keywords: MASS Code MSC 111
section_title: The MASS Code was adopted at MSC 111 and enters into force 1 July 2026. Explain the four Degrees of Autonomy and where the engine room's responsibilities change.
text: The MASS Code was adopted at MSC 111 and enters into force 1 July 2026. Explain the four Degrees of Autonomy and where the engine room's responsibilities change. MASS Code MSC 111 EIF 1 Jul 2026 15-Second Answer The MASS Code, adopted at MSC 111 and effective 1 July 2026, is a non-mandatory, goal-based framework defining four Degrees of Autonomy (DoA 1–4); it does not replace SOLAS, MARPOL, COLREGs or STCW. 60-Second Answer DoA 1 is automated decision-support with seafarers fully in control onboard. DoA 2 is remote control with seafarers onboard able to take over instantly. DoA 3 is remote control with no seafarers onboard, run from a shore-side Remote Operations Centre (ROC). DoA 4 is fully autonomous, with the onboard system making and executing decisions independently. The Code sets minimum safety objectives, requires Remote Operators to hold STCW-equivalent competency, mandates a "minimal risk condition" on system failure, and creates a flag-state certification pathway — but mandatory adoption is targeted for 2030 with entry into force in 2032. Engine-Room Scope Fallback control modes: machinery must default to a defined safe state on loss of remote signal or sensor confidence. IAS/PMS cyber: integration with IACS UR E26 (OT segmentation) and E27 (component resilience). ROC machinery data feeds: sensor validation becomes a safety input, not just a monitoring convenience. UMS as foundation: existing Unmanned Machinery Space practice is treated as the operational baseline MASS builds on. The Unresolved Question Under SOLAS Chapter V, the Master holds absolute overriding authority. Under DoA 3/4, no Master is physically onboard — the ROC operator holds functional command, but legal responsibility under SOLAS Ch.V/ISM Code still sits with flag state, owner and ROC as defined in the SMS. This conflict is unresolved and is expected to be the central issue in the next STCW revision. Key Numbers & Regs EIF (non-mandatory): 1 Jul 2026 — Mandatory adoption target: 1 Jul 2030 — Mandatory EIF: 1 Jan 2032 — MSC 112: Dec 2026, re-establishes working group Regulatory References MSC 111 / MASS Code Goal-based non-mandatory framework, DoA 1–4 structure SOLAS Ch.V Master's overriding authority for safety IACS UR E26/E27 Cyber segmentation and resilience underpinning ROC data links ISM Code SMS must define minimal risk condition and ROC manning/competency CE Oral Tip: Nair and Srivastava both probe this — expect "what are the four DoA levels" followed immediately by "who is legally responsible at DoA 4?" Answer with the SOLAS Ch.V vs ROC tension explicitly; examiners want to hear that you know this is unresolved, not a confident wrong answer. keywords: EPIRB S-100 ECDIS
section_title: What progress was made on EPIRB two-way communication and S-100 ECDIS connectivity at NCSR 13?
text: What progress was made on EPIRB two-way communication and S-100 ECDIS connectivity at NCSR 13? EPIRB S-100 ECDIS NCSR 13, Jun 2026 15-Second Answer NCSR 13 agreed draft amendments to MSC.471(101) adding optional two-way communication via the Galileo SAR Return Link Service to EPIRB standards, and finalised draft circulars on secure IP-based connectivity and route-exchange guidance for S-100 ECDIS — both pending MSC 112. 60-Second Answer For EPIRBs, the amendment introduces two-way communication (TWC) as an optional functionality on 406 MHz float-free EPIRBs via Galileo's SAR Return Link Service, meaning a vessel in distress could receive acknowledgement that the signal was received — guidelines for operational use were deferred pending an ICAO/IMO Joint Working Group. For S-100 ECDIS, NCSR 13 finalised draft guidance for a framework enabling secure, standardised IP-based data exchange between shore facilities and ships for next-generation chart products, plus operational guidance for digital route exchange — addressing the technical, operational and cybersecurity challenges of the S-100 transition. Regulatory References MSC.471(101) EPIRB performance standards — TWC via Galileo SAR RLS amendment agreed S-100 ECDIS Framework IP-based data distribution and route exchange guidance, NCSR 13 MSC 112 (Dec 2026) Expected approval for both items CE Oral Tip: If asked "what's new with EPIRB," the differentiator is "two-way communication via Galileo" — most candidates only know one-way distress alerting. keywords: NAVDAT
section_title: What is NAVDAT, and why was finalisation deferred at NCSR 13?
text: What is NAVDAT, and why was finalisation deferred at NCSR 13? NAVDAT Deferred to NCSR 14, Apr 2027 15-Second Answer NAVDAT is a digital navigational data broadcast system under adopted Performance Standards MSC.569(109); full implementation framework finalisation was deferred from NCSR 13 to NCSR 14 (April 2027) due to time constraints. 60-Second Answer NAVDAT is intended to digitally broadcast navigational and safety information as part of the modernised GMDSS architecture. Performance Standards (MSC.569(109)) and the GMDSS radio services provision (MSC.509(105)/Rev.1) are already adopted, but a nine-item action list remains before service launch — including IEC test/certification standard approval, equipment manufacturing, field trials, coast station establishment, GISIS/GMDSS Master Plan updates, an MSC circular on Terrestrial Broadcast Services, NAVTEX Manual revision, NAVDAT Manual approval, and revision of MSC.1/Circ.1645. NCSR 13 updated the roadmap but could not complete the work, deferring full finalisation to NCSR 14, April 2027. Regulatory References MSC.569(109) NAVDAT Performance Standards, already adopted MSC.509(105)/Rev.1 GMDSS radio services provision NCSR 14 (Apr 2027) Expected finalisation of NAVDAT implementation framework CE Oral Tip: Useful "watch list" answer to show currency — state clearly that Performance Standards exist but full service implementation is still pending, with a named next milestone (NCSR 14). keywords: DGS Circular 33 Security
section_title: The Hormuz corridor paused after a 25 June 2026 attack. What engineering precautions should you take before transiting a high-risk security corridor?
text: The Hormuz corridor paused after a 25 June 2026 attack. What engineering precautions should you take before transiting a high-risk security corridor? Security DGS Circular 33 Jun 2026 15-Second Answer Over 11,000 seafarers and ~600 ships were affected when the Hormuz corridor paused after a 25 June attack; DGS Circular 33 superseded earlier advisories, lifted the blanket restriction conditional on full ISPS compliance, and engineering precautions centre on drill-verified emergency power before transit. 60-Second Answer DGS Circular 31 (13 June) was the most-urgent Gulf advisory following fatal incidents, requiring documented consent for emergency crew change and 24/7 MMDAC contact. DGS Circular 33 (26 June) superseded both Circular 09 and 31, lifting the blanket restriction but mandating full ISPS compliance and documented crew security competency. From an engineering standpoint, route and speed changes under security threat stress steering, propulsion and power systems — emergency power should be drill-verified before transit, and steering gear redundancy confirmed. Action Checklist Drill-verify emergency generator start and load acceptance before transit. Confirm steering gear redundancy and changeover drill currency. Maintain 24/7 MMDAC contact per DGS Circular 31/33 requirements. Document crew security competency per full ISPS compliance requirement. Regulatory References DGS Circular 31 (13 Jun 2026) Most-urgent Gulf advisory after fatal incidents DGS Circular 33 (26 Jun 2026) Supersedes 09 & 31; restriction lifted, full ISPS compliance required ISPS Code Crew security competency documentation requirement CE Oral Tip: Examiners want the engineering angle, not current-affairs commentary — always close with the emergency power/steering redundancy drill point. CT-P1 · Q12 · v1.0 Compiled by Nixon Antony, 2/E, Maersk A/S · Marine Intelligence Weekly · Sources: MIW Issues 17–27, Lloyd's Register NCSR 13 Summary Report (Jun 2026) Corrections: contactus@marineintelligenceweekly.com · Free decarb timeline: marineintelligenceweekly.com/GHGDecarb/timeline.html This material is for oral exam preparation purposes; always verify against current primary IMO/class instruments.

keywords: EU/UK ETS FuelEU
section_title: Three carbon-cost regimes are now live simultaneously — EU ETS, UK ETS and FuelEU Maritime. Explain how they differ and what a single noon report must support.
text: Three carbon-cost regimes are now live simultaneously — EU ETS, UK ETS and FuelEU Maritime. Explain how they differ and what a single noon report must support. EU/UK ETS FuelEU Live 1 Jul 2026 15-Second Answer EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime are assessed Well-to-Wake; UK ETS is assessed Tank-to-Wake — a vessel trading both must keep two separate accounting trails from one noon report. 60-Second Answer EU ETS reached 100% maritime compliance phase-in on 30 April 2026, covering CO2 on a Well-to-Wake basis. UK ETS for shipping went live 1 July 2026 for ships ≥5,000 GT on UK voyages, covering CO2, CH4 and N2O on a Tank-to-Wake basis, with first surrender due 30 April 2028 (2026+2027 combined). FuelEU Maritime requires a Document of Compliance from 30 June 2026 for ≥5,000 GT EU/EEA trade, evaluated Well-to-Wake. Because the boundaries differ, the same noon-report data must be split and reconciled separately for each regime, and PSC actively checks FuelEU DoC carriage. Engineer's Action Items Verify flow/torque/shaft-power meter calibration — these feed all three regimes' fuel-consumption data. Keep noon-report legs separated by jurisdiction (UK / EU / non-covered). Confirm SEEMP III and the vessel's Monitoring Plan explicitly cover UK ETS, not just EU ETS. Cross-check FuelEU DoC issuance with the DPA and THETIS-MRV. Examiner Trap "Aren't EU ETS and UK ETS the same calculation?" — No. EU ETS/FuelEU use Well-to-Wake (full lifecycle, including fuel production); UK ETS uses Tank-to-Wake (onboard combustion only). Conflating the two produces wrong compliance figures. Regulatory References EU Reg 2023/1805 FuelEU Maritime — WTW GHG intensity framework EU ETS Directive 100% maritime compliance from 30 Apr 2026 UK ETS Order 2020 (amended) Live 1 Jul 2026, TTW basis, CO2/CH4/N2O MARPOL Annex VI Reg.28 SEEMP III — must reflect both ETS regimes' monitoring needs CE Oral Tip: Srivastava and Nair like to ask "how would you explain WTW vs TTW to a junior engineer" — give the boundary definition (well/production vs tank/onboard) with a concrete example rather than reciting acronyms. keywords: GFI NZF
section_title: What is the GFI standard under the IMO Net-Zero Framework, and what is the timeline to entry into force?
text: What is the GFI standard under the IMO Net-Zero Framework, and what is the timeline to entry into force? GFI NZF MEPC 85, Nov 2026 15-Second Answer The GFI (GHG Fuel Intensity) standard sets a Well-to-Wake intensity target with a levy on excess intensity; revenue flows to the IMO Net-Zero Fund, with adoption expected at MEPC 85 (Nov 2026) and entry into force 12 months after adoption. 60-Second Answer The Net-Zero Framework path runs: MEPC 83 (drafting continues) → MEPC 84 (further consideration) → MEPC 85, 24–28 Nov 2026 (finalisation and expected adoption) → entry into force roughly 12 months later. GFI inputs include methane slip, fuel choice at the point of bunkering, and use of shore power/renewables — all become financially relevant once the levy applies. Separately, the CII D-rating-for-3-years or E-rating-for-1-year corrective-action trigger continues to operate independently of the NZF timeline — the two systems run in parallel, not as substitutes for each other. Why This Matters Now This is the IMO's first mandatory global carbon levy mechanism. It sits alongside the regional EU/UK ETS and FuelEU regimes already live — meaning vessels may eventually face IMO-level and regional-level carbon costs simultaneously. Key Numbers MEPC 85: 24–28 Nov 2026, IMO HQ London — Expected adoption: Nov 2026 — EIF: ~12 months after adoption (Dec 2027 indicative) — CII trigger: D×3yr or E×1yr independent of NZF Regulatory References MEPC 83/84/85 Progressive NZF drafting and finalisation sessions MARPOL Annex VI Reg.28 CII corrective-action trigger, independent timeline CE Oral Tip: Examiners are currently testing whether candidates can distinguish NZF/GFI (IMO global levy, still pending) from CII (already in force, annual rating). Don't merge the two when answering. Free cross-reference: see the MEPC 84 → NZF entry on the MIW Decarbonisation Timeline (link below) for the full Net-Zero Framework chronology back to 1992. keywords: BWM D-2
section_title: MEPC 84 refined the BWM D-2 standard expectations. What changed, and what must the engine room evidence now?
text: MEPC 84 refined the BWM D-2 standard expectations. What changed, and what must the engine room evidence now? BWM D-2 MEPC 84 15-Second Answer MEPC 84 shifted BWM D-2 enforcement toward active operational performance proof, not just confirmation that a BWMS is installed — surveyors now require detailed logbook evidence. 60-Second Answer Previously, demonstrating compliance largely meant showing the BWMS was fitted and type-approved. The refined approach requires ongoing operational validation: sampling records, UV dose/lamp hours, alarm histories and consumable (chemical/filter) states must be logged and available. A BWMS that is installed but undocumented in active use is now treated as a compliance gap, not just a paperwork gap. Practical Logbook Items Sampling records at each ballast operation UV dose / lamp operating hours (for UV-type systems) Alarm history — any system fault or bypass events Consumable state — filter condition, chemical dosing levels Regulatory References BWM Convention, Reg D-2 Ballast water performance standard MEPC 84 Refinement toward operational performance validation CE Oral Tip: Senthil's exact phrasing on this topic tends to be "is your BWMS installed, or is it performing?" — answer by naming the four logbook categories above, not by describing the treatment technology. keywords: Hydrogen IGF Code
section_title: Lloyd's Register issued the first Type Approval for a 100% hydrogen engine in June 2026. What safety measures does hydrogen require beyond standard IGF Code basics?
text: Lloyd's Register issued the first Type Approval for a 100% hydrogen engine in June 2026. What safety measures does hydrogen require beyond standard IGF Code basics? Hydrogen IGF Code 17 Jun 2026 15-Second Answer LR's BeHydro Type Approval (17 June 2026) makes hydrogen a class-approved propulsion fuel alongside ammonia and methanol, but it demands safety measures beyond standard IGF Code basics given its wide flammability range and near-zero ignition energy. 60-Second Answer Beyond IGF basics, hydrogen systems require double-wall piping with inert gas purge, catalytic or electrochemical hydrogen detection (since hydrogen is colourless, odourless and burns with a near-invisible flame), Emergency Shutdown systems sized for a near-zero ignition threshold, wider hot-work exclusion zones, ventilation engineered for the 4–75% flammability envelope, and embrittlement-aware material selection because hydrogen attacks certain steels over time. Comparative Hazard Profile Hydrogen: flammability range 4–75%, minimum ignition energy ~0.02 mJ — very high relative hazard, buoyant/cryogenic-adjacent handling. LNG: 5–15%, ~0.28 mJ — high hazard, cryogenic, vapour cloud risk. Methanol: 6–36%, ~1.14 mJ — medium hazard, toxic liquid. LPG: 2.1–9.5%, ~10.0 mJ — medium hazard, heavier-than-air, explosion risk. Key Numbers Flammability range: 4–75% — Min ignition energy: ~0.02 mJ — TA date: 17 Jun 2026, LR/BeHydro Regulatory References IGF Code Baseline safety code for gas/low-flashpoint fuels — LNG, methanol, hydrogen IGC Code Governs ammonia-fuelled gas carriers — separate from IGF LR Type Approval — BeHydro First 100% hydrogen engine TA, 17 Jun 2026 CE Oral Tip: Simon's favourite trap on alt-fuels is asking candidates to place a fuel under the wrong code. Memorise: LNG/methanol/hydrogen → IGF; ammonia-fuelled gas carriers → IGC, not IGF. CT-P1 · Q5 · v1.0 6

keywords: Cyber IACS
section_title: Distinguish IACS UR E26 from UR E27 and explain why both matter to your engine control systems.
text: Distinguish IACS UR E26 from UR E27 and explain why both matter to your engine control systems. Cyber IACS Mandatory from 1 Jan 2024 15-Second Answer UR E26 governs the vessel as a whole integrated system (network segmentation between OT and IT); UR E27 governs resilience at the individual product/vendor level — both mandatory for newbuilds contracted from 1 January 2024. 60-Second Answer UR E26 requires physical or robust logical separation — firewalls, VLANs — between Operational Technology (main engine controls, steering gear, navigation) and Information Technology (crew internet, office systems), treating the ship as a holistic cyber system. UR E27 complements it at the component level, requiring that individual third-party systems and product vendors can withstand, mitigate and rapidly recover from an active cyber incident. Together they form the technical floor referenced by the MASS Code for ROC machinery data feeds and IAS/PMS cyber resilience. Examiner Trap "What's the difference between E26 and E27?" — System-level vs component-level. Many candidates answer with generic "cybersecurity rules" and fail to separate the two scopes. Regulatory References IACS UR E26 Cyber security — OT/IT network segmentation, system-level IACS UR E27 Cyber resilience — product/vendor component-level hardening MASS Code (MSC 111) References E26/E27 for ROC machinery data feed integrity CE Oral Tip: Srivastava asks this almost verbatim. Lead with "E26 is system-level, E27 is component-level" before any further detail. CT-P1 · Q6 · v1.0 7

keywords: AI Watchkeeping
section_title: Orca AI is running at fleet scale with class notation. Can an AI alert ever authorise deferring a statutory action or overriding your watch judgement?
text: Orca AI is running at fleet scale with class notation. Can an AI alert ever authorise deferring a statutory action or overriding your watch judgement? AI Watchkeeping 2026 fleet scale 15-Second Answer No. AI tools like Orca AI (94% precision, 98.6% recall, class-notated) are cross-check aids, not a watch substitute — AI alerts never authorise deferring statutory overhauls or surveys. 60-Second Answer Orca AI is now deployed at fleet scale across operators including Gram Car Carriers and Anglo-Eastern, holding class notation from Lloyd's Register following a live trial. The principle examiners want stated explicitly: AI-flagged anomalies must be cross-referenced against manual readings before acting, document overrides are mandatory, and Type Approval (design baseline meets class safety standards) is distinct from Product Certification (specific unit verified to that design). CBM (Condition-Based Maintenance) notations do not remove statutory overhaul requirements. Regulatory References LR Class Notation — Orca AI Collision-avoidance AI under live class-approved trial ISO/IEC 42001 AI Management Systems — accountability and override pathway STCW Watchkeeping Statutory watch requirement unchanged by AI cross-check tools CE Oral Tip: The expected closing line, almost word for word: "AI assists, it doesn't replace professional judgement — and every override gets documented." keywords: Lifting Appliances SOLAS
section_title: SOLAS lifting appliance and PFOS-free foam requirements entered into force 1 January 2026. What is now required for each?
text: SOLAS lifting appliance and PFOS-free foam requirements entered into force 1 January 2026. What is now required for each? SOLAS Lifting Appliances EIF 1 Jan 2026 15-Second Answer Lifting appliances now require overload testing at 110% brake-holding/max line-pull at next renewal survey (Reg. II-1/3-13, MSC.532(107)); fire-fighting foam must be PFOS-free with documented batch traceability, both effective 1 January 2026. 60-Second Answer For lifting appliances — engine room cranes, gantries, davits — the new requirement is overload testing to 110% of brake-holding capacity or maximum line-pull at the next renewal survey, with manuals required either onboard or reconstructed with flag approval if missing. For foam, PFOS substances are completely prohibited; compliance can be proven via one of three routes — manufacturer declaration, laboratory test, or Type Approval under the MED — and the documentation must be traceable to the actual batch installed onboard, not a generic certificate. Key Numbers Overload test: 110% brake-holding/max line-pull — Trigger: next renewal survey — PFOS routes: 3 (manufacturer declaration / lab test / Type Approval-MED) Regulatory References SOLAS Reg. II-1/3-13 Lifting appliances — overload testing requirement MSC.532(107) Implementing resolution for lifting appliance testing SOLAS / PFOS Prohibition PFOS-free foam, batch-traceable documentation, EIF 1 Jan 2026 CE Oral Tip: Senthil tests the documentation trail specifically — be ready to name all three PFOS-free verification routes, not just state that PFOS is banned. keywords: NCSR 13 R-mode VHF
section_title: NCSR 13 finalised several navigation/communications transitions. Summarise the digital VHF transition scheme and the R-mode finalisation.
text: NCSR 13 finalised several navigation/communications transitions. Summarise the digital VHF transition scheme and the R-mode finalisation. NCSR 13 VHF R-mode 22–26 Jun 2026 15-Second Answer NCSR 13 finalised a draft transition scheme for digital VHF voice (retaining GMDSS safety channels) and finalised performance standards for R-mode, a terrestrial GNSS-independent backup; both go to MSC 112 for approval in December 2026. 60-Second Answer The digital VHF transition scheme keeps existing analogue channels 06, 13, 16, 75, 76 plus channel 70 (DSC) and AIS-SART channels active even after digital introduction, to protect GMDSS distress/urgency/safety continuity; new digital channels will be identified within existing ITU frequency allocations, with implementation cost kept minimal. Separately, performance standards for R-mode receivers were finalised — R-mode uses existing terrestrial radio infrastructure as a GNSS-independent positioning backup, directly relevant given rising GNSS jamming/spoofing in conflict zones. Both await MSC 112 approval (December 2026). Why It Matters for the Engine Room GNSS-dependent systems (ECDIS positioning, DP references, some engine telemetry timestamping) are increasingly vulnerable to jamming/spoofing in high-risk areas. R-mode is the IMO's terrestrial answer; understanding it signals current awareness beyond textbook navigation theory. Regulatory References NCSR 13 (Jun 2026) Finalised digital VHF transition draft circular and R-mode performance standards MSC 112 (Dec 2026) Expected approval point for both items GMDSS Safety channel continuity protected through the VHF digital transition CE Oral Tip: Examiners use this to test whether you follow current IMO sessions, not just the syllabus. Name the session (NCSR 13) and the approval body (MSC 112) — generic "IMO is digitising VHF" answers lose marks. CT-P1 · Q9 · v1.0 10

section_subtitle: International Maritime Organization (IMO)
section_title: Q1: What is IMO? Define it precisely.
text: IMO is a specialized agency of the United Nations, established by convention adopted on 17 March 1948 in Geneva, entering into force in 1958. It is the global authority for adopting measures to improve the safety, security, and environmental performance of international shipping. It currently has 176 member states and is headquartered in London.

keywords: IMO structure, International Maritime Organization, IMO organs, Assembly Council Secretariat
section_subtitle: International Maritime Organization (IMO)
section_title: Q2: What is the difference between the Assembly and the Council?
text: The Assembly is the highest governing body, consisting of all 176 member states meeting every two years. It approves the work programme, votes the budget, and elects the Council. The Council is the executive organ, consisting of 40 elected member states, which acts between Assembly sessions and oversees the work of the technical committees.

keywords: IMO structure, International Maritime Organization, IMO organs, Assembly Council Secretariat
section_subtitle: International Maritime Organization (IMO)
section_title: Q3: How is the Council composed — explain the three categories.
text: The Council has 40 members in three categories: Category (a) — 10 states with the largest interest in providing international shipping services (e.g. USA, UK, Greece, Panama, Japan); Category (b) — 10 states with the largest interest in international seaborne trade (e.g. India, Germany, Australia, Brazil); Category (c) — 20 states not in (a) or (b) but with special interests in maritime transport, ensuring equitable geographic representation globally.

keywords: IMO structure, International Maritime Organization, IMO organs, Assembly Council Secretariat
section_subtitle: International Maritime Organization (IMO)
section_title: Q4: What does the Secretariat do?
text: The Secretariat consists of the Secretary General and approximately 300 international personnel based at IMO headquarters in London. It manages administrative duties, coordinates committee sessions, maintains treaty records, and supports technical cooperation activities. The current Secretary General is Mr. Arsenio Dominguez, appointed 01 January 2024.

keywords: IMO structure, International Maritime Organization, IMO organs, Assembly Council Secretariat
section_subtitle: International Maritime Organization (IMO)
section_title: Q5: When was IMO originally called IMCO and why was it renamed?
text: The organization was originally established as IMCO — the Inter-Governmental Maritime Consultative Organization — when the convention entered into force in 1958. In 1982, the name was changed to the International Maritime Organization (IMO) to reflect its broader role beyond consultation and the expanded scope of its mandatory instruments.

keywords: IMO structure, International Maritime Organization, IMO organs, Assembly Council Secretariat
section_subtitle: International Maritime Organization (IMO)
section_title: Q6: How many member states does IMO have?
text: As of 2024, IMO has 176 member states. This figure may change as additional states accede to the IMO Convention.

keywords: IMO structure, International Maritime Organization, IMO organs, Assembly Council Secretariat
section_subtitle: International Maritime Organization (IMO)
section_title: Q7: What powers does the Assembly have that no other body has?
text: Only the Assembly can approve the work programme, vote the budget, determine financial arrangements, and elect the Council. It is also the only body empowered under Article 15(j) to make recommendations to governments on maritime safety and pollution prevention. Technical decisions are delegated to committees, but governance authority rests with the Assembly.

keywords: IMO structure, International Maritime Organization, IMO organs, Assembly Council Secretariat
section_subtitle: International Maritime Organization (IMO)
section_title: Q8: Where is IMO headquartered?
text: IMO headquarters is in London, United Kingdom, at 4 Albert Embankment, London SE1 7SR. It has been based in London since the organization's inception.

section_title: Q10: How does IMO connect to a Chief Engineer's day-to-day work?
text: Every mandatory requirement in the engine room — from ORB entries to OWS 15ppm limits, from NOx Technical Code compliance to ISM Code safety management — derives from an IMO convention adopted through the MSC or MEPC. The Chief Engineer's statutory certificates, surveys, and PSC obligations all have IMO instruments as their legal foundation.

keywords: IMO structure, International Maritime Organization, IMO organs, Assembly Council Secretariat
section_title: International Maritime Organization (IMO)
text: Topic 1 International Maritime Organization (IMO) IMO Governance Uday pp. 2–4 Examiner: Nair ⭐ High Frequency 📖 Definition The International Maritime Organization (IMO) is a specialized agency of the United Nations responsible for adopting measures to improve the safety, security, and environmental performance of international shipping. It acts as the global standard-setting authority, ensuring a uniform regulatory framework applicable to all member states and their flagged vessels engaged in international trade. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) Every statutory certificate on board — IOPP, Safety Equipment, Loadline — is issued under an IMO convention. Without IMO there is no legal basis for these certificates. Port State Control detention is triggered by failure to comply with IMO instruments. A CE who misunderstands IMO hierarchy cannot respond correctly to a PSC deficiency. IMO sets limits for NOx, SOx, GHG, and OWS discharge — direct engine room operational constraints. ISM Code (adopted under IMO) governs the CE's safety management system obligations, authority, and liability. Over 80% of world trade moves by sea — IMO ensures the CE operates under one consistent global framework rather than a patchwork of national rules. 📅 Historical Background 17 Mar 1948 → IMO Convention adopted at UN conference in Geneva 1958 → Convention entered into force; organization began as IMCO (Inter-Governmental Maritime Consultative Organization) 1982 → Name changed to International Maritime Organization (IMO) 2024 → 176 Member States; Mr. Arsenio Dominguez appointed Secretary General (01 Jan 2024, term 2024–2027) ⚖ Regulatory References IMO Convention 1948 Founding instrument establishing the IMO as a UN specialized agency SOLAS 1974 (as amended) Primary safety convention administered through IMO/MSC MARPOL 73/78 Primary pollution prevention convention administered through IMO/MEPC Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (India) In force 15 March 2026; Indian domestic legislation implementing IMO conventions — administered by DGMA (formerly DGS); replaces the repealed 1958 Act. 🔧 IMO Structure IMO — 176 Member States │ ├── ASSEMBLY (All 176 Member States) │ Meets every 2 years (ordinary session) │ Extra-ordinary sessions if required │ Functions: Approve work programme, vote budget, │ determine financial arrangements, │ elect Council, make recommendations │ to governments on maritime safety & │ pollution prevention (Article 15(j)) │ ├── COUNCIL (40 Member States elected by Assembly) │ Executive organ of IMO, elected for 2-year term │ Category (a) — 10 States: largest interest in │ providing international shipping services │ e.g. USA, UK, Korea, Panama, Norway, │ Italy, Japan, Liberia, China, Greece │ Category (b) — 10 States: largest interest in │ international seaborne trade │ e.g. India, UAE, Australia, Brazil, Canada, │ Germany, Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, France │ Category (c) — 20 States: special interest in maritime │ transport or navigation; ensures representation │ of all major geographic areas of the world │ ├── SECRETARIAT │ Secretary General + ~300 international personnel │ Based at IMO HQ, London (Albert Embankment) │ Present SG: Mr. Arsenio Dominguez (2024–2027) │ └── 5 MAIN COMMITTEES (see Topic 2) CE Oral Tip — Nair Sir: Nair routinely asks "What is IMO?" expecting candidates to state the UN specialized agency definition, member state count (176), founding year (convention adopted 17 March 1948), and the name of the current Secretary General. Candidates who say "international organization for shipping" without citing UN specialized agency status are marked down. Always mention Article 15(j) if asked about Assembly powers — it shows depth. 🎯 Oral Q&A — 10 Questions Q1: What is IMO? Define it precisely. IMO is a specialized agency of the United Nations, established by convention adopted on 17 March 1948 in Geneva, entering into force in 1958. It is the global authority for adopting measures to improve the safety, security, and environmental performance of international shipping. It currently has 176 member states and is headquartered in London. Q2: What is the difference between the Assembly and the Council? The Assembly is the highest governing body, consisting of all 176 member states meeting every two years. It approves the work programme, votes the budget, and elects the Council. The Council is the executive organ, consisting of 40 elected member states, which acts between Assembly sessions and oversees the work of the technical committees. Q3: How is the Council composed — explain the three categories. The Council has 40 members in three categories: Category (a) — 10 states with the largest interest in providing international shipping services (e.g. USA, UK, Greece, Panama, Japan); Category (b) — 10 states with the largest interest in international seaborne trade (e.g. India, Germany, Australia, Brazil); Category (c) — 20 states not in (a) or (b) but with special interests in maritime transport, ensuring equitable geographic representation globally. Q4: What does the Secretariat do? The Secretariat consists of the Secretary General and approximately 300 international personnel based at IMO headquarters in London. It manages administrative duties, coordinates committee sessions, maintains treaty records, and supports technical cooperation activities. The current Secretary General is Mr. Arsenio Dominguez, appointed 01 January 2024. Q5: When was IMO originally called IMCO and why was it renamed? The organization was originally established as IMCO — the Inter-Governmental Maritime Consultative Organization — when the convention entered into force in 1958. In 1982, the name was changed to the International Maritime Organization (IMO) to reflect its broader role beyond consultation and the expanded scope of its mandatory instruments. Q6: How many member states does IMO have? As of 2024, IMO has 176 member states. This figure may change as additional states accede to the IMO Convention. Q7: What powers does the Assembly have that no other body has? Only the Assembly can approve the work programme, vote the budget, determine financial arrangements, and elect the Council. It is also the only body empowered under Article 15(j) to make recommendations to governments on maritime safety and pollution prevention. Technical decisions are delegated to committees, but governance authority rests with the Assembly. Q8: Where is IMO headquartered? IMO headquarters is in London, United Kingdom, at 4 Albert Embankment, London SE1 7SR. It has been based in London since the organization's inception. Q9: Who is the current IMO Secretary General? Mr. Arsenio Dominguez, appointed 01 January 2024. He is from Panama and his term runs 2024–2027. Q10: How does IMO connect to a Chief Engineer's day-to-day work? Every mandatory requirement in the engine room — from ORB entries to OWS 15ppm limits, from NOx Technical Code compliance to ISM Code safety management — derives from an IMO convention adopted through the MSC or MEPC. The Chief Engineer's statutory certificates, surveys, and PSC obligations all have IMO instruments as their legal foundation. ✍ Written Exam Questions 5M Describe the structure of the IMO, naming its main bodies and their functions. 10M Explain the composition and functions of the IMO Council. How does it differ from the IMO Assembly? Discuss the significance of the three category system. 15M With the aid of a structural diagram, explain the organization of the IMO from the Assembly down to its technical sub-committees. Discuss how a Chief Engineer on a container vessel is directly affected by the outputs of this structure, citing at least three IMO instruments. 🧠 Memory Box Geneva 1948 → London 1958 — Convention adopted in Geneva (1948), entered into force in London (1958) IMCO → IMO in 1982 — Consultative became full Organization 176 member states, 40-member Council — remember 176 / 40 Council ABC — (a) Shipping services providers, (b) Seaborne trade states, (c) All other special interest states — 10 + 10 + 20 = 40 SG = Arsenio Dominguez, Panama, 2024 ⚡ Quick Revision Item Key Fact Convention adopted 17 March 1948, Geneva Entry into force 1958 Original name IMCO (changed to IMO in 1982) Member states 176 (as of 2024) Assembly All 176 states; meets every 2 years Council 40 states; executive organ; 3 categories (10+10+20) Secretariat SG + ~300 staff; London HQ Current SG Arsenio Dominguez; appointed 01 Jan 2024 Main committees MSC, MEPC, LEG, TCC, FAL ▶ Deep Dive — Full Reference Detail India's IMO Status India is a founding member of IMO and is categorized as a Category (b) state on the Council (largest interest in international seaborne trade). The DGMA (Directorate General of Maritime Administration, renamed from DG Shipping/DGS under the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025) under the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways is India's flag state authority responsible for implementing IMO conventions through the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (in force 15 March 2026, replacing the repealed 1958 Act) and its subordinate rules. Article 15(j) — Assembly Recommendation Power Article 15(j) of the IMO Convention specifically empowers the Assembly to make recommendations to member governments on maritime safety and the prevention and control of marine pollution. This is the constitutional basis for IMO Assembly resolutions — though they are technically recommendations (not binding), they carry significant political weight and are often referenced in PSC inspections. Maersk A/S IMO Interface As a Danish-flagged fleet operator, Maersk A/S interacts with IMO instruments primarily through the Danish Maritime Authority (DMA) as flag state. All class surveys on Maersk container vessels are conducted by recognized organizations (principally DNV or LR acting as ROs for DMA). The CE's ISM obligations flow from IMO → SOLAS Chapter IX → ISM Code → Maersk SMS. Observer Status In addition to 176 member states, IMO has 3 associate members and grants observer status to intergovernmental organizations (e.g. ILO, UN agencies) and non-governmental organizations (e.g. IACS, BIMCO, INTERTANKO, INTERCARGO). NGO observers can participate in technical discussions but cannot vote. 📚 References IMO — About IMO (official) IMO Convention 1948 text DGMA, India 🔗 Related QB Questions: QB4 — ISM Code / IMO Governance QB3 — PSC / MARPOL Notes-p1 · T1 · v1.0

text: Topic 2 IMO Committees — MSC, MEPC, LEG, TCC, FAL IMO Governance Uday pp. 5–9 Examiner: Nair ⭐ High Frequency 📖 Overview IMO has five main committees that develop, adopt, and oversee implementation of international maritime instruments. All committees consist of all member states. The two most technically active — MSC and MEPC — are directly relevant to the Chief Engineer's daily statutory obligations. 🔧 Committee Detail ① Maritime Safety Committee (MSC) The highest technical body within IMO concerned with maritime safety. Consists of all member states . Functions: consider matters within IMO scope concerned with aids to navigation, construction and equipment of vessels, manning from a safety standpoint, rules for prevention of collisions, handling of dangerous cargoes, maritime safety procedures and requirements, hydrographic information, logbooks and navigational records, marine casualty investigation, salvage and rescue, and any other matter directly affecting maritime safety. MSC must carry out duties assigned by the IMO Convention or any other international instrument accepted by the IMO. MSC can adopt amendments to conventions such as SOLAS. ② Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) Consists of all member states. Empowered to consider any matter within IMO scope concerned with the prevention and control of pollution from ships. Particularly concerned with the adoption and amendment of conventions and regulations, and measures to ensure their enforcement. Originally formed as a subsidiary body to the Assembly; raised to full constitutional status in 1985 . ③ Legal Committee (LEG) Consists of all member states. Established in 1967 as a subsidiary body to deal with legal questions arising from the Torrey Canyon disaster. Empowered to deal with any legal matters within the scope of the organization. Also empowered to do duties assigned by any international instrument accepted and recognized by the IMO. ④ Technical Co-operation Committee (TCC) Required to consider any matter within IMO scope concerned with implementation of technical co-operation projects for which the Organization acts as executing or co-operating agency, and any other matters related to the Organization's activities in the technical co-operation field. ⑤ Facilitation Committee (FAL) Consists of all member states. Established as subsidiary body for the Council in 1972 ; became fully institutionalized in December 2008 as a result of an amendment to the IMO Convention. Deals with IMO's work in eliminating unnecessary formalities and red tape in international shipping. Achieved by implementing the Convention on Facilitation of International Maritime Traffic 1965, and any matter within IMO scope concerned with the facilitation of international maritime traffic. By the efforts of this committee, a balance is achieved between maritime security and facilitation of international maritime trade. ⚖ Regulatory References IMO Convention — Article 28 Establishes the MSC as the highest technical safety committee SOLAS 1974 Primary instrument adopted and amended by MSC MARPOL 73/78 Primary instrument adopted and amended by MEPC FAL Convention 1965 Convention on Facilitation of International Maritime Traffic — administered by FAL Committee IMO Convention 2008 Amendment Gave FAL Committee full constitutional status within IMO structure 📊 Comparison Table — MSC vs MEPC Parameter MSC MEPC Focus Maritime safety Marine environment protection Primary convention SOLAS 1974 MARPOL 73/78 Composition All member states All member states Sub-committees Shared — HTW, III, NCSR, SDC, SSE, CCC, PPR Shared — PPR is most MEPC-linked CE interface Machinery safety, fire, LSA, dangerous goods MARPOL compliance, GHG, CII, EEXI Amendment power Can adopt SOLAS amendments Can adopt MARPOL amendments MEPC status history Full committee from establishment Subsidiary until 1985; full status 1985 CE Oral Tip — Nair Sir: Commonly asks "What is the difference between MSC and MEPC?" — candidates must state: MSC = safety; MEPC = environment. Both consist of all member states. MEPC was originally a subsidiary body raised to full constitutional status in 1985. Nair also asks about the Torrey Canyon — connect it to the Legal Committee's establishment in 1967. The FAL Committee date (institutionalized December 2008) occasionally comes up for written exams. 🎯 Oral Q&A — 10 Questions Q1: Name the five main committees of IMO. These amendments are typically passed using the tacit acceptance procedure under SOLAS Article VIII, allowing them to enter into force on a fixed date unless sufficient objections are received. From MEPC: MARPOL Annex VI requirements (NOx, SOx, GHG/CII) have major operational impact on main engine management, fuel selection, and SEEMP compliance on container vessels. Q9: What is the Torrey Canyon and why is it significant for IMO? The Torrey Canyon was a Liberian-flagged supertanker that ran aground on the Seven Stones reef off Cornwall, UK in March 1967, spilling approximately 119,000 tonnes of crude oil — the first major tanker disaster. It exposed major gaps in international maritime law regarding liability, compensation, and coastal state intervention rights, directly leading to the establishment of the IMO Legal Committee in 1967 and later the CLC and Fund Conventions. Q10: Do all IMO committees consist of all member states? Yes. All five main committees — MSC, MEPC, LEG, TCC, and FAL — consist of all 176 IMO member states. Which committee is most relevant to a Chief Engineer on a container vessel and why? 15M The Torrey Canyon disaster of 1967 had a profound impact on the IMO's institutional structure. Explain what happened, how it led to the creation of the Legal Committee, and what subsequent conventions emerged to address the legal gaps exposed by the disaster. 🧠 Memory Box 5 Committees: MSC · MEPC · LEG · TCC · FAL — mnemonic: "My Maritime Life Takes Flight" MEPC full status: 1985 — previously a subsidiary body to Assembly LEG established: 1967 — triggered by Torrey Canyon FAL institutionalized: December 2008 — amendment to IMO Convention MSC = Safety (SOLAS) | MEPC = Environment (MARPOL) ⚡ Quick Revision Committee Full Name Key Instrument Note MSC Maritime Safety Committee SOLAS Highest technical safety body; all member states MEPC Marine Environment Protection Committee MARPOL Full status 1985; was subsidiary to Assembly LEG Legal Committee CLC, Fund Conv. Est. 1967 after Torrey Canyon TCC Technical Co-operation Committee — Technical assistance to developing states FAL Facilitation Committee FAL Convention 1965 Full status December 2008 ▶ Deep Dive — Full Reference Detail MSC Sessions The MSC holds regular sessions (typically 2 per year) and extraordinary sessions when required. Each session has an agenda of items submitted by member states, recognized organizations, and committees. Resolutions and circulars adopted at each session carry the session number — e.g., MSC.520(106) was adopted at MSC 106. MEPC Sessions MEPC similarly holds regular sessions. Recent high-impact MEPC sessions include MEPC 80 (2023) which adopted the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy with a net-zero target by 2050 and interim checkpoints of 20% reduction by 2030 and 70% by 2040 compared to 2008 levels. Torrey Canyon — Full Account The Torrey Canyon grounded 18 March 1967. The UK government ultimately bombed the wreck to burn off remaining cargo — a legally unprecedented action. The disaster demonstrated that no adequate international legal framework existed for: (1) flag state liability for pollution damage; (2) coastal state intervention rights on the high seas; (3) compensation for pollution victims. This directly produced: the Intervention Convention 1969, the CLC 1969, and the Fund Convention 1971. FAL Convention 1965 — Key Requirements The FAL Convention 1965 standardized ship arrival/departure documentation, including the General Declaration, Cargo Declaration, Ship's Stores Declaration, and Crew and Passenger lists. It was significantly updated by the 2002 and later amendments to accommodate e-documentation and Maritime Single Window (MSW) requirements. 📚 References IMO — Maritime Safety Committee IMO — Marine Environment Protection Committee IMO — Legal Committee 🔗 Related QB Questions: QB3 — MARPOL (MEPC instruments) QB4 — ISM / SOLAS (MSC instruments) Notes-p1 · T2 · v1.0

text: Topic 3 IMO Sub-Committees (HTW, III, NCSR, PPR, SDC, SSE, CCC) IMO Governance Uday pp. 3 Examiner: Nair Medium Frequency 📖 Overview The main committees (principally MSC and MEPC) delegate specific technical drafting work to seven sub-committees. These bodies develop the actual technical text, guidelines, and circulars that eventually become mandatory instruments through the MSC or MEPC adoption process. 🔧 Sub-Committee Detail IMO Sub-Committees (under MSC/MEPC) │ ├── HTW — Human Element, Training and Watchkeeping │ STCW standards, fatigue management, model courses, │ engine room resource management (ERRM) │ ├── III — Implementation of IMO Instruments │ IMSAS audits, marine casualty investigation, │ PSC inspection guidelines, flag state compliance │ ├── NCSR — Navigation, Communications and Search & Rescue │ COLREGs, GMDSS, ECDIS, VDR, SAR coordination │ ├── PPR — Pollution Prevention and Response │ MARPOL technical standards, OWS, scrubbers, │ biofouling, BWM, NOx/SOx limits, IBC Code │ ├── SDC — Ship Design and Construction │ SOLAS Ch.II-1, Intact Stability Code, ESP, │ damage stability, structural rules │ ├── SSE — Ship Systems and Equipment │ Fire protection, LSA, FSS Code, FTP Code, │ SOLAS Ch.II-2 and III equipment standards │ └── CCC — Carriage of Cargoes and Containers IMDG Code, solid bulk cargo (IMSBC Code), IGC/IBC codes, container stowage and securing ⚖ Regulatory References IMO Convention — Articles 28–38 Articles governing the MSC and its powers, including authority to establish sub-committees STCW Convention 1978 (as amended) Governed by HTW sub-committee — standards for seafarer training, certification and watchkeeping MARPOL 73/78 — Annexes I–VI Technical standards developed and updated by PPR sub-committee SOLAS Chapter II-2, III Fire protection and LSA equipment standards — developed by SSE sub-committee IMDG Code (MSC.122(75)) Dangerous goods carriage — maintained by CCC sub-committee; mandatory under SOLAS Ch.VII Reg.3 CE Oral Tip — Nair Sir: Examiners rarely ask for all seven sub-committees by name but will ask "which sub-committee deals with pollution?" (PPR) or "which sub-committee handles STCW?" (HTW). Know PPR, HTW, and SSE at minimum — these three have the most direct CE engine room impact. keywords: IMO instruments, conventions protocols amendments codes resolutions
section_title: IMO Instruments — Conventions, Protocols, Amendments, Codes, Resolutions
text: Topic 4 IMO Instruments — Conventions, Protocols, Amendments, Codes, Resolutions IMO Governance Uday pp. 11 Examiner: Nair ⭐ High Frequency 📖 Types of IMO Instruments IMO develops five principal categories of instrument. Understanding the hierarchy and legal status of each is essential for the CE to correctly interpret compliance obligations. IMO Instruments — Hierarchy │ ├── 1. CONVENTIONS │ Formal treaty agreements between member states │ Negotiated under IMO auspices │ Have sub-parts (chapters, annexes, regulations) │ Examples: SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, MLC, BWM Convention │ LEGALLY BINDING on ratifying states │ ├── 2. PROTOCOLS │ Instrument used to introduce significant changes │ to conventions already adopted │ Used when: new chapter added to original convention, │ or any significant change to original text │ Enters into force like a convention (requires ratification) │ NOTE: A state may ratify original convention but │ NOT ratify subsequent protocol │ Binding only on states that ratified the Protocol │ Examples: MARPOL Protocol 1978, SOLAS Protocol 1988 │ ├── 3. AMENDMENTS │ Major changes brought into action via: │ (i) By Protocol │ (ii) By Resolution │ (a) Amendment by consideration within IMO │ (b) Amendment by Conference of Contracting States │ MOST COMMON route: Resolution via Tacit Acceptance │ ├── 4. RECOMMENDATIONS / CODES / GUIDELINES │ Non-mandatory (unless adopted as mandatory by reference │ in a convention) │ Examples: ISM Code (mandatory via SOLAS Ch.IX), │ FSS Code (mandatory via SOLAS Ch.II-2), │ IMDG Code (mandatory via SOLAS Ch.VII) │ └── 5. RESOLUTIONS Formal decisions adopted by IMO bodies Used to adopt amendments, guidelines, codes Identified as: MSC.NNN(XX) or MEPC.NNN(XX) where NNN = sequential number, XX = session number ⚖ Key Instruments — Status Reference SOLAS 1974 Convention — mandatory for contracting states; safety of life at sea MARPOL 73/78 Convention + Protocol — MARPOL 73 merged with Protocol 78 into one instrument ISM Code (MSC.104(73)) Code — made mandatory by incorporation into SOLAS Chapter IX FSS Code (MSC.98(73)) Code — mandatory under SOLAS Chapter II-2 IMDG Code Code — mandatory under SOLAS Chapter VII, Regulation 3 MSC.520(106) Resolution — SOLAS Ch.II-2 amendments, in force 01 January 2026 📊 Comparison — Mandatory vs Non-Mandatory Codes Parameter Mandatory Code Recommendatory Code/Guideline Legal status Binding — referenced in convention regulation Advisory — encourages best practice PSC authority to detain Yes — breach = deficiency No — unless elevated by port state law Examples ISM Code, FSS Code, IGC Code, IBC Code, IMDG Code, LSA Code ISGOTT, BMP5, OCIMF guidelines How made mandatory Convention regulation states "shall comply with [Code]" Convention regulation states "should" or "recommended" CE Oral Tip — Nair Sir: The classic Nair question: "Is the ISM Code mandatory?" Answer: Yes — it is mandatory because SOLAS Chapter IX, Regulation 3 requires ships to comply with the ISM Code. The Code itself is a Resolution (MSC.104(73)) that became mandatory by incorporation into SOLAS. Always explain the mechanism — not just "yes it is mandatory." Also know that ISGOTT and BMP5 are non-mandatory industry guidance documents. 🧠 Memory Box 5 instrument types: Convention → Protocol → Amendment → Code/Guideline → Resolution Code = mandatory only if referenced in a Convention regulation Resolution number format: MSC.520(106) = item 520 adopted at session 106 Protocol = separate legal instrument; needs separate ratification MARPOL 73/78 = the 1978 Protocol so significantly amended MARPOL 1973 that they were merged Notes-p1 · T4 · v1.0

keywords: convention lifecycle, adoption ratification entry into force
section_subtitle: IMO Convention Lifecycle — Draft → Adopt → Ratify → Entry into Force
section_title: Q1: Explain the process by which a new IMO convention enters into force.
text: A convention passes through five stages: (1) Drafting — any member state proposes; committee drafts; (2) Adoption — Diplomatic Conference adopts when majority of states present agree; (3) Ratification — each state gives formal consent via signature, signature subject to ratification, or accession, depositing an Instrument with the Secretary General (Depositary); (4) Entry into force — when a minimum number of states (varying by convention) have ratified; (5) Implementation — each ratifying state incorporates the convention into national law.

keywords: convention lifecycle, adoption ratification entry into force
section_subtitle: IMO Convention Lifecycle — Draft → Adopt → Ratify → Entry into Force
section_title: Q2: What is the Depositary of an IMO convention?
text: The Depositary is the body that keeps an official record of which member states have ratified a convention. For all IMO conventions, the Depositary is the Secretary General of IMO, based in London.

keywords: convention lifecycle, adoption ratification entry into force
section_subtitle: IMO Convention Lifecycle — Draft → Adopt → Ratify → Entry into Force
section_title: Q3: What is the difference between ratification and accession?
text: Ratification is the formal consent given by a state that signed the convention during the open signature window. Accession is the method used by a state to join a convention after the signature window has closed — the state deposits an Instrument of Accession with the Depositary (Secretary General) without having been a signatory.

keywords: convention lifecycle, adoption ratification entry into force
section_subtitle: IMO Convention Lifecycle — Draft → Adopt → Ratify → Entry into Force
section_title: Q4: What happens if India signs a convention "subject to ratification"?
text: India has signed the convention and shown interest, but this is NOT considered official ratification by IMO. India must subsequently obtain parliamentary approval and submit a formal Instrument of Ratification to the Secretary General of IMO. Only after this deposit is India officially a contracting party to the convention.

section_title: Q5: How is a convention implemented in India?
text: Once India ratifies an IMO convention, the provisions must be incorporated into Indian national law. The primary domestic legislation is the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (in force 15 March 2026, replacing the repealed 1958 Act), which is amended or supplemented by DGMA (formerly DGS) notifications and orders to give effect to convention requirements. This makes the convention legally binding on Indian-flagged vessels and persons subject to Indian jurisdiction.

section_title: Q6: What is an "Adoption Conference"?
text: An Adoption Conference is a diplomatic conference convened by the IMO Council or Assembly to formally adopt a draft convention. The draft is circulated to all member states beforehand for comments. At the conference, once the majority of states present agree to the final draft, the convention is formally considered "Adopted" and sent to the Secretary General for distribution.

section_title: Q7: Can a convention bind a state that has not ratified it?
text: No. An IMO convention binds only those states that have ratified it (contracting parties). However, practical enforcement through Port State Control means that even vessels from non-party states may face deficiency notices when calling at ports of contracting states, since PSC officers apply convention standards to all vessels in their ports.

section_title: Q8: What is the minimum ratification threshold for SOLAS to enter into force?
text: SOLAS 1974 required acceptance by at least 25 states representing not less than 50% of the world's gross merchant tonnage. Different conventions have different thresholds — this is specified within each convention text. For the current SOLAS, the entry into force conditions were met before 1980.

text: Topic 5 IMO Convention Lifecycle — Draft → Adopt → Ratify → Entry into Force IMO Governance Uday pp. 12–16 Examiner: Nair ⭐ High Frequency 📖 Overview An IMO convention passes through five sequential stages from initial proposal to legally binding implementation. Understanding this process is essential for the CE to know when a new regulation becomes applicable to the vessel. 🔄 Process Flowchart IMO Convention — 5-Stage Lifecycle STAGE 1: DRAFT CONVENTION ├── Committee sessions held every 6 months ├── Any member state may propose a new convention │ based on information and research ├── If committee is satisfied with merits of proposal, │ it forwards to Council or Assembly as required ├── If Council/Assembly accepts, committee is authorised │ to proceed with detailed drafting └── Committee draws up Draft Convention → sent to Council and Assembly; committee recommends Conference for Adoption STAGE 2: ADOPTION OF THE CONVENTION ├── Council/Assembly sets date for Adoption Conference ├── Draft convention circulated to all member states │ for comments ├── Comments examined; changes made before the Conference ├── At the Conference, draft presented to all member states ├── Majority of states present at conference agree with │ final draft → convention formally "ADOPTED" └── Adopted convention sent to Secretary General of IMO who sends copies to all member states STAGE 3: RATIFICATION ├── Each member state gives formal consent to be bound ├── Three methods of ratification: │ (i) SIGNATURE — most formal; simple signature │ by authorised government representative │ (ii) SIGNATURE SUBJECT TO RATIFICATION, ACCEPTANCE │ OR APPROVAL — state has signed and shown interest │ but needs approval from own parliament; IMO does │ NOT consider this official ratification; state must │ subsequently submit Instrument of Ratification to │ the Depositary of the Convention │ Depositary = Secretary General of IMO │ (iii) ACCESSION — used when signing window has closed; │ see Topic 6 └── Depository of convention = Secretary General of IMO STAGE 4: ENTRY INTO FORCE └── Convention enters into force when a MINIMUM number of member states accepts it (threshold varies by convention) e.g. SOLAS: 25 states representing ≥50% of world gross tonnage STAGE 5: IMPLEMENTATION ├── Member state that ratified must include convention │ in their national laws │ (In India = amend Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 — replaces the repealed 1958 Act) └── When convention enters into force after sufficient countries have ratified, provisions of the convention shall be included in the country's local laws → convention becomes legally binding on the member states that ratified it ⚖ Key Legal Concepts Depository The department which keeps a record of member states that have ratified a convention. For IMO conventions = Secretary General of IMO Instrument of Ratification Formal document submitted by a state to the Depositary confirming acceptance of the convention obligations Instrument of Accession Document submitted when a state joins a convention after the signature window has closed Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (India) In force 15 March 2026; India's national legislation through which IMO conventions are implemented in Indian law (replaces the repealed 1958 Act). 📊 Three Methods of Ratification Method What it means IMO Recognition Signature Most formal; state signs and is immediately bound Official ratification Signature subject to ratification / acceptance / approval State signed and shown interest; needs own parliament approval; must submit Instrument of Ratification to Depositary NOT official until Instrument deposited Accession State joins after signing window closed; deposits Instrument of Accession to Depositary Official from deposit date CE Oral Tip — Nair Sir: The five-stage lifecycle is a written exam favourite at 10–15 marks. In orals, Nair asks: "What is ratification?" and "What is accession?" — candidates must distinguish: ratification = state consenting during the open signature window; accession = state joining after the window closed. Both require deposit of an Instrument with the Depositary (Secretary General). Also asked: "What is the Depositary?" — always answer: the Secretary General of IMO. 🎯 Oral Q&A — 8 Questions Q1: Explain the process by which a new IMO convention enters into force. A convention passes through five stages: (1) Drafting — any member state proposes; committee drafts; (2) Adoption — Diplomatic Conference adopts when majority of states present agree; (3) Ratification — each state gives formal consent via signature, signature subject to ratification, or accession, depositing an Instrument with the Secretary General (Depositary); (4) Entry into force — when a minimum number of states (varying by convention) have ratified; (5) Implementation — each ratifying state incorporates the convention into national law. Q2: What is the Depositary of an IMO convention? The Depositary is the body that keeps an official record of which member states have ratified a convention. For all IMO conventions, the Depositary is the Secretary General of IMO, based in London. Q3: What is the difference between ratification and accession? Ratification is the formal consent given by a state that signed the convention during the open signature window. Accession is the method used by a state to join a convention after the signature window has closed — the state deposits an Instrument of Accession with the Depositary (Secretary General) without having been a signatory. Q4: What happens if India signs a convention "subject to ratification"? India has signed the convention and shown interest, but this is NOT considered official ratification by IMO. India must subsequently obtain parliamentary approval and submit a formal Instrument of Ratification to the Secretary General of IMO. Only after this deposit is India officially a contracting party to the convention. Q5: How is a convention implemented in India? Once India ratifies an IMO convention, the provisions must be incorporated into Indian national law. The primary domestic legislation is the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (in force 15 March 2026, replacing the repealed 1958 Act), which is amended or supplemented by DGMA (formerly DGS) notifications and orders to give effect to convention requirements. This makes the convention legally binding on Indian-flagged vessels and persons subject to Indian jurisdiction. Q6: What is an "Adoption Conference"? An Adoption Conference is a diplomatic conference convened by the IMO Council or Assembly to formally adopt a draft convention. The draft is circulated to all member states beforehand for comments. At the conference, once the majority of states present agree to the final draft, the convention is formally considered "Adopted" and sent to the Secretary General for distribution. Q7: Can a convention bind a state that has not ratified it? No. An IMO convention binds only those states that have ratified it (contracting parties). However, practical enforcement through Port State Control means that even vessels from non-party states may face deficiency notices when calling at ports of contracting states, since PSC officers apply convention standards to all vessels in their ports. Q8: What is the minimum ratification threshold for SOLAS to enter into force? SOLAS 1974 required acceptance by at least 25 states representing not less than 50% of the world's gross merchant tonnage. Different conventions have different thresholds — this is specified within each convention text. For the current SOLAS, the entry into force conditions were met before 1980. 🧠 Memory Box 5 Stages: Draft → Adopt → Ratify → Entry into Force → Implement Depositary = Secretary General of IMO (always) Ratification = during signature window | Accession = after window closed India implementation = amend Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (in force 15 Mar 2026, replaces the repealed 1958 Act) Majority at conference = Adopted; minimum states ratify = Enters into Force Notes-p1 · T5 · v1.0

section_subtitle: Tacit Acceptance & Amendment by Resolution
section_title: Q1: What is tacit acceptance?
text: Tacit acceptance is a procedure whereby a contracting state is deemed to have accepted an IMO amendment if it does not formally oppose it within the prescribed time frame following adoption. Silence constitutes consent. This mechanism, codified in SOLAS Article VIII, allows IMO to update technical regulations quickly without requiring active legislative action by every member state.

keywords: tacit acceptance, amendment by resolution
section_subtitle: Tacit Acceptance & Amendment by Resolution
section_title: Q2: Why was tacit acceptance introduced?
text: Traditional explicit acceptance required every contracting state to positively ratify each amendment through national legislation — an extremely slow process that could delay critical safety updates by years or decades. Tacit acceptance was introduced to ensure that technical safety and environmental amendments enter into force on a fixed, predictable date unless a sufficient number of states actively object.

keywords: tacit acceptance, amendment by resolution
section_subtitle: Tacit Acceptance & Amendment by Resolution
section_title: Q3: What are the voting thresholds for adopting an IMO amendment by Resolution?
text: For successful adoption of an amendment by Resolution at MSC or MEPC: at least one-third of contracting governments must be present for voting, and at least two-thirds of those contracting governments present must vote in favour of the resolution.

keywords: tacit acceptance, amendment by resolution
section_subtitle: Tacit Acceptance & Amendment by Resolution
section_title: Q4: Where is tacit acceptance codified for SOLAS amendments?
text: Tacit acceptance for SOLAS amendments is codified in SOLAS Article VIII — the amendment procedure article. Article VIII specifies the adoption voting thresholds, the circulation period, the time window for objections, and the entry into force date mechanics.

keywords: tacit acceptance, amendment by resolution
section_subtitle: Tacit Acceptance & Amendment by Resolution
section_title: Q5: What is the difference between amendment by Protocol and amendment by Resolution?
text: Amendment by Protocol is used for major structural changes or adding new chapters to a convention already in force. A Protocol is a separate legal instrument requiring independent ratification and binds only states that ratify it. Amendment by Resolution is used for technical updates within existing convention chapters and typically uses tacit acceptance — it is faster and binds all contracting parties that do not formally object.

keywords: tacit acceptance, amendment by resolution
section_subtitle: Tacit Acceptance & Amendment by Resolution
section_title: Q6: Give an example of a recent SOLAS amendment adopted by tacit acceptance.
text: MSC.520(106) — adopted at MSC 106 — amended SOLAS Chapter II-2 (fire protection) and entered into force on 01 January 2026. MSC.496(105) amended SOLAS Chapters II-1, III, IV, and V, entering into force on 01 January 2024. Both were adopted via Resolution using the tacit acceptance procedure under SOLAS Article VIII.

keywords: tacit acceptance, amendment by resolution
section_subtitle: Tacit Acceptance & Amendment by Resolution
section_title: Q7: Can a state object to a tacit acceptance amendment?
text: Yes. A contracting state may formally object to a proposed amendment within the prescribed time frame (typically before the entry into force date). If sufficient states object, the amendment may not enter into force universally. However, in practice, most SOLAS and MARPOL amendments proceed under tacit acceptance with very few formal objections, particularly for technical updates.

keywords: tacit acceptance, amendment by resolution
section_subtitle: Tacit Acceptance & Amendment by Resolution
section_title: Q8: How long is the typical period between adoption and entry into force for a tacit acceptance amendment?
text: Typically 18 to 24 months from adoption to entry into force. This period allows member states to notify their fleets, adjust equipment, obtain class approval for modifications, and update their SMS procedures before the amendment becomes mandatory.

keywords: tacit acceptance, amendment by resolution
section_subtitle: Tacit Acceptance & Amendment by Resolution
section_title: Q9: As a Chief Engineer, what does tacit acceptance mean practically for you?
text: As CE, I must actively monitor MSC and MEPC sessions to identify adopted amendments that will affect my vessel. I cannot wait for the flag state to notify me — tacit acceptance means the amendment is coming regardless. I should update the SMS, procure required equipment or type approvals, arrange class surveys, and brief the crew at least 6 months before the entry into force date. Ignorance is not a defence in a PSC inspection.

keywords: tacit acceptance, amendment by resolution
section_subtitle: Tacit Acceptance & Amendment by Resolution
section_title: Q10: What is an amendment by Conference of Contracting States?
text: This is an alternative amendment route where IMO convenes a separate diplomatic conference of all contracting states to a specific convention. This method is less common and typically used for amendments too significant or politically sensitive for the standard MSC/MEPC resolution route. It resembles the original convention adoption process with a dedicated conference, circulation of the draft, and voting by contracting parties.
