section_title: Q2. The terminal's loading rate is outpacing your deballasting capacity during a BLU Code operation. What is the required response?
text: The duty officer immediately notifies the Terminal Representative via the agreed communication channel to request a reduced loading rate or a temporary halt, per the signed BLU Code Ship/Shore Checklist. If the terminal does not respond promptly and the hull stress monitoring system alarms, the Master or duty officer triggers the agreed Emergency Stop signal, halting all conveyor feeds until ballast pumping brings shear forces and bending moments back within the loading plan's safe limits.

section_title: Q3. What is the practical difference between PES and ACEP for a large container line's fleet?
text: Under PES, each container carries a fixed Next Examination Date and must be formally re-inspected within 30 months of the previous check — administratively simple but requires taking containers out of normal circulation for scheduled inspection. Under ACEP, examination happens naturally every time a container passes through a repair or depot facility, with the ACEP scheme number (not a date) shown on the plate — this suits large fleets where containers are constantly cycling through maintenance touchpoints, avoiding dedicated inspection downtime.

section_title: Q2. Describe the shipboard Can Test and its evidentiary weight.
text: A representative cargo sample half-fills a rigid cylindrical can, which is then struck sharply against a hard deck surface approximately 25 times from a drop height of about 20 cm. If the sample stays dry and crumbly it passes the initial screen; if it thins, settles, or produces free water on the surface, it fails, indicating moisture near or above the flow point. The Can Test is an empirical shipboard screening tool only — it cannot override a certified laboratory report, but a failure gives immediate legitimate grounds to suspend loading and demand formal independent analysis.

section_title: Q3. How does liquefied cargo alter the vessel's transverse stability mathematically?
text: Liquefaction creates a massive free surface effect: as the ship rolls, the fluidised cargo shifts to the low side, producing a virtual rise in the centre of gravity from G to G₁ (GG₁ = i·ρ_cargo / V·ρ_sea). This directly reduces effective GM (GM_eff = KM − KG − GG₁), and the righting lever curve is degraded across all heel angles per GZ_effective = GZ_solid − GG₁sin(θ), sharply reducing reserve stability and increasing capsize risk.

The regulatory purpose of the IMSBC Code's moisture controls is to prevent this transition ever occurring at sea, where its onset can be sudden and catastrophic. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) Liquefaction is a stability, not a strength, failure — it destroys GM through an effective free surface effect, and Rajappan expects candidates to connect the soil-mechanics cause (pore pressure rise) directly to the naval-architecture consequence (GZ curve collapse), not treat them as separate topics. As Chief Engineer, hold bilge system readiness and vibration management during high-risk transits are direct engineering responsibilities that reduce (though never eliminate) the compaction forces driving pore pressure rise. The Master's authority to reject a cargo on visual/Can Test evidence — even against a signed shipper's certificate — is a legal power every officer must be able to explain precisely in an oral exam. 📅 Historical Background 2000s–2010s Series of nickel/iron ore fines capsizes traced to undetected moisture migration Findings Cargoes appeared visually dry but held moisture well above safe transport limits Response IMO transforms the voluntary BC Code into the mandatory IMSBC Code, formalising Group A/B/C classification and TML/FMP testing 📐 Free Surface Effect on Liquefied Cargo (Schematic) Solid cargo (stable) Liquefied cargo (free surface forms) +-----------------+ +-----------------+ |#################| |~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~| +-----------------+ GM unaffected by cargo shift Effective GM reduced (GG1 rise) - same free-surface-moment principle as slack tanks; can precipitate capsize Schematic only — illustrates why a liquefied cargo behaves like a slack tank for GM-reduction purposes, per the standard free-surface-effect treatment in naval architecture references. ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments SOLAS Ch. VI Mandates that solid bulk cargoes be loaded, stowed and carried per the IMSBC Code. IMSBC Code Classifies cargoes into Group A (liquefaction hazard), B (chemical hazard), C (neither); sets TML/FMP testing requirements. IMSBC Appendix 2 Shipboard Can Test procedure for quick moisture-hazard screening. 🧮 Critical Safety Parameters Term Meaning Flow Moisture Point (FMP) Moisture % at which the cargo begins to exhibit fluid flow under standard lab vibration testing Transportable Moisture Limit (TML) Maximum moisture % deemed safe for transit — TML = 0.90 × FMP Rule Actual verified moisture content must be strictly < TML for the cargo to be accepted τ = (σ − u) tan(φ) — as pore water pressure (u) rises toward the normal stress (σ), effective shear strength (τ) collapses toward zero and the material liquefies. Once liquefied, the cargo behaves like a free-surface liquid: GG₁ = (i × ρ_cargo) / (V × ρ_sea) , producing a virtual rise in G and a direct reduction in GM, which degrades the GZ righting-lever curve across all heel angles. 🎓 CE Oral Tip (Rajappan): Rajappan's standard escalation: "The shipper's certificate shows FMP 12.0% and actual moisture 11.2% — is this cargo acceptable?" The Can Test is an empirical shipboard screening tool only — it cannot override a certified laboratory report, but a failure gives immediate legitimate grounds to suspend loading and demand formal independent analysis. "25 strikes, ~20 cm" — the Can Test parameters. section_title: Q1. What is the currently active statutory framework governing Indian vessel registration, and what changed from the earlier law?
text: The currently active law is the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025, in force since 15 March 2026, which repealed the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. Under the 1958 Act, Indian registration required 100% Indian ownership by a citizen, eligible company, or co-operative society. The 2025 Act liberalises this: Indian-flagged vessels may now be wholly or partly owned by Indian citizens, companies, NRIs, OCIs, or other Central-Government-notified entities, with exact partial-ownership thresholds to be prescribed by subordinate Rules rather than fixed in the Act itself. The Director General of Shipping has also been renamed the Director-General of Maritime Administration (DGMA) under the new Act.

section_title: Q3. An Indian company buys a vessel located at a foreign port. How is she registered to make her delivery voyage to India?
text: The Registrar can authorise a local Indian Consular Officer or an RO surveyor to inspect the vessel at the foreign port, verifying ownership documents and the Carving and Marking Note details against the vessel's tonnage. Once satisfied, a Provisional Certificate of Registration is issued, giving the vessel legal flag status for her transit voyage to India, where permanent registration is then completed. (Note: under the 2025 Act the precise validity period and extension/cancellation procedure for this provisional certificate is left to subordinate Rules rather than a fixed figure in the Act — confirm the current prescribed period against the notified Rules rather than quoting a specific number as statute.)

This is now out of date. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (Act No. 24 of 2025) received Presidential assent on 18 August 2025 and its provisions were brought into force from 15 March 2026 — before today's date — so as of this writing the 1958 Act has been repealed and the 2025 Act is the active law . Key operative changes: (1) the office of Director General of Shipping has been renamed Director-General of Maritime Administration (DGMA) , with expanded statutory powers; (2) the rigid "100% Indian ownership" rule is gone — Indian-flagged vessels may now be wholly or partly owned by Indian citizens, companies, NRIs, OCIs, or other Central-Government-notified entities, with the exact ownership thresholds fixed by subordinate Rules rather than the Act itself (draft Registration of Vessels Rules, out for public consultation Dec 2025–Jan 2026, specify a minimum 51% Indian ownership share for partly-owned vessels — this is a draft rule figure, not yet a finalised, gazetted requirement, and should be stated as such); (3) the Act formally enables registration of foreign vessels under a Bareboat Charter-cum-Demise (BBCD) structure (Section 16); (4) Part V "Registration of Indian Ships" language from the 1958 Act is superseded by the 2025 Act's own registration Part (Sections 15–19 cover eligible owners, BBCD registration, and provisional registration). The Registrar of Indian vessels remains the Principal Officer of the Mercantile Marine Department (or a person the Central Government notifies) — this did not change. In an oral exam, state clearly that the 2025 Act is now in force and describe the 1958 Act only as the repealed predecessor framework, not as "currently active." 📖 Definition Flag State Administration is the statutory framework through which a sovereign nation exercises legal authority and technical oversight over vessels flying its flag. Vessel Registry Engineering is the structured legal/technical process of entering a ship into a national register — verifying title, confirming tonnage, and certifying regulatory compliance. In India this framework now sits under the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 , administered by the Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA) through the Mercantile Marine Department (MMD) at regional field offices including Kochi. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) As Chief Engineer you maintain the Continuous Synopsis Record (CSR), Oil Record Book, and engine room log discipline that flag-state and DGMA audits check first — registry compliance is a live, continuous engineering obligation, not a one-time paperwork event. Nair frequently pivots between "1958 Act era" facts and "2025 Act era" facts specifically to test whether candidates are current — stating "2025 Act, now in force" without hesitation is itself part of a strong answer. On a change-of-flag voyage, the engineering department is directly responsible for reprogramming SSAS/AIS/EPIRB/LRIT with new flag identifiers and re-engraving the wheelhouse tonnage plate — this is CE-owned technical work, not administrative-only. 📅 Historical Background 1958 Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 enacted — closed registry, 100% Indian ownership required 2020 Merchant Shipping Bill 2020 proposes 51%/49% equity liberalisation — never enacted as such 2025 18 Aug — Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (Act No. 24 of 2025) receives Presidential assent, repealing the 1958 Act 2026 15 Mar — MS Act 2025 provisions come into force; DG Shipping renamed DGMA ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments UNCLOS Art. 91 Every State fixes conditions for granting nationality/registration to ships; requires a "genuine link" between State and ship. UNCLOS Art. 94 Core duties of the Flag State — effective jurisdiction over the ship, master, officers and crew. Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (Act No. 24 of 2025) In force from 15 March 2026; replaces the 1958 Act; 16 Parts, 325 sections (down from 561 sections in the 1958 Act). The Director General of Shipping has also been renamed the Director-General of Maritime Administration (DGMA) under the new Act. Q2. The Shipping Master supervises the formal engagement and discharge of seafarers in line with national law and the Maritime Labour Convention, hears and arbitrates disputes between Master, owners and crew over wages or working conditions, verifies the vessel meets its Safe Manning Document before issuing port clearances for outbound voyages, and maintains records of Certificates of Competency and seafarers' discharge books. Q3. An Indian company buys a vessel located at a foreign port. How is she registered to make her delivery voyage to India? The Registrar can authorise a local Indian Consular Officer or an RO surveyor to inspect the vessel at the foreign port, verifying ownership documents and the Carving and Marking Note details against the vessel's tonnage. Once satisfied, a Provisional Certificate of Registration is issued, giving the vessel legal flag status for her transit voyage to India, where permanent registration is then completed. (Note: under the 2025 Act the precise validity period and extension/cancellation procedure for this provisional certificate is left to subordinate Rules rather than a fixed figure in the Act — confirm the current prescribed period against the notified Rules rather than quoting a specific number as statute.) ✍ Written Exam Focus 5 State the key differences between the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 regarding vessel ownership eligibility. 10 Detail the complete administrative and technical process to register a newly built commercial vessel under the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025, from name application through to permanent registration. 15 Analyse the technical and regulatory steps in a change-of-flag procedure for an operational cargo vessel — hull marking and wheelhouse tonnage plate modifications, GMDSS/SSAS/LRIT reprogramming, classification society verification, and the statutory audits required for interim certification. 🧠 Memory Box "2025, not 1958" — the active statute is the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025, in force since 15 March 2026. DGS → DGMA — Director General of Shipping renamed Director-General of Maritime Administration. section_title: Q1. You join a vessel that just changed flag from Panama to India. The AIS is still transmitting the old Panamanian MMSI. What do you do, and what's the regulatory risk?
text: This is a serious non-conformity under SOLAS Chapter XI-1, Regulation 3 and the ITU Radio Regulations, and PSC will treat it as an ISPS-linked high-risk item. I would raise it through SMS change-management procedures, obtain the new Indian MMSI and call sign from the provisional Certificate of Registry, and coordinate with an authorised radio technician to reprogram the AIS and GMDSS DSC units, since these are pass-code protected. I would then run a DSC test call with the nearest Coast Radio Station, verify the EPIRB is re-coded with the new country identifier and registered with INMCC, and confirm the physical hull markings and CSR are updated to match.

section_title: Q2. Explain the check-digit logic of the IMO number, and state whether it can be reassigned.
text: The IMO number has 7 digits: the first 6 are data digits, and the 7th is a check digit calculated as (7×d₁ + 6×d₂ + 5×d₃ + 4×d₄ + 3×d₅ + 2×d₆) mod 10. It cannot be reassigned under any circumstances — it stays with the physical hull from keel-laying to scrapping or loss, regardless of ownership, flag, or the vessel's ultimate fate.

text: Part 15 · Topic 1 Ship Identification Systems & Statutory Credentials — IMO Number, MMSI, Call Sign & CSR SOLAS XI-1 · ITU Radio Regs Uday pp. 351–357 (approx.) Examiner: Nair ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: The source draft anchored the Continuous Synopsis Record (CSR) to "SOLAS Chapter XI-1, Regulation 4-1." This is incorrect and has been corrected — the CSR is mandated under SOLAS Chapter XI-1, Regulation 5 (not Regulation 4-1). Regulation 5 requires every ship to which SOLAS Chapter I applies (passenger ships and cargo ships of 500 GT and above on international voyages, plus self-propelled MODUs) to carry a CSR from 1 July 2004, per IMO Resolution A.959(23). This is an important distinction for Nair's line of questioning, since Regulation 4-1 does not exist in the form implied by the draft. All other figures — Resolution A.600(15) of 1987 for the IMO Ship Identification Number Scheme, the 300 GT mandatory threshold under Regulation 3, the check-digit algorithm, and S&P Global Market Intelligence (formerly IHS Markit/Lloyd's Register-Fairplay) as the administering body — were checked against IMO and class-society sources and are correct as given. 📖 Definition Ship identification frameworks are the set of statutory numerical and alphanumeric designations — the IMO number, MMSI, radio call sign, and Official Number — that together give a vessel a traceable, tamper-resistant identity across its operating life. They exist to prevent identity fraud and re-flagging abuse, support search-and-rescue and vessel-traffic monitoring, and ensure that a ship's regulatory history (PSC deficiencies, class conditions, casualties) stays attached to the physical hull regardless of changes in name, ownership, or flag. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) During any flag change, the Chief Engineer directly supervises reprogramming of the AIS, GMDSS DSC radios, EPIRB, and LRIT terminal — this is not simply an administrative form-filling exercise, it is a technical task with PSC/ISPS consequences if done incorrectly or left half-finished. Nair frequently probes whether candidates confuse the four credentials: which one is permanent (IMO number), which changes on flag transfer (MMSI, call sign), and which regulation governs each — mixing these up is one of the fastest ways to lose marks. A mismatch between the AIS-transmitted MMSI and the Certificate of Registry is treated by PSC as a serious ISPS-linked non-conformity, not a paperwork triviality — it can trigger detention. 📅 Historical Background 1987 IMO Res. A.600(15) — Ship Identification Number Scheme introduced (initially voluntary) 2002 SOLAS Ch. XI-1 Reg. 3 amendment makes IMO number scheme mandatory 2002 ISPS Code adopted (12 Dec) — new Reg. 5 (CSR) added to SOLAS Ch. XI-1 2004 SOLAS Ch. XI-1 Reg. 5 (CSR) enters into force — 1 Jul 2009 IMO Unique Company/Registered Owner Numbers added to CSR requirements ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments SOLAS Ch. XI-1, Reg. 3 Mandates the IMO Ship Identification Number Scheme for cargo ships ≥300 GT and all passenger ships on international voyages, subject to statutory exemptions (non-propelled vessels, pleasure yachts, lightships/SAR craft, hopper barges, hydrofoils/ACVs, warships/naval auxiliaries/troopships, primitive wooden-built vessels). IMO Res. A.600(15) 1987 resolution establishing the operational and administrative framework for the IMO Ship Identification Number Scheme. SOLAS Ch. XI-1, Reg. 5 Mandates the Continuous Synopsis Record (CSR) — corrected from the source draft's "Regulation 4-1." In force from 1 July 2004; format/guidelines set out in IMO Res. A.959(23). ITU Radio Regulations, Art. 19 Governs the structural allocation of Maritime Mobile Service Identities (MMSI) and alphanumeric radio call signs. 🔢 The Four Statutory Credentials Credential Format Permanence Governing Instrument IMO Number 7-digit numeric + "IMO" prefix Immutable for the hull's life SOLAS XI-1, Reg. 3 MMSI 9-digit numeric (3-digit MID + 6-digit ship ID) Changes on flag transfer ITU Radio Regs Art. 19 Call Sign Alphanumeric string Changes on flag transfer Flag telecom authority / ITU Official Number Domestic alphanumeric string Changes on flag transfer National flag statute 🎓 CE Oral Tip (Nair): Nair's classic opener here is "walk me through the check-digit formula" followed immediately by "can that IMO number ever be reassigned if the ship sinks?" Know both cold: the check digit is (7d₁+6d₂+5d₃+4d₄+3d₅+2d₆) mod 10 = d₇, and the answer to reassignment is an unqualified no — the number is retired with the hull permanently, regardless of the vessel's fate. 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1. You join a vessel that just changed flag from Panama to India. The AIS is still transmitting the old Panamanian MMSI. What do you do, and what's the regulatory risk? This is a serious non-conformity under SOLAS Chapter XI-1, Regulation 3 and the ITU Radio Regulations, and PSC will treat it as an ISPS-linked high-risk item. I would raise it through SMS change-management procedures, obtain the new Indian MMSI and call sign from the provisional Certificate of Registry, and coordinate with an authorised radio technician to reprogram the AIS and GMDSS DSC units, since these are pass-code protected. I would then run a DSC test call with the nearest Coast Radio Station, verify the EPIRB is re-coded with the new country identifier and registered with INMCC, and confirm the physical hull markings and CSR are updated to match. Q2. Explain the check-digit logic of the IMO number, and state whether it can be reassigned. The IMO number has 7 digits: the first 6 are data digits, and the 7th is a check digit calculated as (7×d₁ + 6×d₂ + 5×d₃ + 4×d₄ + 3×d₅ + 2×d₆) mod 10. It cannot be reassigned under any circumstances — it stays with the physical hull from keel-laying to scrapping or loss, regardless of ownership, flag, or the vessel's ultimate fate. Q3. Which vessel categories are exempt from the mandatory IMO number scheme? Under SOLAS Chapter XI-1, Regulation 3, the exemptions are: vessels without mechanical propulsion, pleasure yachts in non-commercial use, specialised service craft such as lightships and SAR vessels, hopper barges, hydrofoils and air-cushion vehicles, warships/naval auxiliaries/troopships, and wooden vessels of primitive or traditional build. ✍ Written Exam Focus 5 Differentiate between the MMSI and the IMO number regarding structural permanence during a change of flag. 10 Draft a step-by-step engineering management procedure for a Chief Engineer coordinating the physical and electronic transition of ship credentials during a flag-change delivery. 15 Analyse the regulatory framework behind the Continuous Synopsis Record under SOLAS Chapter XI-1, Regulation 5. Explain how historical continuity is maintained across flag changes and the PSC consequences of a broken CSR sequence. 🧠 Memory Box "3-5 split" — Regulation 3 = IMO number (permanent); Regulation 5 = CSR (travels with the ship's history), not Regulation 4-1. MID + 6 — MMSI structure; 224 = Spain, 419 = India. IMO number: never reassigned , ever — even after total loss. ▶ Deep Dive — Flag-Change Identity Transfer Sequence Operational Case Study — 55,000 DWT Crude Oil Tanker, Spain → India Flag Transfer Sequence: weld/paint new hull markings and port of registry → reprogram AIS/DSC/EPIRB/LRIT with the new Indian MMSI block (419XXXXXX) and call sign → insert the new CSR amendment (Form 1/Provisional CSR from DGS) and open Indian official logbooks → execute a DSC test call with a Coast Radio Station to verify the reprogrammed transponder. The internal IMO number carving on the machinery-space bulkhead is verified for legibility but never altered. PSC Integration PSC officers cross-reference the live AIS pilot-plug data against the Certificate of Registry; a mismatch, obscured external hull markings, or a broken CSR page sequence are each treated as standalone, serious deficiencies under ISPS. On My Vessel (Maersk A/S container tonnage) Container ships rarely change flag mid-career, but the same discipline applies at every drydock or reflagging: verify the internal IMO number carving remains legible on the engine-room bulkhead, and confirm the CSR file has no gaps before a class or PSC visit. 📚 References IMO — SOLAS Chapter XI-1, Regulations 3 and 5 IMO — Resolution A.600(15), Ship Identification Number Scheme IMO — Resolution A.959(23), Format and Guidelines for the CSR ITU — Radio Regulations, Article 19 See also — MIW Engineering Management Notes Part 21, Topic 3 : the CSR combined with ISM DOC/SMC certification, and the bareboat-handover sequencing walkthrough. section_title: Q1. Explain the difference between an action in rem and in personam, and why a claimant might prefer the former against a foreign-flagged vessel.
text: An in rem action targets the ship itself as the responsible party; an in personam action targets the individual or corporate owner. Chasing an owner in personam can be difficult if they are based overseas, whereas the vessel is a tangible asset that enters local ports. Under the Admiralty Act, 2017, a claimant can seek an arrest warrant against the ship itself once it enters the jurisdiction of a designated Indian High Court, securing the claim regardless of where the owner is located. In practice, once the owner appears and posts security, the in rem action effectively converts to proceed as if it were in personam against that owner.

keywords: maritime lien, in rem, in personam, Admiralty Act 2017, arrest of ships, mortgage priority, marine engineering assessor, salvage, designated High Court
section_subtitle: Legal Paradigms of Maritime Claims — Liens, Mortgages, Vessel Arrest & Admiralty Jurisdiction
section_title: Q2. What is a maritime lien, and how does its behaviour differ between a private sale and a judicial auction?
text: A maritime lien is a privileged claim against a vessel arising from services rendered or damage caused by the ship; it attaches to the property, not the owner. If the vessel is sold privately, the lien travels with it to the new owner. If the vessel is sold via a court-ordered judicial auction, the sale extinguishes all existing liens, giving the buyer clean title while creditors' claims shift to the auction proceeds instead.

section_title: Q3. What are the statutory qualifications for a Marine Engineering Assessor under the Admiralty Act, 2017, and what is their role?
text: A Marine Engineering Assessor must hold a Class 1 Certificate of Competency as Chief Engineer with at least 1 year served in that rank and a minimum of 5 years' total sea experience, or alternatively a relevant engineering degree with at least 5 years of specialised professional experience. Their role is to act as an independent technical expert to the designated High Court, translating complex engineering and machinery-condition evidence into facts the court can use for its rulings.

The International Convention on Maritime Liens and Mortgages, 1993 and the International Convention on the Arrest of Ships, 1999 were checked against IMO/UNCTAD treaty records and are correctly named and dated. The assessor qualification criteria (Class 1 CoC for a Marine Engineering Assessor, minimum 1 year in rank and 5 years total sea service) reflect the Act's Second Schedule and are stated correctly as a matter of general legal position; candidates should note that exact clause numbers are best confirmed against the Act's current consolidated text before an oral exam, as legal texts are periodically renumbered by amendment. 📖 Definition Maritime claims law gives claimants — crew, salvors, suppliers, lenders — the unique ability to secure a debt directly against a ship itself (the res ), rather than only against the often distant and hard-to-reach shipowner. This proprietary framework, built on the doctrines of in rem and in personam action, exists because a mobile international asset like a merchant vessel would otherwise let owners escape liability simply by moving beyond a claimant's jurisdiction. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) A vessel arrest freezes the ship in port — main propulsion is normally secured while auxiliary power continues under SMS guidelines, so the Chief Engineer's operational judgment directly shapes how smoothly the arrest is managed until security is posted. Nair often tests whether candidates understand that a maritime lien survives a private sale but is wiped out by a judicial auction — this single distinction anchors most of the topic's oral questions. Unpaid crew wages are simultaneously an MLC/PSC detention risk and grounds for a high-priority maritime lien — the two consequences reinforce each other operationally. 📅 Historical Background Medieval Personification doctrine develops — the ship treated as liable in its own right 1993 International Convention on Maritime Liens and Mortgages adopted 1999 International Convention on the Arrest of Ships adopted 2017 Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act enacted in India ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments Intl. Convention on Maritime Liens & Mortgages, 1993 International standards for categorising, prioritising, and enforcing maritime liens and registered mortgages. Intl. Convention on the Arrest of Ships, 1999 Legal framework allowing a claimant to arrest a vessel to secure a maritime claim. Admiralty (Jurisdiction & Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 (India) Vests admiralty jurisdiction in designated High Courts; governs vessel arrest, claim priority, and appointment of nautical/marine engineering assessors. Not affected by the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025. 📊 Priority of Claims on Judicial Sale Tier Claim Type Notes 1 (Highest) Maritime Liens Crew wages, salvage, port/public dues, collision/injury damage — salvage ranks in inverse chronological order 2 Registered Mortgages Bank/financial institution loans secured against the vessel 3 (Lowest) Unsecured Claims Charterparty disputes, general supply invoices 🎓 CE Oral Tip (Nair): Nair likes to ask "does selling the ship privately clear a lien?" followed by "what if it's a court auction instead?" Keep the two clearly separate: private sale — lien survives, attaches to new owner; judicial/in rem auction — lien is wiped out, buyer gets clean title, and creditors' claims shift to the sale proceeds instead. 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1. Explain the difference between an action in rem and in personam, and why a claimant might prefer the former against a foreign-flagged vessel. An in rem action targets the ship itself as the responsible party; an in personam action targets the individual or corporate owner. Chasing an owner in personam can be difficult if they are based overseas, whereas the vessel is a tangible asset that enters local ports. Under the Admiralty Act, 2017, a claimant can seek an arrest warrant against the ship itself once it enters the jurisdiction of a designated Indian High Court, securing the claim regardless of where the owner is located. In practice, once the owner appears and posts security, the in rem action effectively converts to proceed as if it were in personam against that owner. Q2. What is a maritime lien, and how does its behaviour differ between a private sale and a judicial auction? A maritime lien is a privileged claim against a vessel arising from services rendered or damage caused by the ship; it attaches to the property, not the owner. If the vessel is sold privately, the lien travels with it to the new owner. If the vessel is sold via a court-ordered judicial auction, the sale extinguishes all existing liens, giving the buyer clean title while creditors' claims shift to the auction proceeds instead. Q3. What are the statutory qualifications for a Marine Engineering Assessor under the Admiralty Act, 2017, and what is their role? A Marine Engineering Assessor must hold a Class 1 Certificate of Competency as Chief Engineer with at least 1 year served in that rank and a minimum of 5 years' total sea experience, or alternatively a relevant engineering degree with at least 5 years of specialised professional experience. Their role is to act as an independent technical expert to the designated High Court, translating complex engineering and machinery-condition evidence into facts the court can use for its rulings. ✍ Written Exam Focus 5 Explain how priority is determined between two separate salvage claims on the same vessel. 10 Describe the legal pathways by which a maritime lien can be discharged or terminated. 15 Analyse the structure of the Admiralty Act, 2017 — vessel arrest mechanisms, the statutory order of priority on judicial sale, and the role of technical assessors in admiralty litigation. 🧠 Memory Box Priority order: Liens → Mortgages → Unsecured (crew/salvage first, suppliers/charterers last). Private sale = lien survives. Judicial auction = lien wiped clean. Salvage claims rank inverse-chronologically — latest salvor paid first, since their effort preserved the asset for everyone else. ▶ Deep Dive — Vessel Arrest & Court Assessor Cooperation Operational Case Study — 85,000 DWT Post-Panamax Bulk Carrier, Arrest for Unpaid Wages & Berth Damage Sequence: notify owner, management company, and P&I Club immediately → secure main propulsion while maintaining auxiliary power under SMS → lock down and copy engine telegraph logs, bell logbooks, and data logger files for the disputed period → assist the court-appointed Marine Engineering Assessor's inspection of steering gear, propulsion, and maintenance records → once the P&I Club posts security (bank guarantee/letter of undertaking), confirm the designated High Court has lifted the warrant and the port authority clears the vessel to sail. PSC Integration An active arrest warrant is flagged in port databases and independently blocks sailing clearance; systemic wage-payment failures additionally trigger MLC-linked PSC detention alongside the lien itself. On My Vessel (Maersk A/S container tonnage) Meticulous port-entry, pilotage, and tug-service logging under SMS is the practical safeguard here — clean documentation is what protects the ship (and the Chief Engineer's own position) if a berth-damage or supply-invoice dispute later escalates into a lien claim. 📚 References International Convention on Maritime Liens and Mortgages, 1993 International Convention on the Arrest of Ships, 1999 Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 (India) Notes-p15 · P15-T2 · v1.0

section_title: Q1. What Act currently governs the detention of an unsafe ship in India, and what changed recently?
text: The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (Act No. 24 of 2025) currently governs this area — it came into force on 15 March 2026 and repealed the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, which had previously defined unseaworthy and unsafe ships under its Sections 334–338. The Directorate General of Shipping was simultaneously renamed the Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA). The underlying distinction — a general "unseaworthy" condition versus a narrower, immediately dangerous "unsafe ship" category — continues in substance under the new Act.

section_title: Q2. If a critical propulsion defect is found shortly before departure, what are the Chief Engineer's obligations?
text: The Chief Engineer must classify and log the defect under SMS/ISM Code Element 10 procedures, halt departure planning, and notify the Master immediately so the port authority, owner, and the flag administration's local surveyor can be informed. Repairs must be executed under class supervision, and only once the surveyor confirms the vessel is no longer in an unsafe condition can departure proceed.

section_title: Q3. What is the National Shipping Board, and what is its purpose?
text: The National Shipping Board is a permanent statutory advisory body, originally established in 1959 under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, to advise the Government of India on national shipping policy and maritime development. It draws balanced representation from Parliament, shipowners, and seafarers under a designated Chairman. Its statutory basis now sits within the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 framework following the 2026 transition.

text: Part 15 · Topic 3 Statutory Seaworthiness, the "Unsafe Ship" & the National Shipping Board MS Act 1958 → MS Act 2025 Uday pp. 365–370 (approx.) Examiner: Nair Medium Frequency 🔎 Verification note: This is the most significant correction in this Part. The source draft presents the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 (including Section 336's "unsafe ship" provisions and the National Shipping Board's 1959 statutory origin) as the current governing law. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 has since been repealed — the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (Act No. 24 of 2025), a consolidated 16-part, 325-clause statute, came into force on 15 March 2026 and repeals the 1958 Act (retaining only limited savings under Part XIV); the Directorate General of Shipping has been renamed the Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA) . The underlying legal concepts — a ship being "unseaworthy" versus the narrower, higher-danger "unsafe ship" category, and a national maritime policy advisory board — persist in substance under the 2025 Act, but the exact renumbered clause references are not yet available from a citable public consolidated text at the time of writing. The historical section numbers (334–338 for unseaworthy/unsafe ships, and the NSB's 1959 origin) are retained below as accurate historical references and remain useful for understanding how the framework evolved, but candidates should verify the current MS Act 2025 clause numbers against DGMA's own notifications closer to the oral exam, and should be prepared for examiners to ask about the transition itself (old Act → new Act, DG Shipping → DGMA) as a live topic in its own right. 📖 Definition Statutory seaworthiness is the legal and engineering standard requiring a vessel to be structurally sound, properly equipped, adequately manned, and safely loaded before proceeding to sea. Historically codified in India under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 (now superseded by the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025), it distinguishes a general "unseaworthy" condition from the narrower "unsafe ship" category reserved for defects that pose immediate danger to human life. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) A critical machinery defect (main engine, boiler, steering gear, generators) discovered before departure is not just a maintenance item — if it renders the ship "unsafe," the Chief Engineer must halt departure planning and formally notify the Master and flag/PSC channels. Seaworthiness underpins hull and machinery insurance validity and a carrier's due-diligence defence against cargo claims — a breach can void cover entirely, independent of any statutory detention. Nair is likely to test awareness of the ongoing 1958→2025 Act transition itself, not just the old provisions in isolation — know that DG Shipping is now DGMA and that the 1958 Act (except limited savings) is repealed. 📅 Historical Background 1958 Merchant Shipping Act enacted — consolidates colonial-era shipping law 1959 National Shipping Board established under the MS Act, 1958 2025 Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (Act No. 24 of 2025) passed by Parliament 2026 MS Act 2025 enters into force — 15 Mar — repeals the 1958 Act; DG Shipping renamed DGMA ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments SOLAS Ch. II-1 & II-2 International construction, watertight integrity, machinery, and fire-protection standards underpinning structural seaworthiness. SOLAS Ch. V, Reg. 14 Mandates ships be sufficiently and efficiently manned, aligned to Minimum Safe Manning Certificates. International Convention on Load Lines, 1966 Governs reserve buoyancy and structural loading limits to prevent overloading. Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 (historical) → MS Act, 2025 (current) The 1958 Act's Sections 334–338 defined "unseaworthy" and "unsafe" ships and Central Government detention powers; the 2025 Act (in force 15 Mar 2026) now governs this area under DGMA — see verification note above. 🚦 Unseaworthy vs. Unsafe Ship — Historical Criteria (MS Act, 1958 framework) Feature Unseaworthy Ship Unsafe Ship (historically Sec. 336) Definition Materials, master's qualifications, crew complement, cargo/ballast stowage, or hull/machinery condition not fit for the intended voyage A subset of unseaworthiness creating immediate, serious danger to human life Typical Cause Missing minor equipment, uncertified personnel, paperwork gaps Severe hull damage, non-functional propulsion, dangerous overloading Consequence Corrective action required to restore compliance Immediate statutory detention by port authority 🎓 CE Oral Tip (Nair): Nair's standard trap: "which Act governs unseaworthiness right now, in 2026?" The correct answer is the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (in force since 15 March 2026), under DGMA — not the 1958 Act. Be ready to explain the underlying unseaworthy/unsafe distinction using the historical framework, but lead your answer by correctly naming the current governing statute and authority. 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1. What Act currently governs the detention of an unsafe ship in India, and what changed recently? The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (Act No. 24 of 2025) currently governs this area — it came into force on 15 March 2026 and repealed the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, which had previously defined unseaworthy and unsafe ships under its Sections 334–338. The Directorate General of Shipping was simultaneously renamed the Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA). The underlying distinction — a general "unseaworthy" condition versus a narrower, immediately dangerous "unsafe ship" category — continues in substance under the new Act. Q2. If a critical propulsion defect is found shortly before departure, what are the Chief Engineer's obligations? The Chief Engineer must classify and log the defect under SMS/ISM Code Element 10 procedures, halt departure planning, and notify the Master immediately so the port authority, owner, and the flag administration's local surveyor can be informed. Repairs must be executed under class supervision, and only once the surveyor confirms the vessel is no longer in an unsafe condition can departure proceed. Q3. What is the National Shipping Board, and what is its purpose? The National Shipping Board is a permanent statutory advisory body, originally established in 1959 under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, to advise the Government of India on national shipping policy and maritime development. It draws balanced representation from Parliament, shipowners, and seafarers under a designated Chairman. Its statutory basis now sits within the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 framework following the 2026 transition. ✍ Written Exam Focus 5 List the technical criteria that historically rendered a vessel unseaworthy under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. 10 Explain the core strategic goals of the India Maritime Vision 2030 (MIV 2030) regarding port performance, inland waterways, and shipbuilding. 15 Analyse the transition from the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 to the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 as it relates to unsafe-ship detention powers, and describe the steps a shipboard management team must take when a critical propulsion failure occurs just before departure. 🧠 Memory Box 1958 → 2025 → in force 15 Mar 2026: the MS Act timeline; DG Shipping is now DGMA . Unseaworthy = general unfitness; unsafe = immediate danger to life — the narrower, higher bar. NSB, 1959 — Parliament + shipowners + seafarers, under a Chairman, advising on shipping policy. ▶ Deep Dive — Pre-Departure Technical Failure Case Study Operational Case Study — 120,000 DWT Capesize Ore Carrier, Boiler Casing Crack Two Hours Before Departure Sequence: classify the boiler casing crack and emergency generator ATS failure as material defects rendering the vessel unseaworthy, and log under SMS → notify the Master to halt departure; Master informs the port authority, owner, and local flag surveyor → maintain ballast and auxiliary power stability at berth given the near-full-load condition → complete certified shore repairs under class supervision → present repair/testing reports to the visiting surveyor, who clears the "unsafe" classification before departure is permitted. MIV 2030 Context India Maritime Vision 2030 targets world-class port turnaround times, greenfield port infrastructure, inland-waterway cargo growth, e-governance across licensing/inspection, cruise-hub development, domestic shipbuilding capacity, urban water transport, and maritime training excellence — none of these override the baseline statutory seaworthiness requirement, which remains the operational floor beneath all policy ambitions. On My Vessel (Maersk A/S container tonnage) Weekly testing of the emergency generator's automatic transfer switch and the emergency fire pump is the single cheapest insurance against a pre-departure "unsafe ship" finding — a defect caught in routine testing is a maintenance item; the same defect caught by a surveyor two hours before sailing is a detention risk. 📚 References Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 (India) — historical reference, repealed Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (India) — current governing statute DGMA (formerly DG Shipping) — official notifications International Convention on Load Lines, 1966 Notes-p15 · P15-T3 · v1.0

section_title: Q2. Under the Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention, can a shipowner avoid liability simply by abandoning the vessel?
text: No. The Convention imposes strict liability on the registered owner for locating, marking, and removing a hazardous wreck. The owner is exempt from costs only in three narrow situations: an act of war/hostilities, an intentional harmful act by a third party, or negligence by a government authority responsible for navigation marks. The Convention also allows a direct action or claim against the insurer or financial guarantor, bypassing an insolvent owner, and requires compulsory insurance for vessels of 300 GT and above.

Wreck removal frameworks separately provide the legal and technical mechanism for the prompt, safe, and environmentally sound removal of hazardous shipwrecks obstructing navigation or threatening coastal ecosystems. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) Immediately after any casualty, the Chief Engineer's first duty is data preservation — VDR backup, engine automation logs, bell logbooks, physical logbook — under SMS/ISM Code Element 10, before memory of the exact sequence fades or systems overwrite themselves. Nair frequently tests the non-punitive intent of the Casualty Investigation Code alongside the fact that it does not bar a parallel criminal investigation by a coastal state — candidates who present the Code as blanket immunity from prosecution lose marks. The Nairobi Convention's direct-action clause is operationally important: it means insurers can be sued directly for wreck removal costs even if the owner is insolvent, so maintaining valid wreck-removal insurance is a live compliance item, not a formality. 📅 Historical Background 2007 Nairobi International Convention on the Removal of Wrecks adopted — 18 May 2008 IMO Casualty Investigation Code adopted at MSC 84 — May 2015 Nairobi WRC enters into force — 14 Apr 2026 MS Act 2025 in force — casualty inquiry powers reorganised under DGMA — 15 Mar ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments IMO Casualty Investigation Code (Res. MSC.255(84)) Adopted May 2008 at the 84th session of the Maritime Safety Committee; formally the International Standards and Recommended Practices for a Safety Investigation into a Marine Casualty or Marine Incident. SOLAS Ch. XI-1, Reg. 21 / MARPOL Art. 8 & 12 Mandatory anchor requiring flag administrations to conduct safety investigations into serious casualties and report findings to the IMO. UNCLOS Art. 94(7) Requires cooperation between flag states and affected coastal states investigating high-seas casualties involving loss of life or severe environmental damage. Nairobi Intl. Convention on the Removal of Wrecks, 2007 Adopted 18 May 2007, in force 14 April 2015. Covers a state's EEZ (up to 200 nm), with an option to extend to the territorial sea. Merchant Shipping Act (historically Secs. 359/360/373, 1958; now MS Act 2025) Governs statutory Preliminary Inquiries and Formal Investigations for casualties on or near the Indian coast — see verification note above regarding the 2025 renumbering. ⚖ Preliminary Inquiry vs. Formal Investigation (Historical MS Act, 1958 Structure) Parameter Preliminary Inquiry Formal Investigation Objective Fast fact-finding on basic casualty causes Full judicial hearing with binding legal rulings Conducted By Appointed MMD surveyors/nautical examiners Magistrate/Judge, assisted by marine assessors Powers Board/inspect ship and shore premises, gather logs and statements Subpoena witnesses, take formal testimony, rule on certifications Output Written report to Central Government Formal judicial findings and legal determinations 🎓 CE Oral Tip (Nair): Nair's reliable pairing here: "is the Casualty Code punitive?" followed by "so does that mean the coastal state can't prosecute?" No. The Convention imposes strict liability on the registered owner for locating, marking, and removing a hazardous wreck. The owner is exempt from costs only in three narrow situations: an act of war/hostilities, an intentional harmful act by a third party, or negligence by a government authority responsible for navigation marks. The Convention also allows a direct action or claim against the insurer or financial guarantor, bypassing an insolvent owner, and requires compulsory insurance for vessels of 300 GT and above. Q3. Explain the non-punitive intent of the IMO Casualty Investigation Code. Does it block a parallel criminal investigation? The Code's primary purpose is determining technical and operational causes to improve safety, not to assign blame or civil liability. This safety focus does not prevent a coastal state from running a parallel judicial or criminal investigation under its own laws, provided the safety inquiry itself remains protected from outside interference. ✍ Written Exam Focus 5 Define a "Wreck" and a "Hazard" under the Nairobi International Wreck Removal Convention, 2007. 10 Outline the statutory duties and reporting responsibilities of an inquiry officer conducting a Preliminary Inquiry into a marine casualty. 15 Analyse the technical and legal steps a shipboard management team must take following a grounding causing structural damage and a fuel spill, covering reporting channels, environmental containment, and data preservation under both the IMO Casualty Code and the Nairobi Convention. 🧠 Memory Box Casualty Code: non-punitive — safety causes, not blame; doesn't block parallel criminal cases. Nairobi WRC: strict liability + only 3 exceptions + direct action against insurers; ≥300 GT compulsory insurance. Indian MRCC hubs: Mumbai (West), Chennai (East), Port Blair (Andaman & Nicobar). ▶ Deep Dive — Grounding & Fuel Tank Breach Case Study Operational Case Study — 68,000 DWT Panamax Container Ship, EEZ Grounding with Fuel Tank Breach Sequence: sound the alarm, stop engines, sound all tanks/bilges, start emergency bilge pumps → report to DGCOMM/MRCC, flag state, and owner with vessel name, location, damage and cargo/fuel details → transfer fuel from compromised double-bottom tanks to high-level storage under SMS to reduce spill risk → cooperate on wreck marking if not immediately refloated → provide logbooks, fuel transfer logs, and automation alarm histories to the appointed inquiry officer. Reporting Chain (Historical MS Act 1958 Framework) Initial notification → DGCOMM relays to Deputy Nautical Advisor/Nautical Surveyor/Nautical Advisor and the nearest Coast Guard MRCC → the Principal Officer of the local MMD assigns an inquiry officer, who may pursue a Preliminary Inquiry and, if warranted, apply for a Formal Investigation. On My Vessel (Maersk A/S container tonnage) The single most valuable habit here is treating VDR functionality checks as a genuine safety item, not a box-tick — a defective emergency-save function during an actual grounding permanently loses the exact data an investigator needs, regardless of how well the rest of the response is handled. 📚 References IMO — Casualty Investigation Code, Resolution MSC.255(84) IMO — Nairobi International Convention on the Removal of Wrecks, 2007 UNCLOS — Article 94 Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (India) / DGMA — current governing framework Notes-p15 · P15-T4 · v1.0

section_title: Q1. What are the exact prescription periods under the Nairobi Convention, and how do they interact?
text: Claims for the cost of locating, marking, or removing a wreck must be brought within 3 years of the coastal state's formal determination that the wreck constitutes a hazard. Independently, no action may ever be brought more than 6 years after the date of the maritime casualty that caused the wreck — this is an absolute cap that applies even if the hazard determination itself came late. Both time bars must be satisfied; whichever expires first extinguishes the right of action.

section_title: Q3. Differentiate RSV Type I/II from Type III/IV in terms of governing legislation and operational envelope.
text: Type I and II are inland/coastal-fringe classifications limited to fairweather operation within 12 NM of land, governed by the Inland Vessels Act, 2021. Type III and IV are all-weather coastal classifications — Type III capped at a 24-hour voyage and 12 NM (30 NM in the Gulf of Khambhat/Kutch), Type IV unrestricted along the coastline — both governed by the Merchant Shipping Act framework. All four types share the same 3000 GT / 3000 kW upper engineering threshold.

text: Part 16 · Topic 1 Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention, River Sea Vessel (RSV) Classification & India's Sagarmala/Blue Economy Strategy Nairobi Convention · RSV · Sagarmala Uday pp. 376–380 (approx.) Examiner: Nair ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: Checked against the IMO Nairobi International Convention on the Removal of Wrecks, 2007 text and multiple P&I club circulars. The Convention's entry-into-force date (14 April 2015) , the 300 GT compulsory-insurance/certification threshold , and the 3-year / 6-year prescription periods (3 years from formal hazard determination; absolute cap of 6 years from the date of the casualty) in the source draft are all correct and confirmed against Article 13 and Article 12 of the Convention text. The RSV Type I–IV classification, the 3000 GT/3000 kW threshold, and the Sagarmala five-pillar structure are India-specific administrative frameworks (DG Shipping/Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Waterways) rather than IMO instruments; these numbers match the source draft and are consistent with publicly available DGMA RSV guidance, but candidates should cross-check the current RSV notification against the latest DG Shipping/DGMA circular before the oral, since domestic coastal-vessel notifications are amended more frequently than IMO conventions. Also note: as of March 2026 the domestic Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 was repealed and replaced by the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (in force 15 March 2026), and DG Shipping was renamed the Directorate General of Maritime Administration (DGMA) — the RSV framework referenced by the source (originally issued under the 1958 Act) should now be read as continuing under the 2025 Act pending confirmation of a re-notification; Nixon should verify the current statutory basis before this topic is gated. 📖 Definition This topic covers two separate but examinable strands. First, the Nairobi International Convention on the Removal of Wrecks, 2007 — the IMO instrument that gives coastal states a clear legal basis, strict liability regime, and compulsory insurance mechanism to compel the removal of hazardous wrecks. Second, India's domestic River Sea Vessel (RSV) classification system and the linked national strategic programmes — Sagarmala , the Blue Economy , and the Sagar Manthan digital monitoring platform — which a Chief Engineer serving on Indian-flagged or India-trading coastal tonnage is expected to know at MEO Class 1 level. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) The Wreck Removal Certificate is a statutory document for any ship ≥300 GT — as with any P&I-linked "blue card" certificate, the Chief Engineer should know it exists, know it is verified by PSC, and know it is separate from the ship's ordinary H&M/P&I cover. Nair likes to test whether candidates confuse the 3-year window (from formal hazard determination) with the 6-year absolute cap (from the casualty date) — these run on different clocks and only the second is a hard ceiling regardless of when the hazard is formally determined. On coastal/RSV-type tonnage, understanding why a vessel is Type I/II (Inland Vessels Act) versus Type III/IV (Merchant Shipping Act) affects which statutory survey regime, manning scale, and certification pathway applies. 📅 Historical Background 1917 Inland Steam-Vessels Act (India) — original, now-repealed inland vessel statute 1958 Merchant Shipping Act (India) — foundational ocean-going/coastal statute 2007 Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention adopted (Nairobi, Kenya) 2014 Nairobi Convention reaches 10 ratifications — 12-month countdown triggered 2015 Nairobi Convention enters into force — 14 April 2021 Inland Vessels Act, 2021 replaces the 1917 Act 2025 Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 replaces the 1958 Act (in force 15 Mar 2026); DG Shipping renamed DGMA ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments Nairobi Convention 2007 In force 14 Apr 2015. Applies to ships ≥300 GT — compulsory insurance/financial security, Wreck Removal Certificate, direct action against insurers. Article 13 sets the 3-year/6-year prescription periods. LLMC 1976 (as amended) Financial security under Nairobi Art. 12 must match the shipowner's applicable LLMC limitation tonnage bracket. Inland Vessels Act, 2021 Governs RSV Type I & II; repealed and replaced the Inland Steam-Vessels Act, 1917. Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 Governs RSV Type III & IV; repealed the MS Act, 1958, effective 15 Mar 2026 (DG Shipping renamed DGMA). SDG 14 (UN 2030 Agenda) "Life Below Water" — the sustainability framework the Blue Economy programme is aligned to; a policy goal, not binding IMO/domestic regulation. 🚢 RSV Operational Classification (India) Type Operational Range Weather/Time Restriction Governing Act Type I Within 12 NM of nearest land/baseline Fairweather, daylight only Inland Vessels Act, 2021 Type II Between nearby ports, up to 12 NM Fairweather, no daylight restriction Inland Vessels Act, 2021 Type III Up to 12 NM (30 NM in Gulf of Khambhat/Kutch); voyage ≤24 hours All-weather Merchant Shipping Act (2025, successor to 1958) Type IV Any Indian ports along the coastline All-weather, unrestricted distance Merchant Shipping Act (2025, successor to 1958) All four RSV categories are capped at a maximum propulsion power of 3000 kW and a maximum tonnage of 3000 GT — exceeding either threshold takes the vessel out of the RSV framework entirely and into standard ocean-going coastal vessel certification. 🎓 CE Oral Tip (Nair): Nair's classic follow-up after the RSV table is "why does the Act change between Type II and Type III?" The answer is the shift from purely inland/fairweather operation to all-weather coastal operation — Type III/IV vessels face open-sea risk exposure closer to that of standard coastal tonnage, so they sit under the general Merchant Shipping framework rather than the inland-waterways-focused Act. 🇮🇳 National Strategic Frameworks: Sagarmala, Blue Economy & Sagar Manthan The Sagarmala Programme is India's national port-led infrastructure development initiative, executed through five pillars: (1) Port Modernisation & New Port Development, (2) Port Connectivity Enhancement (rail/road/freight-corridor links), (3) Port-Linked Industrialisation, (4) Coastal Community Development, and (5) Coastal Shipping & Inland Waterways Transport. The Blue Economy concept — sustainable economic use of marine resources aligned with SDG 14 — covers offshore renewable energy, the Deep Ocean Mission, and sustainable aquaculture/tourism. Sagar Manthan is the Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Waterways' unified digital dashboard for real-time tracking, data visualisation, and inter-departmental accountability across these national maritime projects. 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1. What are the exact prescription periods under the Nairobi Convention, and how do they interact? Claims for the cost of locating, marking, or removing a wreck must be brought within 3 years of the coastal state's formal determination that the wreck constitutes a hazard. Independently, no action may ever be brought more than 6 years after the date of the maritime casualty that caused the wreck — this is an absolute cap that applies even if the hazard determination itself came late. Both time bars must be satisfied; whichever expires first extinguishes the right of action. Q2. As Chief Engineer, what would you check regarding the Wreck Removal Certificate before departure? That the certificate is valid and matches the vessel's current name, call sign and IMO number; that the financial security provider (typically the P&I Club) is named and active for the voyage; and that the certificate is filed with the ship's statutory documents for PSC presentation. This applies to any ship of 300 GT and above under Article 12 of the Convention. Q3. Differentiate RSV Type I/II from Type III/IV in terms of governing legislation and operational envelope. Type I and II are inland/coastal-fringe classifications limited to fairweather operation within 12 NM of land, governed by the Inland Vessels Act, 2021. Type III and IV are all-weather coastal classifications — Type III capped at a 24-hour voyage and 12 NM (30 NM in the Gulf of Khambhat/Kutch), Type IV unrestricted along the coastline — both governed by the Merchant Shipping Act framework. All four types share the same 3000 GT / 3000 kW upper engineering threshold. ✍ Written Exam Focus 5 Summarise the five pillars of the Sagarmala Programme and how each supports domestic maritime logistics. 10 A 2,500 GT coastal cargo vessel with a 2,200 kW engine plans an 18-hour voyage between two Indian ports. Determine its RSV category, governing Act, and applicable distance/weather constraints. 15 Analyse the regulatory and engineering response to a hard grounding within a foreign coastal state's contiguous zone, covering Wreck Removal Certificate validation, the 3-/6-year liability windows, and the Chief Engineer's hull/pollution-prevention responsibilities. 🧠 Memory Box "3 to determine, 6 to end it" — 3 years from hazard determination; absolute 6-year cap from the casualty date. 300 GT — Nairobi Convention compulsory insurance/certificate threshold. I & II = Inland Act, fairweather; III & IV = MS Act, all-weather — RSV governing-Act split; 3000 GT/3000 kW ceiling applies to all four. ▶ Deep Dive — Grounding Response Sequence Under the Nairobi Framework Immediate Actions Preserve the VDR, conduct full tank soundings/void assessments, and consolidate fuel oil away from breached tanks into intact settling/service tanks to minimise pollution risk before the Coastal State and Flag State are formally notified. Wreck Marking & Certification Once the Coastal State determines the vessel a navigational hazard, physical marking (buoys, AIS hazard transponder) is deployed and the Wreck Removal Certificate is produced to confirm financial security is in place for the salvage/removal costs to follow. Salvage Coordination The shipowner typically contracts salvage under a Lloyd's Open Form (LOF) with SCOPIC clauses; the Chief Engineer's role is to hand over precise fuel-system, ballast and structural-access data to the salvage master to enable safe defueling ahead of any hull-recovery operation. On My Vessel (Maersk A/S container tonnage) Container ships trading deep-sea are outside the RSV framework entirely, but the Nairobi Convention's 300 GT threshold and the Wreck Removal Certificate apply identically — every port call statutory-document check should confirm this certificate alongside the standard P&I blue card. 📚 References IMO — Nairobi International Convention on the Removal of Wrecks, 2007 Inland Vessels Act, 2021 (India) Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (India) — successor to the MS Act, 1958 Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Waterways — Sagarmala Programme / Sagar Manthan Notes-p16 · P16-T1 · v1.0

section_title: Q2. Differentiate Great Circle and Rhumb Line navigation.
text: A Great Circle track is the shortest distance between two points on a sphere but requires continuous heading adjustment as meridians are crossed. A Rhumb Line holds a constant compass heading, simplifying helm control, but is physically longer on transoceanic transits. A Composite Great Circle blends both, capping latitude to avoid hazards like ice fields.

text: Part 16 · Topic 2 Loadicator Statutory Compliance, Controlled Document Transmittal Records & Integrated Bridge System Architecture SOLAS XII/11 · COTR · IBS Uday pp. 381–384 (approx.) Examiner: Paul / Nair Medium Frequency 🔎 Verification note: SOLAS Chapter XII, Regulation 11 (loading and stability computer requirement for bulk carriers ≥150 m in length) and the three mandatory Loadicator documents (Class Certificate, Approved Manual, Approved Test Conditions) were checked against the SOLAS XII text and class-society statutory guidance and are correctly stated. The source draft's LRIT reporting frequency ("four times daily") is consistent with SOLAS V/19-1 and IMO LRIT guidance (default 6-hourly automatic position reporting). Radar frequency bands (S-Band ≈3 GHz, X-Band ≈9 GHz) are standard and correct. No numeric fabrications were found in this topic's source draft; the COTR system is an internal ship-management/document-control practice rather than a named statutory instrument, and is presented here as good-practice terminology rather than a cited regulation. 📖 Definition This topic covers three linked shipboard systems that a senior engineer must understand for both statutory compliance and safe operation: the Loadicator — a ship-specific loading/stability computer; the Controlled Document Transmittal Record (COTR) — the administrative discipline for tracking revision-controlled technical documents; and the sensor/navigation network that makes up the modern Integrated Bridge System (IBS) . ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) The Loadicator's accuracy depends on correct tank-level sensor data — as Chief Engineer you own the calibration of the draft gauges and tank sounding transducers that feed it, even though the Chief Officer runs the calculations. A COTR gap (using an outdated stability booklet or SMS revision) is a documentation deficiency PSC treats as a proxy for wider quality-control failure — keep the ledger current on every structural modification. Great Circle vs Rhumb Line routing directly affects voyage fuel planning and ETA calculations that the engine department must align main engine RPM/consumption schedules against. 📅 Historical Background Pre-1980s Manual hydrostatic-table stress/stability calculations 1980s–90s Digital microprocessor-based Loadicators introduced fleet-wide 1997 SOLAS Chapter XII adopted (bulk carrier structural safety, incl. loading computer mandate) 2000s Bridge instruments progressively networked into Integrated Bridge Systems (IBS) ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments SOLAS Ch XII, Reg 11 Bulk carriers ≥150 m length must carry a type-approved loading instrument capable of providing hull girder shear force/bending moment and stability data. SOLAS Ch V, Reg 19 Mandatory carriage requirements for Gyro Compass, Echo Sounder, Radar/ARPA, ECDIS, AIS, and VDR by ship type/tonnage. SOLAS Ch V, Reg 19-1 Long-Range Identification and Tracking (LRIT) — automatic position reporting to the Flag State/data centres, standard interval 6-hourly. 📋 Loadicator Statutory Documentation & Testing Requirement Content Class Certificate Formal approval of the software/hardware configuration for the specific hull Approved Manual Operating instructions, input constraints, default execution guidelines Approved Test Conditions Standard loading profiles used to cross-check computer output against shipyard data Crew must periodically re-run the approved test conditions per the ship's SMS and compare outputs to the manual; a Class Surveyor witnesses this test annually at Class Renewal Survey. 🧭 Great Circle vs Rhumb Line Navigation Great Circle: shortest physical distance between two points on the globe; requires continuous heading changes as the vessel crosses meridians. Rhumb Line: constant compass heading throughout; visually straight on a Mercator chart, but a longer physical track on ocean transits. Composite Great Circle: hybrid — follows a Great Circle path but caps maximum latitude to avoid polar ice/heavy-weather hazards. 🎓 CE Oral Tip (Paul): Paul's typical probe is "what happens if the Loadicator fails during cargo operations?" The expected answer: stop loading, switch to the secondary/backup terminal or manual hydrostatic-table calculation, cross-check tank sensor data against manual soundings, and only resume once the discrepancy is diagnosed and the Class Surveyor (if survey-linked) has re-witnessed the test conditions. 📡 Integrated Bridge System Components Component Function Common Failure Mode Gyro Compass True-north heading reference Spin-motor breakdown, power inverter fault Radar/ARPA Target detection, collision-risk tracking (S-Band ≈3 GHz, X-Band ≈9 GHz) Magnetron degradation, waveguide moisture ECDIS Electronic chart display integrated with position/target data Chart update omissions, data corruption AIS Broadcasts ship identity/position via VHF Antenna damage, GPS sync fault LRIT Reports position to Flag State via satellite (typically 6-hourly) Satellite terminal/power loss 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1. What three documents must be on board to validate a Loadicator under SOLAS Chapter XII? The Class Certificate for the Loadicator, the Class Approved Loadicator Manual, and the Class Approved Loadicator Test Conditions. Routine crew verification against the approved test conditions is required per the SMS, plus annual witnessed testing during Class Renewal Survey. Q2. Differentiate Great Circle and Rhumb Line navigation. A Great Circle track is the shortest distance between two points on a sphere but requires continuous heading adjustment as meridians are crossed. A Rhumb Line holds a constant compass heading, simplifying helm control, but is physically longer on transoceanic transits. A Composite Great Circle blends both, capping latitude to avoid hazards like ice fields. Q3. What is a COTR and why does it matter to a Chief Engineer? A Controlled Document Transmittal Record is the administrative ledger tracking revision numbers and distribution of safety-critical documents — stability booklets, SMS manuals, structural drawings. The Chief Engineer must ensure machinery drawings and structural modification records are logged and outdated revisions archived, since PSC treats document-control gaps as evidence of wider quality-management weakness. ✍ Written Exam Focus 5 Explain the role of the Loadicator under SOLAS Chapter XII and the difference between routine crew testing and annual Class witnessing. 10 Sketch a block diagram of data flow between the Gyro Compass, GPS, Echo Sounder and ECDIS, and describe the consequences of a sudden Gyro heading step-error. 15 The primary Loadicator terminal fails hardware pre-loading. Outline (a) the alternative stability-verification steps, and (b) the documentation/testing process to restore full Class compliance via the COTR. 🧠 Memory Box "C-M-T" — Class Certificate, Manual, Test Conditions: the three statutory Loadicator documents. ≥150 m bulk carriers — SOLAS XII/11 loading-computer applicability threshold. GC = shortest, changing heading; RL = constant heading, longer — the core navigation-geometry contrast. ▶ Deep Dive — Loadicator Verification Failure Case Study Scenario During annual survey, a re-run of the approved test conditions on an 85,000 DWT Capesize bulker showed a bending-moment discrepancy against the manual's printed values. Response Sequence Isolate the primary terminal and switch to the backup unit → re-run the same test profile on the backup (confirming the fault is local to the primary database, not the sensor network) → cross-check tank radar readings against manual tape soundings → reinstall the approved hydrostatic profile on the primary terminal under Class technical guidance → re-run and re-witness the test conditions → Class endorses the certificate and the event is logged in the COTR. On My Vessel (Maersk A/S container tonnage) Container ships are not SOLAS XII bulk-carrier-mandated for a Loadicator, but virtually all carry an equivalent stability/loading computer for lashing and GM verification — the same verification-test discipline against a backup terminal applies before every loading operation. 📚 References SOLAS Chapter XII (Additional Safety Measures for Bulk Carriers) SOLAS Chapter V (Safety of Navigation) IMO Performance Standards for ECDIS Notes-p16 · P16-T2 · v1.0

Examiner: Srivastava / Nair ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: Checked against IMO Resolution MSC.496(105), class-society statutory circulars (Bureau Veritas, Lloyd's Register, ABS) and SAFETY4SEA coverage. The 1 January 2024 entry-into-force date , the replacement of "Inmarsat" with the generic term Recognized Mobile Satellite Service (RMSS) , the removal of the NBDP carriage requirement , and the exclusion of VHF-EPIRB as a substitute for satellite EPIRB in Sea Area A1 are all confirmed correct. One correction to the source draft: MSC.496(105) was adopted in April 2022 (not simply described as originating from "the modernization program" with no adoption date) and entered into force 1 January 2024 — both dates are now stated. The GMDSS reserve source of energy duration (1 hour with an emergency generator fitted, 6 hours without) was not explicitly numbered in the source draft's Chief Engineer responsibilities section; this figure has been added and verified against SOLAS Chapter IV, Regulation 13, since it is a standard, high-frequency oral-exam number. The Sea Area A₁ line-of-sight formula (𝒜 = 2.5·(√H + √h)) is the standard ITU/IMO VHF coverage approximation and is correctly stated. 📖 Definition The Global Maritime Distress and Safety System (GMDSS) was comprehensively modernized under IMO Resolution MSC.496(105) , adopted April 2022 and effective 1 January 2024 , replacing satellite-provider-specific and obsolete terrestrial-telegraphy requirements with generalized, technology-neutral terminology. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) The GMDSS console's electrical supply chain — main, emergency, and reserve source — is a Chief Engineer responsibility; a battery bank that cannot sustain the required duration is a PSC detention risk under SOLAS Chapter IV. Post-2024, a Safety Radio Certificate must name the specific RMSS provider (e.g. Inmarsat or Iridium) fitted — a mismatch between the certificate and the actual installed terminal is grounds for detention. Weekly battery load testing, specific-gravity checks, and confirming automatic boost-to-float charger transition remain core engine-room GMDSS maintenance tasks unaffected by the 2024 modernization. 📅 Historical Background 1988 GMDSS framework established under SOLAS Chapter IV 1992–99 Phased GMDSS implementation across SOLAS fleet 2022 Res. MSC.496(105) adopted (April) — GMDSS modernization 2024 MSC.496(105) enters into force — 1 January ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments Res. MSC.496(105) In force 1 Jan 2024. Full rewrite of SOLAS Chapter IV: RMSS terminology, NBDP removal, VHF-EPIRB exclusion from A1, consolidated SART/AIS-SART carriage. SOLAS Ch IV, Reg 13 GMDSS reserve source of energy: must sustain full radio operation for 1 hour (emergency generator fitted) or 6 hours (no emergency generator); recharge to minimum within 10 hours. ITU Radio Regulations Governs DSC/satellite operating frequencies and transmission power limits. 🌐 GMDSS Sea Areas Sea Area Definition A1 VHF DSC coastal coverage; 𝒜 = 2.5·(√H + √h) NM, H = coast antenna height, h = ship antenna height (both in metres) A2 MF DSC coverage, excluding A1; boundary set per Coastal State per ITU guidance A3 RMSS/SES satellite coverage, excluding A1 & A2; coverage now varies by the specific RMSS constellation installed A4 Remaining polar/other areas outside A1–A3; relies on HF or non-geostationary RMSS terminals 🎓 CE Oral Tip (Srivastava): Srivastava frequently asks candidates to state the A1 formula and correctly identify which variable is the coastal station's antenna height and which is the ship's. He then follows with "what changed for A3 after 2024?" — the expected answer is that A3 coverage is no longer a fixed geostationary boundary but depends on the specific RMSS/SES system fitted, which must now be explicitly named on the Safety Radio Certificate. 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1. List the major structural changes introduced by Resolution MSC.496(105). Replacement of "Inmarsat" with the generic "Recognized Mobile Satellite Service (RMSS)"; removal of the mandatory Narrow-Band Direct Printing (NBDP) carriage requirement; consolidation of SART/AIS-SART carriage directly into Chapter IV; exclusion of VHF-EPIRB as a substitute for satellite EPIRB in Sea Area A1; and a requirement for the Safety Radio Certificate to name the specific RMSS terminal fitted. Q2. State the GMDSS reserve source of energy duration requirement. Under SOLAS Chapter IV, Regulation 13, the reserve battery bank must sustain full GMDSS radio operation for 1 hour if the vessel is fitted with an emergency generator, or 6 hours if it is not. The batteries must recharge to the required minimum capacity within 10 hours, and capacity must be tested at intervals not exceeding 12 months. Q3. Give the Sea Area A1 line-of-sight formula and define each term. 𝒜 = 2.5 × (√H + √h), where 𝒜 is the maximum theoretical VHF coverage radius in nautical miles, H is the coastal VHF station's antenna elevation above sea level in metres, and h is the vessel's primary VHF antenna height above sea level in metres. This approximates the radio line-of-sight limit accounting for Earth's curvature. ✍ Written Exam Focus 5 Compare a 9 GHz Radar SART and an AIS-SART regarding transmission method and display on an approaching rescue vessel. 10 Sketch the GMDSS console power supply schematic, showing the main AC board, emergency switchboard link, automatic battery charger, reserve battery bank, and DC bus feeding the RMSS terminal. 15 During an A4 transit, the HF transceiver and main satellite terminal fail simultaneously due to an electrical surge. Outline (a) alternative distress-alerting arrangements available, and (b) the testing/certification steps required post-repair under the modernized GMDSS framework. 🧠 Memory Box 1 Jan 2024 — MSC.496(105) entry into force (adopted April 2022). 1 hr / 6 hr — GMDSS reserve energy: with / without emergency generator. RMSS replaces Inmarsat; NBDP removed; VHF-EPIRB excluded from A1 — the three headline 2024 changes. ▶ Deep Dive — Distress Alerting Sequence in Sea Area A3 Scenario A fire in the auxiliary machinery space causes total loss of the main switchboard while transiting Sea Area A3. Response Sequence Activate the primary RMSS/SES distress button → transmit a backup MF/HF DSC alert → GMDSS console automatically transfers to the reserve battery bank as main power fails → shed non-essential bridge loads to preserve the reserve duration → establish MRCC voice contact via the RMSS terminal → if abandonment becomes necessary, deploy the satellite EPIRB and activate both radar SART and AIS-SART. On My Vessel (Maersk A/S container tonnage) Weekly GMDSS battery load tests and specific-gravity checks are logged in the radio log per the SMS — confirming the reserve source meets its rated duration is a standing engine-room task irrespective of the 2024 RMSS terminology change. 📚 References IMO Resolution MSC.496(105) — Amendments to SOLAS Chapter IV SOLAS Chapter IV — Radiocommunications COMSAR.1/Circ.32/Rev.3 — Harmonization of GMDSS Requirements Notes-p16 · P16-T3 · v1.0
