section_title: General Average, the York-Antwerp Rules (2016) & the New Jason Clause
text: Part 18 · Topic 4 General Average, the York-Antwerp Rules (2016) & the New Jason Clause GA · YAR 2016 · New Jason Clause Uday pp. 445–450 (approx.) Examiner: Nair ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: The Rule Paramount and Rule A four-pillar test (Extraordinary, Intentional, Common Safety, Real Peril), Rule C's exclusion of environmental pollution cleanup costs, and Rule D (fault does not bar contribution, but does not bar counter-actions either) are confirmed against the structure and content of the York-Antwerp Rules 2016 as adopted by the CMI. The New Jason Clause mechanics (requiring cargo to contribute to GA for losses arising from any cause, negligent or not, where the carrier is statutorily exempt under COGSA/the Harter Act — but not for unseaworthiness absent due diligence) are confirmed against published legal commentary on the clause and the underlying US case law ( The Irrawaddy , The Jason ). The worked numerical GA apportionment example is internally consistent and correctly illustrates the proportional contribution principle. 📖 Definition General Average (GA) is the principle that all parties in a common maritime adventure — ship, cargo, and freight interests — must share proportionally in any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure reasonably made to save the venture from a real peril. In plain terms: if the Master jettisons your cargo to save the ship (and everyone else's cargo with it), you don't bear that loss alone — everyone whose property was saved chips in according to what they had at stake. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) GA lets the Master act decisively in an emergency without first negotiating terms with hundreds of individual cargo owners — as Chief Engineer, your logs of the emergency (fuel used, damage sustained, decisions taken) become the technical backbone of the Average Adjuster's later calculation. Understanding Rule A's four pillars lets you correctly judge, in real time, whether an emergency action you're asked to take (e.g. running the main engine hard aground) will actually qualify for GA treatment later. Nair frequently gives a grounding or fire scenario and asks candidates to test it against the four pillars live in the oral — this is one of the highest-yield "apply the rule" topics at Class 1 level. 📅 Historical Background Ancient Lex Rhodia (Rhodian Law) — earliest known GA-style loss-sharing principle 1890 York-Antwerp Rules first unified internationally 1994 / 2004 Periodic revisions to modernise the Rules 2016 York-Antwerp Rules 2016 — current standard, incorporated by reference into bills of lading/charter parties ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments York-Antwerp Rules 2016 International standard governing which sacrifices/expenditures qualify for GA; applies only if incorporated by reference into the Bill of Lading or Charter Party. SOLAS Ch. III & V Seaworthiness/safety obligations — if a GA incident stems from unseaworthiness, contribution rights can be legally challenged (Rule D). New Jason Clause Bill of Lading/Charter Party clause preserving the shipowner's GA contribution rights under US COGSA/Harter Act law. 🧮 GA Apportionment — Worked Example Contribution Factor (C f ) = Total GA Expense (E GA ) ÷ Total Saved Value (V T ) Example: a hijacking incident incurs ransom + fees totalling E GA = $110,000. Saved values: Ship $500,000, Cargo Owner 1 $300,000, Cargo Owner 2 $200,000 → V T = $1,000,000. C f = 110,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 11% . Each party then pays 11% of their own saved value: Ship pays $55,000, Cargo Owner 1 pays $33,000, Cargo Owner 2 pays $22,000 — proportional to what each party had at stake in the saved venture, not a flat split. 🧭 The Four Pillars of Rule A Extraordinary: beyond ordinary duties — routine operations or standard cargo-delivery obligations do not qualify. Intentional: deliberately executed — flooding a burning hold on purpose qualifies; accidentally striking a submerged wreck does not. Common Safety: protects the entire venture, not one cargo unit — diverting for a single reefer container's breakdown does not qualify. Real Peril: the danger must be genuine and imminent, not minor or imagined. Rule Paramount sits above all of these: no allowance is made for any sacrifice or expenditure unless it was reasonable — an unnecessary commercial service ordered when the ship remained functional is excluded regardless of intent. Rule C excludes environmental pollution cleanup costs and environmental damage claims from GA entirely. Rule D preserves the right to contribution even where the casualty was caused by one party's fault — but if that fault was the shipowner providing an unseaworthy vessel, the cargo owners retain the right to counter-claim their contributions back. ⚔ GA vs Particular Average (PA) Feature General Average (GA) Particular Average (PA) Who bears the cost Shared proportionally by all saved interests Borne solely by the specific owner of the damaged asset Example Jettisoning cargo to stabilise a damaged hull Heavy weather tearing a forecastle door Environmental costs Excluded (Rule C) Handled under separate P&I liability policies 📜 The New Jason Clause Under US maritime law, shipowners historically could not claim GA contributions from cargo owners if the casualty was caused by crew negligence. The New Jason Clause overcomes this: when inserted into the Bill of Lading or Charter Party, it requires cargo to contribute to GA for losses from any cause whatsoever, negligent or not , provided the carrier is statutorily exempt from liability for that cause under COGSA or the Harter Act — chiefly errors in navigation/management of the ship, but the language extends to any statutory exemption except unseaworthiness arising from a lack of due diligence at the start of the voyage. 🎓 CE Oral Tip (Nair): Nair's classic trap question is a localised equipment failure (e.g. one reefer container compressor) versus a ship-wide threat — always check the Common Safety pillar first, since a localised problem, however serious for that cargo, is Particular Average, not GA. 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1. A cargo hold fire is extinguished by flooding, destroying part of the cargo. Is this General Average? Yes. All four Rule A pillars are satisfied: flooding the hold was an extraordinary, intentional action taken reasonably for the common safety of the entire vessel and remaining cargo against a real, active fire peril. The value of the water-damaged cargo and the operation's costs are shared proportionally by all saved interests. Q2. Explain the legal scope of the New Jason Clause. The New Jason Clause requires cargo interests to contribute to GA for losses arising from any cause whatsoever, negligent or not, provided the carrier is statutorily exempt from liability for that cause under COGSA or the Harter Act. It chiefly protects the shipowner for errors in navigation or ship management, but its wording covers any statutory exemption — so long as the shipowner exercised due diligence to make the vessel seaworthy at the start of the voyage. Q3. A vessel diverts to a port of refuge because one reefer container's compressor fails. Can the deviation costs be claimed under GA? No. This fails the Common Safety pillar — the breakdown threatens only that one cargo unit, not the ship or the remaining cargo as a whole. This is a Particular Average loss for that cargo owner, not a General Average act. ✍ Written Exam Focus 5 Define the Rule Paramount within the York-Antwerp Rules 2016 and explain its effect on emergency expenditures ordered by a Master. 10 Explain the relationship between Rule D and the New Jason Clause, focusing on how cargo contribution rights are handled where crew negligence is involved. 15 A vessel runs aground; the Master orders the main engine run at full power to refloat, causing sand ingestion damage to the cooling system; the vessel is then towed to a port of refuge. Analyse this under the York-Antwerp Rules 2016 and outline how the final adjustment will be apportioned. 🧠 Memory Box E-I-C-P — Extraordinary, Intentional, Common safety, real Peril: the four pillars of Rule A. Rule C excludes pollution; Rule Paramount demands reasonableness above all else. GA/YAR only bind if written into the Bill of Lading or Charter Party. ▶ Deep Dive — Sandbar Grounding & Engine Sacrifice Case Study Scenario A steering failure causes the vessel to shear out of a restricted channel and ground on a sandbar with the tide falling. Sequence Master orders tank soundings and confirms hull integrity, then declares GA given the risk of structural stress. To refloat before the next low tide, the main engine is intentionally run at maximum load alongside emergency tugs, drawing sand into the cooling system and damaging the seawater pumps and auxiliary coolers. The vessel refloats successfully and is towed to a port of refuge. Adjustment Because the cooling-system damage was an intentional sacrifice for the common safety of the entire adventure, it is treated as GA — all cargo owners contribute proportionally toward the repair bills and tug expenses, alongside the Ship's own proportional share. On My Vessel (Maersk A/S container tonnage) If ever ordered to run machinery outside normal parameters during an emergency, log explicitly that the action was ordered by the Master for the common safety of the vessel — this single logbook entry is often the deciding evidence for whether the resulting damage is accepted into the GA adjustment. 📚 References York-Antwerp Rules 2016 (CMI) US Carriage of Goods by Sea Act (COGSA) & Harter Act, 1893 The Jason , 225 U.S. 32 (1912) — validity of the Jason Clause See also — MIW Engineering Management Notes Part 19, Topic 1 : the deeper operational treatment — lien on cargo and the four security mechanisms, the Average Adjuster's role, Rule VII machinery damage, and the Rule XXIII time bar. section_title: Q1. The vessel is aground and the Master orders maximum astern power to refloat. The main engine suffers scored liners and a cracked cylinder head. Is this damage allowed in General Average?
text: Yes, under York-Antwerp Rules Rule VII (Damage to Machinery and Boilers), provided two conditions are satisfied: the ship was ashore and in a position of peril, and the damage arose from an actual intention to float the ship for the common safety. Both are met here — the vessel was hard aground and the engine was deliberately worked beyond its design limits specifically to refloat. The damage is therefore an intentional sacrifice rather than accidental wear, and the repair cost is made good in GA and shared by all contributing interests. Had the vessel been afloat, Rule VII excludes such damage in any circumstances, even if the engine was being worked hard to escape a genuine peril.

section_title: Q2. Cargo interests at the discharge port refuse to provide a General Average Bond or deposit. What happens, and what is your part in it?
text: The shipowner exercises the possessory lien on cargo conferred by the charterparty and bill of lading, and does not release the cargo until acceptable security is provided — a GA bond, an underwriter's average guarantee, a bank guarantee, or a cash deposit paid into a separate joint-name account under Rule XXII. My part is technical support to the Master in maintaining the ship's custody of that cargo: continuing to run and log reefer power, hold ventilation and bilge monitoring so that no cargo-care claim arises during the detention, keeping auxiliary machinery available for the extended stay, and recording the additional fuel and stores consumed so those costs can be presented to the adjuster. I would not unilaterally isolate cargo-gear power — enforcement of the lien is the Master's and the owner's decision, and I act on the Master's instruction.

section_title: Q4. A GA adjustment was issued 14 months ago and the owner has only now started proceedings against a cargo interest. Is there a problem?
text: Yes, if YAR 2016 or YAR 2004 is incorporated into the contract of carriage. Rule XXIII extinguishes the right to GA contribution — including any right to claim under a GA bond or guarantee — unless action is brought within one year of the date the adjustment was issued, subject to any mandatory time limitation in the applicable law. The right is extinguished, not merely barred as a remedy. There is also an absolute six-year long stop running from termination of the common maritime adventure, and the periods can be extended only by agreement made after the adventure terminated. If YAR 1994 is the incorporated version, Rule XXIII does not exist and national limitation law governs instead — which is why the first question in any GA dispute is which version the charterparty incorporates.

text: Part 19 · Topic 1 General Average — Principles, Security Mechanisms and the York-Antwerp Rules 2016 GA Principles · YAR 2016 · Lien & Security · Average Adjuster Uday pp. 451–457 (approx.) Examiner: Nair ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: Three corrections were applied to the source draft. (1) Time bar: the draft stated that the York-Antwerp Rules "do not universally prescribe a fixed, global time-bar". That is true of YAR 1994, but not of YAR 2004 or YAR 2016. Rule XXIII of YAR 2016 expressly extinguishes rights to GA contribution — including rights under GA bonds and guarantees — unless action is brought within one year of the date the GA adjustment is issued , with an absolute six-year long stop from termination of the common maritime adventure ; the periods are subject to any mandatory time limitation in the applicable law, may be extended by agreement made after termination of the adventure, and do not apply as between a GA party and its own insurers. The draft's internal contradiction (its own black-letter list correctly described Rule XXIII as imposing limitation windows) has been resolved in favour of the verified rule text. (2) Apportionment formula: retained but explicitly kept labelled as a pedagogical model — it is not algebraic text appearing in the Rules. (3) Overlap: Part 18 Topic 4 already covered General Average at the level of the New Jason Clause and the YAR framework; this topic is the deeper operational treatment (security enforcement, the adjuster, Rule VII machinery damage) and is deliberately not a repeat. 📖 Definition General Average (GA) is a principle of private maritime law under which all parties to a common maritime adventure proportionally share any loss arising from a voluntary, intentional sacrifice of part of the ship or cargo, or from an extraordinary expenditure, incurred for the purpose of preserving the remaining property from a real and imminent common peril. Its purpose is to ensure that the party whose property is deliberately sacrificed for the common good does not bear that loss alone — which in turn frees the Master to make fast, objective decisions in an emergency without weighing individual cargo-owner claims against the safety of the venture. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) GA is the reason a Master can order jettison, voluntary stranding, or destructive firefighting without hesitating over which cargo owner will sue — the economics are settled afterwards, not during the emergency. The Chief Engineer is the technical custodian of the evidence on which the entire adjustment rests. If bunker consumption during the extraordinary act cannot be isolated from routine consumption, that expenditure may simply not be allowed in GA. Rule VII is one of the few places in commercial maritime law where a deliberate engineering decision — running the main engine beyond its design limits — converts directly into a recoverable claim, but only if two narrow conditions are satisfied. The version of YAR incorporated into the charterparty or B/L (1994, 2004 or 2016) changes the answer to real questions — most sharply on the time bar. GA is driven by contract, not by a mandatory global convention. 📅 Historical Background c. 800 BC Lex Rhodia (Rhodian Law) — what is given for all must be replaced by the contribution of all 6th c. AD Absorbed into Roman law via the Digesta of Justinian 12th c. Rolls of Oleron and medieval sea codes carry the custom into Northern Europe 1890 First York-Antwerp Rules — international standardisation of GA adjustment 1906 UK Marine Insurance Act s.66 gives GA a statutory definition in English law 1994 YAR 1994 — long the most commonly incorporated version; contains no GA time bar 2004 YAR 2004 — introduces the Rule XXIII time bar; not accepted by shipowning interests 5 May 2016 YAR 2016 settled at CMI conference, New York; approved by BIMCO; retains Rule XXIII ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments YAR 2016, Rule VII Damage to machinery and boilers — allowed in GA only when the ship is ashore and in a position of peril and the damage arose from an actual intention to refloat for the common safety. YAR 2016, Rule XI Wages and maintenance of master, officers and crew, and fuel and stores consumed, during the extra period of detention at a port of refuge. YAR 2016, Rule XVII Contributory values — assessed on actual net values at the termination of the adventure. YAR 2016, Rule XXII Cash deposits to be paid into a separate account in the joint names of representatives of the shipowner and the depositors. YAR 2016, Rule XXIII Time bar — one year from issue of the adjustment; six-year long stop from termination of the common maritime adventure; subject to mandatory applicable law. MIA 1906, s.66 Statutory English-law definition of a general average act, loss and contribution. SOLAS Ch. V, Reg. 34-1 Master's discretion — the Master is not to be constrained by the owner, charterer or any other person from taking any decision necessary for safety of life at sea and protection of the marine environment. New Jason Clause Contractual clause preserving the carrier's right to GA contribution where the casualty arose from negligent navigation or management — required because of the US decision in The Jason . 🧮 Apportionment — the Contributory Value Mechanism Settlement rests on the contributory value of each interest — ship, cargo and freight at risk — assessed at the place and time the adventure ends. Each party contributes in the ratio its saved value bears to the total value of all property that benefited, including the value of the property sacrificed (the sacrificed property contributes towards making good its own loss). Contribution of party i : C i = (V i ÷ V total ) × L GA Where V i is that party's net contributory value, V total the aggregate of all contributory values, and L GA the total of allowed sacrifices and extraordinary expenditure. This is a teaching model, not rule text — no such equation appears in the York-Antwerp Rules. Say so if you write it on the board; presenting a self-made formula as convention text is exactly the trap Nair looks for. 🔒 Lien on Cargo and the Four Security Mechanisms The shipowner is usually the largest single contributor because the saved ship is the most valuable interest, but the shipowner also holds the leverage. Where cargo interests will not commit to contribute, the owner exercises a possessory lien on the cargo — a contractual right expressly written into the charterparty and bill of lading. The cargo is not released until acceptable security is in hand. [Casualty] ──> [GA Declared] ──> [Owner asserts possessory lien] │ Has acceptable security been given? ├── YES ──> [Cargo released to consignee] └── NO ──> [Cargo retained; storage costs accrue] Security Type Instrument Who is bound Practical strength General Average Bond Lloyd's Average Bond (LAB 77) or equivalent Cargo owner / consignee A contractual promise only — normally taken together with a guarantee or deposit, rarely alone. Average Guarantee Underwriter's GA guarantee Cargo underwriter Strongest in practice — backed by an insurer's balance sheet and standard market wording. Bank Guarantee Irrevocable bank guarantee Commercial bank Used where cargo is uninsured or the underwriter is unrated. Cash Deposit GA deposit receipt Cargo owner (payer) Held in a separate joint-name account under Rule XXII — not in the owner's general funds. Note the Rule XXII point: cash deposits must be paid into a separate account in the joint names of a representative of the shipowner and a representative of the depositors. Mixing GA deposits with the owner's working capital is a breach of the Rules. ⚖ The Average Adjuster One party — normally the shipowner — appoints the Average Adjuster , a specialist in marine insurance and GA practice. The appointment does not make the adjuster that party's advocate. Collects all evidence following the GA act — logs, soundings, surveys, repair accounts, port-of-refuge invoices. Prepares the statement of general average, allocating allowed losses and calculating each interest's contribution. Collects GA security from each interest and administers deposits. Issues the adjustment — the document that starts the Rule XXIII one-year clock running. The CMI Guidelines Relating to General Average state that the adjuster is expected to act impartially and independently so as to act fairly to all parties in the adventure, regardless of who appointed and pays them. A proposal to write that duty expressly into the 2016 Rules was considered and not adopted; it lives in the Guidelines, not the Rules. That distinction is a precise answer if pushed. 📜 The Numbered Rules — Working Map Rule Subject Engineer's relevance I–II Jettison of cargo; loss by sacrifice for common safety Collateral damage caused during the sacrifice is itself allowed. III Extinguishing fire on board Water, foam and CO₂ damage to ship and cargo is GA — smoke and heat damage from the fire itself is not. IV–V Cutting away wreck; voluntary stranding Rule IV allows only cutting away what is already broken or effectively lost by accident. VI Salvage remuneration Salvage under LOF or contract brought into the adjustment. VII Damage to machinery and boilers The engineer's rule — see the analysis below. VIII–IX Lightening a ship when ashore; cargo used as fuel Barge hire, discharge and reloading; cargo burnt only in a genuine emergency shortage. X–XII Port of refuge expenses; crew wages and maintenance; damage in discharging The bulk of most real adjustments sits here. XIII–XIV Deductions from cost of repairs ("new for old"); temporary repairs YAR 2016 removed the cap on temporary repairs of accidental damage at a port of refuge. XV–XIX Loss of freight; amount made good; contributory values; damage to ship; undeclared cargo Rule XIX: wrongfully declared cargo is not made good but still contributes if saved. XX–XXIII Provision of funds; interest; cash deposits; time bar YAR 2016 dropped the commission provision of YAR 1994 Rule XX; Rule XXIII is the time bar. ⚙ Rule VII — Damage to Machinery and Boilers The rule allows in general average damage caused to any machinery and boilers of a ship which is ashore and in a position of peril , in endeavouring to refloat, when shown to have arisen from an actual intention to float the ship for the common safety; but where a ship is afloat , no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers is in any circumstances made good as general average. Condition 1 — ashore and in peril. The vessel must actually be aground and in danger. Thrashing the engine to claw off a lee shore while still afloat is excluded, however extreme the weather and however genuine the peril. Condition 2 — actual intention to refloat for the common safety. The machinery must have been deliberately worked beyond normal limits with that specific intent. This is why the engineer's contemporaneous technical report matters: it is the primary evidence of intention. [Machinery worked beyond normal limits] │ ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐ Ship AGROUND & in peril Ship AFLOAT │ │ Intent to refloat for EXCLUDED in all the common safety? circumstances ├── YES ──> ALLOWED (Rule VII) (ordinary wear / └── NO ──> EXCLUDED operational loss) The asymmetry is deliberate. Working the engine while afloat is what a ship is for ; the resulting wear is an ordinary operating cost, not an extraordinary sacrifice. Once aground, the same act becomes extraordinary because the machinery is being used for a purpose, and at a stress level, outside its intended service. 🎓 CE Oral Tip (Nair): Nair's standard follow-up on Rule VII is the mirror case: "and if the ship had been afloat?" The expected answer is excluded in any circumstances — those words are in the rule. If you then volunteer that the YAR version matters, and that under YAR 2016 Rule XXIII the adjustment itself starts a one-year clock with a six-year long stop, you have moved from a memorised answer to a working one. Do not claim the Rules are silent on time bars — that was true only up to YAR 1994. 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1. The vessel is aground and the Master orders maximum astern power to refloat. The main engine suffers scored liners and a cracked cylinder head. Is this damage allowed in General Average? Both are met here — the vessel was hard aground and the engine was deliberately worked beyond its design limits specifically to refloat. The damage is therefore an intentional sacrifice rather than accidental wear, and the repair cost is made good in GA and shared by all contributing interests. Had the vessel been afloat, Rule VII excludes such damage in any circumstances, even if the engine was being worked hard to escape a genuine peril. Q2. Cargo interests at the discharge port refuse to provide a General Average Bond or deposit. What happens, and what is your part in it? The shipowner exercises the possessory lien on cargo conferred by the charterparty and bill of lading, and does not release the cargo until acceptable security is provided — a GA bond, an underwriter's average guarantee, a bank guarantee, or a cash deposit paid into a separate joint-name account under Rule XXII. I would not unilaterally isolate cargo-gear power — enforcement of the lien is the Master's and the owner's decision, and I act on the Master's instruction. Q3. Who pays the engine room crew's wages while the vessel is detained at a port of refuge for emergency repairs? Under YAR Rule XI, the wages and maintenance of the master, officers and crew, together with fuel and stores consumed during the extra period of detention at a port of refuge, are allowed in general average, provided the detention was necessary for the common safety or to enable the vessel to complete the voyage safely. The cost is not borne by the shipowner alone: the average adjuster pools it into the total GA losses and it is distributed across all interests in proportion to their contributory values under Rule XVII. YAR 2016 specifically reinstated the allowance for wages and maintenance during detention at a place of refuge that the 2004 Rules had restricted. Q4. A GA adjustment was issued 14 months ago and the owner has only now started proceedings against a cargo interest. Is there a problem? Yes, if YAR 2016 or YAR 2004 is incorporated into the contract of carriage. Rule XXIII extinguishes the right to GA contribution — including any right to claim under a GA bond or guarantee — unless action is brought within one year of the date the adjustment was issued, subject to any mandatory time limitation in the applicable law. The right is extinguished, not merely barred as a remedy. There is also an absolute six-year long stop running from termination of the common maritime adventure, and the periods can be extended only by agreement made after the adventure terminated. If YAR 1994 is the incorporated version, Rule XXIII does not exist and national limitation law governs instead — which is why the first question in any GA dispute is which version the charterparty incorporates. ✍ Written Exam Focus 5 Outline the role of the Average Adjuster following a declaration of General Average, and list the four types of security that may be collected from cargo interests. 10 A vessel suffers an engine room fire extinguished by the fixed CO₂ system, and subsequently grounds after losing power. Differentiate the damages allowed under York-Antwerp Rule III (Extinguishing Fire on Board) and Rule V (Voluntary Stranding), stating the operational boundaries of each. 15 Analyse the technical and administrative responsibilities of a Chief Engineer before, during and after a General Average event involving machinery damage at sea. Address engine logbook entries, quantification of bunker and resource consumption, preservation of physical evidence for Class and the adjuster, and the basis of contributory value under Rule XVII. 🧠 Memory Box P.I.E.R. — the four tests of a GA act: P eril (real and imminent), I ntentional, E xtraordinary, R easonable. Rule VII: aground = allowed, afloat = never. Two conditions — ashore and in peril, and actual intention to refloat for the common safety. Rule XXIII: 1 year from the adjustment, 6-year long stop from the end of the adventure — YAR 2004 and 2016 only, not YAR 1994. Security quartet: Bond, Underwriter's Guarantee, Bank Guarantee, Cash Deposit. Deposits go into a separate joint account (Rule XXII). Rule XI = crew wages at the port of refuge. Rule XVII = contributory values. ▶ Deep Dive — Engine Room Fire and Refloating — Full Incident Chronology Chronology 0200 LT — fuel line rupture in the auxiliary engine room on a laden container vessel; severe fire. 0215 — Master releases the fixed CO₂ system; fire contained but all main propulsion and auxiliary power lost, vessel adrift in a narrow channel. 0330 — tidal set drives the unpowered vessel hard onto a mud bank. 0500 — Master declares General Average. 0800 — Chief Engineer prepares the main engine for maximum astern to refloat before the next low water exposes the hull to excessive stress. 0930 — engine run significantly past thermal limits for 45 minutes; liner scoring, bearing damage and a cracked cylinder head result; the vessel refloats. Which losses fall where CO₂ discharge and any water or foam damage to ship and cargo: Rule III. The grounding itself was accidental, not voluntary, so Rule V (voluntary stranding) does not apply — a common trap in this scenario. The machinery damage from the refloating attempt: Rule VII, because the ship was ashore and in peril and the engine was worked with actual intention to refloat. Port of refuge expenses and crew wages during detention for repairs: Rules X and XI. Chief Engineer's evidence checklist Verify and lock the CO₂ battery release counters and timestamps. Sound every fuel tank immediately before and after the refloating attempt to isolate extraordinary consumption. Isolate and preserve the cracked cylinder head, damaged bearings and scored liner segments for the surveyor and the adjuster — do not scrap or send them for reconditioning. Extract and duplicate engine control room data logger parameters covering 0800–1015 LT. Draft a technical report stating why the engine had to be worked beyond normal limits — this is the primary evidence of the intention required by Rule VII. On my vessel (Maersk A/S container tonnage) If the ECR data logger dies with the power, designate an engineer to keep a handwritten log of jacket water temperature, exhaust temperatures, scavenge pressure and lube oil pressure at fixed intervals. A contemporaneous manual log in the duty engineer's handwriting is accepted evidence; a reconstruction written up two days later is not, and the adjuster will treat it accordingly. 📚 References York-Antwerp Rules 2016 (Comité Maritime International, adopted New York, 5 May 2016) — Rules VII, XI, XVII, XXII, XXIII CMI Guidelines Relating to General Average (2016) UK Marine Insurance Act 1906, s.66 SOLAS Chapter V, Regulation 34-1 (Master's discretion) Association of Average Adjusters — Rules of Practice Notes-p19 · P19-T1 · v1.0

section_title: Q1. Explain the difference between a Clean and a Claused Bill of Lading, and why a Master would refuse to sign clean.
text: A clean B/L states that the carrier received the cargo in apparent good order and condition, with no notation of defect or shortage. A claused or "dirty" bill carries an express remark recording damage, shortage, staining, wet packaging or similar. The Master has a duty to ensure the bill accurately reflects the apparent condition of the goods as received. Signing clean for visibly damaged cargo binds the carrier to deliver in that stated good condition, so any damage found at discharge becomes the carrier's liability even though it existed before loading. The Master therefore clauses the bill, or refuses to sign it clean. Shippers commonly offer a letter of indemnity to obtain a clean bill — accepting one to conceal known damage is a misrepresentation to the bank and the LOI is generally unenforceable and outside P&I cover.

section_title: Q2. A shipper says the contract of carriage is fully contained in the Bill of Lading. Evaluate that statement.
text: It is inaccurate as between the original parties. The B/L is evidence of the contract of carriage, not the contract itself; the contract is concluded earlier, at booking or under the governing charterparty. The proof is that if cargo is damaged after loading but before the bill is issued, the shipper can still claim under the pre-existing contract. There is a refinement worth stating: once the bill is transferred to a third-party endorsee who took it in good faith, the terms on the face of the bill generally become the contract as against that endorsee, because they were never party to the original booking and can only rely on the document they hold.

section_title: Q3. What is the legal basis for an electronic Bill of Lading, and what makes it as secure as paper?
text: The legal basis is domestic legislation giving electronic transferable records the same effect as paper documents — the UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Transferable Records of 2017, enacted for example by the UK Electronic Trade Documents Act 2023 — together with the contractual rulebook that binds all users of an approved platform. The technology, whether distributed ledger or a centralised registry, provides the two properties the law requires: a reliable method of identifying the record as unique so there cannot be two originals, and of establishing exclusive control so that transfer of control functions as endorsement and delivery. The Rotterdam Rules also provide for electronic transport records, but they are not in force and cannot be relied on as operative law.

section_title: Q4. What are your specific duties as Chief Engineer in relation to what is written on the Bill of Lading?
text: My duties are evidential. Before loading, I confirm hold bilge systems, bilge alarms and hold ventilation are tested and logged, and support hold tightness and hatch cover ultrasonic testing so the vessel can demonstrate cargo spaces fit to receive the cargo. Tank soundings are taken and recorded immediately before and after loading so that no shipboard liquid transfer can be alleged to have affected cargo weight or condition. During the voyage I log reefer power continuity, any interruption and its duration, and the daily bilge soundings for every hold. All bunker delivery notes and fuel change-over records are retained. The purpose is to establish that the carrier exercised due diligence and cared properly for the cargo — which is what preserves the liability limits and immunities under the carriage regime that the B/L incorporates.

section_title: Bills of Lading — Legal Framework, Operational Typologies and the Electronic B/L
text: Part 19 · Topic 2 Bills of Lading — Legal Framework, Operational Typologies and the Electronic B/L Triple Function · B/L Typologies · Endorsement · e-B/L Uday pp. 457–463 (approx.) Examiner: Nair ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: Four corrections were applied. (1) The draft repeatedly referred to India's " Bills of Lading Bill, 2025 " as pending legislation. It is no longer a Bill: the Bills of Lading Act, 2025 received Presidential assent on 24 July 2025 and was published in the Gazette Extraordinary the same day, repealing the Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856. All references have been updated to the Act. (2) The draft cited the Rotterdam Rules (2008) as providing "the statutory foundation for electronic equivalents". The Rotterdam Rules have not entered into force — they require 20 ratifications and remain well short. They are a signpost to the future, not operative law, and the framing has been corrected. (3) The draft stated that blockchain enforces the integrity of the e-B/L. Distributed-ledger technology is one implementation; the legal effect of an electronic B/L derives from MLETR-based national legislation (e.g. the UK Electronic Trade Documents Act 2023) and from contractual rulebooks binding the users of an approved platform. That distinction has been added. (4) The draft's claim that a straight B/L generally need not be presented at delivery is contested; the House of Lords in The Rafaela S [2005] UKHL 11 held a straight bill to be a document of title requiring presentation. The safe examination position is given below. 📖 Definition A Bill of Lading (B/L) is a transport document issued by or on behalf of the carrier to the shipper, recording the type, quantity, apparent condition and destination of goods received for carriage by sea. It is the pivot around which the seller, buyer, carrier and financing bank all operate — it is what allows cargo to be sold, resold and financed while it is physically in the middle of an ocean. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) The B/L is the document against which a cargo claim is measured. Every technical record the engine room keeps — bilge soundings, hold ventilation, reefer power logs — exists partly to defend the carrier's position against what the B/L says about apparent condition on loading. A Master signing a clean B/L for visibly damaged cargo converts a shipper's problem into the owner's liability. Understanding why the Master clauses a bill explains why the Chief Engineer's records of hold condition and tightness testing are demanded before loading. Misdelivery — releasing cargo without the original B/L — is one of the few exposures a P&I club will not cover as of right. It is a contractual and criminal risk, not merely a commercial one. e-B/L adoption is now moving fast under MLETR-based law; the shipboard consequence is that data-transfer protocols and documentary timings change, while the underlying liability principles do not. 📅 Historical Background 16th–17th c. Master's book entries evolve into separate portable signed receipts 1855 / 1856 UK Bills of Lading Act 1855; Indian Bills of Lading Act 1856 codifies transfer of rights 1924 Hague Rules — mandatory minimum carrier obligations under a B/L 1968 / 1979 Visby Protocol and SDR Protocol modernise limits and package definitions 2008 Rotterdam Rules adopted — includes electronic transport records; NOT in force 2017 UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Transferable Records (MLETR) adopted 2023 UK Electronic Trade Documents Act 2023 gives electronic trade documents legal parity 24 Jul 2025 India: Bills of Lading Act, 2025 assented — repeals the 1856 Act ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments Bills of Lading Act, 2025 (India) Assented 24 July 2025; repeals the Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856. Restructures and simplifies the transfer of rights and liabilities to consignees and endorsees, and empowers the Central Government to issue directions for implementation. Substance of the 1856 rule is preserved. Hague / Hague-Visby Rules Mandatory minimum carrier obligations, immunities and liability limits applicable to contracts covered by a B/L. Rotterdam Rules 2008 Adopted but not in force — provides for electronic transport records; cannot be cited as operative law. UNCITRAL MLETR 2017 Model law giving electronic transferable records the same legal effect as paper, where enacted domestically. SOLAS Ch. VI, Reg. 2 Cargo information — shipper to provide accurate cargo information, including verified gross mass, before loading. SOLAS Ch. VII / IMDG Code Dangerous goods documentation — the description and UN number on the B/L must match what is physically loaded. 🔺 The Triple Function ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ THE B/L TRIAD │ └──────────────┬───────────────┘ ┌─────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ [DOCUMENT OF TITLE] [RECEIPT FOR GOODS] [EVIDENCE OF CONTRACT] Entitles the lawful Records quantity, date Proves the terms agreed holder to delivery and apparent order and before loading — but is at the discharge port condition on loading NOT the contract itself Document of title. The lawful holder presenting an original B/L is entitled to delivery from the carrier. Note the precision: it confers the right to possession from the carrier, not ownership . Ownership passes under the sale contract between buyer and seller, on entirely separate terms. Receipt for goods. It records the date of receipt, place of issue, load and discharge ports, and quantity or weight — and, critically, apparent order and condition, which is the phrase that makes clausing matter. Evidence of the contract of carriage. It is evidence, not the contract. The contract is concluded earlier, at booking or under the charterparty. If cargo is damaged after loading but before the B/L is issued, the shipper can still sue on the pre-existing contract. There is one important refinement: as between the carrier and a third-party endorsee who took the bill in good faith, the B/L generally becomes the contract itself rather than mere evidence of it, because the endorsee was never party to the original booking and can only look to the document in their hands. Between the original shipper and the carrier it remains evidence. 📄 Operational Typologies Type Transferability Delivery requirement Typical use Straight B/L Non-negotiable — consigned to a named party Presentation of an original is the safe practice (see note below) Intra-group transfers; established, stable trading relationships Order B/L Negotiable by endorsement ("to order" / "to order of X") Presentation of a properly endorsed original The standard form in global commodity and container trade Bearer B/L Negotiable by physical delivery alone — no endorsement needed Presentation of the physical document Specialised open-market trading; high fraud exposure Claused ("dirty") B/L Depends on the underlying type Presentation of the original Issued where cargo shows shortage or visible damage at loading Clean B/L Depends on the underlying type Presentation of the original Cargo received in apparent good order and condition — what banks require under an L/C Note on the straight bill. Older texts state that a straight B/L need not be presented at delivery because the consignee is named and can be identified. The House of Lords in The Rafaela S [2005] UKHL 11 held that a straight bill is a document of title requiring presentation, and that the Hague-Visby Rules apply to it. In the oral, the defensible answer is: practice varies by jurisdiction and by the wording of the bill, but presentation of an original is the safe operational rule, and delivering without presentation exposes the carrier to a misdelivery claim that the P&I club may decline to cover. Endorsement mechanics. A full (special) endorsement names the new party — "deliver to X" — and is signed and stamped by the current holder. An endorsement in blank is a signature and stamp on the reverse with no named party, which converts the bill into one transferable by delivery alone. Blank endorsement is convenient and is the reason a lost or stolen original is a serious fraud exposure. 💻 The Electronic Bill of Lading An e-B/L is a functional electronic equivalent of the paper bill, issued and transferred on an approved platform. Its legal effect does not come from the technology: it comes from MLETR-based national legislation where enacted, and from the contractual rulebook that binds every user of the platform to treat electronic transfer as equivalent to endorsement and delivery. Distributed-ledger or centralised-registry technology is how uniqueness and exclusive control are enforced — it is the mechanism, not the source of legal validity. Speed. Transfer is effectively instantaneous, removing the courier leg that routinely delays cargo release and drives demand for letters of indemnity. Cost. Removes printing, courier and re-issue costs, and the LOI exposure created when cargo arrives before the paper does. Security. Cryptographic control prevents duplicate originals and retroactive alteration — the two classic paper-B/L frauds. Constraint. Recognition is jurisdiction-dependent. An e-B/L is only as good as the law at the place of delivery and the P&I club's approval of the platform. [Paper] Shipper ─> Courier ─> Bank ─> Courier ─> Consignee ─> Master (days; risk of loss; LOI often needed if cargo beats the paper) [e-B/L] Shipper ─> [Approved platform — exclusive control transferred] ─> Consignee (minutes; no LOI; validity depends on MLETR-based law at delivery) 🎓 CE Oral Tip (Nair): If Nair asks about India's new legislation, be precise about status and date — Bills of Lading Act , 2025, assented 24 July 2025, repealing the 1856 Act . Candidates who say "Bill" signal they learned it from a news article a year old. Then add the honest qualifier that the substance is largely unchanged: the reform simplifies language, restructures the provisions, and adds a Central Government direction power — it does not alter the underlying liability principles, which still sit in the carriage regime. 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1. Explain the difference between a Clean and a Claused Bill of Lading, and why a Master would refuse to sign clean. A clean B/L states that the carrier received the cargo in apparent good order and condition, with no notation of defect or shortage. A claused or "dirty" bill carries an express remark recording damage, shortage, staining, wet packaging or similar. The Master has a duty to ensure the bill accurately reflects the apparent condition of the goods as received. Signing clean for visibly damaged cargo binds the carrier to deliver in that stated good condition, so any damage found at discharge becomes the carrier's liability even though it existed before loading. The Master therefore clauses the bill, or refuses to sign it clean. Shippers commonly offer a letter of indemnity to obtain a clean bill — accepting one to conceal known damage is a misrepresentation to the bank and the LOI is generally unenforceable and outside P&I cover. Q2. A shipper says the contract of carriage is fully contained in the Bill of Lading. Evaluate that statement. It is inaccurate as between the original parties. The B/L is evidence of the contract of carriage, not the contract itself; the contract is concluded earlier, at booking or under the governing charterparty. The proof is that if cargo is damaged after loading but before the bill is issued, the shipper can still claim under the pre-existing contract. There is a refinement worth stating: once the bill is transferred to a third-party endorsee who took it in good faith, the terms on the face of the bill generally become the contract as against that endorsee, because they were never party to the original booking and can only rely on the document they hold. Q3. What is the legal basis for an electronic Bill of Lading, and what makes it as secure as paper? The legal basis is domestic legislation giving electronic transferable records the same effect as paper documents — the UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Transferable Records of 2017, enacted for example by the UK Electronic Trade Documents Act 2023 — together with the contractual rulebook that binds all users of an approved platform. The technology, whether distributed ledger or a centralised registry, provides the two properties the law requires: a reliable method of identifying the record as unique so there cannot be two originals, and of establishing exclusive control so that transfer of control functions as endorsement and delivery. The Rotterdam Rules also provide for electronic transport records, but they are not in force and cannot be relied on as operative law. Q4. What are your specific duties as Chief Engineer in relation to what is written on the Bill of Lading? My duties are evidential. Before loading, I confirm hold bilge systems, bilge alarms and hold ventilation are tested and logged, and support hold tightness and hatch cover ultrasonic testing so the vessel can demonstrate cargo spaces fit to receive the cargo. Tank soundings are taken and recorded immediately before and after loading so that no shipboard liquid transfer can be alleged to have affected cargo weight or condition. During the voyage I log reefer power continuity, any interruption and its duration, and the daily bilge soundings for every hold. All bunker delivery notes and fuel change-over records are retained. The purpose is to establish that the carrier exercised due diligence and cared properly for the cargo — which is what preserves the liability limits and immunities under the carriage regime that the B/L incorporates. ✍ Written Exam Focus 5 State the three functions of a Bill of Lading and distinguish clearly between the right of possession and the right of ownership. 10 Compare a Straight Bill of Lading and an Order Bill of Lading, explaining how transferability affects the requirement to present an original document at the discharge port, and the carrier's exposure on misdelivery. 15 Discuss the modernisation of bill of lading law, using India's Bills of Lading Act, 2025 as a case study. Contrast statutory reform with the operational advantages of MLETR-based electronic bills of lading, assessing transaction speed, administrative cost, document security and the residual jurisdictional risks. 🧠 Memory Box T.R.E. — T itle, R eceipt, E vidence of contract. Title = possession, not ownership. Straight = named, Order = endorsed, Bearer = whoever holds it. Clean vs claused turns on "apparent order and condition". LOI for a clean bill on known damage = unenforceable, no P&I cover. India: Bills of Lading Act 2025 (assent 24 Jul 2025) replaced the 1856 Act. Say "Act", not "Bill". e-B/L legality = MLETR-based law + platform rulebook. Blockchain is the mechanism, not the legal basis. Rotterdam Rules are NOT in force. ▶ Deep Dive — Misdelivery, Letters of Indemnity and Why P&I Cover Falls Away The commercial pressure On short sea legs and in oil trades, the vessel routinely arrives before the original bills have completed the banking chain. The receiver cannot present an original, and demurrage starts accruing. The standard fix is a letter of indemnity from the charterer or receiver asking the carrier to deliver without presentation. Why this is dangerous Delivery without presentation of an original bill is a breach of the contract of carriage and, if the goods go to the wrong party, a conversion. P&I clubs exclude liability arising from delivery of cargo without production of the original bill of lading from standard cover. The owner is then relying entirely on the creditworthiness of whoever signed the LOI — which is exactly the party most likely to have disappeared when a fraud unwinds. Two distinct LOI situations — do not confuse them An LOI offered to obtain a clean bill for known damaged cargo is a misrepresentation to the bank and the endorsee, and English courts have held such indemnities unenforceable as founded on fraud. An LOI offered for delivery without production of originals is not inherently fraudulent and is commercially common — but it still moves the risk outside P&I cover onto the indemnifier's balance sheet. The Chief Engineer's practical involvement is limited but real: the accuracy of your cargo-care records is what determines whether the underlying claim is defensible in the first place. 📚 References Bills of Lading Act, 2025 (India) — assented 24 July 2025; repeals the Indian Bills of Lading Act, 1856 UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Transferable Records (MLETR), 2017 UK Electronic Trade Documents Act 2023 J I MacWilliam Co Inc v Mediterranean Shipping Co SA (The Rafaela S) [2005] UKHL 11 SOLAS Chapter VI Regulation 2; SOLAS Chapter VII and the IMDG Code United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Carriage of Goods Wholly or Partly by Sea, 2008 (Rotterdam Rules) — adopted, not in force Notes-p19 · P19-T2 · v1.0

section_title: Q1. Under a time charter the charterer supplies fuel that causes fuel pump scoring and filter clogging. What are your immediate actions and who is liable?
text: Immediate actions: change over to a tank of known-good fuel; isolate the suspect tank and stop further transfer from it; increase purification efficiency and adjust settling and purifier temperatures; monitor and log fuel pump, filter differential pressure, exhaust temperatures and any power limitation; inform the Master at once so a Letter of Protest can be issued and the charterer notified. Evidence: secure the MARPOL Annex VI Regulation 18 retained sample drawn at the receiving ship's manifold — unopened, sealed and jointly signed — together with the Bunker Delivery Note, the ship's own drip samples and the change-over record, and request a joint analysis at an accredited laboratory. On liability: under a time charter the charterer supplies and pays for bunkers and warrants that they meet the specification stated in the charterparty and the statutory MARPOL requirements. If off-spec fuel causes machinery damage or performance shortfall, the owner has a claim against the charterer — but that claim stands or falls on the sample chain of custody, which is my responsibility.

section_title: Q2. A vessel on a voyage charter arrives at the load port 12 hours after the cancelling date because of heavy weather. What is the position?
text: The charterer is entitled to reject the vessel and cancel the charterparty. The cancelling date in the laycan is an absolute contractual right; the reason for the delay is irrelevant, so heavy weather, machinery breakdown or congestion elsewhere provide no defence. In practice the charterer will often not cancel if the market has moved against them, and may instead seek a reduced rate, but the legal right exists. The operational consequence for us is that the achievable service speed must be assessed honestly and early — if it becomes clear the vessel cannot make the cancelling date, the Master and owner need to know while there is still time to negotiate an extension rather than after the window has closed.

section_subtitle: Charterparty Frameworks, Off-Hire and Commercial Ship Management
section_title: Q3. Explain off-hire and give two engine-room events that would trigger it.
text: Off-hire is the mechanism in a time charter that suspends the charterer's obligation to pay hire for the period during which the vessel is prevented from providing full working service, for a cause listed in the off-hire clause. Two engine-room examples: a main engine breakdown requiring a stoppage or a significant power reduction at sea, and failure of cargo-handling machinery such as a crane or hatch cover system during cargo operations. Whether the whole period or only the net time lost is deducted depends on the clause wording — a net loss of time clause deducts only time actually lost, while a period clause runs from the event until full efficiency is restored, which can be far more expensive for the owner. Throughout the off-hire period the owner continues to pay crew, insurance and stores, so the loss is pure revenue.

section_title: Q4. What changes for you technically when a vessel goes on bareboat charter?
text: Under a bareboat charter the charterer takes possession and becomes responsible for crewing, technical management, insurance, maintenance and the statutory survey cycle, and normally becomes the "Company" for ISM purposes. Practically that means a new Document of Compliance and Safety Management Certificate, a new entry on the Continuous Synopsis Record, possibly a change of flag and of Recognised Organisation, and a new planned maintenance system and spares supply chain. The handover is a high-risk period: Class and PSC treat a change of manager as a targeting factor, so I would expect an expanded inspection at the next port and would make sure the maintenance records, oil record books, PMS history and certificates are complete and consistent with the new management entity before the handover is signed off.

section_title: Charterparty Frameworks, Off-Hire and Commercial Ship Management
text: Part 19 · Topic 3 Charterparty Frameworks, Off-Hire and Commercial Ship Management Voyage / Time / Bareboat · Laytime & Laycan · Off-Hire · Performance Claims Uday pp. 463–469 (approx.) Examiner: Senthil ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: One substantive correction. The draft stated that BIMCO's BARECON variants allocate insurance as: " BARECON A — owner pays the premium for short-period chartering; BARECON B — charterer pays for long period; BARECON C — a combination ". This is not correct . BIMCO first issued the bareboat form in 1974 in two versions: BARECON A , for the chartering of commissioned vessels with or without an existing mortgage, and BARECON B , a financial-type charter for newbuildings financed by mortgage . The distinction was the subject vessel and the financing structure, not the insurance premium or the charter duration. The two were amalgamated into BARECON 89 , revised as BARECON 2001 (Parts I–V, with Part III applying to newbuildings only), and the current form is BARECON 2017 . There is no "BARECON C". Insurance in the modern form is dealt with by alternative clauses under which either the Charterers or the Owners insure — an option selected in Part I, not a lettered form variant. The fictitious A/B/C insurance scheme has been removed and replaced with the verified position. 📖 Definition A charterparty is a contract by which a shipowner places a vessel, or her cargo-carrying capacity, at the disposal of a charterer for a specific voyage or a defined period. Its function is to allocate cost, risk and control between the two: who buys the bunkers, who pays port dues, who employs and directs the crew, who carries the delay risk, and what happens to the money when the ship stops performing. The name comes from charta partita — the medieval practice of writing the agreement twice on one parchment and cutting it in a jagged line, each party keeping a half. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) The charter type determines who the Chief Engineer's technical decisions cost money. Under a time charter the charterer buys the fuel, so every hour of poor combustion efficiency is a claim waiting to be raised against the owner under the speed and consumption warranty. Off-hire is the single commercial term most directly driven by the engine room. A breakdown that stops the vessel suspends hire — the owner's revenue stops while costs continue. Planned maintenance scheduling is therefore a commercial decision as much as a technical one. Under a time charter the charterer supplies the bunkers but the owner carries the machinery. Fuel-quality damage claims sit exactly on that boundary, and they are won or lost on the manifold sample and the bunker records the engine room controls. Under bareboat the charterer takes over technical management including the survey cycle — which is why a bareboat handover triggers heightened PSC and Class scrutiny. 📅 Historical Background Medieval Charta partita — the indented, cut-in-two contract 1905 BIMCO founded; standard forms begin to displace bespoke drafting 1913 NYPE (New York Produce Exchange) time charter form first issued 1939 BALTIME time charter form 1974 BIMCO BARECON A and BARECON B issued 1989 BARECON A and B amalgamated into BARECON 89 2001 / 2017 BARECON 2001 (Parts I–V); current form BARECON 2017 2015 / 2020s BIMCO fuel-compliance, sulphur cap and CII operation clauses added to time charter practice ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments and Standard Forms BIMCO NYPE / BALTIME Standard time charter forms — contain the speed and consumption warranty, off-hire clause, and bunker specification clause. BIMCO BARECON 2017 Current standard bareboat charter. BARECON 2001 structure: Part I data, Part II standard terms, Part III newbuildings only, Parts IV–V optional (hire/purchase, flag-state registry provisions). BIMCO GENCON The most widely used voyage charter form — laytime, demurrage, despatch and lien provisions. MARPOL Annex VI, Reg. 14 & 18 Sulphur limits and fuel oil quality/availability — the statutory floor beneath any contractual bunker specification clause. MARPOL Annex VI, Reg. 28 Operational carbon intensity (CII) rating — the driver behind modern CII clauses allocating operational responsibility to charterers. ISM Code (SOLAS Ch. IX) Identifies the "Company" — under a bareboat charter this normally becomes the charterer, which changes the DOC and the Continuous Synopsis Record. 🚢 The Three Chartering Regimes ┌──────────────────────────┐ │ CHARTERING REGIMES │ └────────────┬─────────────┘ ┌───────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ [VOYAGE CHARTER] [TIME CHARTER] [BAREBOAT CHARTER] Port A to Port B. Hired for a period. Hull leased outright. Owner: bunkers, crew, Owner: crew + technical. Charterer: everything — port costs. Charterer: bunkers + crew, bunkers, insurance, Paid as FREIGHT. port costs. Paid as HIRE. maintenance. Paid as HIRE. Voyage charter. The owner sells a transport service between named ports. Payment is freight , on a per-tonne or lump-sum basis. The owner bears bunkers, crew and (subject to the cargo-handling terms agreed, such as FIOST) port costs. The owner carries the delay risk — which is why laytime and demurrage exist. Time charter. The owner sells the use of the vessel for a period. Payment is hire , usually per day. The owner retains the crew and technical management; the charterer directs employment, nominates ports, and buys the bunkers. This split is the source of nearly all time-charter disputes: performance, fuel quality, and off-hire. Bareboat (demise) charter. The charterer takes possession and full control — crewing, technical management, insurance, maintenance and the statutory survey cycle. Hire is lower because the owner's risk is lower. It is essentially a financing instrument: it lets an investor own tonnage and hand operation to a manager. A useful analogy for the oral: a voyage charter is hiring a taxi — you pay the fare and nothing else; a time charter is hiring a car with a driver — you pay for the fuel and tell the driver where to go; a bareboat charter is leasing the car — you insure it, service it, and hire your own driver. 📊 Responsibility Matrix Cost / responsibility Voyage Charter Time Charter Bareboat Charter Bunkers Owner Charterer Charterer Crew wages and manning Owner Owner Charterer Port costs and dues Owner Charterer Charterer Technical management and maintenance Owner Owner Charterer Hull & Machinery insurance Owner Owner Charterer (or Owner — optional clause in BARECON) Statutory survey cycle / Class Owner Owner Charterer ISM "Company" Owner / manager Owner / manager Charterer (normally) Payment mechanism Freight Hire Hire Delay risk at port Owner (laytime/demurrage) Charterer (ship remains on hire) Charterer ⏱ Laytime, Demurrage, Despatch and Laycan Laytime — the time allowed by the charterparty for loading and discharging, without additional payment. It begins on tendering a valid Notice of Readiness and the expiry of any turn time. Demurrage — liquidated damages payable by the charterer to the owner for each day (and pro rata) that laytime is exceeded. Once on demurrage, always on demurrage: exceptions that would have interrupted laytime generally do not interrupt demurrage unless expressly stated. Despatch — a payment by the owner to the charterer when cargo work finishes before laytime expires, conventionally at half the demurrage rate. Laycan (laydays / cancelling) — the window within which the vessel must arrive and tender readiness. Arrive early and the charterer need not accept before the first layday; arrive after the cancelling date and the charterer has an absolute right to cancel, whatever the reason for the delay. The laycan point is the harsh one and examiners like it: heavy weather, a breakdown, or congestion at the previous port are all irrelevant to the charterer's cancelling right. This is why the passage plan, the achievable service speed and the Chief Engineer's honest assessment of what the machinery can sustain are commercial inputs, not just technical ones. A Contract of Affreightment (COA) sits above individual voyages: an undertaking to carry a stated quantity of cargo over a period, across multiple shipments, with the specific vessel nominated later. It fixes freight, laycan windows, cargo specification, laytime terms, lien provisions and jurisdiction, and gives both sides volume certainty without tying up a named ship. 🛑 Off-Hire and the Performance Warranty Off-hire suspends the charterer's obligation to pay hire for the period the vessel is prevented from giving full working service, for causes listed in the off-hire clause — typically breakdown of machinery, damage to hull, deficiency of crew, drydocking, or detention. The wording matters: a net loss of time clause deducts only time actually lost, while a period clause deducts the whole period from the event until full efficiency is restored. Typical engine-room triggers: main engine breakdown at sea; turbocharger or auxiliary blower failure preventing full power; steering gear defect; cargo crane or hatch cover machinery failure during cargo work; generator shortage forcing reduced operations. The owner keeps paying crew, insurance and stores throughout — off-hire is pure revenue loss, and it is directly attributable to the machinery. This is the commercial argument for spending on planned maintenance rather than deferring it. Speed and consumption warranty: the owner warrants a service speed at a stated daily consumption, usually in good weather up to a defined Beaufort/sea-state limit. Underperformance gives the charterer a claim for the time lost and the excess fuel burned. Hull and propeller fouling, poor combustion, and turbocharger fouling are the usual technical causes. Fuel supplied by the charterer. Under a time charter the charterer buys the bunkers and warrants that they meet the specification in the charterparty and the statutory requirements of MARPOL Annex VI. If off-spec fuel scores fuel pumps, blocks filters or damages the engine, the owner has a claim — but only if the evidence chain holds. The MARPOL Annex VI Regulation 18 retained sample drawn at the receiving ship's manifold, properly sealed, jointly signed and correctly stored, is the single most important piece of evidence in the case. 🎓 CE Oral Tip (Senthil): Senthil's line of questioning on charterparties usually starts commercial and lands on your records. Expect: "charterer's fuel damaged your fuel pumps — what do you do?" The answer he wants is a sequence, not an opinion: change over to a known-good tank, increase purifier throughput and lower throughput temperature margin, log all parameters, inform the Master, preserve the MARPOL manifold sample unopened, retain the BDN and the ship's own drip samples, and request a joint analysis. Then, and only then, the legal conclusion — the charterer warranted the specification, so the owner claims. Leading with "the charterer is liable" without the evidence chain reads as commercially aware but technically thin. 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1. Under a time charter the charterer supplies fuel that causes fuel pump scoring and filter clogging. What are your immediate actions and who is liable? Immediate actions: change over to a tank of known-good fuel; isolate the suspect tank and stop further transfer from it; increase purification efficiency and adjust settling and purifier temperatures; monitor and log fuel pump, filter differential pressure, exhaust temperatures and any power limitation; inform the Master at once so a Letter of Protest can be issued and the charterer notified. Evidence: secure the MARPOL Annex VI Regulation 18 retained sample drawn at the receiving ship's manifold — unopened, sealed and jointly signed — together with the Bunker Delivery Note, the ship's own drip samples and the change-over record, and request a joint analysis at an accredited laboratory. On liability: under a time charter the charterer supplies and pays for bunkers and warrants that they meet the specification stated in the charterparty and the statutory MARPOL requirements. If off-spec fuel causes machinery damage or performance shortfall, the owner has a claim against the charterer — but that claim stands or falls on the sample chain of custody, which is my responsibility. Q2. A vessel on a voyage charter arrives at the load port 12 hours after the cancelling date because of heavy weather. What is the position? The charterer is entitled to reject the vessel and cancel the charterparty. The cancelling date in the laycan is an absolute contractual right; the reason for the delay is irrelevant, so heavy weather, machinery breakdown or congestion elsewhere provide no defence. In practice the charterer will often not cancel if the market has moved against them, and may instead seek a reduced rate, but the legal right exists. The operational consequence for us is that the achievable service speed must be assessed honestly and early — if it becomes clear the vessel cannot make the cancelling date, the Master and owner need to know while there is still time to negotiate an extension rather than after the window has closed. Q3. Explain off-hire and give two engine-room events that would trigger it. Off-hire is the mechanism in a time charter that suspends the charterer's obligation to pay hire for the period during which the vessel is prevented from providing full working service, for a cause listed in the off-hire clause. Two engine-room examples: a main engine breakdown requiring a stoppage or a significant power reduction at sea, and failure of cargo-handling machinery such as a crane or hatch cover system during cargo operations. Whether the whole period or only the net time lost is deducted depends on the clause wording — a net loss of time clause deducts only time actually lost, while a period clause runs from the event until full efficiency is restored, which can be far more expensive for the owner. Throughout the off-hire period the owner continues to pay crew, insurance and stores, so the loss is pure revenue. Q4. What changes for you technically when a vessel goes on bareboat charter? Under a bareboat charter the charterer takes possession and becomes responsible for crewing, technical management, insurance, maintenance and the statutory survey cycle, and normally becomes the "Company" for ISM purposes. Practically that means a new Document of Compliance and Safety Management Certificate, a new entry on the Continuous Synopsis Record, possibly a change of flag and of Recognised Organisation, and a new planned maintenance system and spares supply chain. The handover is a high-risk period: Class and PSC treat a change of manager as a targeting factor, so I would expect an expanded inspection at the next port and would make sure the maintenance records, oil record books, PMS history and certificates are complete and consistent with the new management entity before the handover is signed off. ✍ Written Exam Focus 5 Explain the difference between demurrage and despatch under a voyage charterparty, and state who pays whom in each case. 10 A container vessel on time charter suffers an auxiliary blower failure causing reduced main engine speed and increased daily fuel consumption. Analyse the commercial liabilities under the speed and consumption warranty and the off-hire clause, and describe the technical records the Chief Engineer must provide to the owner. 15 Compare the operational, financial and legal structures of voyage, time and bareboat charters, with reference to the development of the BIMCO BARECON forms. Detail which party bears crew costs, port dues, bunker procurement, insurance and technical maintenance under each, and assess the effect of each model on shipboard management and the statutory survey cycle. 🧠 Memory Box Voyage = FREIGHT. Time = HIRE, charterer buys fuel. Bareboat = HIRE, charterer buys everything. Taxi / car-with-driver / leased car — voyage / time / bareboat. Laycan: early = need not accept; late = absolute right to cancel , whatever the reason. Once on demurrage, always on demurrage. Despatch is conventionally half the demurrage rate. BARECON A = commissioned vessels; BARECON B = newbuildings financed by mortgage. Amalgamated into BARECON 89 → 2001 → 2017. There is no BARECON C. ▶ Deep Dive — The Bunker Quality Dispute — Building a Claim That Survives Why most claims fail Charterer-supplied fuel disputes are usually lost not on the science but on the evidence. The commonest failures are: the MARPOL retained sample was not drawn continuously at the receiving ship's manifold; the sample seals were broken or the joint signature is missing; the ship's own drip sample was taken from the barge side rather than the manifold; or the change-over record does not establish which fuel was actually in the engine when the damage occurred. The chain that works Draw the MARPOL Annex VI Regulation 18 sample continuously throughout delivery at the receiving ship's manifold, using a fitting dedicated to that purpose. Seal it with a unique identification number, have the barge representative and the ship's officer both sign the label, and record the number on the BDN. Retain it under the ship's control for the period required, in a safe place outside accommodation. Take the ship's own additional samples at the same point at the same time. Record the exact time of change-over to and from the disputed fuel against the running hours and the damage timeline. Technical evidence to add Filter differential pressure trend before and after change-over; purifier sludge discharge frequency and appearance; fuel pump plunger and barrel condition with photographs and part numbers; exhaust temperature deviation by unit; measured viscosity and settling tank temperature; any cat-fines analysis, since aluminium plus silicon above the fuel's stated limit is the classic mechanism for accelerated liner and pump wear. Present these as a timeline, not a list — the aim is to show the damage tracks the fuel. On my vessel (Maersk A/S container tonnage) The practical discipline is that the sample locker and the BDN file are audited as carefully as the Oil Record Book. A missing joint signature on a seal label is a small administrative failure that can extinguish a six-figure claim, and it is entirely within the engine room's control to prevent. 📚 References BIMCO BARECON 2017 standard bareboat charter (successor to BARECON 2001, BARECON 89, and the 1974 BARECON A and B forms) BIMCO NYPE and BALTIME standard time charter forms; GENCON voyage charter form MARPOL Annex VI, Regulations 14, 18 and 28 SOLAS Chapter IX and the ISM Code (identification of the "Company") Laytime Definitions for Charter Parties (BIMCO / CMI / FONASBA) Notes-p19 · P19-T3 · v1.0

section_title: Q1. An LCL package measures 2.0 m × 1.5 m × 2.0 m and weighs 4.5 tonnes. How is the ocean freight assessed?
text: LCL shipments are charged on weight or measurement, whichever is greater. The volume is 2.0 × 1.5 × 2.0 = 6.0 cubic metres. On the ocean freight convention one cubic metre is charged as approximately one tonne, so 6.0 CBM is equivalent to 6.0 revenue tonnes. That exceeds the actual weight of 4.5 tonnes, so the shipment is billed on the volumetric basis of 6.0 CBM. The same package moving by air would be assessed very differently, because the IATA volumetric divisor of 6,000 cubic centimetres per kilogram values one cubic metre at only about 167 kg — around 6 cubic metres to the tonne — which is why bulky, light cargo is heavily penalised in air freight.

section_title: Q2. What is WS100, and what does a fixture at WS150 mean?
text: WS100 is the Worldscale flat rate for a specific route — the freight in US dollars per tonne calculated by the Worldscale Associations for a nominal standard vessel of 75,000 tonnes deadweight, 14.5 knots service speed, 55 tonnes per day bunker consumption, a fixed hire element of US$12,000 per day and four days total port time, on a round-voyage basis including the ballast leg. Flat rates are recalculated annually. A fixture at WS150 means the charterer pays 150% of that published flat rate for the route. The system exists so that owners and charterers can negotiate a single percentage figure rather than recalculating full voyage economics for every one of thousands of route and cargo combinations.

section_title: Q3. Under CIF terms, cargo is damaged during the ocean passage. Who bears the loss, and why does this surprise people?
text: The buyer bears the risk. Under CIF the seller pays the cost of carriage and marine insurance to the named destination port, but the risk of loss or damage passes to the buyer when the goods are placed on board the vessel at the port of shipment. Cost and risk therefore separate, which is what surprises people: the seller is still paying freight for a voyage during which the goods are already at the buyer's risk. The buyer's remedy is against the insurance the seller was obliged to arrange — and under Incoterms 2020 that obligation for CIF is still only minimum cover, Institute Cargo Clauses (C), whereas the multimodal equivalent CIP was upgraded to all-risks Clauses (A). It is also worth noting that the old "ship's rail" boundary was deleted in Incoterms 2010; the test is now whether the goods have been placed on board.

section_title: Q4. Which Incoterm places the greatest burden on the seller, and what does that mean operationally?
text: DDP, Delivered Duty Paid. The seller bears all costs and risks of bringing the goods to the named destination place, including main carriage, insurance arrangements, inland delivery, import customs clearance and payment of all import duties and taxes. Operationally it means the seller must be able to act as importer of record in the buyer's country, which is often impractical or legally impossible for a foreign seller — one reason DDP is used less than its apparent simplicity suggests. At the opposite end, EXW places the minimum obligation on the seller, who need only make the goods available at their own premises.
