Those are the wrong way round: the industry convention is expressed as volume per tonne , or equivalently as a weight per cubic metre. Ocean LCL: 1 CBM ≈ 1,000 kg (1 CBM per tonne). Road groupage: 1 CBM ≈ 333 kg, i.e. 3 CBM per tonne . Air: the IATA volumetric divisor of 6,000 cm³/kg gives 1 CBM ≈ 167 kg , i.e. 6 CBM per tonne — not 6 tonnes per CBM, which would be physically absurd for air cargo. The table has been rewritten in the correct direction. The draft's worked ocean example was unaffected and is retained. (2) "Ship's rail". The draft's FOB/CIF diagram used the ship's rail as the risk-transfer boundary. That concept was deleted in Incoterms 2010 ; under FOB, CFR and CIF risk now passes when the goods are placed on board the vessel. (3) Worldscale detail stripped. The draft's claims that the standard vessel allows "24 hours for each canal transit" and that the bunker index uses "March to September of the preceding year" could not be verified against a primary source — the Worldscale schedule is a proprietary publication. Rather than publish unverified specifics, those two figures have been removed. The widely published core parameters of the nominal standard vessel are retained and flagged as commercial benchmarks, not statutory values. 📖 Definition Maritime economics , in the ship-management sense, is the set of commercial frameworks that determine how shipping revenue is generated and how transport costs are allocated: how freight is built up and surcharged, where cost and risk pass between seller and buyer under standard trade terms, and how tanker freight is benchmarked. None of it is IMO law — Incoterms are published by the International Chamber of Commerce, and Worldscale is administered by the private Worldscale Association. They operate alongside statutory requirements, not under them. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) Bunker consumption is the largest controllable variable cost in most trades. On a Worldscale-rated voyage the freight is fixed by the index and the market percentage; every tonne of fuel saved against the voyage estimate falls straight to the owner's margin. The Bunker Adjustment Factor exists because fuel price volatility cannot be absorbed in a quoted rate. Understanding it explains why fuel-efficiency measures are visible at board level, not just in the engine room. Incoterms decide who is exposed when cargo is damaged. The point at which risk passes governs whether the carrier's claim exposure runs to the seller or the buyer — and which party's insurer will be pursuing the ship. Deadweight and draft verification is an engineering task with a direct commercial consequence: the tonnage actually loaded is what is billed, and a discrepancy between draft survey and manifest is a dispute. 📅 Historical Background 1936 ICC publishes the first Incoterms rules 1969 Worldscale introduced — joint venture of the Worldscale Associations, London and New York 2010 Incoterms 2010 — the "ship's rail" concept deleted; risk passes on placement on board 2020 Incoterms 2020 — DAT renamed DPU; CIP insurance raised to Institute Cargo Clauses (A) Annual Worldscale flat rates recalculated and published, effective 1 January each year ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments ICC Incoterms 2020 Eleven trade terms defining delivery, cost and risk transfer between seller and buyer. A private ICC publication, not a convention. Parties must state the edition — Incoterms 2020 does not automatically supersede 2010 in an existing contract. Worldscale (World Tanker Nominal Freight Scale) Privately administered tanker freight index; flat rates recalculated annually. Rates negotiated as WS points, where WS100 equals the published flat rate for that route. SOLAS Ch. VI, Reg. 2 Verified Gross Mass — the shipper must provide a verified gross mass for a packed container before it is loaded. SOLAS Ch. VII / IMDG Code Dangerous goods manifest, correct UN numbers and packing details — a documentation failure here is a detainable deficiency. MARPOL Annex VI, Reg. 18 Bunker Delivery Notes and retained samples — the documentary basis for proving fuel compliance and consumption. 💰 Building Up a Freight Rate Base ocean freight — the carriage element itself. Terminal Handling Charge (THC) — terminal costs for lifting and positioning at each end. Inland transport — pre-carriage and on-carriage where the quotation is door-to-door. Bunker Adjustment Factor (BAF) — a variable surcharge tracking marine fuel price movements, so the base rate need not be requoted every time fuel moves. Currency Adjustment Factor (CAF) — a percentage surcharge covering exchange-rate exposure between the currency of the tariff and the currency of the carrier's costs. Documentation fees — B/L issue, amendment and release charges. FCL versus LCL. For a Full Container Load, price attaches to the box — its size, type and whether it is a reefer. For Less than Container Load, the shipment is charged on weight or measurement, whichever is greater (the classic "W/M" basis), which is why volumetric weight matters. Volume in cubic metres: CBM = L (m) × W (m) × H (m) Mode Charging equivalence Expressed as volume per tonne Effect Ocean (LCL) 1 CBM ≈ 1,000 kg 1 CBM per tonne Balanced — dense cargo pays on weight, light cargo on volume. Road (groupage) 1 CBM ≈ 333 kg 3 CBM per tonne Moderate penalty on low-density cargo. Air 1 CBM ≈ 167 kg (IATA divisor 6,000 cm³/kg) 6 CBM per tonne Heavy penalty on bulky, low-density cargo. Worked example. An LCL package 2.0 m × 1.5 m × 2.0 m weighs 4.5 tonnes. Volume = 6.0 CBM. On the ocean basis 6.0 CBM is equivalent to 6.0 tonnes, which exceeds the actual 4.5 tonnes, so the shipment is charged on 6.0 CBM. 🌍 Incoterms 2020 — the Eleven Rules Any mode of transport (7): EXW (Ex Works), FCA (Free Carrier), CPT (Carriage Paid To), CIP (Carriage and Insurance Paid To), DAP (Delivered at Place), DPU (Delivered at Place Unloaded), DDP (Delivered Duty Paid). Sea and inland waterway only (4): FAS (Free Alongside Ship), FOB (Free On Board), CFR (Cost and Freight), CIF (Cost, Insurance and Freight). EXW — minimum seller obligation; buyer collects at the seller's premises and bears everything thereafter. FAS / FOB — seller delivers alongside, or on board, the vessel at the named load port. Under FOB risk passes when the goods are placed on board . CFR / CIF — seller pays freight (and, under CIF, marine insurance) to the destination port, but risk still passes on placement on board at the load port. The split between where cost ends and where risk ends is the single most examinable feature of these two terms. CPT / CIP — the multimodal equivalents; risk passes on handing over to the first carrier. Under Incoterms 2020, CIP requires all-risks cover (Institute Cargo Clauses A), while CIF still requires only minimum cover (Clauses C). DAP / DPU / DDP — seller carries risk to destination. DPU (renamed from DAT in 2020) is the only rule requiring the seller to unload. DDP places maximum obligation on the seller, including import clearance and duties. [Seller's works] ──> [Load port] ══(ON BOARD — risk passes)══> [Ocean] ──> [Discharge port] │ FOB: seller's cost stops here ............ risk passes on board CIF: seller's cost runs to destination ... risk STILL passes on board (cost and risk part company — this is the trap) 🛢 The Worldscale System Worldscale is a nominal freight scale for tanker chartering. Rather than pricing every one of thousands of route combinations from scratch, the Worldscale Associations publish an annual flat rate in US dollars per tonne for each route, calculated for a defined nominal standard vessel on a round-voyage basis. That flat rate is WS100 . The market then negotiates in Worldscale points: WS120 is 120% of the flat rate, WS80 is 80%. Nominal standard vessel parameter Value Deadweight 75,000 tonnes Service speed 14.5 knots Bunker consumption at sea 55 tonnes per day Fixed hire element US$12,000 per day Port time allowance 4 days total for the round voyage Voyage basis Laden Port A → Port B, ballast return to Port A These are commercial benchmarks published by a private association , not statutory values, and the schedule itself is proprietary. Quote them as the standard-vessel assumptions underlying the index; do not present them as regulation. Flat rates are recalculated annually and take effect on 1 January. [Worldscale Association publishes annual FLAT RATE per route] │ FLAT RATE = WS100 ($/tonne) │ ┌─────────────────────┴─────────────────────┐ Strong market Weak market ▼ ▼ Fixed at WS150 → charterer pays Fixed at WS70 → charterer pays 150% of the flat rate 70% of the flat rate The engineering consequence is direct: the index assumes 55 tonnes per day for the nominal vessel, but the owner earns on the actual ship. Candidates who cite Incoterms as if it were a convention lose credibility for the rest of the answer. Sea-only: FAS, FOB, CFR, CIF. CIF: cost to destination, risk on board at loading. Ship's rail was deleted in 2010. WS100 = the published flat rate. ▶ Deep Dive — Why the Engine Room Owns the Voyage Margin The structure of the exposure On a voyage charter or a Worldscale-rated fixture, the freight is fixed at the moment of fixing. Every variable cost thereafter is the owner's. Bunkers are typically the largest single item, so the voyage result is decided by the difference between the consumption assumed in the voyage estimate and the consumption actually achieved. Where the tonnes actually go Hull roughness and biofouling: a fouled hull can add a double-digit percentage to propulsive power demand at constant speed, and the penalty compounds with time since the last cleaning. Propeller roughness and blade damage act similarly but are cheaper to correct. Air cooler fouling raises scavenge air temperature and reduces charge density, worsening combustion. Turbocharger fouling reduces available air, forcing later, hotter combustion. Poor injector condition raises specific fuel consumption directly. Excessive auxiliary load, particularly unnecessary running of pumps and compressors in parallel, is a quiet continuous drain. Making it visible Trend specific fuel oil consumption against corrected shaft power, not against speed over ground, so that current and weather are removed from the comparison. Log hull performance indicators consistently so that hull cleaning can be justified commercially rather than argued for on general principles. Where a CII rating clause exists in the charter, the same data set serves two purposes — commercial performance evidence and regulatory rating management. section_title: Q1. What is meant by an ad valorem declaration and how does it affect the carrier's liability?
text: An ad valorem declaration is a statement by the shipper, made before shipment, of the nature and value of the goods, which is then inserted into the bill of lading. Its effect is to displace the package limitation: instead of being capped at 666.67 SDR per package or unit or 2 SDR per kilogram of gross weight, whichever is higher, the carrier becomes liable up to the declared value. The carrier will charge a higher freight to reflect the increased exposure. Under the original Hague Rules the same mechanism displaced the £100 gold-value limit. Where no declaration is made, the statutory limits apply regardless of the actual value of the goods, which is why high-value cargo either declares or is separately insured.

section_title: Q2. Distinguish a latent defect from a failure to exercise due diligence.
text: A latent defect is a hidden flaw in material or manufacture that could not have been discovered by reasonable inspection, testing or routine maintenance — for example a fatigue crack propagating from a subsurface inclusion in a forging, where the non-destructive testing was carried out at the correct interval and passed. Where such a defect causes cargo loss, the carrier has a defence under Article IV rule 2. A failure of due diligence is different in kind: the condition was known or reasonably discoverable and was not acted upon — an overdue planned maintenance job, a rising bearing temperature trend that was recorded but ignored, or a deferred defect carried without assessment. That invalidates the carrier's exemptions and exposes the owner to the full claim. The distinction is decided on records, which is why the engine room's documentation is the carrier's primary defence.

section_title: Q3. Why must due diligence be exercised "before and at the beginning of the voyage"?
text: Those words fix the temporal window in which the seaworthiness obligation applies. It runs from the commencement of loading until the vessel breaks ground for the voyage. Within that window the carrier must exercise due diligence to make the ship seaworthy, properly manned, equipped and supplied, and to make the holds and cool chambers fit for the cargo. The obligation is one of due diligence, not an absolute warranty of seaworthiness, but it is non-delegable, so the carrier answers for the negligence of a repair yard or servicing contractor. If a defect arises genuinely at sea and could not have been detected beforehand by due diligence, the carrier does not breach Article III rule 1 and can rely on the statutory exceptions. This is why maintenance and test records for the period immediately before departure are decisive in most cargo claims.

section_title: Q4. What is the current Indian statutory position on carriage of goods by sea?
text: The Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 has been repealed. The Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025, Act No. 19 of 2025, received Presidential assent on 8 August 2025 and commenced on 10 September 2025. Its Schedule applies the Hague Rules as amended by the Visby Protocol of 23 February 1968 and the Protocol of 21 December 1979, so India now operates on a Hague-Visby basis with SDR limits — 666.67 SDR per package or unit or 2 SDR per kilogram of gross weight, whichever is higher. The Act applies to ships carrying goods from any port in India to any other port, whether in or outside India, and requires bills of lading issued in India to state expressly that they take effect subject to the Rules. It also empowers the Central Government to amend the Schedule by notification, so India can adopt future conventions without new primary legislation. It was enacted alongside the Bills of Lading Act, 2025 and the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025.

text: Part 19 · Topic 5 Carriage of Goods Regimes — the Hague Rules, Hague-Visby and the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 2025 Hague / Hague-Visby · Due Diligence · Package Limitation · COGSA 2025 Uday pp. 472–475 (approx.) Examiner: Nair ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: Four corrections. (1) Entry into force. The draft said the Hague-Visby Rules "came into force in 1968". 1968 is the date the Visby Protocol was signed (Brussels, 23 February 1968); it entered into force on 23 June 1977 . The SDR Protocol of 21 December 1979, which replaced the gold-franc limits with Special Drawing Rights, entered into force on 14 February 1984. (2) Liability limits left vague. The draft's comparison table described the Hague-Visby limit only as "set via Special Drawing Rights or modern currency units". The actual figures are examinable and have been inserted: 666.67 SDR per package or unit, or 2 SDR per kilogram of gross weight of the goods lost or damaged, whichever is the higher . (3) Indian law is out of date in the draft. The Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 has been repealed. The Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 (Act No. 19 of 2025) received Presidential assent on 8 August 2025 and commenced on 10 September 2025 ; its Schedule applies the Hague Rules as amended by the Visby Protocol of 1968 and the Protocol of 21 December 1979. India therefore now operates on a Hague-Visby basis, not the old 1925 Hague basis. (4) Missing regimes added. The draft compared only Hague and Hague-Visby; the Hamburg Rules (in force 1 November 1992) and the Rotterdam Rules (adopted 2008, not in force ) have been added for completeness, since examiners ask for the full progression. 📖 Definition An international carriage of goods regime is a body of rules fixing the minimum obligations, the immunities, and the maximum financial liability of a sea carrier under a bill of lading. Its purpose is a bargain: carriers accept a floor of non-excludable duties — principally due diligence to make the ship seaworthy and proper care of the cargo — and in exchange receive a defined list of defences and a ceiling on liability. Before these regimes, carriers used freedom of contract to exclude liability even for their own crews' negligence, and cargo interests and their financing banks had no reliable recourse. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) The carrier's entire package of immunities and limits depends on proving due diligence to make the ship seaworthy before and at the beginning of the voyage . That proof is built almost entirely from engine room records — planned maintenance history, survey reports, test records and defect close-outs. Unseaworthiness is not confined to the hull. Inoperative hold bilge systems, defective hatch cover seals, a failed hold ventilation fan or an undermanned engine room can each render a vessel unseaworthy for the intended cargo and voyage. The distinction between a latent defect (a defence) and a failure to maintain (not a defence) is decided on documentation. A component that failed with no prior indication in the records is a latent defect; the same failure with two years of ignored condition-monitoring trends is negligence. India moved to a Hague-Visby basis in 2025. For a Kochi MMD candidate this is the single most current and most examinable fact in this topic. 📅 Historical Background 25 Aug 1924 Hague Rules adopted at Brussels — first international carriage regime 2 Jun 1931 Hague Rules enter into force 1925 Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 gives the Hague Rules effect in India 23 Feb 1968 Visby Protocol signed at Brussels 23 Jun 1977 Visby Protocol enters into force — the Hague-Visby Rules 21 Dec 1979 SDR Protocol — gold francs replaced by Special Drawing Rights 14 Feb 1984 SDR Protocol enters into force 1 Nov 1992 Hamburg Rules 1978 enter into force — abolish the nautical fault defence 2008 Rotterdam Rules adopted — not in force 8 Aug 2025 India: Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 (Act 19 of 2025) assented; commenced 10 September 2025 ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments Hague Rules, Art. III r.1 Carrier to exercise due diligence before and at the beginning of the voyage to make the ship seaworthy, properly man, equip and supply her, and make holds and cool chambers fit and safe for reception, carriage and preservation of the goods. Hague Rules, Art. III r.2 Carrier to properly and carefully load, handle, stow, carry, keep, care for and discharge the goods. Hague-Visby, Art. III r.6 One-year time bar — suit must be brought within one year of delivery, or of the date when the goods should have been delivered. Hague-Visby, Art. IV r.2 The seventeen listed defences (a)–(q), including nautical fault, fire without actual fault or privity, perils of the sea, act of God, inherent vice and insufficiency of packing. Hague-Visby, Art. IV r.5(a) Limitation: 666.67 SDR per package or unit or 2 SDR per kilogram of gross weight, whichever is higher . Hague-Visby, Art. IV r.5(c) Container clause — where packages are enumerated in the bill of lading as packed in a container, each enumerated package counts as a package for limitation. Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 (India) Act No. 19 of 2025; assent 8 August 2025, commenced 10 September 2025; repeals the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 and applies the Hague Rules as amended by the 1968 and 1979 Protocols. ⚖ The Three Core Carrier Obligations Seaworthiness. Due diligence to make the ship seaworthy — an obligation of due diligence , not an absolute warranty, but one that is non-delegable: the carrier remains answerable for the negligence of a repair yard or a servicing contractor. Manning, equipping and supplying. Properly manned, equipped and supplied for the intended voyage — including sufficient bunkers, stores, spares and a competent, rested crew. Cargoworthiness and cargo care. Holds, refrigerating and cool chambers fit and safe for the reception, carriage and preservation of the goods; and thereafter proper and careful loading, handling, stowage, carriage, custody, care and discharge. The timing phrase "before and at the beginning of the voyage" is doing heavy lifting. The duty attaches to the period from the start of loading until the vessel breaks ground for the voyage. A defect arising genuinely at sea, which could not have been detected by due diligence beforehand, does not breach Article III rule 1 — which is precisely why the maintenance record for the period before departure decides most cases. 🛡 Defences, and the Latent Defect Distinction Act of God; act of war; act of public enemies; arrest or restraint of princes. Perils, dangers and accidents of the sea or other navigable waters. Fire, unless caused by the actual fault or privity of the carrier . Act or omission of the shipper; inherent vice, wastage in bulk or weight; insufficiency of packing or of marks. Strikes, lockouts, restraint of labour; saving or attempting to save life or property at sea. Nautical fault — act, neglect or default of the master, mariner, pilot or servants of the carrier in the navigation or management of the ship. This survives in Hague-Visby but was abolished by the Hamburg Rules . Latent defects not discoverable by due diligence. Latent defect (defence available) Failure of due diligence (no defence) Nature A hidden material or manufacturing flaw not discoverable by reasonable inspection or routine testing A known or reasonably discoverable condition that was not acted upon Typical evidence Metallurgical failure analysis; clean condition-monitoring history; NDT within interval and passed Ignored vibration or wear trends; overdue PMS jobs; deferred defects; expired or waived surveys Engine room example Crankshaft fatigue crack originating from a subsurface inclusion Bearing failure after three months of rising temperature trend with no intervention Outcome Carrier exempt Carrier liable — and the limitation may be at risk if the conduct is reckless The practical lesson is uncomfortable but useful: a good condition-monitoring system creates evidence both ways . It proves diligence when the trend was clean, and it proves negligence when the trend was clear and nothing was done. Recording a trend and not acting on it is worse, evidentially, than not measuring at all — which is an argument for closing out defects, not for measuring less. 📐 Limitation of Liability Across the Regimes Regime In force Package / unit limit Weight limit Notes Hague Rules 1924 2 June 1931 £100 gold value per package or unit None — package basis only No weight alternative; hence the container problem Hague-Visby (Visby 1968 + SDR 1979) 23 Jun 1977 / 14 Feb 1984 666.67 SDR per package or unit 2 SDR per kg gross weight Whichever is higher ; container enumeration clause Art. IV r.5(c) Hamburg Rules 1978 1 November 1992 835 SDR per package or unit 2.5 SDR per kg gross weight Nautical fault defence abolished; carrier's period of responsibility extended Rotterdam Rules 2008 Not in force 875 SDR per package or unit 3 SDR per kg gross weight Door-to-door scope; electronic transport records Ad valorem declaration. Under all these regimes the limit falls away if the shipper declares the nature and value of the goods before shipment and that declaration is inserted in the bill of lading. The carrier is then liable up to the declared value — and will charge a correspondingly higher freight. "Ad valorem" is the correct term; avoid informal abbreviations in an oral. The container problem and its fix. Under the 1924 Rules, with only a package basis and no weight alternative, a carrier could argue that a container holding 500 cartons was a single "package", capping liability at one limit for the whole box. Article IV rule 5(c) of Hague-Visby resolves this: where the number of packages inside the container is enumerated in the bill of lading , each enumerated package counts separately. Where it is not enumerated, the container itself is the package. This is why the description on the face of the bill matters commercially and not merely administratively. 🇮🇳 The Indian Position after 2025 The Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 (Act No. 19 of 2025) received assent on 8 August 2025 and commenced on 10 September 2025, repealing the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925. Its Schedule applies the Hague Rules as amended by the Brussels Protocol of 23 February 1968 and the Protocol of 21 December 1979 — that is, the Hague-Visby Rules with SDR limits . The Act applies to carriage of goods by sea in ships carrying goods from any port in India to any other port, whether in or outside India — the outward-cargo scope inherited from the 1925 Act. Every bill of lading or similar document of title issued in India that evidences a contract to which the Rules apply must carry an express statement that it has effect subject to the Rules. The Central Government is empowered to amend the Schedule by notification, allowing India to adopt future international carriage conventions without fresh primary legislation. It sits alongside the Bills of Lading Act, 2025 (assented 24 July 2025) and the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 in the same wave of maritime law reform. For the oral, the sequence worth having ready is: 1925 Act was Hague-based → repealed → 2025 Act is Hague-Visby based with SDR limits → therefore the Indian package limitation is now 666.67 SDR per package or 2 SDR per kilogram, whichever is higher, not the old gold-value figure. 🎓 CE Oral Tip (Nair): Nair's favourite entry point here is the phrase "before and at the beginning of the voyage" — he will ask you to explain why those exact words matter. The complete answer has three parts: they fix the window in which the seaworthiness duty bites; the duty is due diligence rather than an absolute warranty; and it is non-delegable, so engaging a competent repair yard does not transfer the responsibility. Then bring it home to your own department: the evidence that due diligence was exercised is the PMS history, the survey and test records, and the closed-out defect list — all of which are mine. If he moves to limits, give the current figures and, if it is an Indian-law question, the 2025 Act. 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1. Analyse the claim under the Hague-Visby Rules, addressing due diligence, perils of the sea, and the applicable limitation of liability. 15 Critically evaluate the progression from the Hague Rules 1924 through the Visby and SDR Protocols to the Hamburg and Rotterdam Rules. Identify the commercial deficiencies that drove each revision, compare the limitation regimes, and assess the significance of India's Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 for a vessel trading from Indian ports. 🧠 Memory Box Hague 1924 → in force 2 June 1931. Visby Protocol signed 1968 → in force 23 June 1977. SDR Protocol 1979 → in force 14 Feb 1984. Signature year and force year are different — do not merge them. Hague-Visby limit: 666.67 SDR per package OR 2 SDR per kg, whichever is HIGHER. Hamburg: 835 / 2.5. Rotterdam: 875 / 3 (not in force). "Before and at the beginning of the voyage" — due diligence, not absolute warranty, and non-delegable. Nautical fault survives in Hague-Visby, abolished by Hamburg. India: COGSA 2025 (Act 19 of 2025), commenced 10 Sept 2025 — Hague-Visby basis. The 1925 Act is gone. ▶ Deep Dive — Proving Due Diligence — What the Engine Room Actually Has to Show The evidential burden Once cargo damage is established, the carrier must show either that the loss falls within one of the Article IV rule 2 exceptions, or that due diligence was exercised to make the ship seaworthy before and at the beginning of the voyage. Where unseaworthiness is alleged as the cause, the burden of proving due diligence rests on the carrier — it is not for the cargo interest to prove negligence. The document set that carries the burden Planned maintenance system history for the systems implicated, showing jobs raised, done and closed with dates and running hours. Condition monitoring records — vibration, lube oil analysis, bearing temperatures, performance data — with evidence that adverse trends were investigated. Class and statutory survey status with no overdue or conditionally waived items relevant to the failure. Test records for hold bilge systems, bilge alarms, hold ventilation, hatch cover ultrasonic tightness testing and cargo hold fixed detection. Defect list with each open item risk-assessed and reported. Spares inventory demonstrating that critical spares were on board as required. The three failure modes that lose cases First, retrospective completion — PMS jobs signed off in a block after the incident, which is obvious from the system audit trail and destroys credibility. Second, trend data recorded but not acted on, which converts a latent-defect defence into proof of negligence. Third, an open defect carried without a documented risk assessment or notification to the office, which makes the unseaworthiness knowing rather than inadvertent. On my vessel (Maersk A/S container tonnage) For container tonnage the reefer plant deserves specific attention, because reefer cargo claims are frequent, high-value and technically well-documented on both sides. Continuous logging of supply and return air temperatures, power interruption events with durations, defrost cycles and any alarm acknowledgements gives a defensible record. The absence of that record, on a cargo that is designed to be temperature-monitored, is itself read as a failure of care. 📚 References International Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules of Law relating to Bills of Lading, Brussels, 25 August 1924 (Hague Rules) — in force 2 June 1931 Protocol to amend the 1924 Convention, Brussels, 23 February 1968 (Visby Protocol) — in force 23 June 1977 Protocol of 21 December 1979 (SDR Protocol) — in force 14 February 1984 United Nations Convention on the Carriage of Goods by Sea, 1978 (Hamburg Rules) — in force 1 November 1992 Rotterdam Rules, 2008 — adopted, not in force The Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 (Act No. 19 of 2025), India — indiacode.nic.in Notes-p19 · P19-T5 · v1.0

text: Topic 10 MARPOL Annex I — Statutory Certification, Record-Keeping & Oily Waste Management MARPOL Annex I Uday pp. 46–50 Examiner: Nair ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: Two corrections applied to the original draft: (1) the Special Areas list was missing Southern South African waters , and "Oman area" is formally "Oman area of the Arabian Sea" — both added below. (2) The original draft stated cargo-tank-washing discharge must stay "below 34 ppm" — MARPOL Annex I Regulation 34 does not use a fixed ppm threshold for tanker ODMCS operations; it uses instantaneous-rate (≤30 L/NM) and total-quantity (≤1/30,000 of cargo) limits. 15 ppm is the separate machinery-bilge discharge limit. The 34 ppm figure has been removed and replaced with the correct rate/quantity criteria. 📖 Definition This topic covers the statutory framework for preventing oil pollution under MARPOL Annex I — international certification (IOPP), the Oil Record Book (Parts I & II), the physics of the Load on Top (LOT) procedure, and the structural/volumetric design criteria for slop tanks. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) Oil pollution carries some of the most severe consequences in shipping — criminal liability for engineering officers, heavy fines, and immediate detention. Falsified ORB entries or "magic pipe" bypasses are treated as serious criminal offences in most jurisdictions. Every entry the CE signs in the ORB must reconcile with physical tank soundings — discrepancies are read by PSC as evidence of concealment. 📅 Historical Background 1973 → MARPOL adopted but insufficient ratification to enter into force 1976–77 → Series of severe tanker accidents drives revision 1978 → Protocol of 1978 modifies the convention 2 Oct 1983 → MARPOL 73/78 (with Annex I) enters into force ⚖ Regulatory References MARPOL Annex I, Reg.13 Defines Special Areas and their operational discharge criteria MARPOL Annex I, Reg.17 Oil Record Book Part I — carriage, format, entry criteria MARPOL Annex I, Reg.31 Oil Discharge Monitoring and Control Systems (ODMCS) MARPOL Annex I, Reg.34 Operational discharge criteria for cargo/ballast water from oil tankers 🌊 MARPOL Annex I Special Areas (Current List — Corrected) Mediterranean Sea area Baltic Sea area Black Sea area Red Sea area Gulfs area Gulf of Aden area Antarctic area North West European waters Oman area of the Arabian Sea Southern South African waters (added — missing from original draft) 📜 Statutory Certification & Record-Keeping IOPP Certificate: mandatory for oil tankers ≥150 gross tonnage and all other ships ≥400 gross tonnage. Supplement Form A (non-tankers) / Form B (tankers). Oil Record Book: retained onboard ≥3 years from the date of the last entry. ORB Part I (Machinery Space, all ships ≥400 GT, tankers ≥150 GT): Codes A–I covering bunkering, sludge disposal, bilge discharge, and filtering-equipment condition. ORB Part II (Cargo/Ballast, tankers ≥150 GT): Codes A–R covering loading, COW, ballasting, slop discharge, and ODMCS condition. ⚗ The Physics of Load on Top (LOT) 1. TANK WASHINGS → wash water routed to slop tank 2. GRAVITY SEPARATION → oil floats, water settles 3. DECANTING → clean bottom water discharged via ODMCS; oil residue retained 4. CO-MINGLED LOADING → next cargo loaded on top of retained residue 📏 Tanker Discharge Criteria — Regulation 34 (Corrected) Outside a designated Special Area More than 50 nautical miles from the nearest land Vessel underway, en route, at ≥7 knots Instantaneous rate of discharge ≤ 30 litres per nautical mile Total oil discharged ≤ 1/30,000 of the total quantity of the particular cargo from which the residue formed ODMCS and slop tank arrangement operational — oil content and discharge rate are governed by these rate/quantity limits monitored by the ODMCS, not by a fixed ppm figure (that 15 ppm limit applies to machinery-space bilge discharge under Reg. 15, a separate regime) 🛢 Slop Tank Structural Capacity Configuration Minimum Slop Tank Capacity Standard baseline 3% of total oil carrying capacity Eductor-supply tank washing only 2% Segregated Ballast Tanks (SBT) 2% SBT + eductor-supply washing 1.5% Combination carrier, smooth bulkheads 1% Combination carrier, eductor-supply washing 0.8% All new oil tankers of 70,000 DWT and above must be fitted with at least two slop tanks. (Per MARPOL Annex I slop tank design criteria and associated IMO guidelines — raw citation markers from the source draft removed.) CE Oral Tip — Nair Sir: Never quote a fixed ppm figure for tanker cargo-washing discharge — Nair specifically tests for this confusion. State the rate (30 L/NM) and quantity (1/30,000) limits, and reserve 15 ppm strictly for machinery-space bilge water under Regulation 15. 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1: Explain the mandatory discharge parameters for an oil tanker discharging cargo tank washings under Regulation 34. The vessel must be outside a designated Special Area, more than 50 NM from the nearest land, underway en route, with the instantaneous discharge rate not exceeding 30 L/NM, and the total oil discharged not exceeding 1/30,000 of the cargo quantity from which the residue formed, with an operational ODMCS and slop tank arrangement. Q2: Under what code must a routine bilge water transfer and discharge be recorded in the Oil Record Book Part I? Internal transfer of bilge water from the bilge wells to the holding tank is logged under Code (D); the subsequent processing and discharge via the 15 ppm oily water separator is logged separately, recording start/stop times, the processing tank, and confirmation that the filtering equipment was operational below the 15 ppm alarm threshold. Q3: What are the slop tank capacity rules for a tanker fitted with Segregated Ballast Tanks (SBT)? The baseline 3% requirement drops to 2% for SBT-fitted tankers, and further to 1.5% if the tank-washing system also relies on eductor water supply rather than cargo pumps. ✍ Written Exam Questions 5M List the 10 designated Special Areas under MARPOL Annex I and identify the geographical boundaries of the Mediterranean Sea Special Area. 10M Draw a flowchart of the Load on Top (LOT) process and explain the physics that allow gravity separation to prevent pollution. 15M Analyze the regulatory and legal liabilities associated with shipboard record-keeping under MARPOL Annex I. Tanker discharge (Reg. 34): ≥7 kn, >50 NM, ≤30 L/NM, ≤1/30,000 of cargo — never "34 ppm." IOPP thresholds: tankers ≥150 GT, all others ≥400 GT. ORB retention: 3 years from last entry. ⚡ Quick Revision Item Key Fact MARPOL 73/78 in force 2 October 1983 Special Areas (current count) 10 (incl. Southern South African waters, Oman area of the Arabian Sea) IOPP threshold Tankers ≥150 GT / others ≥400 GT ORB retention 3 years from last entry Machinery bilge limit <15 ppm (Reg. 15 — separate from tanker Reg. 34) Tanker discharge rate limit ≤30 L/NM, ≤1/30,000 of cargo (Reg. 34 — no fixed ppm) New tanker (≥70,000 DWT) slop tanks Minimum 2 tanks ▶ Deep Dive — Full Reference Detail Why 34 ppm was wrong MARPOL Annex I distinguishes two separate discharge regimes: machinery-space bilge water (Regulation 15, 15 ppm limit, applies to all ships) and tanker cargo-tank washings/oily mixtures from slop tanks (Regulation 34, rate- and quantity-based limits, applies to oil tankers). section_title: Q2: What are the precise legal conditions for a MARPOL amendment to be rejected via tacit acceptance?
text: A valid blocking minority of contracting governments must file formal written objections with the IMO Secretary-General within the tacit-acceptance window (minimum 10 months for MARPOL). Rejection requires either (1) at least one-third of all contracting governments to object, or (2) objecting states whose combined merchant fleets represent not less than 50% of world gross merchant shipping tonnage. If neither threshold is met, the amendment is deemed accepted and enters into force exactly 6 months later.

section_title: The IMO Legislative Framework & Amendment Mechanisms
text: Topic 7 The IMO Legislative Framework & Amendment Mechanisms IMO Governance Uday pp. 26–33 Examiner: Nair ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: The quorum (⅓ present) and adoption (⅔ majority) figures below are correctly aligned with SOLAS Article VIII and MARPOL Article 16. The "1/3–2/3–50%" blocking-minority rule is an accurate exam mnemonic summarising those articles, not a word-for-word quotation — for written answers always cite SOLAS Article VIII / MARPOL Article 16 directly rather than quoting the mnemonic as convention text. 📖 Definition This topic establishes the structural framework of maritime legislation — the legal hierarchy that governs a Chief Engineer's statutory liabilities — and explains how international instruments are proposed, adopted, and systematically amended to keep pace with evolving technology and safety needs. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) A uniform legislative framework prevents conflicting unilateral regional rules — every flag applies the same technical baseline. Understanding how a resolution becomes binding law is critical to avoiding PSC detentions, contractual delays, or criminal liability for non-compliance. Knowing municipal legal hierarchy (Acts → Rules → Regulations) explains why a flag state notice, not the IMO resolution itself, is what actually binds the vessel. 📅 Historical Background Historically, amendments required "explicit acceptance" — a fixed percentage (typically two-thirds) of contracting states had to formally ratify before entry into force, a process that could take up to a decade. To fix this dangerous lag, IMO introduced Tacit Acceptance through convention revisions in the early 1970s, flipping the legal default from "rejected unless explicitly accepted" to "accepted unless explicitly objected to." ⚖ Regulatory References IMO Convention, Part XI Functions and interactions of the principal committees SOLAS Article VIII Legal framework, timeframes and criteria for amending SOLAS MARPOL Article 16 Procedures for adopting and enforcing MARPOL amendments 🏛 Hierarchy of IMO Instruments CONVENTIONS → Binding primary treaties (SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW) PROTOCOLS → Major structural amendments to an existing convention CODES → Mandatory technical rules once referenced by a convention chapter (ISM, IGF, ISPS) RESOLUTIONS → Formal committee-approved mandates (Assembly / MSC / MEPC) CIRCULARS → Interpretative guidance and clarifications (non-mandatory) 🔢 Statutory Nomenclature Resolution format — Body.Number(Session): e.g. MSC.374(93) = 374th resolution of the Maritime Safety Committee, adopted at its 93rd session. Circular format — Body.Category/Circ.Number: e.g. MSC.1/Circ.1501 = sub-category 1 under MSC, informational circular #1501. ⏱ The Amendment Lifecycle — Explicit vs. Tacit Acceptance 1. PROPOSAL → submitted to IMO Secretary-General by a contracting government 2. REVIEW & DRAFT → routed to MSC or MEPC for technical drafting 3. ADOPTION → quorum ≥⅓ of contracting governments present; vote ≥⅔ of those present and voting 4. ACCEPTANCE → tacit period runs (SOLAS min. 15 months / MARPOL min. 10 months, max. 24 months) unless a blocking minority objects 5. ENTRY INTO FORCE → exactly 6 months after acceptance, for both SOLAS and MARPOL Criterion Amendment by Conference Tacit Acceptance Quorum ≥⅓ of contracting states attend ≥⅓ of contracting states present for the vote Adoption vote ≥⅔ majority of attendees ≥⅔ majority of committee present & voting Acceptance Explicit ratification by each state Assumed accepted unless a blocking minority objects Blocking minority Not applicable — non-signers simply not bound ≥⅓ of states object, OR objectors represent ≥50% of world gross merchant tonnage Timeframe Historically 5–12 years, unpredictable SOLAS ≥15 months / MARPOL ≥10 months, max 24 months to acceptance, +6 months buffer to force CE Oral Tip — Nair Sir: When Nair asks about tacit acceptance, always name the source articles (SOLAS Article VIII, MARPOL Article 16) before reciting the 1/3–2/3–50% figures — reciting numbers without the legal source reads as a memorised mnemonic rather than regulatory knowledge, and he marks that down. 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1: Explain the fundamental difference between an IMO Resolution and an IMO Circular, and how each affects your day-to-day management. A Resolution is a formal legislative instrument adopted by the Assembly, MSC, or MEPC to adopt conventions, protocols, or amendments; once it passes tacit acceptance and enters into force it becomes a mandatory international requirement enforced through domestic flag-state law. A Circular is an informational document issued by a committee or sub-committee providing technical clarification or uniform interpretation — generally non-mandatory, but widely used by PSC officers and ROs as the definitive technical benchmark during surveys. As Chief Engineer, I treat resolutions as mandatory structural/operational targets and circulars as the practical guide for meeting them. Q2: What are the precise legal conditions for a MARPOL amendment to be rejected via tacit acceptance? A valid blocking minority of contracting governments must file formal written objections with the IMO Secretary-General within the tacit-acceptance window (minimum 10 months for MARPOL). Rejection requires either (1) at least one-third of all contracting governments to object, or (2) objecting states whose combined merchant fleets represent not less than 50% of world gross merchant shipping tonnage. If neither threshold is met, the amendment is deemed accepted and enters into force exactly 6 months later. Q3: Decode MSC.1/Circ.1501. "MSC.1/" identifies the originating body (Maritime Safety Committee) and its technical sub-category; "Circ." identifies the instrument as an informational/interpretative circular rather than a mandatory resolution; "1501" is the unique chronological index number. Operationally it provides unified global interpretation of a safety matter which shipboard management should align with for flag-state and PSC expectations. ✍ Written Exam Questions 5M Outline the precise voting and quorum requirements mandated within the MSC for the legal adoption of a SOLAS amendment. 10M Explain the structural and legal distinctions between a Convention, a Protocol, and a mandatory Technical Code. Detail how a code transitions from a non-binding recommendation into a mandatory statutory instrument. 15M Analyze the historical transition from Explicit Acceptance to Tacit Acceptance for maritime amendments. Construct a detailed timeline of a SOLAS amendment's lifecycle from proposal to shipboard entry into force, explaining the legal parameters governing each phase. 🧠 Memory Box 1/3 – 2/3 – 50% Rule (exam mnemonic, not literal article text): ⅓ = minimum quorum to hold a vote; ⅔ = majority needed to adopt; ⅓ of states (or states representing ≥50% of global gross tonnage) can block via formal objection before the tacit deadline. 6-month buffer — fixed for both SOLAS and MARPOL between acceptance and entry into force. Acts → Rules → Regulations — Parliament → ministerial decree → statutory technical directive. ⚡ Quick Revision Item Key Fact Adoption quorum ≥⅓ of contracting states present Adoption vote ≥⅔ majority of present & voting Tacit rejection threshold ≥⅓ of states object, or objectors = ≥50% of global gross tonnage Entry-into-force buffer Exactly 6 months post-acceptance (SOLAS & MARPOL) Resolution format Body.Number(Session) — e.g. MSC.374(93) Circular format Body.Category/Circ.Number — e.g. MSC.1/Circ.1501 ▶ Deep Dive — Full Reference Detail Failure to Implement — PSC Consequence Any failure to implement an adopted amendment after its formal entry-into-force date is a high-risk PSC detention ground. Claiming ignorance of a tacitly accepted amendment, or a delay in receiving a company circular, is not accepted as a valid defense by boarding officers. Municipal Transposition International conventions are not self-executing — they must be transposed into domestic legislation. In India, the Merchant Shipping Act provides the constitutional/legal authority; rules and regulations issued under DGS authority give the technical detail that flag-state surveyors and PSC actually enforce. 📚 References IMO — Amendment Procedure (official) SOLAS 1974 consolidated text — Article VIII 🔗 Related QB Questions: QB4 — IMO Governance QB3 — MARPOL & PSC Notes-p2 · T7 · v1.0

SDG 6 (Clean Water & Sanitation): aligns with MARPOL Annex IV controls on sewage and graywater discharge. SDG 13 (Climate Action): aligns with the IMO GHG Strategy via EEDI, EEXI, and CII. SDG 14 (Life Below Water): supports Ballast Water Management, oil-spill prevention, underwater-noise mitigation. Global data indicates women make up approximately 1.2% of the global seafarer workforce — an industry statistic, not a regulatory figure — reflecting an estimated 45.8% increase since 2015, driven by targeted training, visibility, and recognition programs. text: MEPC-83 approved in principle a market-based GHG pricing framework applying financial penalties tied to a vessel's emissions relative to its targets, structured as a higher-priced tier for larger deficits and a lower-priced tier for smaller deficits, with over-compliant vessels earning tradeable surplus units. section_title: Q1. How would you demonstrate due diligence to a surveyor after a cargo damage claim alleging hold flooding?
text: I would produce a chronological technical file proving the vessel was seaworthy and cargoworthy before and at the beginning of the voyage. First, hatch cover integrity: ultrasonic leak detection or hose test reports dated before loading, identifying the compartments tested, together with the inspection record of rubber packing, compression bars, drain channels and non-return valves. Second, maintenance history: planned maintenance system records showing hatch gasket renewals, cleat overhauls and drainage servicing carried out on schedule with no overdue safety-critical items. Third, bilge management: daily sounding logs for each hold bilge well with actual figures, function test records for the hold bilge high level alarms, and maintenance entries for suction valves and stripping pumps. Fourth, operational data: engine room logs and automated records showing pumping frequency, confirming no abnormal accumulation attributable to mechanical failure. The point I would make to the surveyor is that a flat, credible sounding record through the heavy weather period is positive evidence that no ingress occurred, not merely an absence of evidence.

section_title: Q2. What is inherent vice, and how does the engine department's documentation support that defence?
text: Inherent vice is a quality or defect within the cargo itself that causes it to deteriorate without any external operational fault — classically bulk grain loaded above its safe storage moisture content, which self-heats and moulds when the cargo passes through changing climatic zones. It is a listed carrier exception under Article IV rule 2(m) of the Hague-Visby Rules. The engine department supports the defence with the ventilation record: daily ambient and hold dew points, cargo temperatures, and the ventilation decision taken with its reason, showing that ventilation was applied or suspended correctly under the Dew Point Rule or the Three Degree Rule. Combined with the pre-shipment quality certificate showing the loaded moisture content, that record shows the damage was a property of the cargo rather than a failure of care. Without the ventilation log the defence generally fails, because the carrier cannot show it discharged its Article III rule 2 duty to care for the goods.

section_title: Q3. Distinguish tackle-to-tackle from port-to-port liability, and explain why it matters to the P&I club.
text: Tackle-to-tackle is the Hague-Visby period of responsibility defined in Article I(e): from the time the goods are loaded on to the time they are discharged from the ship. Damage occurring on the quay before loading begins, or after discharge is complete, falls outside the statutory regime. Port-to-port is the Hamburg Rules scope, covering the whole period the goods are in the carrier's charge at the port of loading, during carriage, and at the port of discharge, including shore-side storage and transhipment. It matters to the P&I club because the port-to-port regime substantially widens the owner's exposure to risks the ship's staff do not control — stevedore handling, terminal storage, transhipment custody — which changes both the premium and the documentation the club will require. Note that the older textbook phrasing of "the ship's rail" is not the statutory test; the Rules speak of loading on and discharging from the ship.

section_title: Q4. Under Hague-Visby, when can the carrier lose the right to limit liability altogether?
text: Under Article IV bis rule 4, the carrier is not entitled to the benefit of the limitation of liability if it is proved that the damage resulted from an act or omission of the carrier done with intent to cause damage, or recklessly and with knowledge that damage would probably result. This is a deliberately high threshold — ordinary negligence, even serious negligence, does not break the limit. What can reach it is a documented decision taken with knowledge: sailing with a hatch cover known to be leaking and known to be over that cargo, or operating a system that has been formally condemned. It is worth noting that Article IV bis also extends the Rules' defences and limits to claims brought in tort and to the carrier's servants and agents, which is why the same limits protect the crew personally.

Examiner: Nair ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: Three corrections. (1) Wrong Article cited for limitation. The draft twice attributed the 666.67 SDR / 2 SDR per kilogram limits to " Article IV bis ". They are in Article IV, rule 5(a) . Article IV bis is a different provision — inserted by the Visby Protocol — which extends the carrier's defences and limits to claims framed in tort and to the carrier's servants and agents (the "Himalaya" provision), and removes the limit where damage resulted from an act or omission done with intent to cause damage or recklessly with knowledge that damage would probably result. Both citations have been corrected and the Article IV bis content added, because the recklessness carve-out is itself examinable. (2) "Ship's rail" used as the liability boundary. Article I(e) of the Hague-Visby Rules defines carriage of goods as covering the period from the time the goods are loaded on to the time they are discharged from the ship. "Tackle-to-tackle" is the accepted shorthand for that period, but the ship's rail is not the statutory test and the phrase was deleted from Incoterms in 2010 for the same reason. Corrected throughout. (3) Deck cargo comparison row. The draft's table said deck cargo is excluded under Hague-Visby "unless explicitly agreed or in container ships". More precisely: Article I(c) excludes from the definition of "goods" cargo which by the contract of carriage is stated as being carried on deck and is so carried . Containers carried on deck on a purpose-built containership are generally treated as within the Rules because that carriage is not a departure from the contract. Reworded. 📖 Definition A cargo liability regime allocates risk between carrier and cargo interest by fixing a floor of non-excludable carrier duties, a defined list of defences, and a ceiling on financial exposure. Part 19 Topic 5 dealt with how these regimes came into being and what they say. This topic deals with the operational question that follows: how does a regime actually attach to a given voyage, and what evidence does the engine room have to produce when a claim lands? ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) A charterparty is a private contract — no cargo regime applies to it automatically. The Clause Paramount is the mechanism that brings the Rules in, and with them the carrier's defences and limits. Without it, the owner is exposed on ordinary common-law terms. The liability period defines what you are answerable for. Under tackle-to-tackle, damage on the quay before loading is not the carrier's problem; under port-to-port it may be. That single boundary decides whether a claim is even admissible. The due diligence defence is proved almost entirely from engineering records — ultrasonic hatch cover tests, hold bilge alarm function tests, daily sounding logs, ventilation and dew point records. These are not paperwork chores; they are the evidence file. Inherent vice is the carrier's strongest defence on wet bulk cargo damage, but it only works if the ventilation record proves the crew did everything right. A missing ventilation log converts a shipper's problem into an owner's liability. 📅 Historical Background 1924 Hague Rules — tackle-to-tackle scope; £100 gold per package 1968 Visby Protocol — raises limits to 10,000 Poincaré gold francs per package or 30 francs per kg; inserts Article IV bis 1979 SDR Protocol — gold francs replaced by IMF Special Drawing Rights 1978 Hamburg Rules — port-to-port scope; presumed fault; nautical fault abolished 2008 Rotterdam Rules — door-to-door scope; not in force 2016 SDR basket composition: USD, EUR, CNY, JPY, GBP 10 Sep 2025 India: Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 commences — Hague-Visby basis ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments Hague-Visby, Art. I(e) Defines "carriage of goods" as the period from the time the goods are loaded on to the time they are discharged from the ship — the tackle-to-tackle period. Hague-Visby, Art. I(c) Excludes from "goods" cargo stated in the contract as carried on deck and so carried, and live animals. Hague-Visby, Art. III r.1 Due diligence before and at the beginning of the voyage: make the ship seaworthy; properly man, equip and supply her; make holds, refrigerating and cool chambers fit and safe for reception, carriage and preservation. Hague-Visby, Art. IV r.2 Seventeen exceptions (a)–(q) — nautical fault, fire without actual fault or privity, perils of the sea, act of God, inherent vice (m), insufficiency of packing, and the catch-all (q). Hague-Visby, Art. IV r.5(a) Limitation: 666.67 SDR per package or unit, or 2 SDR per kilogram of gross weight, whichever is higher. Hague-Visby, Art. IV bis Defences and limits apply to claims in tort and extend to servants and agents; the limit is lost where damage resulted from an act or omission done with intent to cause damage, or recklessly and with knowledge that damage would probably result. SOLAS Ch. II-1 Watertight integrity, bilge pumping arrangements — the technical baseline for cargoworthiness. SOLAS Ch. VI, Reg. 2 & 5 Cargo information (including verified gross mass) and stowage and securing. STCW Convention Competency of the crew — the manning limb of Article III rule 1. 📎 The Clause Paramount A Clause Paramount is a contractual clause in a bill of lading or charterparty that expressly incorporates a cargo liability regime — normally the Hague or Hague-Visby Rules — into the contract, and provides that the incorporated Rules prevail over any inconsistent term. It exists because the Rules apply compulsorily only in defined circumstances. A charterparty is a freely negotiated private contract and is expressly excluded from compulsory application. Without a Clause Paramount, the owner has neither the statutory defences of Article IV rule 2 nor the limitation of Article IV rule 5 — the exposure reverts to whatever the contract and the governing common law provide. Is the regime enacted in the country of SHIPMENT? ├── YES ──> applies compulsorily to outbound shipments └── NO │ Is the regime enacted in the country of DESTINATION? ├── YES ──> may apply compulsorily to inbound shipments └── NO │ Does the contract contain a CLAUSE PARAMOUNT? ├── YES ──> the regime applies contractually └── NO ──> local law / common law governs That decision tree is a teaching model of how municipal enactments bite, not a uniform IMO hierarchy. The detail varies by enacting state — for India, the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 2025 applies to ships carrying goods from any port in India to any other port, whether in or outside India, and requires bills issued in India to state expressly that they take effect subject to the Rules. 📏 Scope: Tackle-to-Tackle, Port-to-Port, Door-to-Door Regime Period of responsibility Practical consequence Hague / Hague-Visby Tackle-to-tackle — from loading on to discharge from the ship (Art. I(e)) Damage on the quay before loading or after discharge falls outside the statutory liability window. Hamburg Rules Port-to-port — the whole period the goods are in the carrier's charge at the port of loading, in carriage, and at the port of discharge Extends exposure to shore-side custody and transhipment; demands far tighter custody documentation. Rotterdam Rules Door-to-door — receipt to delivery, including inland legs ( not in force ) Would bring multimodal legs inside a single maritime-plus regime. I(c)); containers on deck of a containership normally inside Covered, with conditions Covered Time bar 1 year (Art. III r.6) 2 years 2 years 🧮 SDR Mechanics and the Limitation Calculation The Special Drawing Right is an international reserve asset created by the International Monetary Fund, valued against a basket of five currencies — US dollar, euro, Chinese renminbi, Japanese yen and pound sterling. Using SDR rather than a national currency insulates the limit from the inflation and devaluation that destroyed the £100 gold limit of 1924. Maximum liability: L max = the greater of (N × 666.67) and (W × 2) , in SDR where N is the number of packages or units and W the gross weight in kilograms of the goods lost or damaged. The higher figure applies, so the claimant in practice selects whichever basis favours them. For heavy, low-count cargo the weight basis wins; for numerous light packages the package basis wins. Worked check. 100 drums, total gross weight 40,000 kg, all damaged. Package basis: 100 × 666.67 = 66,667 SDR. Weight basis: 40,000 × 2 = 80,000 SDR. The weight basis is higher, so the limit is 80,000 SDR. Reverse the numbers — 500 cartons of 20 kg each, total 10,000 kg — and the package basis (333,335 SDR) far exceeds the weight basis (20,000 SDR). Container enumeration (Art. IV r.5(c)). Where the bill of lading enumerates the packages inside a container, each enumerated package counts. Where it does not, the container itself is one package. Loss of the limit (Art. IV bis r.4). The carrier cannot limit at all where the damage resulted from an act or omission done with intent to cause damage, or recklessly and with knowledge that damage would probably result — a high threshold, but one that a documented decision to sail with a known unrepairable defect can reach. 🔍 Building the Due Diligence Evidence File Hatch cover weathertightness. Ultrasonic leak detection or hose test results dated before loading, with the tested compartments identified. Physical condition record of rubber packing, compression bars, drain channels and non-return valves. Hold bilge system. Function test of each hold bilge high level alarm, with date and result per hold. Strum box condition, suction valve operation, stripping pump capacity test. Daily soundings. Every hold bilge well, every day, recorded with an actual figure — not "dry" as a standing entry. A flat, plausible record with no spike through heavy weather is affirmative proof that no ingress occurred. Ventilation and dew point. Ambient and cargo temperatures, dew points, and the ventilation decision taken with the reason. This is what defeats a moisture-damage claim. PMS and defect status. No overdue safety-critical jobs on the systems implicated; open defects risk-assessed and reported. Ventilation rules for hygroscopic bulk cargo. The Dew Point Rule : ventilate only when the dew point of the outside air is lower than the dew point of the air in the hold. The Three Degree Rule : ventilate when the outside air temperature is at least 3 °C below the average cargo temperature at loading. Either rule is defensible if applied consistently and logged; what is not defensible is ventilating on instinct and recording nothing. Inherent vice. If the pre-shipment quality certificate shows grain loaded above its safe storage moisture content — for maize commonly cited around 14 to 14.5% — self-heating and mould are a property of the cargo, not a failure of the ship. Scope ladder: tackle-to-tackle (HV) → port-to-port (Hamburg) → door-to-door (Rotterdam, not in force). F-P-I-N-S — the headline Article IV r.2 immunities: F ire (no actual fault or privity), P erils of the sea, I nherent vice, N avigation or management error, in S ufficiency of packing. Dew Point Rule: ventilate only when outside dew point is LOWER than hold dew point. Three Degree Rule: outside air at least 3 °C below cargo temperature at loading. ▶ Deep Dive — Case Study — Bulk Corn, Hold No. 3, New Orleans to Rotterdam The claim A 65,000 DWT Panamax discharges 60,000 tonnes of yellow corn at Rotterdam. The consignee finds microbiological degradation, caking and mould across the top 1.5 metres of Hold No. 3 and alleges unseaworthiness — specifically that defective hatch cover sealing admitted seawater during the North Atlantic passage. Rotterdam is a Hague-Visby jurisdiction, so the Rules apply compulsorily. Step 1 — secure the record before anything else On notification, print, sign and stamp the engine room logbook extracts, the PMS history for hatch cover and bilge systems, and the automated data logger records for hold bilge pumping. Doing this immediately, and dating it, forecloses any later allegation that records were reconstructed after the claim was known. Step 2 — hatch cover integrity Retrieve the pre-loading ultrasonic leak detection report for Hold No. 3 and confirm it identifies that hatch specifically. Physically inspect rubber packing for permanent set, cracking and compression, the compression bars for distortion, the drain channels for blockage, and the non-return drain valves for correct seating. Photograph everything before any remedial work. Step 3 — bilge evidence Extract the daily Hold No. 3 bilge well soundings. If the readings are flat and low through the heavy weather period, with no step change, seawater ingress through the hatch covers is effectively excluded — water entering a hold does not stay in the cargo, it drains to the well. Support this with the high level alarm function test record and the stripping pump capacity check. On my vessel (Maersk A/S container tonnage) The container analogue is the reefer claim. The same logic applies: continuous supply and return air temperature logs, power interruption events with durations, and defrost cycles are what separate "the cargo was already deteriorating" from "the ship failed to care for it". section_title: Q1. The charterer's surveyor records a bunker ROB significantly below your engine room figures at an on-hire survey. What do you do?
text: I would not sign the surveyor's figure as presented, and I would not simply refuse to sign either, since that delays delivery and creates a separate claim. I would request a joint re-measurement and conduct it methodically. First, manual soundings of every tank on board using the ship's certified sounding tapes and water-finding paste — bunker tanks, settling, service, overflow, drain and sludge tanks — with trim and list recorded and the sounding table corrections applied. Second, take the temperature of each tank and correct the observed volume to 15 degrees using the volume correction factor from ASTM Table 54B, then apply the density at 15 degrees from the Bunker Delivery Note, less 0.0011 for weight in air. Third, account separately for unpumpable dead bottoms below the suction bellmouths and for fuel held in the transfer and treatment piping, purifiers, heaters and service system — this is usually where a surveyor's figure goes low. Fourth, produce the flow meter calibration certificates and confirm the anti-tamper seals are intact. If the surveyor still will not align, I sign the statement of quantity under formal protest with a tank-by-tank annexure of the differences, and issue a Letter of Protest to the owner and the P&I club the same day.

section_title: Q2. When does a bill of lading stop being merely prima facie evidence of what was received?
text: Under Article III rule 4 of the Hague-Visby Rules, the bill of lading is prima facie evidence of receipt of the goods as described, meaning that as between the carrier and the original shipper the carrier may prove the contrary — for example that the actual weight differed from the declared figure. However, proof to the contrary is not admissible once the bill has been transferred to a third party acting in good faith. At that point the description becomes conclusive against the carrier. This is the practical reason a Master clauses a bill rather than signing clean over visibly damaged or short cargo: once the bill is endorsed to a good-faith purchaser, the opportunity to contest the description is gone. Article III rule 5 gives the carrier a counterbalance, in that the shipper is deemed to guarantee the accuracy of the marks, number, quantity and weight and indemnifies the carrier against inaccuracies — but that is a claim against the shipper, not a defence against the endorsee.

section_title: Q3. Why is a bareboat redelivery survey more demanding than a time charter off-hire survey?
text: Because the technical history of the ship during the charter is not the owner's. Under a time or voyage charter the owner retains technical management and crewing, so the maintenance record and machinery condition are the owner's own and continuous. Under a bareboat charter the charterer has taken possession and run the vessel entirely — its own crew, its own planned maintenance system, its own spares policy, and often a different Class society and flag. The redelivery survey therefore has to establish the actual condition of the asset from scratch: open up machinery to assess wear against running hours, inspect tank internals and coating condition, review the complete maintenance and class records for gaps or deferred work, and verify spares and consumables inventories. The commercial purpose is to distinguish fair wear and tear, which the owner accepts, from degradation beyond it, which is a claim against the charterer. It is also a high-risk PSC period, because a change of manager and ISM Company is a targeting factor.

section_title: Q4. Give the calculation sequence from a sounding to a bunker figure in metric tonnes.
text: Take the manual sounding or ullage with the tape, note trim and list, and enter the tank calibration table to obtain the observed volume, applying the trim and list corrections. Measure the tank temperature. Apply the volume correction factor for the observed temperature and density, from ASTM Table 54B for generalised products, to convert observed volume to volume at the standard temperature of 15 degrees Celsius. Multiply that corrected volume by the density at 15 degrees taken from the Bunker Delivery Note. If the figure is required as metric tonnes in air, which is the commercial convention, subtract 0.0011 from the density at 15 degrees before multiplying. Finally, add the quantities held in the treatment and transfer system and identify unpumpable dead bottoms separately, so the total on board and the pumpable quantity are both clear on the statement.

Examiner: Senthil ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: Two corrections and one clarification. (1) e-B/L legal basis. The draft stated that "digital signatures and blockchain-backed tokens carry the same legal weight as traditional paper endorsements". As corrected in Part 19 Topic 2, legal equivalence comes from MLETR-based national legislation — for example the UK Electronic Trade Documents Act 2023 — together with the platform rulebook and, commercially, from the International Group of P&I Clubs' approval of the specific system. The technology is the mechanism for uniqueness and exclusive control, not the source of legal effect. (2) Weight formula incomplete. The draft gave Weight = Volume × ρ t without the volume correction step. In practice the measured (observed) volume is corrected to a standard temperature of 15 °C using the volume correction factor from ASTM Table 54B, and the standard density at 15 °C is then applied, with a weight-in-air correction of 0.0011 subtracted from density for the customary metric tonnes in air figure. The full sequence is given below. (3) Clarification. The draft describes the on-hire dispute as arising "transitioning from a Bareboat Charter to a fixed-term Time Charter". Bunker ROB disputes arise on any delivery or redelivery where bunkers change hands for value — the procedure below applies to all of them, not only to bareboat-to-time transitions. 📖 Definition Charter party operational management is the day-to-day work of making the ship's technical reality match the contract's commercial assumptions — and of proving it when the two are alleged to differ. Part 19 Topic 3 set out the structure of the three chartering regimes. This topic covers the two places where that structure produces disputes the Chief Engineer personally owns: the bunker quantity on delivery and redelivery , and the condition of the ship at handover . ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) The on-hire and off-hire bunker figure is money changing hands on the strength of a measurement the Chief Engineer takes. A 180-tonne discrepancy on VLSFO is a six-figure argument settled by soundings, temperature and correction tables. The independent surveyor's figure is not automatically right. Surveyors routinely miss unpumpable dead bottoms and fuel held in treatment piping, and misapply or omit temperature correction. Signing their statement without checking transfers the error to the owner. A bareboat redelivery survey is the most exhaustive technical audit a Chief Engineer will face outside a renewal survey, because the whole point is to establish whether the returning charterer degraded the asset beyond fair wear and tear. Under a time charter, the same records that defend a bunker figure also defend the speed and consumption warranty. One evidence discipline serves both. 📅 Historical Background 11th c. Bill of lading originates as a ship's clerk's ledger entry 16th c. Becomes a standalone document issued to the shipper 19th c. Develops as a document of title, decoupling trade finance from physical arrival 1968 Hague-Visby Art. III rr.3–5 codify the B/L as prima facie evidence and conclusive against a good-faith transferee 2023 UK Electronic Trade Documents Act gives electronic trade documents legal parity Current International Group of P&I Clubs maintains the list of approved electronic B/L systems ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments Hague-Visby, Art. III r.3 Carrier to issue a bill of lading showing leading marks, number of packages or pieces, or quantity or weight as furnished in writing by the shipper, and the apparent order and condition of the goods. Hague-Visby, Art. III r.4 The bill is prima facie evidence of receipt; proof to the contrary is not admissible once it has been transferred to a third party acting in good faith . Hague-Visby, Art. III r.5 The shipper is deemed to guarantee the accuracy of marks, number, quantity and weight, and indemnifies the carrier against inaccuracies. Hague-Visby, Art. III r.7 Shipped bill of lading to be issued once the goods are loaded. MARPOL Annex VI, Reg. 18 Bunker Delivery Note content and the representative retained sample — the evidential anchor of any fuel dispute. ASTM D1250 / Table 54B Volume correction factor for generalised products, correcting observed volume to 15 °C. ISO 8217 Specification for marine fuels — the technical standard a charterparty bunker clause normally incorporates. 📑 B/L Points That Bite Operationally Prima facie versus conclusive. As between carrier and shipper, the bill is prima facie evidence of what was received — the carrier can prove the contrary. Once it is transferred to a third party acting in good faith, Article III rule 4 makes it conclusive . That is why a clean bill signed over visibly damaged cargo cannot be unwound later. Shipper's guarantee. Under Article III rule 5 the shipper guarantees the accuracy of quantity and weight and indemnifies the carrier — which is the legal reason draft surveys and tank dips matter, since they are the carrier's independent check on the figure it is being asked to certify. "To order" versus named consignee. A "to order" bill is negotiable by endorsement and delivery and is what makes mid-voyage resale possible. A straight bill names the consignee and is not negotiable. Presentation of an original remains the safe operational rule for both (see Part 19 Topic 2 and The Rafaela S ). Misdelivery. Delivery without production of an original bill is outside standard P&I cover. Commercial pressure from a charterer does not change that, and a letter of indemnity moves the risk onto the indemnifier's balance sheet rather than removing it. ⛽ The Bunker Quantity Dispute — Full Procedure Scenario. On an on-hire survey a 300,000 DWT VLCC shows a 180 tonne discrepancy in VLSFO between the outgoing figure and the incoming charterer's independent surveyor. The allegation is either concealed fuel or miscalibrated flow meters. The dispute is settled by measurement, not argument. Step 1 — sound everything, manually. Every fuel oil bunker tank, settling tank, service tank, overflow tank, drain tank and sludge tank, using the vessel's certified sounding tapes and water-finding paste. Manual soundings override automated gauge readings, which drift and are frequently uncalibrated. Record trim and list at the time of sounding and apply the correct sounding table corrections. Step 2 — correct for temperature. Measure the actual temperature of each tank. Take the observed volume from the tables, apply the volume correction factor from ASTM Table 54B to obtain the volume at 15 °C, then multiply by the density at 15 °C from the Bunker Delivery Note. For metric tonnes in air, use density at 15 °C minus 0.0011. Step 3 — account for what cannot be pumped. Unpumpable dead bottoms below the suction bellmouth, fuel held in the transfer and treatment piping, in the purifiers and heaters, and in the service system. This is the single commonest cause of a surveyor's figure reading low, and it is a legitimate part of the quantity on board. Step 4 — check the metering. Calibration certificates for the Coriolis mass flow meters, physical integrity of anti-tamper seals on the fuel system, and consistency between the daily engine room logs, the flow meter totals and the Oil Record Book Part I entries. Step 5 — resolve or protest. Present the audited tank-by-tank spreadsheet, jointly signed if the surveyor agrees. If not, sign the statement of quantity under protest , annexing the tank-by-tank differences, and issue a Letter of Protest to the owner and the P&I club the same day.
