Surveyor low? Look for dead bottoms and system hold-up. Surveyor high? Look for a missing temperature correction. Sign under protest, never refuse outright. Letter of Protest to owner and club the same day. B/L: prima facie against the shipper, conclusive against a good-faith transferee (Art. III r.4). Bareboat redelivery = the deepest survey — the charterer, not the owner, held technical control. ▶ Deep Dive — Where the 180 Tonnes Actually Went The four usual explanations First, temperature. VLSFO in a heated tank at 50 °C occupies materially more volume than the same mass at 15 °C. If the surveyor read observed volume and applied a density figure without the volume correction factor, or applied it in the wrong direction, a large apparent difference appears with no fuel having moved. Second, dead bottoms. On a VLCC the volume below the suction bellmouth across all bunker tanks is substantial and is genuinely on board even though it cannot be pumped — it belongs in the total, identified separately. Third, system hold-up: transfer lines, settling and service tanks, purifier bowls, heaters and the supply and circulating system hold a real and calculable quantity. Fourth, tables and trim: an uncorrected sounding at significant trim on a long tank produces a large error. What almost never explains it Concealment. The allegation is made because it is the only explanation a surveyor can offer for a difference they cannot reconcile, but it requires the fuel to physically exist somewhere unmeasured. Sounding every tank on board, including sludge, overflow and drain tanks, closes that argument definitively — which is why the audit must be exhaustive rather than confined to the bunker tanks in dispute. Making the audit stand up Present the result as a tank-by-tank spreadsheet: tank, sounding, trim/list correction, observed volume, temperature, VCF, volume at 15 °C, density at 15 °C, mass in air, and a remarks column for dead bottom or system content. Invite the surveyor to sound jointly and co-sign each line. A jointly signed spreadsheet ends the dispute at source; a unilateral one still stands as evidence, but only if it was produced on the day. On my vessel (Maersk A/S container tonnage) Liner container tonnage rarely sees full bareboat handovers, but redelivery and delivery bunker surveys on period charters are routine, and the same discipline applies. section_title: Q1. An auxiliary engine piston is pulled at sea. How do you obtain survey credit under a CSM arrangement?
text: Class rules generally allow a qualified and approved Chief Engineer to carry out the examination of certain machinery items at sea, with the attending surveyor granting credit at the next visit on the strength of the documentation. To secure that credit I would assemble the package at the time of the overhaul, not afterwards. First, an official entry in the planned maintenance system and the engine room logbook recording the date, the running hours at overhaul and the reason. Second, complete measurement records taken with calibrated instruments — liner wear at the defined measuring positions, piston ring vertical and radial clearances, gudgeon pin and bearing dimensions, all against the manufacturer's new and maximum-wear figures. Third, dated photographs of the components before cleaning and again after measurement, showing crown condition, ring groove condition and liner cross-hatching. Fourth, the part numbers and batch details of everything fitted. I would then present the compiled package at the next annual attendance so the item is credited without opening the unit again. The exact code letter used to record the credit differs between classification societies, so I would confirm the notation with our own society.

section_title: Q2. What is Form E and how does it relate to the Safety Equipment Survey?
text: Form E is the Record of Equipment for Cargo Ship Safety Equipment, the mandatory supplement to the Cargo Ship Safety Equipment Certificate issued under SOLAS Chapter I Regulation 8 to cargo ships of 500 gross tonnage and above. It lists the exact type, quantity and specification of the life-saving appliances, fire-fighting appliances, navigational equipment and signalling equipment the ship is required to carry. During the Safety Equipment Survey and during any Port State Control inspection it is the primary checklist: the inspector works down Form E and verifies each item physically. Any discrepancy between the record and what is actually on board — a missing immersion suit, an expired pyrotechnic, a lifebuoy light that does not work — is a statutory deficiency, and because Form E is a certificate supplement rather than a ship's document, the discrepancy goes directly against the certificate.

section_title: Q3. Explain the requirements for bottom inspections and when an in-water survey may substitute for drydocking.
text: A minimum of two inspections of the outside of the ship's bottom must be carried out within each five-year certificate period, and the interval between two consecutive inspections must not exceed 36 months. Classification society rules generally permit an in-water survey to substitute for one of those two inspections, typically for ships below about fifteen years of age, provided the ship carries the appropriate in-water survey class notation. The notation prerequisites are usually a high-durability underwater coating system in good condition, external hull markings that reference internal frames and bulkheads so any finding can be located precisely, and arrangements permitting sea inlets and underwater valves to be blanked and examined from outside while afloat. The survey itself is conducted by approved divers or an ROV with real-time video and a surveyor in attendance, covering hull plating, rudder and pintle clearances, propeller condition and sea chest gratings. For older ships both inspections normally have to be carried out in dry dock. The age threshold is class rule, not SOLAS text, and differs between societies.

section_title: Q4. What happens if an annual survey window is missed?
text: Under SOLAS Chapter I Regulation 14, the annual survey must be carried out within three months before or after each anniversary date of the certificate. If the survey is not completed within that period, the certificate ceases to be valid. It becomes valid again on satisfactory completion of the survey. What it does not automatically do is trigger a complete re-survey and re-issue — whether anything beyond the outstanding survey is required is a decision for the flag State on the facts, and there are limited harmonisation and extension provisions in the HSSC guidelines for specific circumstances such as a ship not in a port where a survey can be carried out. The practical position is that the ship should not sail on a certificate that has ceased to be valid; Port State Control treats an invalid statutory certificate as a detainable deficiency, and the P&I and hull cover may also be affected.

section_title: Marine Survey Regimes — HSSC, Drydocking and In-Water Survey, Continuous Machinery Survey and Safety Equipment Certification
text: Part 20 · Topic 3 Marine Survey Regimes — HSSC, Drydocking and In-Water Survey, Continuous Machinery Survey and Safety Equipment Certification HSSC Windows · Drydock vs IWS · CSM · SEQ & Form E Uday pp. 492–500 (approx.) Examiner: Paul ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: Two corrections and one caution. (1) Superseded resolution numbers. The draft cited resolutions A.1156(32) and A.1186(33) for the HSSC Survey Guidelines. Both are revoked. The current instrument is resolution A.1207(34), Survey Guidelines under the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification (HSSC), 2025 , adopted by the 34th IMO Assembly in December 2025, which revokes A.1186(33). The Guidelines are revised on a two-year cycle, so always state the edition year as well as the number and confirm the current one before an examination. A.1207(34) also covers survey items entering into force between 1 January 2023 and 31 December 2025, adds survey requirements for the Code of Safety for Ships Carrying Industrial Personnel, and deletes the Anti-Fouling System Certificate survey provisions (the AFS Convention requires certification but no periodic survey beyond initial issue). (2) Certificate invalidity overstated. The draft said missing an annual survey window "automatically invalidates the certificate, requiring a full re-survey and formal re-authorization". The accurate position under SOLAS I/14 is that the certificate ceases to be valid if the required survey is not completed within the specified period; it is reinstated on satisfactory completion of that survey. A full re-survey is not automatically triggered — that is a flag- and case-specific outcome. Corrected. (3) Caution on CSM code letters. The draft's "Code O / Code C / Code G" nomenclature could not be verified as universal terminology — the substance (open-up in the surveyor's presence; Chief Engineer's survey credited on documentation; approved alternatives to opening up) is standard, but the letter codes vary between classification societies. The concepts are retained; the codes are presented as class-specific administrative labels to be checked against the ship's own society. (4) Cross-reference — Parts 1–18. The general HSSC survey-window and certificate-extension mechanics set out here are also applied, certificate-by-certificate, in Part 3 Topic 13 (MARPOL Annex I Survey Framework — the same rules applied specifically to the IOPP Certificate) and Part 11 Topic 48 (Statutory Survey Engineering — the same rules applied specifically to the Load Line Certificate). Read together for the general framework alongside two worked certificate-specific applications; the underlying survey-window numbers are consistent across all three. 📖 Definition The Harmonized System of Survey and Certification (HSSC) is the IMO framework that aligns the survey intervals and certificate validity periods of SOLAS, Load Lines, MARPOL and the associated mandatory codes into a single five-year cycle with common windows and terminology. Before it, each convention ran its own schedule and the ship was interrupted repeatedly through the year. Continuous Machinery Survey (CSM) and Planned Maintenance System (PMS) survey arrangements then distribute the machinery examination burden across that cycle instead of concentrating it at renewal. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) The survey calendar is the Chief Engineer's operational calendar. Every window has a hard edge, and a certificate that ceases to be valid stops the ship — commercially this is indistinguishable from a machinery breakdown. CSM is the difference between a manageable rolling workload and a crushing renewal-year overhaul programme. Managing the CSM ledger is a planning skill examiners test directly. Survey credit for work done at sea is real money and real time saved, but only if the documentation package — measurements, photographs, running hours, logbook entries — is assembled at the time of the overhaul, not reconstructed for the surveyor. Safety equipment deficiencies are the highest-frequency detention items in the engine department's area: emergency fire pump, lifeboat engine, quick-closing valves. 📅 Historical Background Pre-1988 SOLAS, Load Line and MARPOL surveys run on separate, misaligned schedules 1988 SOLAS and Load Line Protocols introduce the harmonized system 3 Feb 2000 HSSC enters into force MEPC.39(29) / MEPC.132(53) HSSC introduced into MARPOL, and into MARPOL Annex VI 2021 A.1156(32) — HSSC Survey Guidelines 2021 (revoked) 6 Dec 2023 A.1186(33) — HSSC Survey Guidelines 2023 (revoked) Dec 2025 A.1207(34) — HSSC Survey Guidelines, 2025 — current ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments SOLAS Ch. I, Regs. 6–11 Survey and certification framework — inspection and survey, surveys of cargo ship structure, machinery and equipment, maintenance of conditions after survey. SOLAS Ch. I, Reg. 8 Surveys of life-saving appliances and other equipment of cargo ships — the basis of the Cargo Ship Safety Equipment Certificate. SOLAS Ch. I, Reg. 14 Duration and validity of certificates — a certificate ceases to be valid if the required surveys are not completed within the specified periods. Resolution A.1207(34) Survey Guidelines under the HSSC, 2025 — current edition; revokes A.1186(33). Revised biennially. SOLAS Ch. II-1, Reg. 43/44 Emergency source of electrical power — the emergency generator to start and supply the emergency switchboard automatically within 45 seconds. SOLAS Ch. II-2, Reg. 10 Fire fighting — emergency fire pump capacity and the two-jet requirement. IACS UR Z / class rules Continuous survey machinery arrangements, Chief Engineer's survey, PMS survey approval, and in-water survey notations. 🗓 The HSSC Survey Hierarchy Yr 0 Yr 1 Yr 2 Yr 3 Yr 4 Yr 5 [INITIAL]-------[ANNUAL]--------[ANNUAL]--------[ANNUAL]--------[ANNUAL]--------[RENEWAL] ±3 months ±3 months ±3 months ±3 months expiry └──── INTERMEDIATE replaces the 2nd OR 3rd annual ────┘ └─ renewal may commence at the 4th annual ─┘ Survey Window Scope Initial Before the ship enters service Complete inspection of structure, machinery and equipment against approved drawings and the applicable certificates. Annual ±3 months of each anniversary date General inspection to confirm the ship has been maintained and remains fit — hatch covers, coamings, cleats, ventilation dampers, sounding pipes, safety systems. Intermediate ±3 months of the 2nd or 3rd anniversary; replaces that annual Extended scope — operational testing of bilge and ballast systems, localised thickness gauging where corrosion is evident. Periodical At intervals specified by the Administration Radio installation and certain navigational equipment. Renewal Every 5 years; may commence at the 4th annual and be progressed through the year Comprehensive — thickness measurements, tank testing, machinery open-ups, safety system overhauls; new certificates issued. Additional After a casualty, defect or significant repair General or partial, scoped to the event. Consequence of missing a window. Under SOLAS Chapter I Regulation 14, a certificate ceases to be valid if the required survey is not completed within the specified period. Validity is restored on satisfactory completion. Whether anything more than that survey is required is a flag State decision on the facts — but the ship should not be sailing on an invalid certificate in the meantime, and PSC will treat it as a detainable deficiency. 🛠 Bottom Inspections — Drydock and In-Water Survey A minimum of two inspections of the outside of the ship's bottom must be carried out within each five-year certificate period, and the interval between any two consecutive inspections must not exceed 36 months . Drydocking survey. Hull plating condition and thickness, rudder and pintle clearances, propeller and shaft condition, stern tube bearing wear (poker gauge), sea chest gratings and internal coatings, sacrificial anode wastage, anchor cables ranged and gauged. In-water survey (IWS). Carried out afloat by approved divers or ROV with real-time video and a surveyor in attendance. Class rules generally permit an IWS to substitute for one of the two bottom inspections, typically for ships below about 15 years of age, provided the ship carries the appropriate class notation. The usual notation prerequisites are a high-durability underwater coating system, clear external hull markings referencing internal frames and bulkheads so that findings can be located precisely, and arrangements allowing sea inlets and underwater valves to be blanked and examined from outside while afloat. Age limit caveat. The 15-year threshold is a classification society rule, not convention text, and differs between societies. State it as class practice, not as SOLAS. ⚙ Continuous Machinery Survey and PMS Survey Under a CSM arrangement, the machinery items that would otherwise all be examined at renewal are distributed across the five-year cycle so that roughly 20% are surveyed each year . The surveyor attends annually to audit completed items and witness key open-ups. The alternative is a PMS survey arrangement, in which the ship's approved computerised planned maintenance system, audited periodically, provides the basis for credit against running hours and condition rather than against a fixed list. Parameter Continuous Machinery Survey PMS Survey 5-Year Special Survey Distribution Rolling 5-year cycle, ~20% of items per year Continuous, driven by running hours and condition via an approved database Concentrated in the renewal window Surveyor attendance Annual audit of completed items; witnesses key open-ups Periodic system audit; individual items largely credited from records Attendance for the full programme of open-ups Engine room workload Even, plannable Even, but administratively demanding Severe spike, usually needing riding squads Main benefit Minimises downtime concentrated at renewal Condition-based — maximises component life Administratively simple, operationally punishing Main risk Ledger drift — items slipping to the final year Audit failure if PMS discipline lapses Cost and off-hire exposure at the end of the cycle Open-up in the surveyor's presence. The item is opened, cleaned and measured with the surveyor attending, and credited immediately. Chief Engineer's survey (confirmatory credit). Where an essential item has to be opened at sea, class rules generally allow a qualified and approved Chief Engineer to carry out the examination, with the surveyor granting credit at the next attendance on the strength of the documentation package. Alternative to opening up. Certain items may be credited on the basis of approved non-destructive examination, performance analysis or condition monitoring in lieu of disassembly, preserving established running clearances. The documentation package that earns Chief Engineer's credit: PMS and logbook entry with date, running hours and reason for the overhaul; calibrated micrometer and clearance sheets (liner wear at defined positions, ring vertical and radial clearances, pin and bearing dimensions); dated photographs before cleaning and after measurement showing crown condition, ring grooves and liner cross-hatching; part numbers and batch details of components fitted. The letter codes used to record these categories vary between classification societies. Learn the substance — attended open-up, Chief Engineer's survey, approved alternative — and check the coding used by the ship's own society rather than quoting a code letter that may not exist in that society's system. 🧯 Safety Equipment Survey and Form E Cargo ships of 500 GT and above must hold a Cargo Ship Safety Equipment Certificate issued under SOLAS Chapter I Regulation 8, supplemented by the Record of Equipment, Form E . Form E lists the exact type, quantity and specification of the equipment the ship is required to carry, and functions as the checklist against which both the survey and any PSC inspection are conducted. Any discrepancy between Form E and the physical equipment on board is a statutory deficiency. System Survey focus Test method Lifeboat launching appliances Davit arm structure, sheaves, suspension hooks, on-load release gear Five-yearly dynamic winch brake test using water weights; annual and five-yearly examination of release gear Fixed fire-extinguishing systems Cylinder contents and weights, distribution piping, release manifold, alarms Blow-through of distribution piping with air to confirm nozzles are clear; alarm and ventilation damper function test Emergency fire pump Prime, discharge pressure, independence of power supply Live test delivering the required two jets at the required pressure Emergency generator Automatic start and connection, fuel supply, battery condition Dead-ship simulation — must start and supply the emergency switchboard within 45 seconds Navigation and radio Gyro error, radar alignment, EPIRB and SART currency, battery endurance Comparison against magnetic compass; battery endurance test; date checks on pyrotechnics, EPIRB battery and hydrostatic release The three recurring detention items in this area: an emergency fire pump that will not prime or cannot hold pressure; lifeboat engines that will not start on their own batteries; and fuel tank quick-closing valves that have been wire-tied, wedged or otherwise disabled. The last is the most damaging, because it is not a maintenance failure — it is visible evidence of a deliberate decision to defeat a safety system, and it colours the inspector's view of everything else on board. 🎓 CE Oral Tip (Paul): Paul examines surveys as a system, not as a list of dates. Expect him to give you a scenario — "your intermediate survey window closes next month and you are mid-ocean" — and watch whether you know the window is ±3 months around the second or third anniversary and that it replaces that annual survey, not supplements it. On resolutions, quote the current edition with its year: A.1207(34), Survey Guidelines under the HSSC, 2025 . Candidates still quoting A.1156(32) are giving a 2021 answer. If he moves to CSM, the winning detail is the documentation package for Chief Engineer's credit — micrometer sheets, dated photographs, running hours, PMS entry — assembled at the time of the overhaul. 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1. An auxiliary engine piston is pulled at sea. How do you obtain survey credit under a CSM arrangement? Class rules generally allow a qualified and approved Chief Engineer to carry out the examination of certain machinery items at sea, with the attending surveyor granting credit at the next visit on the strength of the documentation. To secure that credit I would assemble the package at the time of the overhaul, not afterwards. First, an official entry in the planned maintenance system and the engine room logbook recording the date, the running hours at overhaul and the reason. Second, complete measurement records taken with calibrated instruments — liner wear at the defined measuring positions, piston ring vertical and radial clearances, gudgeon pin and bearing dimensions, all against the manufacturer's new and maximum-wear figures. Third, dated photographs of the components before cleaning and again after measurement, showing crown condition, ring groove condition and liner cross-hatching. Fourth, the part numbers and batch details of everything fitted. I would then present the compiled package at the next annual attendance so the item is credited without opening the unit again. The exact code letter used to record the credit differs between classification societies, so I would confirm the notation with our own society. Q2. What is Form E and how does it relate to the Safety Equipment Survey? Form E is the Record of Equipment for Cargo Ship Safety Equipment, the mandatory supplement to the Cargo Ship Safety Equipment Certificate issued under SOLAS Chapter I Regulation 8 to cargo ships of 500 gross tonnage and above. It lists the exact type, quantity and specification of the life-saving appliances, fire-fighting appliances, navigational equipment and signalling equipment the ship is required to carry. During the Safety Equipment Survey and during any Port State Control inspection it is the primary checklist: the inspector works down Form E and verifies each item physically. Any discrepancy between the record and what is actually on board — a missing immersion suit, an expired pyrotechnic, a lifebuoy light that does not work — is a statutory deficiency, and because Form E is a certificate supplement rather than a ship's document, the discrepancy goes directly against the certificate. Q3. Explain the requirements for bottom inspections and when an in-water survey may substitute for drydocking. A minimum of two inspections of the outside of the ship's bottom must be carried out within each five-year certificate period, and the interval between two consecutive inspections must not exceed 36 months. Classification society rules generally permit an in-water survey to substitute for one of those two inspections, typically for ships below about fifteen years of age, provided the ship carries the appropriate in-water survey class notation. The notation prerequisites are usually a high-durability underwater coating system in good condition, external hull markings that reference internal frames and bulkheads so any finding can be located precisely, and arrangements permitting sea inlets and underwater valves to be blanked and examined from outside while afloat. The survey itself is conducted by approved divers or an ROV with real-time video and a surveyor in attendance, covering hull plating, rudder and pintle clearances, propeller condition and sea chest gratings. For older ships both inspections normally have to be carried out in dry dock. The age threshold is class rule, not SOLAS text, and differs between societies. Q4. What happens if an annual survey window is missed? Under SOLAS Chapter I Regulation 14, the annual survey must be carried out within three months before or after each anniversary date of the certificate. If the survey is not completed within that period, the certificate ceases to be valid. It becomes valid again on satisfactory completion of the survey. What it does not automatically do is trigger a complete re-survey and re-issue — whether anything beyond the outstanding survey is required is a decision for the flag State on the facts, and there are limited harmonisation and extension provisions in the HSSC guidelines for specific circumstances such as a ship not in a port where a survey can be carried out. The practical position is that the ship should not sail on a certificate that has ceased to be valid; Port State Control treats an invalid statutory certificate as a detainable deficiency, and the P&I and hull cover may also be affected. ✍ Written Exam Focus 5 State the scheduling windows for the annual and intermediate surveys under the HSSC and explain the effect on certificate validity of failing to complete a survey within its window. 10 A ten-year-old cargo ship is preparing for a mid-cycle bottom inspection. (a) Detail the technical requirements that must be satisfied before an in-water survey may substitute for drydocking under classification society rules. (b) Describe the checks a surveyor performs on the rudder and propeller assembly during an in-water survey using divers or an ROV. 15 Compare the Continuous Machinery Survey arrangement with the traditional five-year special survey. Draft an engineering procedure for preparing, executing and documenting the five-yearly full-load operational testing of the emergency power supply and emergency fire pumping systems, stating the regulatory performance benchmarks that must be demonstrated. 🧠 Memory Box Annual ±3 months. Intermediate ±3 months of the 2nd or 3rd anniversary, replacing that annual. Renewal may start at the 4th annual. Two bottom inspections in 5 years, maximum 36 months apart. IWS may replace one, class notation and (typically) under 15 years. CSM ≈ 20% of machinery items per year. Credit routes: attended open-up · Chief Engineer's survey · approved alternative to opening up. Current HSSC Survey Guidelines: A.1207(34), 2025 edition — revoked A.1186(33), which revoked A.1156(32). Revised every two years. S-L-E-R-P — Safety Construction, Load Line, Safety Equipment, Safety Radio, IOPP. Emergency generator: on the board within 45 seconds. ▶ Deep Dive — Running a Combined Renewal, Drydock and CSM Closeout The problem A 180,000 DWT Capesize enters its fifth anniversary window with fifteen CSM line items outstanding, a drydock booked, and a Safety Equipment Certificate to renew. The failure mode is predictable: the CSM ledger has drifted, the heavy items were left to last because they need the ship stopped, and the yard period is not long enough to absorb them all. Sequencing Split the outstanding items into three groups. Items that can only be done in dock — tailshaft, rudder, sea valves, anodes, hull. Items that can be done alongside with the plant down — main air compressors, turbochargers, coolers. Items that were already done at sea and only need the documentation presented — these should never be occupying yard time at all. Clear the third group in the pre-arrival submission, so the surveyor's attendance in dock is spent on the first group. Under-water clearance measurements Rudder stock palm and pintle clearances by dial gauge against the class wear limits; record the datum and the measuring positions so the next docking is comparable. Stern tube bearing wear down by poker gauge, taken at the same relative shaft angular position each time — a wear-down record is only useful if it is measured consistently. Propeller blade edges, cavitation erosion, and cone and cap security. Sea chest internal coatings and grating security, and anode wastage expressed as a percentage so the next docking interval can be planned from it. The safety demonstration The surveyor will want to see systems work, not read that they were tested. Simulate the dead-ship condition and time the emergency generator onto the emergency switchboard — it must be inside 45 seconds. Run the emergency fire pump from cold and deliver the required jets at the required pressure. Function-test the fixed fire system alarms and the ventilation dampers and closing appliances together, because the failure is usually in the interlock rather than in either component. On my vessel (Maersk A/S container tonnage) The discipline that prevents the whole problem is monthly review of the CSM ledger against the remaining months of the cycle, not annual review. If the ledger is reviewed monthly, every item that could have been done at sea is done at sea, and the yard period is spent only on what genuinely requires the ship out of the water. 📚 References Resolution A.1207(34) — Survey Guidelines under the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification (HSSC), 2025 SOLAS Chapter I, Regulations 6–11 and 14; Regulation 8 (safety equipment surveys) 1988 Protocols to SOLAS 74 and the Load Line Convention 1966 (HSSC, in force 3 February 2000) Resolutions MEPC.39(29) and MEPC.132(53) — HSSC in MARPOL and MARPOL Annex VI SOLAS Chapter II-1 Regulations 43/44; Chapter II-2 Regulation 10 Classification society rules for continuous survey of machinery, Chief Engineer's survey and in-water survey notations Notes-p20 · P20-T3 · v1.0

section_title: Q1. Define the anniversary date and state the survey windows under the HSSC.
text: The anniversary date is the day and month of each year corresponding to the expiry date of the certificate. Annual, intermediate and periodical surveys must be carried out within a window of three months before to three months after the anniversary date — a six-month window in total. The intermediate survey is carried out within that window at either the second or the third anniversary and replaces the annual survey for that year rather than being additional to it. The renewal survey may commence at the fourth annual survey and be progressed through the following year, but must be completed before the certificate expires. If a required survey is not completed within its window, the certificate ceases to be valid until the survey is completed. The current guidance is resolution A.1207(34), the Survey Guidelines under the HSSC, 2025 edition, which revoked A.1186(33); the guidelines are revised every two years, so the edition should always be confirmed.

section_title: Q2. A renewal survey is completed two months before the certificate expires. When does the new certificate expire, and is any validity lost?
text: Because the survey was completed within the three months preceding the expiry date, the new certificate is dated from completion of the survey but is valid to a date not exceeding five years from the expiry date of the existing certificate. No validity is lost — the five-year cycle continues unbroken from the original expiry date. The rule differs if the survey is completed more than three months before expiry: in that case the new certificate is valid only to a date not exceeding five years from the date of completion, so surveying too early actually shortens the effective cycle and costs the owner the difference. If the survey is completed after the certificate has already expired, the new certificate is again dated from the original expiry date, so the lapsed period is neither recovered nor added.

section_title: Q3. The certificate is about to expire and the ship is at a port with no survey facilities. What can be done?
text: The company applies to the flag Administration under SOLAS Chapter I Regulation 14(e) for an extension. Where a ship at the time a certificate expires is not in a port in which it is to be surveyed, the Administration may extend the validity of the certificate, but the extension is granted only for the purpose of allowing the ship to complete its voyage to the port in which it is to be surveyed, and only where it appears proper and reasonable to do so. The maximum extension is three months, and no ship may leave the survey port under that extension without a new certificate. Critically, the new certificate is then dated from the original, un-extended expiry date, so the extension is repaid out of the next cycle rather than added to it. In support of the application I would compile the planned maintenance system records, recent self-assessment checklists and machinery condition data to demonstrate the ship is being properly maintained. Two other provisions exist and should not be confused with this one: Regulation 14(d) allows the existing certificate to be endorsed as valid for up to five further months where the renewal survey has been completed but the new certificate cannot yet be issued or placed on board, and Regulation 14(f) allows a grace period of up to one month for ships engaged on short voyages.

section_title: Q4. What makes an electronic certificate valid, and how does a PSC officer verify it?
text: Under IMO circular FAL.5/Circ.39/Rev.2, an electronic certificate has the same status as a paper certificate provided four conditions are met. It must follow the format and layout of the model form required by the relevant convention. It must have technical measures protecting it against unauthorised alteration, such as a secure file format, controlled access and verification against the issuer's system. It must carry a Unique Tracking Number that identifies that specific document on the issuing authority's system. And it must include a printable, visible verification feature — normally a QR code or hyperlink — that resolves to the flag State or Recognised Organisation verification portal. The officer verifies it by following that link and confirming the tracking number returns a current, valid document issued to that ship. The practical implication on board is that connectivity must be available during the inspection and a printed copy should be to hand as a fallback; a certificate whose tracking number cannot be resolved is treated as unverified, which is a deficiency in itself.

text: Part 21 · Topic 1 The HSSC Certification Framework — Certificate Typologies, Validity Windows, Extensions and Electronic Certificates Certificate Typology · Anniversary Date · SOLAS I/14 Extensions · e-Certificates Uday pp. 501–508 (approx.) Examiner: Paul ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: Four corrections. (1) Superseded resolution. The draft anchors the survey windows to A.1156(32) (2021) . That has been revoked twice over. The current instrument is resolution A.1207(34), Survey Guidelines under the HSSC, 2025 , adopted at the 34th Assembly in December 2025, revoking A.1186(33), which had revoked A.1156(32). (2) A.883(21) mischaracterised. The draft calls it "the foundational enabling instrument establishing the harmonized system". It is not. The harmonized system was introduced by the 1988 Protocols to SOLAS 74 and the Load Line Convention 1966 and by corresponding MARPOL amendments (resolutions MEPC.39(29) and, for Annex VI, MEPC.132(53)), entering into force 3 February 2000 . Resolution A.883(21) is guidance on the global and uniform implementation of that system — important, but not the enabling instrument. Corrected. (3) Wrong issuing regulations for certificates. The draft attributes the Cargo Ship Safety Equipment Certificate to "SOLAS Chapter III" and the Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate to "Chapter II-1". Both are issued under SOLAS Chapter I, Regulation 12 ; the chapters cited describe the subject matter the certificates attest to, not the issuing provision. (4) Renewal and extension rules incomplete. The draft gives only "renewal window = expiry − 3 months". SOLAS I/14 in fact provides three distinct dating rules and three separate extension mechanisms, all examinable; the complete position is set out below. (5) Cross-reference — Parts 1–18. Part 11 Topic 48 (Statutory Survey Engineering — Load Line Framework, HSSC Protocols & Certificate Extensions) already sets out the same core SOLAS I/14 survey-window and extension mechanics — the five-year validity, the ±3-month annual/intermediate window, and the three extension provisions — anchored to the Load Line Certificate specifically. This topic generalises that mechanics across all statutory certificate types and adds the three-category classification (statutory / commercially mandatory / classification) and the electronic-certificate treatment under FAL.5/Circ.39/Rev.2, neither of which appears in Part 11 Topic 48 or elsewhere in Parts 1–18. Study the two together rather than assuming either is a full substitute for the other. 📖 Definition The HSSC certification framework is the administrative half of the harmonized system. Part 20 Topic 3 dealt with the surveys themselves — what is inspected and when. This topic deals with the paper that results: which certificates exist, what legal category each falls into, how validity is calculated from the anniversary date, what happens when a survey cannot be completed on time, and how an electronic certificate is verified. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) A certificate that has ceased to be valid stops the ship as effectively as a seized main engine, and unlike machinery it cannot be repaired at sea. The dating rules under SOLAS I/14 are counter-intuitive: completing a renewal survey early can cost the owner validity if it falls outside the three-month window. Knowing the rule is worth real money. Extensions exist and are legitimate, but each has a different trigger, a different maximum, and a different effect on the next certificate's expiry. Confusing them in an oral is an easy fail. Electronic certificates are now routine, and PSC officers verify them online. If the ship cannot demonstrate the verification path, the certificate is treated as unverified. 📅 Historical Background Pre-2000 SOLAS, Load Line and MARPOL run separate survey intervals and validity periods 1988 Protocols to SOLAS 74 and LL 66 introduce the harmonized system 1999 Resolution A.883(21) — guidance on global and uniform implementation of the HSSC 3 Feb 2000 Harmonized system enters into force MEPC.39(29) / MEPC.132(53) HSSC introduced into MARPOL and into MARPOL Annex VI 2016 FAL.5/Circ.39/Rev.2 — guidelines for the use of electronic certificates Dec 2025 A.1207(34) — Survey Guidelines under the HSSC, 2025 (current) ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments SOLAS Ch. I, Reg. 12 Issue or endorsement of certificates — the provision under which the Cargo Ship Safety Construction, Safety Equipment and Safety Radio Certificates are actually issued. SOLAS Ch. I, Reg. 14 Duration and validity of certificates — the five-year maximum, the anniversary date, the renewal dating rules and the extension provisions. Resolution A.1207(34) Survey Guidelines under the HSSC, 2025 — current edition; revised biennially. Resolution A.883(21) Global and uniform implementation of the harmonized system of survey and certification — implementation guidance, not the enabling instrument. 1988 SOLAS & Load Line Protocols The instruments that actually introduced the harmonized system; in force 3 February 2000. FAL.5/Circ.39/Rev.2 Guidelines for the use of electronic certificates — format, integrity protection, unique tracking number and verification. MARPOL Annexes I, II, IV, VI IOPP, NLS, Sewage and IAPP certificates brought within the harmonized cycle. 🗂 Three Categories of Certificate Statutory certificates Commercially mandatory certificates Classification certificates Legal basis International convention as given effect by the flag State — SOLAS, MARPOL, Load Lines, Tonnage, MLC National port-State regulation or commercial/underwriting requirement Rules of the classification society; referenced indirectly by SOLAS through the RO framework Effect of not holding it The ship may not lawfully proceed to sea The ship may sail, but is barred from specific ports, terminals or trades Loss of class — hull and machinery cover and most financing covenants fall away, making trading impossible in practice Examples Cargo Ship Safety Construction, Safety Equipment, Safety Radio, Load Line, IOPP, IAPP, ISSC, SMC/DOC, MLC P&I Certificate of Entry, US Certificate of Financial Responsibility, Blue Cards for CLC/Bunkers Convention Certificate of Class (Hull), Certificate of Class (Machinery) Who issues Flag Administration or an authorised Recognised Organisation Insurer, club, or the relevant national authority The classification society Harmonised statutory set on a typical cargo ship: Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate; Cargo Ship Safety Equipment Certificate with Record of Equipment Form E ; Cargo Ship Safety Radio Certificate with Form R ; International Load Line Certificate; IOPP (MARPOL Annex I) with Form A or B; IAPP (Annex VI); International Sewage Pollution Prevention Certificate (Annex IV); NLS Certificate (Annex II) where applicable; and for chemical and gas carriers, the Certificate of Fitness under the IBC or IGC Code. 📅 Anniversary Dates and Validity Rules The anniversary date is the day and month of each year corresponding to the expiry date of the certificate. Every window is measured from it. Maximum validity is five years for cargo ship certificates and twelve months for the Passenger Ship Safety Certificate. Survey Window Annual Anniversary date ±3 months Intermediate Anniversary date ±3 months, at the 2nd or 3rd anniversary, replacing that annual survey Periodical (radio) Anniversary date ±3 months Renewal May commence at the 4th annual survey and be progressed; must be completed before the certificate expires The three renewal dating rules (SOLAS I/14) — this is where candidates lose marks: Completed within 3 months before expiry: the new certificate runs from completion of the renewal survey to a date not exceeding five years from the expiry date of the existing certificate . No validity is lost. Completed after the expiry date: same rule — new certificate valid to a date not exceeding five years from the existing expiry date. The lost period is not recovered but neither is it added. Completed more than 3 months before expiry: the new certificate runs from completion to a date not exceeding five years from the date of completion . Surveying too early therefore shortens the effective cycle — this is the counter-intuitive one. The three extension mechanisms — different triggers, different maxima: Situation Provision Maximum Effect on the next certificate Renewal survey completed but the new certificate cannot be issued or placed on board before expiry SOLAS I/14(d) Existing certificate endorsed as valid for a further 5 months New certificate dated from the original expiry as normal Ship is not in a port in which it is to be surveyed when the certificate expires SOLAS I/14(e) Extension of up to 3 months , granted by the Administration Extension is only to allow the ship to complete its voyage to the survey port; the new certificate is dated from the original, un-extended expiry date Ship engaged on short voyages, not previously extended SOLAS I/14(f) Grace period of up to 1 month New certificate dated from the original expiry date The critical point common to all three: an extension does not move the five-year cycle . The new certificate's expiry is calculated from the original expiry date, so the extension is repaid out of the following cycle rather than added to it. 💻 Electronic Certificates Under FAL.5/Circ.39/Rev.2 , an electronic certificate has the same legal force as a paper certificate provided it satisfies four conditions: Format. The presentation must correspond to the model form required by the relevant convention. Integrity protection. Technical measures preventing unauthorised alteration — secure file formats, controlled access, and verification against the issuer's own system. Unique Tracking Number. A dedicated alpha-numeric identifier allowing the specific document to be located on the issuing authority's system. Visible verification feature. A printable, visible symbol — typically a QR code or hyperlink — resolving to the flag State or RO verification portal so an inspector can confirm authenticity independently. Two practical consequences. First, the ship must be able to demonstrate the verification path on demand — a PSC officer who cannot resolve the UTN will treat the certificate as unverified, so connectivity and a printed fallback matter. Second, the electronic certificate remains the flag State's document: it can be revoked or amended centrally without anything changing on board, which is why the onboard file must be refreshed after any survey, endorsement or company change. 🎓 CE Oral Tip (Paul): Paul's high-yield question in this area is the dating trap: "you complete the renewal survey five months before expiry — when does the new certificate run out?" The answer is five years from the date of completion , not from the old expiry, because it was completed more than three months before expiry. The ship loses two months of cycle. Only a renewal completed within the three-month window (or after expiry) is dated from the original expiry date. Have the three extension provisions ready with their maxima — 5 months, 3 months, 1 month — and be able to say which one applies to which situation. And quote the current guidelines: A.1207(34), 2025 edition . 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1. Define the anniversary date and state the survey windows under the HSSC. The anniversary date is the day and month of each year corresponding to the expiry date of the certificate. Annual, intermediate and periodical surveys must be carried out within a window of three months before to three months after the anniversary date — a six-month window in total. The intermediate survey is carried out within that window at either the second or the third anniversary and replaces the annual survey for that year rather than being additional to it. The renewal survey may commence at the fourth annual survey and be progressed through the following year, but must be completed before the certificate expires. If a required survey is not completed within its window, the certificate ceases to be valid until the survey is completed. The current guidance is resolution A.1207(34), the Survey Guidelines under the HSSC, 2025 edition, which revoked A.1186(33); the guidelines are revised every two years, so the edition should always be confirmed. Q2. A renewal survey is completed two months before the certificate expires. When does the new certificate expire, and is any validity lost? Because the survey was completed within the three months preceding the expiry date, the new certificate is dated from completion of the survey but is valid to a date not exceeding five years from the expiry date of the existing certificate. No validity is lost — the five-year cycle continues unbroken from the original expiry date. The rule differs if the survey is completed more than three months before expiry: in that case the new certificate is valid only to a date not exceeding five years from the date of completion, so surveying too early actually shortens the effective cycle and costs the owner the difference. If the survey is completed after the certificate has already expired, the new certificate is again dated from the original expiry date, so the lapsed period is neither recovered nor added. Q3. The certificate is about to expire and the ship is at a port with no survey facilities. What can be done? The company applies to the flag Administration under SOLAS Chapter I Regulation 14(e) for an extension. Where a ship at the time a certificate expires is not in a port in which it is to be surveyed, the Administration may extend the validity of the certificate, but the extension is granted only for the purpose of allowing the ship to complete its voyage to the port in which it is to be surveyed, and only where it appears proper and reasonable to do so. The maximum extension is three months, and no ship may leave the survey port under that extension without a new certificate. Critically, the new certificate is then dated from the original, un-extended expiry date, so the extension is repaid out of the next cycle rather than added to it. In support of the application I would compile the planned maintenance system records, recent self-assessment checklists and machinery condition data to demonstrate the ship is being properly maintained. Two other provisions exist and should not be confused with this one: Regulation 14(d) allows the existing certificate to be endorsed as valid for up to five further months where the renewal survey has been completed but the new certificate cannot yet be issued or placed on board, and Regulation 14(f) allows a grace period of up to one month for ships engaged on short voyages. Q4. What makes an electronic certificate valid, and how does a PSC officer verify it? Under IMO circular FAL.5/Circ.39/Rev.2, an electronic certificate has the same status as a paper certificate provided four conditions are met. It must follow the format and layout of the model form required by the relevant convention. It must have technical measures protecting it against unauthorised alteration, such as a secure file format, controlled access and verification against the issuer's system. It must carry a Unique Tracking Number that identifies that specific document on the issuing authority's system. And it must include a printable, visible verification feature — normally a QR code or hyperlink — that resolves to the flag State or Recognised Organisation verification portal. The officer verifies it by following that link and confirming the tracking number returns a current, valid document issued to that ship. The practical implication on board is that connectivity must be available during the inspection and a printed copy should be to hand as a fallback; a certificate whose tracking number cannot be resolved is treated as unverified, which is a deficiency in itself. ✍ Written Exam Focus 5 State the differences between a statutory certificate, a commercially mandatory certificate and a classification certificate, giving two practical examples of each carried on a cargo vessel. 10 Explain the rules governing the duration and validity of statutory certificates under SOLAS Chapter I Regulation 14. Include the three dating rules for the issue of a certificate following a renewal survey, and the three extension provisions with their respective maxima. 15 A cargo vessel is trading in a remote region where the local port has neither the facilities nor the surveyors to complete a statutory renewal survey before the certificate expires. Detail the regulatory procedure and communications required to obtain an extension, state its maximum duration, and analyse its effect on the anniversary date and validity of the certificate subsequently issued. 🧠 Memory Box Anniversary date = day and month of the EXPIRY date. Annual / intermediate / periodical: ±3 months. Renewal dating: within 3 months of expiry (or after expiry) → 5 years from the OLD expiry. More than 3 months early → 5 years from COMPLETION. Early surveying costs cycle. Extensions: 5 months (certificate not yet issued) · 3 months (not in a survey port) · 1 month (short voyages). None of them moves the cycle. Certificates are issued under SOLAS I/12; validity is governed by SOLAS I/14. e-Certificate: Format · Integrity · UTN · Visible verification feature (FAL.5/Circ.39/Rev.2). HSSC in force 3 Feb 2000 via the 1988 Protocols. A.883(21) is implementation guidance; A.1207(34) is the current Survey Guidelines. ▶ Deep Dive — Audits and Surveys — Two Different Instruments Why the distinction matters Ship safety oversight runs on two parallel methodologies that are frequently confused in orals. A technical survey examines the physical condition of an asset. An administrative audit examines whether a management system is functioning. They answer different questions, use different methods, and produce different remedies. Focus and direction of travel A survey looks forward: it asks whether this hull, this machinery, this equipment can be expected to remain fit until the next scheduled inspection. An audit looks backward: it samples historical records — training, drills, maintenance, non-conformity handling — to judge whether the system has been working, and infers from that whether it will continue to. Method A survey is a complete physical examination of the defined scope: every hatch cover, every specified thickness measurement point. An audit is deliberately a sampling exercise: the auditor cannot read every record and does not try, but selects a sample sufficient to test whether the system is systematically applied. This is why an audit finding on one record is treated as evidence about the whole system, not as an isolated defect. Remedy A survey deficiency is closed by rectification — repair the defect, re-present the item. An audit non-conformity is closed by root cause analysis and corrective action — fixing the individual instance is not enough, because the finding is evidence of a systemic gap. This is the distinction that catches candidates out: replacing the missing entry does not close an ISM non-conformity; explaining why the entry was missing, and changing the process so it cannot recur, does. On my vessel (Maersk A/S container tonnage) The practical test of whether the two are properly integrated is what happens between surveys. The SMS is what keeps the ship in survey condition — the maintenance schedules, the defect reporting loop, the drills. If the engine department only reaches statutory condition in the fortnight before a surveyor is due, the survey may still pass while the audit correctly fails, and the audit is the one that reflects reality. 📚 References SOLAS Chapter I, Regulations 12 and 14 Resolution A.1207(34) — Survey Guidelines under the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification (HSSC), 2025 Resolution A.883(21) — Global and uniform implementation of the harmonized system of survey and certification 1988 Protocols to SOLAS 74 and the International Convention on Load Lines 1966 FAL.5/Circ.39/Rev.2 — Guidelines for the use of electronic certificates Resolutions MEPC.39(29) and MEPC.132(53) Notes-p21 · P21-T1 · v1.0

section_title: Q1. Define substantial corrosion and explain what follows once an area is so designated.
text: Substantial corrosion is an extent of corrosion such that the assessed wastage has reached 75% or more of the allowable margin established by the classification society, while still remaining within acceptable limits — so the plating is not yet below its minimum permitted thickness, but it is well down the path towards it. It is identified by ultrasonic thickness measurement plotted against the as-built scantlings and the class allowable reduction. Once identified, the surveyor records the coordinates in the Condition Evaluation Report as a suspect area. The consequence is that those locations must then be subjected to close-up survey and thickness gauging at every subsequent annual survey, so that the rate of decay can be tracked rather than a single value. That is a permanent recurring burden — for a ballast tank it means gas freeing, ventilating, staging and entering that tank annually for the rest of the ship's life. The alternative is to crop and renew the affected plating to original specification, after which re-gauging clears the suspect designation. Either way the underlying cause must be dealt with: coating breakdown, anode depletion or standing water, because renewing steel into an unchanged environment only resets the clock.

section_title: Q2. What is the ESP File and why does the surveyor care about its continuity?
text: The ESP File is the dedicated documentation file that a bulk carrier or oil tanker subject to the Enhanced Survey Programme must maintain on board throughout its life. It contains the hull structure survey reports, the Condition Evaluation Report identifying problem areas and suspect areas with the actions taken, and the complete thickness measurement reports referenced to the structural drawings, together with the survey planning document, repair history and coating and anode records. Its continuity matters because a single set of thickness readings tells the surveyor only a present value. It is the comparison against the previous datasets that establishes a corrosion rate, and it is the rate that determines whether the structure will remain above its minimum thickness until the next survey. If the historical data is missing or cannot be correlated to specific locations, the surveyor has no basis for that projection and will take the conservative route — more gauging, wider close-up survey, or a class condition. So a well-kept ESP File directly reduces survey scope and cost.

section_title: Q3. Distinguish ESP, CAS and CAP.
text: ESP is statutory and mandatory. It is the Enhanced Survey Programme required by SOLAS Chapter XI-1 Regulation 2 and given effect by the ESP Code, resolution A.1049(27) as amended, applying to bulk carriers and oil tankers from delivery, with the scope of close-up survey and thickness measurement escalating as the ship ages. CAS, the Condition Assessment Scheme under MARPOL Annex I and resolution MEPC.94(46), was also statutory but served a single narrow purpose: verifying the structural condition of Category 2 and 3 single-hull tankers over 5,000 deadweight and over 15 years of age so that they could continue trading under the phase-out extensions. Every date in that scheme has now passed — Category 1 tankers were prohibited from 2005 and the extensions expired in 2015 or at 25 years of age — so CAS is examinable history rather than live compliance. CAP, the Condition Assessment Programme, is neither statutory nor mandatory. It is a commercial scheme bought by owners at the request of charterers and underwriters, typically for ships past about fifteen years, involving deep gauging, structural strength and fatigue analysis and detailed machinery assessment, and producing a graded rating from CAP-1 very good down to CAP-4 poor, split between CAP-Hull and CAP-Machinery and cargo systems. The key contrast is that CAS answered a yes or no statutory question while CAP answers a graded commercial one.

section_title: Q4. What is your role as Chief Engineer in preparing the vessel for an ESP renewal survey?
text: My role is to make the structure accessible and the data available. On access: coordinating tank cleaning, gas freeing, ventilation, lighting and staging so the close-up survey positions can actually be reached safely, and managing the enclosed space entry permits and standby arrangements for the thickness measurement team and the surveyor. On the plant side: ensuring the ballast system, tank level gauging and bilge arrangements are fully operational so tanks can be emptied, checked and re-ballasted on the survey programme without holding up the yard. On condition: assessing and reporting coating breakdown in ballast tanks and anode wastage as a percentage, so corrosion control decisions are based on measurement rather than impression. On documentation: keeping the ESP File complete and in order, with the previous thickness measurement reports correlated to the drawings, the repair history and the previous Condition Evaluation Report, so the surveyor can establish trends. And on planning: making sure known suspect areas are on the docking specification in advance, so a decision to crop and renew is taken before the ship is in the dock rather than as an expensive variation once it is.
