text: Part 21 · Topic 2 Enhanced Structural Inspection Regimes — ESP, CAS and CAP, Substantial Corrosion and Suspect Areas ESP Code · CAS · CAP Ratings · Substantial Corrosion Uday pp. 508–517 (approx.) Examiner: Paul ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: Three corrections. (1) "ESP Code 2017" is not a recognised designation. The instrument is the International Code on the Enhanced Programme of Inspections during Surveys of Bulk Carriers and Oil Tankers, 2011 (ESP Code), adopted by resolution A.1049(27) and subsequently amended by MSC resolutions , made mandatory by SOLAS Chapter XI-1, Regulation 2 . References to a "2017 Code" have been replaced with the correct citation and a note that amendments are issued periodically, so the applicable amendment set should be confirmed against the ship's class. (2) CAS is now historical for operational purposes. The draft presents the single-hull phase-out as live regulation. Every date in the scheme has passed: Category 1 tankers were prohibited from 2005, and the Category 2 and 3 extensions expired in 2015 or at 25 years of age. CAS is retained here because it remains examinable and because the Category 1/2/3 definitions still appear in oral questions, but it is now presented as the historical mechanism it is, not as a current compliance obligation. (3) Surveyor attendance. The draft's statement about dual surveyor attendance has been retained with its own hedge intact, because the tonnage and age thresholds are genuinely RO-specific and no single figure could be verified as universal. 📖 Definition The Enhanced Survey Programme (ESP) is the mandatory, prescriptive framework of close-up surveys, thickness measurements and tank testing applied to bulk carriers and oil tankers, whose structural failure modes proved that a general visual survey was not enough. CAS was the statutory verification scheme that policed the single-hull tanker phase-out. CAP is neither statutory nor mandatory: it is a commercially driven condition rating bought by owners to satisfy charterers that an older ship is better than its age suggests. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) ESP is why the Chief Engineer's docking and survey preparation includes safe tank entry — gas freeing, ventilation, lighting, staging and access for the thickness measurement team. Poor preparation does not just delay the survey; it can force close-up items to be deferred, which becomes a class condition. The 75% substantial corrosion threshold is a decision point with commercial consequences: accept it and live with annual close-up tracking of those points forever, or crop and renew now and clear the designation. Corrosion control is engineering work the department owns — anode condition and renewal, coating breakdown assessment in ballast tanks, and keeping bilge and drainage arrangements clear so water does not stand against steel. CAP ratings determine whether an older ship can be fixed at all with the major charterers. A CAP-1 or CAP-2 rating is a commercial asset; CAP-4 effectively ends the ship's trading life with those charterers. 📅 Historical Background 1990s Repeated bulk carrier losses from side-shell and bulkhead failure drive the enhanced survey concept 1993 Resolution A.744(18) — original Guidelines on the Enhanced Programme of Inspections 2002 Resolution MEPC.94(46) — Condition Assessment Scheme adopted 2011 Resolution A.1049(27) — the ESP Code, restructured as a mandatory code 1 Jan 2014 ESP Code made mandatory through SOLAS Chapter XI-1, Regulation 2 2005 Category 1 single-hull tankers prohibited 2010 / 2015 Category 2 and 3 phase-out, with CAS-conditional extension to 2015 or 25 years of age — now expired ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments SOLAS Ch. XI-1, Reg. 2 Requires bulk carriers and oil tankers to be surveyed in accordance with the ESP Code — the provision that makes ESP mandatory. Resolution A.1049(27), as amended International Code on the Enhanced Programme of Inspections during Surveys of Bulk Carriers and Oil Tankers, 2011 (ESP Code). Annex A — bulk carriers (Part A single side skin, Part B double side skin). Annex B — oil tankers (Part A double hull, Part B non-double hull). MARPOL Annex I, Regs. 20 and 21 Single-hull tanker phase-out scheme and the Condition Assessment Scheme requirement. Resolution MEPC.94(46), as amended Condition Assessment Scheme (CAS). IACS UR Z10 series Unified requirements for hull surveys of bulk carriers and oil tankers — the class-level implementation of ESP. SOLAS Ch. XII Additional safety measures for bulk carriers — structural strength, water level detectors, and the survey regime that supports them. 📘 The ESP Code Structure and the ESP File Annex Applies to Parts Annex A Bulk carriers Part A — single side skin construction; Part B — double side skin construction Annex B Oil tankers Part A — double hull construction; Part B — other than double hull ESP requirements are not a separate survey: they are integrated into the existing annual, intermediate and renewal surveys, with the scope escalating sharply with the age of the ship. What changes with age is the number of tanks subject to close-up survey, the number of thickness measurement locations, and the extent of tank pressure testing. The ESP File must be maintained on board throughout the ship's life and made available to the surveyor. It contains, as a minimum: Survey reports — the record of every hull structure inspection, including close-up survey findings. Condition Evaluation Report — the surveyor's summary identifying problem areas, wear trends, suspect areas and the action taken. Thickness measurement reports — the complete ultrasonic gauging dataset, by location, with the readings referenced to the structural drawings. Supporting material: survey planning document, structural drawings, previous repair history, coating condition and anode records, and the ship's own inspection reports. A missing or disordered ESP File is not a paperwork problem. Without the previous thickness measurement dataset the surveyor cannot establish a corrosion rate , only a present value, and will default to the conservative outcome — more gauging, more close-up survey, or a class condition. 📉 Substantial Corrosion and Suspect Areas Substantial corrosion is an extent of corrosion such that the assessed wastage is 75% or more of the allowable margin set by the classification society, but still within acceptable limits. The plate is not yet below the minimum permitted thickness — it is on the trajectory towards it. W measured ≥ 0.75 × W max allowable → substantial corrosion Original as-built thickness ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ◄───────────── maximum allowable reduction (100%) ─────────► ┌────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┐ │ acceptable wastage (0 – 75%) │ SUBSTANTIAL CORROSION │ │ │ (75 – 100%) │ └────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────┘ ▲ 75% threshold — becomes a SUSPECT AREA Identification. The thickness measurement team maps the structure by ultrasonic gauging; readings are plotted against the as-built scantlings and the class allowable reduction. Designation. The surveyor records the coordinates as suspect areas in the Condition Evaluation Report. Consequence. Suspect areas are subject to close-up survey and thickness gauging at every subsequent annual survey , so the surveyor can measure the rate of decay rather than a single value. That is a permanent recurring burden on the ship until it is cleared. Options. Either accept the annual tracking, or crop and renew the affected plating to original specification. Renewal removes the suspect designation on re-gauging and the item is cleared from the report. Mitigation. Whichever route is taken, the underlying cause must be addressed — coating breakdown, anode depletion, standing water, or a drainage path that keeps the area wet. Renewing steel into an unchanged corrosive environment simply resets the clock. The engineering judgement: annual close-up tracking of a bulkhead in a ballast tank means gas freeing, ventilating, staging and entering that tank every year for the rest of the ship's life. The cost of that, compounded, very often exceeds the cost of cropping and renewing at the next docking — which is the argument the Chief Engineer needs to be able to make to the superintendent with the numbers attached. ⚖ ESP versus CAS versus CAP ESP CAS CAP Legal status Statutory and mandatory — SOLAS XI-1/2 and the ESP Code Statutory — MARPOL Annex I; now historically spent Commercial and voluntary — charterer and underwriter driven Applies to Bulk carriers and oil tankers Category 2 and 3 single-hull oil tankers ≥ 5,000 DWT Oil tankers, chemical tankers and bulk carriers Trigger From delivery, throughout the ship's life; scope escalates with age Once the tanker exceeded 15 years of age Typically requested once a ship passes about 15 years, at charterer's discretion What it produces Close-up survey findings, thickness measurements, Condition Evaluation Report A statement of compliance permitting continued single-hull operation to a fixed end date A numerical condition rating , split into CAP-Hull and CAP-Machinery/Cargo systems Current relevance Fully current Expired — all phase-out dates passed; examinable as history and definitions Fully current and commercially decisive for older tonnage CAS and the single-hull categories — retained because the definitions are still asked: Category Definition Phase-out Category 1 "Pre-MARPOL" tankers — crude ≥ 20,000 DWT, product ≥ 30,000 DWT, without protectively located segregated ballast tanks Prohibited from 2005 Category 2 "MARPOL" tankers — same size thresholds, but with protectively located SBT Phase-out from 2010; CAS-conditional extension to 2015 or 25 years of age, whichever earlier Category 3 Smaller oil tankers — 5,000 DWT up to the Category 1/2 thresholds As Category 2 CAP ratings: CAP-1 very good · CAP-2 good · CAP-3 satisfactory/acceptable · CAP-4 poor. The rating is derived from extensive gauging, structural strength and fatigue analysis, and detailed machinery and cargo system assessment — it is a far deeper technical exercise than a statutory survey, which is exactly why charterers pay attention to it. Note the asymmetry with CAS: CAS answered a yes/no statutory question, whereas CAP answers a graded commercial one. 🎓 CE Oral Tip (Paul): Paul's reliable question here is the definition of substantial corrosion, and the answer that scores is the full one: wastage of 75% or more of the allowable margin, still within acceptable limits , recorded as a suspect area, and therefore subject to close-up survey and gauging at every subsequent annual survey . Most candidates give the 75% and stop; the annual tracking consequence is what shows you understand why it matters. If he asks about CAS, say plainly that the scheme is spent — every phase-out date has passed — and then give the Category 1/2/3 definitions, which is what he is really testing. And cite the ESP Code correctly: resolution A.1049(27) as amended, mandatory under SOLAS XI-1/2. 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1. Define substantial corrosion and explain what follows once an area is so designated. Substantial corrosion is an extent of corrosion such that the assessed wastage has reached 75% or more of the allowable margin established by the classification society, while still remaining within acceptable limits — so the plating is not yet below its minimum permitted thickness, but it is well down the path towards it. It is identified by ultrasonic thickness measurement plotted against the as-built scantlings and the class allowable reduction. Once identified, the surveyor records the coordinates in the Condition Evaluation Report as a suspect area. The consequence is that those locations must then be subjected to close-up survey and thickness gauging at every subsequent annual survey, so that the rate of decay can be tracked rather than a single value. That is a permanent recurring burden — for a ballast tank it means gas freeing, ventilating, staging and entering that tank annually for the rest of the ship's life. The alternative is to crop and renew the affected plating to original specification, after which re-gauging clears the suspect designation. Either way the underlying cause must be dealt with: coating breakdown, anode depletion or standing water, because renewing steel into an unchanged environment only resets the clock. Q2. What is the ESP File and why does the surveyor care about its continuity? The ESP File is the dedicated documentation file that a bulk carrier or oil tanker subject to the Enhanced Survey Programme must maintain on board throughout its life. It contains the hull structure survey reports, the Condition Evaluation Report identifying problem areas and suspect areas with the actions taken, and the complete thickness measurement reports referenced to the structural drawings, together with the survey planning document, repair history and coating and anode records. Its continuity matters because a single set of thickness readings tells the surveyor only a present value. It is the comparison against the previous datasets that establishes a corrosion rate, and it is the rate that determines whether the structure will remain above its minimum thickness until the next survey. If the historical data is missing or cannot be correlated to specific locations, the surveyor has no basis for that projection and will take the conservative route — more gauging, wider close-up survey, or a class condition. So a well-kept ESP File directly reduces survey scope and cost. Q3. Distinguish ESP, CAS and CAP. ESP is statutory and mandatory. It is the Enhanced Survey Programme required by SOLAS Chapter XI-1 Regulation 2 and given effect by the ESP Code, resolution A.1049(27) as amended, applying to bulk carriers and oil tankers from delivery, with the scope of close-up survey and thickness measurement escalating as the ship ages. CAS, the Condition Assessment Scheme under MARPOL Annex I and resolution MEPC.94(46), was also statutory but served a single narrow purpose: verifying the structural condition of Category 2 and 3 single-hull tankers over 5,000 deadweight and over 15 years of age so that they could continue trading under the phase-out extensions. Every date in that scheme has now passed — Category 1 tankers were prohibited from 2005 and the extensions expired in 2015 or at 25 years of age — so CAS is examinable history rather than live compliance. CAP, the Condition Assessment Programme, is neither statutory nor mandatory. It is a commercial scheme bought by owners at the request of charterers and underwriters, typically for ships past about fifteen years, involving deep gauging, structural strength and fatigue analysis and detailed machinery assessment, and producing a graded rating from CAP-1 very good down to CAP-4 poor, split between CAP-Hull and CAP-Machinery and cargo systems. The key contrast is that CAS answered a yes or no statutory question while CAP answers a graded commercial one. Q4. What is your role as Chief Engineer in preparing the vessel for an ESP renewal survey? My role is to make the structure accessible and the data available. On access: coordinating tank cleaning, gas freeing, ventilation, lighting and staging so the close-up survey positions can actually be reached safely, and managing the enclosed space entry permits and standby arrangements for the thickness measurement team and the surveyor. On the plant side: ensuring the ballast system, tank level gauging and bilge arrangements are fully operational so tanks can be emptied, checked and re-ballasted on the survey programme without holding up the yard. On condition: assessing and reporting coating breakdown in ballast tanks and anode wastage as a percentage, so corrosion control decisions are based on measurement rather than impression. On documentation: keeping the ESP File complete and in order, with the previous thickness measurement reports correlated to the drawings, the repair history and the previous Condition Evaluation Report, so the surveyor can establish trends. And on planning: making sure known suspect areas are on the docking specification in advance, so a decision to crop and renew is taken before the ship is in the dock rather than as an expensive variation once it is. ✍ Written Exam Focus 5 Define substantial corrosion under the ESP Code and state the consequences for the subsequent survey regime once an area has been designated as a suspect area. 10 Describe the structure and contents of the ESP File and explain how thickness measurement data is used by the surveyor to determine survey scope. Include the effect of an incomplete historical dataset. 15 Explain the quantitative criteria distinguishing ordinary structural wear from substantial corrosion. Formulate a step-by-step procedure for the Chief Engineer to manage, rectify and document structural defects in cooperation with the Recognised Organisation surveyors, and analyse the long-term survey and commercial implications of retaining worn plating rather than executing immediate steel renewal. 🧠 Memory Box Substantial corrosion = 75% or more of the allowable margin, still within limits. Result: suspect area → close-up survey and gauging at EVERY annual thereafter. ESP = statutory (SOLAS XI-1/2, ESP Code A.1049(27)). CAS = statutory but spent. CAP = commercial and graded. ESP Annex A = bulk carriers (single/double side skin); Annex B = oil tankers (double hull / other). ESP File trio: survey reports · Condition Evaluation Report · thickness measurement reports. CAP-1 very good · CAP-2 good · CAP-3 satisfactory · CAP-4 poor. Split CAP-Hull and CAP-Machinery. Single-hull categories: Cat 1 pre-MARPOL no SBT (out 2005); Cat 2 MARPOL with SBT; Cat 3 5,000 DWT up to the Cat 1/2 thresholds. ▶ Deep Dive — Corrosion Control as an Engineering Programme, Not a Docking Task Where the steel actually goes Ballast tanks are the dominant loss mechanism: alternating wet and dry cycles, warm cargo adjacent, oxygen-rich seawater and coating breakdown at edges, welds and stiffener toes. Cargo hold tank tops and lower hopper plating on bulk carriers lose steel to mechanical damage from grabs and bulldozers, which removes coating and exposes bare steel to residual moisture and cargo acids. Under-deck and upper wing structures suffer from condensation. In each case the corrosion follows the coating failure, which follows the mechanical damage or the surface preparation defect. What the department controls Anodes: condition assessed and recorded as a percentage consumed at each tank entry, not a subjective note — a consistent percentage record allows the renewal interval to be set from data. Coatings: breakdown assessed against a defined scale by area and location, photographed and logged; touch-up carried out where surface preparation can actually be achieved rather than painting over rust. Drainage: bilge suctions, strums and drain paths kept clear so water does not stand — the single commonest local cause of accelerated wastage. Ballast management: minimising unnecessary partial filling that leaves a waterline oscillating in the same band of plating. Making the renewal case The argument to the superintendent should be built as a cost comparison over the remaining survey cycles, not as an appeal to good practice. Annual close-up tracking of a suspect area in a ballast tank carries a recurring cost: cleaning, gas freeing, ventilation, staging, enclosed-space entry manning, surveyor attendance and the operational time. Multiply that by the number of annual surveys remaining before the next planned docking window in which renewal could be done anyway, and compare it with the cropping and renewal cost at the next docking. In most cases where the ship has meaningful life left, renewal wins on cost alone. On my vessel (Maersk A/S container tonnage) Container tonnage is not ESP tonnage, but the same logic governs ballast tank and void space condition, and the same corrosion-rate discipline applies to the class hull survey. The habit worth carrying across is recording anode and coating condition quantitatively at every tank entry, so that when the docking specification is written the decisions are made from a trend rather than from the last person's recollection. 📚 References SOLAS Chapter XI-1, Regulation 2; SOLAS Chapter XII Resolution A.1049(27), as amended — International Code on the Enhanced Programme of Inspections during Surveys of Bulk Carriers and Oil Tankers, 2011 (ESP Code) MARPOL Annex I, Regulations 20 and 21 Resolution MEPC.94(46), as amended — Condition Assessment Scheme IACS Unified Requirements Z10 series — hull surveys of bulk carriers and oil tankers Classification society Condition Assessment Programme (CAP) rules and rating scales Notes-p21 · P21-T2 · v1.0

section_title: Q1. What is the Continuous Synopsis Record and why is a break in it treated so seriously?
text: The Continuous Synopsis Record is required by SOLAS Chapter XI-1 Regulation 5. It is a continuous, chronological record of the ship's history, issued by the flag Administration and kept on board for the life of the ship, recording the flag State and date of registration, the IMO number, the ship's name and port of registry, the registered owner and owner identification number, any bareboat charterer, the ISM Company and Company identification number, the classification society, and the bodies that issued the Document of Compliance, the Safety Management Certificate and the International Ship Security Certificate. Every change to those particulars produces an amendment and a new numbered document, and all superseded documents, the amendment forms and the index remain on board. When the ship changes flag, the outgoing Administration transmits the complete file to the incoming one, so the chain is never restarted. A break in the chain is serious because the entire purpose of the instrument is to make substandard ownership traceable — a missing intermediate document or an unindexed transition is exactly what would be produced by an attempt to obscure a period of the ship's history, and Port State Control treats it as a detainable finding for that reason.

section_title: Q2. An ISM auditor raises a major non-conformity. What happens next?
text: A major non-conformity is an identifiable deviation posing a serious threat to personnel, the ship or the environment and requiring immediate corrective action, or the absence of effective and systematic implementation of a requirement of the ISM Code. The immediate requirement is that it must be downgraded to a non-conformity before the audit team leaves the ship, by taking corrective action that removes the serious threat. If it cannot be downgraded, the Safety Management Certificate is withdrawn or its validity suspended — and if the finding is against the shore organisation, the Document of Compliance is withdrawn, which withdraws the SMC of every ship that DOC covers. It is important not to confuse downgrading with closing out. Downgrading only removes the immediate danger; the non-conformity remains open and must be closed within the agreed timeframe by correction of the instance, root cause analysis establishing why the system permitted it, corrective action changing the process so it cannot recur, and verification of effectiveness at the following audit.

section_title: Q3. State the validity periods and verification requirements for the DOC and the SMC.
text: The Document of Compliance is issued to the Company, for each type of ship it operates, and is valid for five years, subject to annual verification within three months before or after each anniversary date. A copy must be carried on board. The Safety Management Certificate is issued to the ship, is valid for five years, and requires at least one intermediate verification carried out between the second and third anniversary dates. An SMC can only be issued to a ship whose Company holds a valid DOC covering that ship type. There are also interim certificates: an interim DOC valid for twelve months, issued to a new Company or where an existing Company takes on a new ship type, and an interim SMC valid for six months, issued for a new ship, a change of flag or a change of Company, which the Administration may extend for a further six months. The certificates are invalidated if the periodical verifications are not carried out within their windows, if major non-conformities are left unrectified, or if unauthorised changes are made to the management system or the Company.

section_title: Q4. A vessel is transferring to a new manager under a bareboat charter. What documentation must change and in what order?
text: The ISM Company changes, so the certification chain has to be rebuilt rather than amended. The incoming manager must hold a Document of Compliance covering that ship type — if they do not, an interim DOC valid for twelve months is issued after an initial audit of the shore organisation. The existing Safety Management Certificate becomes invalid on the change of Company, so an interim SMC valid for six months is issued to the ship following an initial verification, extendable by the Administration for a further six months, during which the full SMC audit is carried out. The Continuous Synopsis Record must be amended under SOLAS XI-1 Regulation 5 to record the new bareboat charterer, the new ISM Company and Company identification number, and the issuing body of the new DOC and SMC, with the amendment form completed and a new numbered CSR document issued, all previous documents retained on board. If flag or class changes as well, those entries and the corresponding statutory and class certificates change too, and the previous Administration must transmit the CSR file to the new one. The practical risk is sequencing: if the ship sails after the change of Company but before the interim certification is in place, it is trading without valid ISM certification, which is a detention at the next port.

text: Part 21 · Topic 3 Statutory Documentation and Operational Auditing — the Continuous Synopsis Record, ISM Certification and Non-Conformity Management CSR Chain of Custody · DOC & SMC · Non-Conformities · Audit vs Survey Uday pp. 517–525 (approx.) Examiner: Senthil ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: Two corrections and one scoping decision. (1) ISPS citation. The draft refers to "ISPS Code Part A & Form A" as governing the International Ship Security Certificate. The ISSC is issued under ISPS Code Part A, section 19 , with the certificate form set out in the appendix to Part A; "Form A" is not the designation for it (Form A and Form B are the supplements to the IOPP Certificate under MARPOL Annex I, which is a different instrument entirely). Corrected. (2) Non-conformity handling stated loosely. The draft says a major non-conformity means the RO "will take immediate steps to handle or invalidate the certificate". The precise position is given below: a major non-conformity must be downgraded to a non-conformity before the audit team departs, by immediate corrective action, or the SMC or DOC is withdrawn or its validity suspended. The distinction between downgrading and closing out is examinable and has been added. (3) Scoping. The draft's SIRE and CDI material has deliberately not been expanded here. The full vetting treatment — SIRE 2.0, CDI and TMSA — is the subject of Part 22 Topic 1 , and splitting one subject across two Parts would break the series rule that a topic sits wholly within one Part. This topic keeps only the boundary point: vetting is commercial, not statutory. (4) Cross-reference — Parts 1–18. This topic's ISM/DOC/SMC/non-conformity content overlaps substantially with Part 13 Topic 2 (The International Safety Management (ISM) Code — SMS Architecture, DOC/SMC Certification & Non-Conformity Management), which already covers the NC/MNC/Observation taxonomy and the DOC/SMC validity table in comparable depth. Its CSR content overlaps with Part 15 Topic 1 (Ship Identification Systems & Statutory Credentials — IMO Number, MMSI, Call Sign & CSR), which already covers the CSR's contents and amendment mechanics. This topic's distinct contribution is the explicit downgrade-versus-close-out procedural distinction, the bareboat-handover certification-sequencing walkthrough, and the pattern analysis of why engine-room findings specifically escalate to major non-conformities — material not present in either existing topic. Treat Part 13 Topic 2 and Part 15 Topic 1 as the primary references and this topic as the applied, cross-cutting companion, not as three independent sources to memorise separately. 📖 Definition This topic covers the ship's administrative compliance layer: the documents that establish who the ship is and who is responsible for it, and the audits that verify the management system behind them. The Continuous Synopsis Record (CSR) is the ship's unbroken identity history. The Document of Compliance and Safety Management Certificate are the ISM Code's evidence that a functioning safety management system exists ashore and on board. Together they answer the question a surveyor cannot answer by looking at machinery: who is accountable for this ship, and is their system working? ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) A break in the CSR chain is a detainable finding that no amount of engine room condition can offset. It is also the classic marker of a ship whose ownership history someone has tried to obscure. A major non-conformity raised against the SMS can suspend the Safety Management Certificate. That stops the ship as surely as a main engine failure, and the trigger is very often an engine department item — an untracked defect, a bypassed alarm, an unrecorded maintenance interval. Non-conformities are closed by root cause analysis, not by repair. An engineer who fixes the item and reports it fixed has not closed the finding, and the follow-up audit will say so. Under a bareboat charter or a management change, the ISM "Company" changes — new DOC, new SMC, new CSR entry. Getting this sequence wrong at handover is a common and entirely avoidable detention. 📅 Historical Background 1993 OCIMF introduces the Ship Inspection Report Programme (SIRE) — commercial vetting standardised 1 Jul 1998 ISM Code enters into force for tankers, bulk carriers, gas carriers and passenger ships 1 Jul 2002 ISM Code applies to all cargo ships of 500 GT and above 1 Jul 2004 ISPS Code and SOLAS Chapter XI-2 enter into force 1 Jul 2004 SOLAS XI-1/5 — Continuous Synopsis Record becomes mandatory 2004 onward SOLAS XI-1/3 ship identification number permanently marked externally and internally 2024 SIRE 2.0 replaces the VIQ7 regime — see Part 22 Topic 1 ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments SOLAS Ch. XI-1, Reg. 5 Continuous Synopsis Record — issued by the Administration, kept on board for the life of the ship, recording the full history of flag, ownership, management, class and certification. SOLAS Ch. XI-1, Reg. 3 Ship identification number — the IMO number permanently marked in a visible external position and in an accessible internal location. SOLAS Ch. IX / ISM Code Safety management — Document of Compliance for the Company and Safety Management Certificate for the ship; audit and verification regime. ISM Code, para. 13 Certification and periodical verification — DOC and SMC validity, annual and intermediate verification. ISM Code, para. 14 Interim certification — interim DOC and interim SMC. ISPS Code Part A, s.19 Verification and certification for ships — issue of the International Ship Security Certificate; certificate form in the appendix to Part A. SOLAS Ch. XI-1, Reg. 3-1 Company and registered owner identification number. 📜 The Continuous Synopsis Record The CSR is a continuous, chronological record of a ship's history, issued by the flag Administration and kept on board for the life of the ship. Its purpose is to make ownership, management and flag history traceable and un-erasable , so that substandard ownership cannot be laundered through a change of name and register. When a ship changes flag, the outgoing Administration transmits the complete CSR file to the incoming one; the chain is never restarted. Contents required by SOLAS XI-1/5: # Item # Item 1 Flag State the ship is entitled to fly 8 Name and address of bareboat charterer(s), if applicable 2 Date of registration with that State 9 Name of the Company responsible under the ISM Code 3 Ship identification (IMO) number 10 Company identification number 4 Name of the ship 11 Name of the classification society or societies 5 Port of registry 12 Administration or organisation that issued the DOC 6 Name and registered address of the registered owner(s) 13 Administration or organisation that issued the SMC 7 Registered owner identification number 14 Administration or organisation that issued the ISSC Any change to any of these particulars triggers an amendment . The Company completes the amendment form and the Administration issues a revised, numbered CSR document. Every document in the sequence stays on board — the current CSR, all superseded CSRs, the index of amendments, and the amendment forms. The file is the evidence; a gap in the numbering is a gap in the chain. The date on which the ship ceased to be registered under a previous flag must appear, so there is no unaccounted period. The CSR is verified at statutory surveys and is a standing PSC target. A missing intermediate document or an unindexed history page following an ownership or flag transition is a detainable finding. Related and often examined alongside it: SOLAS XI-1/3 requires the ship identification number to be permanently marked in a visible place on the stern or on the ship's sides, and in an easily accessible place inside the ship — on a transverse bulkhead of a machinery space, or on a hatchway, or on the inside of a ro-ro space. A mismatch between the marked number and the number on the certificates is treated as a serious documentary discrepancy. 📋 DOC, SMC and the Verification Cycle Certificate Issued to Validity Periodical verification Document of Compliance (DOC) The Company , for each ship type operated 5 years Annual verification within 3 months before or after each anniversary date Safety Management Certificate (SMC) The ship 5 years At least one intermediate verification between the 2nd and 3rd anniversary date Interim DOC A new Company, or an existing Company adding a new ship type 12 months — Interim SMC A new ship, a change of flag, or a change of Company 6 months, extendable by the Administration for a further 6 months — ISSC The ship, under the ISPS Code 5 years At least one intermediate verification between the 2nd and 3rd anniversary date A copy of the DOC must be carried on board. The SMC is only issued to a ship whose Company holds a valid DOC covering that ship type — so a DOC problem ashore invalidates certification afloat, which is why a management change has to be sequenced correctly rather than announced retrospectively. ⚠ Non-Conformities — the Distinction That Matters Observation. A statement of fact made during an audit and substantiated by objective evidence. It is not a finding of non-compliance; it flags something that could develop into one. Non-conformity. An observed situation where objective evidence indicates the non-fulfilment of a specified requirement. Closed by corrective action within an agreed timeframe. Major non-conformity. An identifiable deviation posing a serious threat to personnel, ship safety or the environment, requiring immediate corrective action — or the absence of effective and systematic implementation of a requirement of the ISM Code. The critical procedural point. A major non-conformity must be downgraded to a non-conformity before the audit team leaves the ship , by taking immediate corrective action that removes the serious threat. If it cannot be downgraded, the SMC — or, if the finding is against the shore organisation, the DOC — is withdrawn or its validity suspended. Downgrading is not the same as closing out: the underlying non-conformity remains open and must still be closed by root cause analysis and corrective action within the agreed period. [Major non-conformity raised] │ Can immediate action remove the serious threat before the team departs? ├── YES ──> DOWNGRADED to a non-conformity │ └─> still open: root cause analysis + corrective action + verification └── NO ──> SMC (or DOC) WITHDRAWN / SUSPENDED └─> ship cannot trade until re-verified Closing out is not repairing. The remedy for a non-conformity is: correction (fix the instance), root cause analysis (establish why the system permitted it), corrective action (change the process so it cannot recur), and verification of effectiveness at the next audit. An engineer who replaces the missing entry and reports the finding closed has completed step one of four. This is the single most common weakness in engine department audit responses. Invalidation triggers for DOC and SMC: periodical verifications not carried out within their windows; major non-conformities left unrectified; and unauthorised or unnotified changes to the management system or the Company. Loss of the DOC withdraws the SMC of every ship it covers. 🏷 The Commercial Vetting Boundary Vetting inspections are commercial, not statutory. SIRE, introduced by OCIMF in 1993, and the CDI scheme for chemical and gas carriers, are risk-assessment tools operated by cargo interests, charterers and underwriters. No international convention requires them. They are nonetheless a practical prerequisite to trading with the oil and chemical majors, and a poor report can end a ship's employment prospects faster than a PSC detention. The Chief Engineer's standing obligations in this area are the same regardless of scheme: maintenance records that match the actual condition of the equipment; a defect list that is live rather than decorative; clean bilges and a demonstrably functioning oily water separator with an intact 15 ppm alarm and no bypass arrangements; steering gear and emergency systems that work on demand; and factual, unembellished clarification of any disputed observation at the closing meeting. The full treatment of SIRE 2.0, CDI and TMSA — architecture, question library, risk-based inspection targeting and the human-factors dimension — is Part 22, Topic 1 . 🎓 CE Oral Tip (Senthil): Senthil examines this area through the ISM lens and his tell-tale follow-up is: "the auditor raises a major non-conformity — what happens?" The answer that scores is procedural, not remedial: it must be downgraded to a non-conformity before the audit team leaves the ship by immediate corrective action removing the serious threat, failing which the SMC is withdrawn or suspended — and downgrading is not closing out, because the non-conformity remains open pending root cause analysis and corrective action. If he then asks how you close it, do not say "we repaired it". Say correction, root cause, corrective action, verification of effectiveness. That four-step answer separates candidates who have been audited from candidates who have read about auditing. 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1. What is the Continuous Synopsis Record and why is a break in it treated so seriously? The Continuous Synopsis Record is required by SOLAS Chapter XI-1 Regulation 5. It is a continuous, chronological record of the ship's history, issued by the flag Administration and kept on board for the life of the ship, recording the flag State and date of registration, the IMO number, the ship's name and port of registry, the registered owner and owner identification number, any bareboat charterer, the ISM Company and Company identification number, the classification society, and the bodies that issued the Document of Compliance, the Safety Management Certificate and the International Ship Security Certificate. Every change to those particulars produces an amendment and a new numbered document, and all superseded documents, the amendment forms and the index remain on board. When the ship changes flag, the outgoing Administration transmits the complete file to the incoming one, so the chain is never restarted. A break in the chain is serious because the entire purpose of the instrument is to make substandard ownership traceable — a missing intermediate document or an unindexed transition is exactly what would be produced by an attempt to obscure a period of the ship's history, and Port State Control treats it as a detainable finding for that reason. Q2. An ISM auditor raises a major non-conformity. What happens next? A major non-conformity is an identifiable deviation posing a serious threat to personnel, the ship or the environment and requiring immediate corrective action, or the absence of effective and systematic implementation of a requirement of the ISM Code. The immediate requirement is that it must be downgraded to a non-conformity before the audit team leaves the ship, by taking corrective action that removes the serious threat. If it cannot be downgraded, the Safety Management Certificate is withdrawn or its validity suspended — and if the finding is against the shore organisation, the Document of Compliance is withdrawn, which withdraws the SMC of every ship that DOC covers. It is important not to confuse downgrading with closing out. Downgrading only removes the immediate danger; the non-conformity remains open and must be closed within the agreed timeframe by correction of the instance, root cause analysis establishing why the system permitted it, corrective action changing the process so it cannot recur, and verification of effectiveness at the following audit. Q3. State the validity periods and verification requirements for the DOC and the SMC. The Document of Compliance is issued to the Company, for each type of ship it operates, and is valid for five years, subject to annual verification within three months before or after each anniversary date. A copy must be carried on board. The Safety Management Certificate is issued to the ship, is valid for five years, and requires at least one intermediate verification carried out between the second and third anniversary dates. An SMC can only be issued to a ship whose Company holds a valid DOC covering that ship type. There are also interim certificates: an interim DOC valid for twelve months, issued to a new Company or where an existing Company takes on a new ship type, and an interim SMC valid for six months, issued for a new ship, a change of flag or a change of Company, which the Administration may extend for a further six months. The certificates are invalidated if the periodical verifications are not carried out within their windows, if major non-conformities are left unrectified, or if unauthorised changes are made to the management system or the Company. Q4. A vessel is transferring to a new manager under a bareboat charter. What documentation must change and in what order? The ISM Company changes, so the certification chain has to be rebuilt rather than amended. The incoming manager must hold a Document of Compliance covering that ship type — if they do not, an interim DOC valid for twelve months is issued after an initial audit of the shore organisation. The existing Safety Management Certificate becomes invalid on the change of Company, so an interim SMC valid for six months is issued to the ship following an initial verification, extendable by the Administration for a further six months, during which the full SMC audit is carried out. The Continuous Synopsis Record must be amended under SOLAS XI-1 Regulation 5 to record the new bareboat charterer, the new ISM Company and Company identification number, and the issuing body of the new DOC and SMC, with the amendment form completed and a new numbered CSR document issued, all previous documents retained on board. If flag or class changes as well, those entries and the corresponding statutory and class certificates change too, and the previous Administration must transmit the CSR file to the new one. The practical risk is sequencing: if the ship sails after the change of Company but before the interim certification is in place, it is trading without valid ISM certification, which is a detention at the next port. ✍ Written Exam Focus 5 State the purpose of the Continuous Synopsis Record and list eight of the particulars it must contain. 10 Distinguish an observation, a non-conformity and a major non-conformity under the ISM Code. Explain the action required when a major non-conformity is raised during a shipboard audit and describe the process by which a non-conformity is properly closed out. 15 Analytically compare an administrative safety audit with a technical statutory survey with respect to focus, methodology and deficiency resolution. Explain how the two regimes are integrated within a shipboard Safety Management System to maintain continuous compliance between statutory surveys, using engine department examples. 🧠 Memory Box CSR = SOLAS XI-1/5. Ship identification number = XI-1/3. Company and owner ID numbers = XI-1/3-1. Every superseded CSR stays on board. A gap in the numbering is a break in the chain — detainable. DOC = Company, 5 years, annual verification ±3 months. SMC = ship, 5 years, one intermediate between the 2nd and 3rd anniversary. Interim DOC 12 months · Interim SMC 6 months (+6). Major NC: downgrade before the team leaves, or the SMC/DOC goes. Downgrading ≠ closing out. Close-out = Correction → Root cause → Corrective action → Verification. Vetting (SIRE, CDI) is commercial, not statutory. ▶ Deep Dive — Why Engine Department Findings Become Major Non-Conformities The pattern Major non-conformities raised against the engine department rarely concern a broken component. They concern evidence that a system for controlling risk was not operating: a critical equipment defect that was never entered on the defect list, a safety device found isolated with no risk assessment or authorisation, a maintenance interval that has silently lapsed across several cycles, or an Oil Record Book entry that cannot be reconciled with the tank soundings and the transfer log. Why these are treated as major Each of them satisfies the second limb of the definition — the absence of effective and systematic implementation of an ISM requirement — rather than the first limb about immediate physical danger. An isolated bilge alarm is a component fault; an isolated bilge alarm with no entry anywhere in the system is evidence that the ship's defect control process is not functioning, and the auditor is entitled to conclude that other defects are being handled the same way. That inference is what escalates the finding. The three habits that prevent it First, everything isolated gets a record: a defect entry, a risk assessment, an authorisation, and a notification to the office if it affects critical equipment. An authorised, documented isolation is a managed risk; an undocumented one is a system failure. Second, overdue maintenance is declared rather than absorbed — an overdue job with a reason, a risk assessment and a plan is a finding at worst, while an overdue job hidden by a back-dated sign-off is a major non-conformity and a credibility problem for every other record on board. Third, the Oil Record Book is reconciled against soundings and the transfer log before it is signed, not after a question is asked. On my vessel (Maersk A/S container tonnage) The most useful discipline is treating the defect list as the audit's primary exhibit rather than an internal working document. If every isolation, deferral and overdue item on board appears on it, with a date, a reason, a risk assessment and an owner, then the auditor's sampling will keep confirming that the system works. The engine room is then being judged on how it manages problems, which is what the ISM Code actually asks, rather than on whether it has any — which no ship can claim. 📚 References SOLAS Chapter XI-1, Regulations 3, 3-1 and 5 International Safety Management (ISM) Code, paragraphs 13 and 14; SOLAS Chapter IX Resolution A.1118(30) — Revised Guidelines on the implementation of the ISM Code by Administrations ISPS Code Part A, section 19 and appendix; SOLAS Chapter XI-2 MSC/Circ. and flag State guidance on CSR amendment procedures OCIMF Ship Inspection Report Programme (SIRE) — see Part 22 Topic 1 Notes-p21 · P21-T3 · v1.0

section_title: Q1. A SIRE 2.0 inspector grades an engine room observation "Not As Expected". What do you do?
text: I would first ask to review the observation with the inspector on the device while we are still in the space, so that the factual basis is clear before it is finalised. If the grading arises from a misunderstanding of our specific machinery configuration, I would present the approved technical manual and the system drawing to show the design arrangement, and ask that the narrative reflect it. If the observation is correct, I acknowledge it without argument, take immediate mitigating action if safety is affected, and photograph the item myself showing the surrounding context and the action taken, so the ship's record matches the inspector's. I would then log the observation into the safety management system so that root cause analysis and a corrective action plan are initiated with the Designated Person Ashore, rather than treating it as a one-off repair. The important thing is that under SIRE 2.0 a negative variance carries a narrative, not just a mark, so the quality of the explanation recorded at the time affects how the finding reads to every charterer who later opens the report.

section_title: Q2. Explain the difference between core, rotational and campaign questions in SIRE 2.0.
text: Core questions are the critical safety, pollution-prevention and statutory checkpoints that carry the highest consequence of failure, and they are generated automatically for every single inspection regardless of ship or operator. Rotational questions are drawn dynamically from the much larger OCIMF question library appropriate to that ship type and vary from one inspection to the next, so that the crew cannot predict the checklist and must maintain readiness across all systems rather than preparing to a fixed list. Campaign questions are selected by OCIMF to target a specific industry-wide trend or a recurring failure mode identified from the aggregated inspection data, so they change as the industry's problems change. The combined effect is that the inspection is compiled for that ship on that day, which is the essential difference from the VIQ7 regime it replaced in 2024, where every ship faced the same static set of roughly three hundred questions.

section_title: Q3. How does TMSA-3 affect what you do on board?
text: TMSA-3 is the operator's own structured self-assessment of its shore management and fleet against thirteen elements, each scored across maturity levels one to four, filed with OCIMF. It matters on board because the SIRE inspection tests whether the declared maturity is real. The element that bears directly on my department is Element 4, Vessel Reliability and Maintenance, where the company declares its planned maintenance discipline, how critical equipment is identified, how defects are managed and what its critical spares policy is. The inspector will use my planned maintenance system records, my defect list and my critical spares inventory to test those declarations. So if the office has declared a high maturity level and my PMS shows unexplained overdue jobs, or my critical spares list does not match what is physically in the store, the damage is not confined to this ship — it undermines the operator's whole self-assessment across the fleet. In practice that means my records have to be accurate rather than merely complete.

section_title: Q4. Why is vetting sometimes commercially more damaging than a PSC detention?
text: A Port State Control detention is a public but discrete event: the deficiencies are rectified, the ship is released, and while the detention affects the flag and company performance record and may raise the ship's targeting factor, the ship can trade again immediately. A poor vetting report is different in kind. It sits in the OCIMF or CDI database, accessible to every charterer, trader and terminal operator for its validity period, and each of them applies their own acceptance criteria to it. A ship that fails to meet those criteria is simply not fixed — there is no appeal to compliance, because vetting is a commercial judgement about acceptable risk, not a legal finding. For a tanker operator, losing acceptance with a major oil company can remove a substantial part of the ship's addressable market, and regaining it requires a subsequent clean inspection plus evidence that the underlying management issues have been corrected. That is why findings suggesting deliberate circumvention of safety systems are so serious: they speak to culture rather than condition.

Examiner: Senthil ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: Two clarifications, no factual reversals. (1) SIRE 2.0 status and timing. The draft presents SIRE 2.0 as "modern" against VIQ7 as "legacy" without dating the transition. SIRE 2.0 was developed by OCIMF over several years and phased into full operation during 2024 , replacing the static VIQ7 questionnaire regime. Candidates should say when, not just what. (2) Question counts. The draft's "~300 static questions" for VIQ7 is an approximation of the order of magnitude and is retained as such; the SIRE 2.0 set is compiled dynamically per inspection from a much larger question library, so no fixed count exists and none is stated here. (3) TMSA version. TMSA-3 (13 elements) is presented as current. OCIMF revises TMSA periodically and the self-assessment is tightly coupled to the SIRE regime, so the applicable edition should be confirmed against the company's own submission before an examination. Carried forward from Part 21 Topic 3: vetting is a commercial risk-assessment practice, not a statutory requirement — no IMO instrument mandates SIRE, CDI or TMSA. 📖 Definition Commercial vetting is the process by which cargo interests, charterers and terminals satisfy themselves that a ship and its operator are an acceptable risk, independently of statutory compliance. SIRE (Ship Inspection Report Programme), operated by OCIMF since 1993, is the dominant scheme for tankers. CDI serves the chemical trades. TMSA is the operator's own structured self-assessment of its shore management, verified against what an inspector finds on board. A ship can hold every statutory certificate and still be commercially unemployable on a poor vetting record. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) SIRE 2.0 grades the crew , not only the equipment. A correctly maintained system operated by an engineer who cannot explain it now scores "Not As Expected" — which changes what preparation means. The question set is no longer predictable. Rotational and campaign questions mean the engine room cannot be prepared to a checklist; it has to be in order across the board. TMSA is the company's declaration of its own maturity. A SIRE inspector cross-checks shipboard reality against that declaration, so a gap between office claims and engine room practice damages the operator far beyond the single ship. The findings that end vetting acceptance are almost all engine department items: bypassed interlocks, unauthorised jumpers, temporary pipe repairs, an OWS with a questionable history. 📅 Historical Background 1993 OCIMF introduces SIRE — vetting standardised into a shared database 2004 onward TMSA introduced; operators self-assess shore management against KPIs 2017 TMSA-3 issued — 13 elements, integrated with the SIRE data flow 2024 SIRE 2.0 enters full operation , replacing the static VIQ7 regime Ongoing CDI-Marine for bulk chemical tankers; MPCAS for packed chemical cargo ⚖ Regulatory References Reference Framework (note: none of these is a statutory instrument) OCIMF SIRE 2.0 Risk-based, digitally captured tanker inspection regime; question sets compiled per inspection; graded rather than binary responses. OCIMF TMSA-3 Tanker Management and Self Assessment — 13 elements, each scored across maturity levels 1 to 4. CDI-Marine Chemical Distribution Institute inspection scheme for bulk chemical tankers. MPCAS Marine Packed Cargo Audit Scheme — packaged chemical cargo, container packing, securing and terminal interfaces. ISM Code (SOLAS Ch. IX) The statutory system that vetting verifies in practice — findings are fed back into the SMS as non-conformities or observations. MARPOL Annex I, Reg. 14 Oily water separating equipment and the 15 ppm alarm — the single most scrutinised engine room item in any vetting inspection. 🧩 SIRE 2.0 Architecture SIRE 2.0 replaced a fixed paper questionnaire with a dynamically compiled, risk-targeted question set delivered on an inspector's handheld device. Three consequences follow, and each is examinable. [OCIMF question library + vessel factors, history, operator TMSA data] │ dynamically compiled per inspection │ ┌───────────────────┬───────────────────┬───────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ CORE QUESTIONS ROTATIONAL QS CAMPAIGN QS every inspection vary between industry-wide themes (critical safety inspections selected by OCIMF and pollution) (unpredictable) └───────────────────┴───────────────────┘ │ each question assessed across FOUR elements, graded not binary: HUMAN · PROCESS · HARDWARE · PHOTOGRAPH Core questions — mandatory on every inspection; the critical safety, pollution-prevention and statutory checkpoints where failure carries the highest consequence. Rotational questions — drawn dynamically from the wider library and varied between inspections, so the crew cannot anticipate the checklist and must maintain readiness across all systems. Campaign questions — selected by OCIMF to probe an industry-wide trend or a recurring failure mode identified from the aggregated data. The four elements. Each question is assessed against: Human — crew familiarity, training and actual execution; Process — whether the company's SMS procedure is adequate and was followed; Hardware — physical condition, certification and maintenance; Photograph — photographic evidence substantiating what was found. The mnemonic H-P-H-P is a revision aid, not an OCIMF term. Graded responses. Observations are recorded as As Expected , Not As Expected or Better Than Expected , with supporting narrative for any variance in either direction. This is the structural change that matters: the old binary yes/no recorded whether a thing existed; the graded response records how well it was being operated. A fully compliant, fully certificated system operated by an engineer who cannot explain its logic can now be graded Not As Expected. 🧪 CDI and TMSA CDI-Marine. Operated by the Chemical Distribution Institute, a non-commercial trade association, for bulk chemical tankers. It produces a detailed technical report against a standardised questionnaire, used by chemical companies for risk assessment. It is more prescriptive and hardware-focused than SIRE 2.0. MPCAS. The Marine Packed Cargo Audit Scheme extends CDI's approach to packaged chemicals moving in containers — packing, securing, documentation and the terminal logistics interface. TMSA-3. The operator self-assesses its shore organisation and fleet against 13 elements , scoring each across maturity levels 1 to 4 . The result is filed with OCIMF and becomes part of the data the SIRE inspection is compiled against. The engine department's direct connection is TMSA Element 4, Vessel Reliability and Maintenance . That element is where the company declares its planned maintenance discipline, critical equipment identification, defect management and spares policy — and it is the shipboard PMS, defect list and critical spares inventory that a SIRE inspector uses to test whether the declared maturity level is real. VIQ7 (legacy) SIRE 2.0 CDI-Marine TMSA-3 Scope Tanker hardware checklist Risk-based tanker assessment Chemical tanker audit Operator self-assessment Method Static paper list Dynamically compiled digital set Standardised technical questionnaire Office and fleet KPI matrix Size ~300 fixed questions Compiled per inspection from a large library Fixed audit book 13 elements Human factors Minimal — hardware-centric Central — crew performance graded Moderate — technical competence High — management culture and KPIs Output Binary yes/no As / Not As / Better Than Expected Compliance score Maturity levels 1–4 🔧 The Engine Room in a Vetting Inspection Before: pre-inspection questionnaire and certificate data uploaded and accurate; PMS current with no unexplained overdue items; defect list live, with each open item risk-assessed, dated and owned; critical spares inventory verified against the declared list, not against the software. During: the Chief Engineer escorts the inspector throughout — never allow unescorted movement through machinery spaces. Where the inspector photographs a finding, take an identical photograph showing the surrounding context and any immediate action taken, so the ship's record matches the inspector's. Known high-scrutiny items: oily water separator and the 15 ppm alarm, with no bypass arrangement and a coherent Oil Record Book that reconciles to soundings; bilges visibly clean and dry; emergency generator and emergency fire pump on demand; steering gear including the emergency changeover drill; fixed firefighting release arrangements and their alarms and dampers. If it is correct, acknowledge it, take immediate mitigating action if safety is affected, and log it into the SMS so root cause analysis and corrective action begin with the DPA. They are evidence of deliberate circumvention: an electrical jumper across a trip, a bypassed machinery interlock, a temporary soft patch on a pressure line, a wire-tied quick-closing valve. No IMO instrument mandates SIRE, CDI or TMSA. SIRE 2.0 questions: Core (always) · Rotational (varies) · Campaign (industry themes). Four elements: Human · Process · Hardware · Photograph. Graded: As / Not As / Better Than Expected. TMSA-3 = 13 elements, maturity levels 1–4. Element 4 = Vessel Reliability and Maintenance — the engine department's element. CDI-Marine = bulk chemical tankers. MPCAS = packed chemical cargo. Vetting killers: jumpers, bypassed interlocks, soft patches, wire-tied quick-closing valves. ▶ Deep Dive — Preparing for an Unpredictable Inspection Why checklist preparation no longer works Under VIQ7 a competent Chief Engineer could work the questionnaire in the week before an inspection and close the gaps. SIRE 2.0 removed that possibility deliberately: the rotational element means the specific questions are unknown until the inspector is on board, and the campaign element means the emphasis shifts across the industry without notice. The only viable preparation is a plant and a set of records that are continuously in order. The human element is the real change Grading crew performance means the inspector will ask a watchkeeper to explain a system, not just show it. The failure mode is a well-maintained installation that nobody on the current crew fully understands — common after a crew change, and common with equipment retrofitted between dockings. The defence is familiarisation that is genuinely completed rather than signed: walkthroughs on the actual plant, with the responsible engineer explaining the system logic aloud, recorded as training. Photographic discipline Every finding is photographed by the inspector and the photograph travels with the report. A close-up of an oil-stained tank top conveys something quite different from a wide shot showing a clean machinery space with one localised leak under repair. Taking a matching contextual photograph at the moment the inspector takes theirs is not defensive gamesmanship; it is how the ship ensures its own record of the same fact exists. On my vessel (Maersk A/S container tonnage) Container tonnage is outside the SIRE and CDI regimes, but the same logic has migrated into charterer and terminal inspections and into the company's own internal audits. The transferable discipline is the graded mindset: assume the question is not "does this work?" but "can the duty engineer explain why it works, show me the record, and tell me what happens when it fails?" section_subtitle: Global Climate Accords and the Legal Genesis of Maritime Decarbonisation — Kyoto, Doha and Paris
section_title: Q1. What is the legal basis for the IMO regulating greenhouse gas emissions from ships?
text: It derives from Article 2, paragraph 2 of the Kyoto Protocol, under which the Annex I Parties agreed to pursue limitation or reduction of emissions of greenhouse gases not controlled by the Montreal Protocol from aviation and marine bunker fuels, working through the International Civil Aviation Organization and the International Maritime Organization respectively. That provision assigned international shipping emissions to the IMO rather than to national emissions inventories, and it is the origin of everything that followed — the 2011 energy efficiency amendments introducing EEDI and SEEMP into MARPOL Annex VI, the Data Collection System, EEXI and CII, and the Initial and Revised GHG Strategies. The Paris Agreement did not disturb that assignment: it does not expressly address international shipping at all, so the sector remains outside Nationally Determined Contributions and the IMO route remains the only global one. That structural fact is also why regional measures such as the EU Emissions Trading System extension and FuelEU Maritime emerged — regional actors filling the gap left by the pace of global consensus.

section_title: Q2. List the Kyoto Protocol Annex A gases and identify those with direct shipboard relevance.
text: The original six controlled gases are carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, hydrofluorocarbons, perfluorocarbons and sulphur hexafluoride. Nitrogen trifluoride was added as a seventh for the second commitment period by the Doha Amendment of 2012. Four have direct shipboard relevance. Carbon dioxide is the dominant emission and the subject of the entire EEDI, EEXI and CII framework. Methane matters because of methane slip from low-pressure dual-fuel LNG engines, which is significant in well-to-wake accounting and can materially erode the apparent carbon benefit of LNG. Hydrofluorocarbons are the refrigerants in the provision plant and air conditioning system, which is why refrigerant leakage control and log-keeping have become an environmental compliance matter rather than a purely technical one. Sulphur hexafluoride is the insulating medium in high-voltage switchgear, relevant on ships with high-voltage installations. Nitrous oxide is a minor combustion product but is included in carbon dioxide equivalent accounting. Perfluorocarbons are industrial process gases and are not a normal ship emission.

section_title: Q3. Compare the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement in structure.
text: Kyoto was top-down and differentiated. Binding quantified emission limitation targets were negotiated and assigned to Annex I Parties only — developed countries and economies in transition — while non-Annex I developing countries took no binding commitments. Compliance was supported by three market mechanisms: the Clean Development Mechanism generating Certified Emission Reductions from projects in developing countries, Joint Implementation generating Emission Reduction Units between Annex I Parties, and International Emissions Trading in surplus assigned amounts. Paris is bottom-up and universal. Every Party prepares, communicates and maintains a Nationally Determined Contribution stating its own targets, reviewed on a five-year ratchet under which each successive contribution must represent a progression. The legal obligation attaches to the process of submitting and maintaining an NDC rather than to achieving the number in it. The overall goal shifted from an aggregate percentage against 1990 to a temperature outcome — well below two degrees, pursuing efforts towards one and a half. For shipping the critical structural difference is that Kyoto expressly assigned international bunker fuel emissions to the IMO under Article 2.2, whereas Paris does not mention international shipping, leaving that assignment in place by default.

section_title: Q4. Why is progress on IMO greenhouse gas measures so slow compared with other MARPOL amendments?
text: Because two legitimate principles collide. From the UNFCCC and Kyoto comes common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities — the position that developed States, having caused the historical accumulation, should bear the greater burden, and that developing States should not have their development constrained. From the IMO comes no more favourable treatment, the principle that a ship is regulated according to where it trades rather than whose flag it flies, which is what makes MARPOL enforceable at all — without it, tonnage would migrate to whichever register imposed the least. A measure that differentiates by flag or by the nationality of the owner undermines enforceability; a measure that treats all ships identically is resisted as ignoring differentiated responsibility. Every carbon pricing proposal at the IMO has had to navigate that, usually by treating ships uniformly while redistributing the revenue differentially. The October 2025 extraordinary session of the MEPC, which adjourned adoption of the Net-Zero Framework by a vote of 57 to 49 with 21 abstentions, is the clearest demonstration of how unresolved that tension remains.

text: Part 22 · Topic 2 Global Climate Accords and the Legal Genesis of Maritime Decarbonisation — Kyoto, Doha and Paris Kyoto Art. 2.2 · Annex A Gases · CDM/JI/ET · Paris NDCs Uday pp. 533–542 (approx.) Examiner: Simon ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: One significant addition and two clarifications. (1) The missing link. The draft explains Kyoto and Paris but never states why a marine engineer studies them. The connection is Kyoto Protocol Article 2, paragraph 2 , under which Annex I Parties agreed to pursue limitation or reduction of greenhouse gases from aviation and marine bunker fuels working through ICAO and the IMO respectively . That single provision is the legal origin of the IMO's mandate over shipping GHG, and it is the reason international shipping sits outside national inventories. It has been added, because without it the chapter is climate history rather than maritime regulation. (2) Paris and shipping. The Paris Agreement does not expressly mention international shipping or aviation — the reference in the draft text of the agreement was removed before adoption. International shipping emissions therefore fall outside Nationally Determined Contributions, which is precisely why the IMO route matters and why the point is examinable. Added. (3) Doha Amendment entry into force. The draft describes the second commitment period without noting that the Doha Amendment did not enter into force until 31 December 2020 — the day the period it governed ended. Added, because it explains why the second period had little practical effect. 📖 Definition The UNFCCC (1992) is the framework convention; the Kyoto Protocol (1997) was its first binding implementing instrument, imposing quantified targets on developed countries only; the Paris Agreement (2015) replaced that architecture with universal participation through self-determined national pledges. For a marine engineer their significance is narrow and specific: Kyoto assigned international shipping emissions to the IMO rather than to national inventories, and Paris left that assignment untouched. Everything in MARPOL Annex VI Chapter 4 traces back to that assignment. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) Kyoto Article 2.2 is why the IMO — and not the flag State's environment ministry — regulates ship GHG. Every subsequent instrument, from EEDI to CII to the Net-Zero Framework, sits on that foundation. International shipping falls outside national NDCs. That structural gap explains both the IMO's slow consensus-based progress and the willingness of the EU to act unilaterally through the ETS and FuelEU Maritime. Kyoto's Annex I / non-Annex I split created the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, which collides directly with the IMO's own principle of no more favourable treatment. That collision is the substantive reason IMO GHG negotiations are difficult, and it is a strong oral answer. The Kyoto market mechanisms — CDM, JI and emissions trading — are the conceptual ancestors of every maritime carbon pricing proposal now on the table. 📅 Historical Background 1992 UNFCCC adopted at the Rio Earth Summit 11 Dec 1997 Kyoto Protocol adopted 16 Feb 2005 Kyoto Protocol enters into force 2008–2012 First commitment period — collective reduction of about 5% against 1990 levels 8 Dec 2012 Doha Amendment adopted — second commitment period and NF₃ added 12 Dec 2015 Paris Agreement adopted at COP 21 4 Nov 2016 Paris Agreement enters into force; India ratified 2 October 2016 31 Dec 2020 Doha Amendment finally enters into force — on the last day of the period it governed Nov 2021 COP 26 — India announces net-zero by 2070 and the associated 2030 targets ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments UNFCCC, 1992 Framework convention; establishes the objective of stabilising GHG concentrations and the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities. Kyoto Protocol, Art. 2(2) Annex I Parties shall pursue limitation or reduction of greenhouse gases from aviation and marine bunker fuels, working through ICAO and the IMO respectively. The legal origin of the IMO's GHG mandate. Kyoto Protocol, Annex A The controlled gases: CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, HFCs, PFCs and SF₆ — with NF₃ added for the second commitment period by the Doha Amendment. Kyoto Protocol, Arts. 6, 12, 17 Joint Implementation, the Clean Development Mechanism, and International Emissions Trading. Doha Amendment, 2012 Second commitment period 2013–2020; 18% reduction target against 1990 for participating Parties; in force 31 December 2020. Paris Agreement, 2015 Well below 2 °C, pursuing efforts towards 1.5 °C; universal participation via Nationally Determined Contributions on a five-year ratchet cycle. Does not expressly address international shipping. ⚗ The Kyoto Architecture Gas Note Carbon dioxide (CO₂) The dominant ship emission; the entire EEDI/EEXI/CII framework addresses it Methane (CH₄) Directly relevant to shipping through methane slip from low-pressure dual-fuel LNG engines Nitrous oxide (N₂O) A minor but non-zero combustion product; included in well-to-wake CO₂-equivalent accounting Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) Refrigerants — the link to the shipboard refrigeration and air-conditioning plant Perfluorocarbons (PFCs) Industrial process gases; not a normal ship emission Sulphur hexafluoride (SF₆) Electrical switchgear insulation medium — relevant to high-voltage installations Nitrogen trifluoride (NF₃) Added by the Doha Amendment for the second commitment period — the seventh gas Party categories. Annex I — developed countries and economies in transition, which accepted quantified targets. Annex II — a subset of Annex I (developed countries excluding the economies in transition), additionally obliged to provide finance and technology transfer. Non-Annex I — developing countries, with no binding quantified commitments. India is non-Annex I. Commitment periods. First, 2008–2012: a collective reduction of about 5% against a 1990 baseline across participating Annex I Parties, with differentiated national figures — the EU accepting 8% and Germany 21%. Second, 2013–2020, established by the Doha Amendment with an 18% target against 1990 for participating Parties. India accepted the Doha Amendment on 8 August 2017 as the 80th Party to do so. The amendment did not enter into force until 31 December 2020 , the final day of the period it governed, which is why the second period is of limited practical significance. Clean Development Mechanism (Art. 12). An Annex I Party finances an emission-reduction project in a developing country and earns Certified Emission Reductions (CERs) , one CER equalling one tonne of CO₂ equivalent, usable against its own target. Joint Implementation (Art. 6). The same project-based logic between two Annex I Parties, generating Emission Reduction Units (ERUs) . International Emissions Trading (Art. 17). Parties that overachieve may sell surplus assigned amount to Parties that fall short — the first genuine international carbon market. Sinks. Land use, land-use change and forestry, allowing sequestration to be counted against emissions. 🌍 The Paris Shift Kyoto Protocol Paris Agreement Participation Binding targets on Annex I Parties only Universal — every Party submits a contribution Target setting Top-down, negotiated and assigned Bottom-up, self-determined (NDCs) Legal character of the target Binding quantified emission limitation Binding obligation to prepare, communicate and maintain an NDC; the target itself is not internationally enforceable Goal Aggregate reduction against 1990 levels Well below 2 °C, pursuing 1.5 °C above pre-industrial Cycle Fixed commitment periods Five-year ratchet — successive NDCs must represent a progression Gases The Annex A list (6, later 7) All anthropogenic greenhouse gases International shipping Expressly assigned to the IMO by Article 2(2) Not expressly addressed — remains with the IMO by default Why the omission matters. Because international shipping is not in any NDC, no State's national target is affected by what its flagged fleet emits. That removes the domestic political driver that operates in every other sector, and leaves progress dependent on consensus at the IMO — where the Kyoto-derived principle of common but differentiated responsibilities is pressed by developing States against the IMO's own long-standing principle of no more favourable treatment , under which a ship is regulated by where it trades rather than by whose flag it flies. That tension is the substantive explanation for the pace of IMO GHG regulation, and it produced the October 2025 adjournment discussed in Topic 3. India's position — worth having precisely for a Kochi MMD oral. Ratified the Paris Agreement on 2 October 2016. At COP 26 (Glasgow, 2021) announced: reduce the emissions intensity of GDP by 45% below 2005 levels by 2030; 500 GW of non-fossil energy capacity by 2030; meet 50% of energy requirements from renewables by 2030; reduce projected emissions by one billion tonnes by 2030; and achieve net-zero by 2070 . Forest and tree cover expansion supports the additional carbon sink commitment. 🎓 CE Oral Tip (Simon): Simon uses this material as the setup for the technical questions that follow, so the answer he is listening for is the bridge, not the history. Then the consequence — international shipping is outside national inventories and outside NDCs, and the Paris Agreement does not mention it.
