Explain why international shipping falls outside Nationally Determined Contributions, and assess how the tension between common but differentiated responsibilities and no more favourable treatment has shaped the pace of IMO measures. 🧠 Memory Box Kyoto Art. 2(2) = the IMO's mandate over ship GHG. Aviation to ICAO, marine bunkers to IMO. Annex A gases: CO₂ · CH₄ · N₂O · HFCs · PFCs · SF₆ , plus NF₃ added by the Doha Amendment (seventh). CDM → CERs (Annex I into developing). JI → ERUs (Annex I into Annex I). Emissions Trading → surplus assigned amount. Kyoto: top-down, Annex I only. Paris: bottom-up, universal, NDCs on a 5-year ratchet. Paris does NOT mention international shipping — so it stays with the IMO and outside NDCs. CBDR (UNFCCC) vs No More Favourable Treatment (IMO) — the structural tension behind every GHG negotiation. India: Paris ratified 2 Oct 2016 · net-zero 2070 · 45% intensity cut vs 2005 by 2030 · 500 GW non-fossil by 2030. ▶ Deep Dive — Why the Regional Measures Appeared The gap If international shipping is outside every national inventory and outside every NDC, then no State can improve its own reported position by regulating the ships that call at its ports. The only lever is the IMO, and the IMO moves by consensus among States with sharply divergent economic interests. That gap — a sector nobody counts, regulated by a body that cannot move quickly — is what regional measures were designed to close. What the EU did Two instruments, deliberately complementary. The EU Emissions Trading System was extended to maritime transport from 2024, requiring surrender of allowances against verified emissions on a phased basis — a proportion in the first years rising to full surrender — covering voyages within the EU in full and voyages into and out of the EU at half. Separately, FuelEU Maritime (Regulation (EU) 2023/1805) applies from 1 January 2025 and limits the greenhouse gas intensity of the energy used on board, on a well-to-wake basis against a 2020 fleet baseline of 91.16 gCO₂eq/MJ , tightening on a defined schedule. The distinction that must not be blurred These are separate regulatory tracks with different accounting boundaries, and conflating them is a known examination trap. CII under MARPOL Annex VI Regulation 28 is tank-to-wake : it counts what comes out of the funnel, using fixed carbon factors per fuel type, and takes no account of how the fuel was produced. FuelEU Maritime and the IMO's proposed GHG Fuel Intensity metric are well-to-wake : they count the whole fuel lifecycle including production and distribution. A fuel can therefore look excellent under CII and mediocre under a well-to-wake metric, which is exactly the case for fossil LNG. Never write a causal sentence connecting a CII outcome to a FuelEU outcome without checking the boundary. On my vessel (Maersk A/S container tonnage) For a European-trading container operator these regimes overlap in practice: the same voyage generates an ETS allowance liability, a FuelEU intensity balance and a CII rating contribution, computed on different boundaries from the same bunker data. The engine room consequence is that fuel consumption reporting has to be accurate at a granularity none of these schemes required ten years ago — by fuel grade, by voyage leg, and reconciled to bunker delivery notes — because three separate compliance calculations now depend on the same underlying figures. 📚 References United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, 1992 Kyoto Protocol to the UNFCCC, 1997 — Article 2(2), Articles 6, 12 and 17, and Annex A Doha Amendment to the Kyoto Protocol, 2012 — in force 31 December 2020 Paris Agreement, 2015 — in force 4 November 2016 India's Nationally Determined Contribution and COP 26 announcements Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 (FuelEU Maritime); Directive (EU) 2023/959 (EU ETS extension to maritime transport) Notes-p22 · P22-T2 · v1.0

section_title: Q1. Compare the Initial and Revised IMO GHG Strategies.
text: The Initial Strategy, adopted at MEPC 72 in 2018, set a carbon intensity target of at least a forty per cent reduction in CO2 emissions per transport work by 2030 while pursuing efforts towards seventy per cent by 2050, and a target of reducing total annual greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping by at least fifty per cent by 2050, both against a 2008 baseline, with a vision of phasing out emissions entirely within this century. The Revised Strategy, adopted at MEPC 80 in July 2023, retained the forty per cent carbon intensity target for 2030 but changed the character of the headline goal from intensity to absolute reduction. It sets net-zero greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping by or around 2050, with indicative checkpoints of at least twenty per cent striving for thirty per cent absolute reduction by 2030, and at least seventy per cent striving for eighty per cent by 2040, both against 2008. It also adds a technology target that zero or near-zero greenhouse gas emission technologies, fuels and energy sources should represent at least five per cent, striving for ten per cent, of the energy used by international shipping by 2030. The important conceptual point is that an intensity target can be met while total emissions rise if trade grows; an absolute target cannot.

section_title: Q2. What is the current status of the IMO Net-Zero Framework?
text: It is approved but not adopted, and it is not in force. The Framework was approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025 as draft amendments that would insert a new Chapter 5 into MARPOL Annex VI, combining a goal-based greenhouse gas fuel intensity standard on a well-to-wake basis with an economic pricing and reward mechanism, under which ships exceeding the required intensity acquire remedial units and ships outperforming it may earn surplus units. It was submitted for formal adoption at the second extraordinary session of the Marine Environment Protection Committee, held in London from the fourteenth to the seventeenth of October 2025. The session did not adopt it: a motion to adjourn for one year carried by fifty-seven votes to forty-nine with twenty-one abstentions. The Committee returned to it at MEPC 84, held from the twenty-seventh of April to the first of May 2026 and preceded by the twenty-first Intersessional Working Group on GHG emissions, but again reached no final agreement — reporting describes a continuing split between states wanting the original text adopted with minimal change and states wanting a more market-ready approach, although the balance of support was reported to have shifted towards adoption since the October 2025 vote. Work continues through two further intersessional working groups scheduled for September and November 2026, reporting to MEPC 85, which is planned for the thirtieth of November to the third of December 2026, immediately followed by a one-day resumption of the extraordinary session on the fourth of December 2026 — that date is the current decision point, superseding the October 2026 date originally announced in 2025. So the correct statement is that it is a draft instrument that operators should plan for but which has no legal effect, and any figure associated with it, including the 93.3 grams of CO2 equivalent per megajoule reference baseline discussed at MEPC 83, is a draft figure.

section_title: Q3. Which of the energy efficiency measures do you actually influence as Chief Engineer, and how?
text: EEDI is fixed at design and construction and I cannot change it; my only concern there is that the ship-specific EEDI Technical File is maintained on board and that no machinery or structural modification takes the ship outside its approved design assumptions. EEXI is a one-off calculation for existing ships, most commonly satisfied by engine or shaft power limitation, so my role is to ensure the limitation arrangement is correctly installed, sealed, and that the override arrangement and its recording are understood, since misuse of the override is a compliance failure. The measure I genuinely influence is the CII, the operational carbon intensity rating under MARPOL Annex VI Regulation 28, which is recalculated every year from reported fuel consumption and distance sailed and produces a rating from A to E against a reduction factor that tightens annually. The levers are hull and propeller cleanliness, which is usually the largest single recoverable loss; waste heat recovery output, which degrades with economiser soot fouling and steam leakage; turbocharger and air cooler cleanliness, which govern charge air density and therefore combustion quality; injector condition and timing; use of the shaft generator in place of auxiliary engines where the load profile allows; thermal insulation of exhaust and steam systems; and auxiliary load discipline. The SEEMP Part III is where those measures are formally recorded, and if the ship is rated D for three consecutive years or E once, a plan of corrective actions must be developed and incorporated into it.

section_title: Q4. Explain the difference between tank-to-wake and well-to-wake accounting and why it matters.
text: Tank-to-wake accounting counts only the emissions produced on board from the fuel as burned, using fixed carbon conversion factors for each fuel type. That is the basis of the CII under MARPOL Annex VI Regulation 28: fuel consumed multiplied by its carbon factor, divided by transport work. It takes no account of how the fuel was produced, extracted, refined or transported. Well-to-wake accounting counts the entire lifecycle, including upstream production and distribution emissions, and is expressed as greenhouse gas intensity per unit of energy in grams of CO2 equivalent per megajoule. That is the basis of FuelEU Maritime under EU Regulation 2023/1805, and of the greenhouse gas fuel intensity metric in the draft IMO Net-Zero Framework. The distinction matters because a fuel can look very different on the two bases. Fossil LNG performs well tank-to-wake because of its favourable carbon-to-hydrogen ratio, but performs considerably less well well-to-wake once upstream methane leakage and any onboard methane slip are counted. Blue and green fuels can show the reverse pattern. The practical rule is that the two are separate regulatory tracks with separate baselines — the draft IMO figure of 93.3 grams of CO2 equivalent per megajoule is a 2008 fleet average, while the FuelEU baseline of 91.16 is a 2020 EU fleet average — and no causal statement should be made across them without checking which boundary applies.

text: Part 22 · Topic 3 The IMO GHG Strategy, Market-Based Measures and Technical Energy Efficiency — EEDI, EEXI, CII and the Net-Zero Framework 2023 GHG Strategy · EEDI/EEXI/CII · NZF Status · WHRS Uday pp. 542–550 (approx.) Examiner: Simon ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: One major status update and three additions. (1) The Net-Zero Framework has NOT been adopted. The draft states only that "the exact economic instrument has not yet been finally adopted into statutory law", which was accurate when written but is now datable and materially incomplete. The position: the IMO Net-Zero Framework was approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025 as draft amendments introducing a new Chapter 5 to MARPOL Annex VI , combining a goal-based GHG fuel intensity standard with a pricing and reward mechanism. It was submitted for adoption at the 2nd extraordinary session of the MEPC (MEPC/ES.2), held 14–17 October 2025 . The session adjourned for one year without adopting the amendments , on a vote of 57 in favour of adjournment, 49 against, 21 abstentions . This note has been updated a second time following MEPC 84 (27 April – 1 May 2026) , held after this topic was first drafted: MEPC 84, preceded by ISWG-GHG 21 (20–24 April 2026), considered the Framework but reached no final agreement — reports describe a continuing split between States wanting the April 2025 text adopted with minimal change and States wanting a more market-ready approach. The Committee agreed to press on rather than abandon it: two further intersessional GHG working groups are scheduled (September and November 2026), reporting to MEPC 85 (30 November – 3 December 2026) , immediately followed by a one-day resumption of MEPC/ES.2 on 4 December 2026 — now the operative decision point, superseding the "October 2026" date originally announced in October 2025. Every reference to the Framework in this topic is therefore flagged as draft and not in force , in the reg box, in the tables and in the CE tip. (2) 2023 Strategy incomplete in the draft. The draft omits the retained carbon-intensity element — the Revised Strategy keeps the commitment to reduce CO₂ emissions per transport work by at least 40% by 2030 compared with 2008, alongside the new absolute checkpoints. Added. (3) EEXI and CII absent. The draft covers EEDI but not EEXI or CII, which are the measures actually biting on existing tonnage today. Added. (4) Regulation numbering. The energy efficiency regulations within MARPOL Annex VI Chapter 4 were renumbered by the 2021 amendments (in force 1 November 2022). Only Regulation 28 (operational carbon intensity rating) is cited here by number; other measures are cited by name and chapter, and the current consolidated text should be checked before quoting a regulation number in an oral. (5) Cross-reference — Parts 1–18, and a currency note for that topic. Part 2 Topic 9 (Decarbonisation Pathways & the IMO Net-Zero Framework (MEPC-83)) already covers the Framework in more commercial depth — the draft two-tier GHG pricing figures, the Net-Zero Fund's dual purpose, and the draft Z-factor trajectory through 2030 — none of which is repeated here; this topic instead covers the broader Strategy history (2018 vs 2023), the in-force EEDI/EEXI/SEEMP/CII technical measures, and the tank-to-wake/well-to-wake distinction, which Part 2 Topic 9 does not. Read together. Separately: Part 2 Topic 9's own verification note currently states adoption was "rescheduled to November 2026" — that was accurate when written but is now superseded by the confirmed 4 December 2026 date verified in this topic (following MEPC 84's no-agreement outcome in April–May 2026). That note has not been edited as part of this build; flagging it here so it can be corrected for consistency. 📖 Definition The IMO's greenhouse gas regime has three layers. A strategy setting the ambition — the Initial Strategy of 2018, replaced by the Revised Strategy adopted at MEPC 80 in July 2023. A set of in-force technical and operational measures in MARPOL Annex VI Chapter 4 — EEDI for new ships, EEXI for existing ships, the SEEMP, and the CII operational rating. And a proposed economic layer , the Net-Zero Framework, which combines a GHG fuel intensity standard with carbon pricing — approved in April 2025 but not yet adopted , with the next scheduled decision point a resumed extraordinary session on 4 December 2026. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) EEDI is fixed at design; EEXI is a one-off calculation usually satisfied by power limitation; CII is the one that recurs every year and is driven by how the ship is operated — which makes it the Chief Engineer's measure. A D rating for three consecutive years, or a single E, forces a corrective action plan into SEEMP Part III. That is a commercial and administrative penalty arising directly from engine room and voyage performance. Waste heat recovery, shaft generators, hull and propeller condition and auxiliary load management are the levers that move CII within a given trade pattern — they are engineering decisions with a regulatory rating attached. The Net-Zero Framework, if adopted, would shift the metric from carbon intensity per transport work to GHG intensity per unit of energy on a well-to-wake basis. That changes which fuels look good, and it is why the tank-to-wake versus well-to-wake distinction has to be understood rather than memorised. 📅 Historical Background 2011 MEPC.203(62) — EEDI and SEEMP added to MARPOL Annex VI as Chapter 4; in force 1 January 2013 Apr 2018 MEPC 72 — Initial IMO GHG Strategy 2019 onward IMO Data Collection System for fuel oil consumption operational Jun 2021 MEPC.328(76) — EEXI, CII and SEEMP Part III adopted; in force 1 November 2022 1 Jan 2023 EEXI and CII requirements take effect; first CII ratings assigned for calendar year 2023 Jul 2023 MEPC 80 — 2023 Revised IMO GHG Strategy Apr 2025 MEPC 83 — Net-Zero Framework approved as draft MARPOL Annex VI Chapter 5 14–17 Oct 2025 MEPC/ES.2 adjourns for one year without adopting the NZF — 57 / 49 / 21 27 Apr–1 May 2026 MEPC 84 (preceded by ISWG-GHG 21, 20–24 Apr) — no final agreement reached ; work continues 4 Dec 2026 MEPC/ES.2 due to resume for one day, immediately after MEPC 85 (30 Nov–3 Dec 2026) — current decision point ⚖ Regulatory References Key Instruments MARPOL Annex VI, Chapter 4 Regulations on energy efficiency for ships — EEDI (new ships), EEXI (existing ships), SEEMP and the operational carbon intensity requirements. Renumbered by the 2021 amendments (in force 1 November 2022). MARPOL Annex VI, Reg. 28 Operational carbon intensity — required annual operational CII and the A to E rating. Tank-to-wake basis using fixed carbon factors per fuel. Resolution MEPC.328(76) 2021 revised MARPOL Annex VI — introduced EEXI, CII and SEEMP Part III. Resolution MEPC.377(80) 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships. International Energy Efficiency (IEE) Certificate Issued on verification of the attained EEDI/EEXI and the SEEMP; the ship-specific EEDI Technical File is its supporting document. IMO Net-Zero Framework Draft — approved MEPC 83 (April 2025); NOT adopted. Adjourned at MEPC/ES.2 (Oct 2025, 57/49/21); MEPC 84 (Apr–May 2026) reached no final agreement; MEPC/ES.2 due to resume 4 December 2026, after MEPC 85. Would insert a new Chapter 5 into MARPOL Annex VI: a goal-based GHG fuel intensity standard on a well-to-wake basis plus a pricing and reward mechanism. 🎯 Initial Strategy (2018) versus Revised Strategy (2023) Initial Strategy — MEPC 72, 2018 Revised Strategy — MEPC 80, 2023 Carbon intensity (per transport work) At least 40% reduction by 2030, pursuing 70% by 2050, vs 2008 Retained — at least 40% by 2030 vs 2008 Absolute GHG — 2030 — At least 20%, striving for 30% , reduction vs 2008 (indicative checkpoint) Absolute GHG — 2040 — At least 70%, striving for 80% , reduction vs 2008 (indicative checkpoint) Absolute GHG — 2050 At least 50% reduction vs 2008 Net-zero by or around 2050 Zero/near-zero fuels — At least 5%, striving for 10% , of the energy used by international shipping by 2030 Long-term Phase out GHG entirely within this century, consistent with Paris Net-zero by or around 2050, consistent with 1.5 °C pathways Two points that gain marks. First, the 2030 and 2040 figures are indicative checkpoints , not binding limits — the binding instruments are the MARPOL measures beneath the strategy. Second, the Revised Strategy did not simply raise the numbers: it changed the type of target, from a carbon-intensity metric (emissions per transport work, which can improve while total emissions rise) to absolute GHG reduction, which cannot. The three horizons of candidate measures. Short-term — the technical and operational measures now in force (EEXI, CII, SEEMP Part III), subject to review. Mid-term — a technical element , being a goal-based marine fuel standard regulating a phased reduction of fuel GHG intensity, and an economic element , being a maritime GHG emissions pricing mechanism. These two together form the Net-Zero Framework. Long-term — full decarbonisation through zero-emission fuels and propulsion by or around 2050. 📐 EEDI, EEXI, SEEMP and CII — What Is Actually in Force EEDI = CO₂ emissions ÷ transport work , in grams of CO₂ per tonne-nautical mile Measure Applies to Nature Engineer's lever EEDI New ships (by ship type and size) Design index, fixed at construction; attained EEDI must not exceed the required EEDI for the applicable phase None once built — but the EEDI Technical File constrains later modification EEXI Existing ships ≥ 400 GT One-off calculated index; commonly satisfied by engine or shaft power limitation Verification of the power limitation arrangement and its override SEEMP All ships ≥ 400 GT Ship-specific management plan; Part III required for ships subject to CII, containing the implementation plan and, where triggered, the corrective action plan Direct — the measures in it are executed by the engine department CII Ships ≥ 5,000 GT Annual operational rating A to E based on reported fuel consumption and distance, against a reduction factor that tightens each year Direct and continuous EEDI phases. Phase 0 from 2013, Phase 1 a 10% reduction, Phase 2 a 20% reduction, Phase 3 a 30% reduction against the reference line for most ship types, with Phase 3 brought forward to 2022 for several types including container ships, gas carriers, general cargo ships and LNG carriers, and with the largest container ship size bands facing reductions above 30%. CII consequence. A ship rated D for three consecutive years, or E for a single year , must develop a plan of corrective actions and incorporate it into SEEMP Part III, verified by the Administration or RO. There is no direct fine, but the rating is visible to charterers and financiers, and charterparty CII clauses now allocate responsibility for it commercially. Boundary discipline. CII is tank-to-wake , calculated from fuel consumed and distance sailed using fixed carbon conversion factors per fuel type. It says nothing about how the fuel was produced. The proposed GHG fuel intensity metric under the Net-Zero Framework is well-to-wake , as is FuelEU Maritime. Do not build a causal argument across the two boundaries. ⏸ The Net-Zero Framework — Current Status Status as at this Part: approved but NOT adopted, and not in force. The Framework was approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025 as draft amendments creating a new Chapter 5 of MARPOL Annex VI . It has two limbs: a goal-based GHG fuel intensity standard requiring a phased reduction in the well-to-wake GHG intensity of the energy used on board against a fleet-average baseline, and an economic mechanism under which ships exceeding the required intensity acquire remedial units while ships outperforming it may earn surplus units — a pricing and reward structure rather than a simple levy. MEPC 83 (Apr 2025) ──── approved as draft MARPOL Annex VI Chapter 5 │ MEPC/ES.2 (14–17 Oct 2025) ── submitted for ADOPTION │ └── vote to adjourn for one year: 57 for · 49 against · 21 abstentions │ ▼ MEPC 84 (27 Apr–1 May 2026) ── considered the NZF again — NO FINAL AGREEMENT │ └── work continues: 2 intersessional GHG groups (Sep & Nov 2026) │ ▼ MEPC 85 (30 Nov–3 Dec 2026) ── report back │ ▼ MEPC/ES.2 RESUMES — 4 December 2026 (one day) — current decision point The reference baseline discussed at MEPC 83 for the GHG Fuel Intensity metric is a 2008 fleet-average figure of 93.3 gCO₂eq/MJ . That figure belongs to the draft IMO instrument and is not the same as the FuelEU Maritime baseline of 91.16 gCO₂eq/MJ , which is a 2020 EU fleet-average under Regulation (EU) 2023/1805. The two are different regimes with different baselines, different scopes and different compliance mechanics, and conflating them is a documented examination trap. Momentum since the adjournment. The October 2025 vote to adjourn was itself close — 57 to 49, with 21 abstentions. By MEPC 84 in April–May 2026, reporting suggests the balance of States had shifted towards accepting the April 2025 text as the basis for moving forward, though a market-readiness camp remains, and no agreement was actually reached. The direction of travel is informative for an oral, but it is not a substitute for the fact that the instrument remains unadopted. How to state this in an oral. Say the Framework is approved but not adopted; give the October 2025 adjournment (57/49/21); note that MEPC 84 in April–May 2026 discussed it again and still reached no final agreement; and give the current decision point — a resumed MEPC/ES.2 on 4 December 2026, immediately after MEPC 85. Say that if adopted, entry into force would follow the tacit acceptance sequence, so the sector should plan for it without treating it as law. Presenting it as being in force, or citing the original "October 2026" reconvening date as still current, are both factual errors an examiner will test for. 🔥 Shipboard Carbon Reduction — the Engineering Levers Waste heat recovery. Exhaust gas economiser raising steam for a turbo-generator, and where fitted a power turbine on the exhaust bypass, displacing auxiliary diesel generator load. Output degrades with soot fouling of the economiser tube nest, with air cooler and turbocharger fouling reducing exhaust energy quality, and with steam system leakage — all of which are maintainable causes, not inevitable decline. Shaft generator / PTO. Producing electrical power from the main engine at its far better specific fuel consumption instead of running an auxiliary engine, wherever the load profile and the propulsion mode allow. Hull and propeller condition. The single largest recoverable loss on most ships. Fouling raises the power required at a given speed continuously between cleanings, and the penalty compounds. Air path and combustion. Turbocharger and air cooler cleanliness govern charge air density; injector condition and correct timing govern combustion quality. Both act directly on specific fuel consumption at every load. Thermal insulation. Exhaust manifolds, steam lines and heated tanks — cheap to restore, and the loss is continuous. Auxiliary load management. Avoiding unnecessary parallel running of pumps and compressors, and using variable frequency drives where fitted rather than throttling. Wind assistance and solar. Rotor sails, suction wings and photovoltaic arrays — real but ship- and route-specific; treat as a design or retrofit decision rather than an operational lever. Measuring honestly. Trend specific fuel oil consumption against corrected shaft power rather than against speed over ground, so that current, wind and draught are removed from the comparison. Only then can a claimed improvement be attributed to the intervention. That same corrected dataset is what supports a hull cleaning business case, a charterparty performance defence and the CII narrative — one measurement discipline serving three purposes. 🎓 CE Oral Tip (Simon): Simon is the GHG examiner and he tests currency above all. Two things will mark you out. First, state the Net-Zero Framework status precisely and unprompted: approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025, submitted for adoption at the extraordinary MEPC session in October 2025, adjourned for one year on a vote of 57 to 49; MEPC 84 in April–May 2026 discussed it again and still reached no final agreement; the current decision point is a resumed MEPC/ES.2 on 4 December 2026, straight after MEPC 85 — approved, not adopted, not in force. Candidates who stop at the October 2025 adjournment, or who quote the original "reconvenes October 2026" line without knowing it was superseded at MEPC 84, are giving a stale answer. Second, keep the boundaries clean: CII is tank-to-wake under Regulation 28 with fixed carbon factors; the draft GFI and FuelEU Maritime are well-to-wake, and their baselines differ — 93.3 gCO₂eq/MJ in the IMO draft against 91.16 gCO₂eq/MJ under FuelEU. If he asks what you personally control, the answer is CII, and the levers are hull and propeller condition, waste heat recovery output, air path cleanliness and auxiliary load. 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1. Compare the Initial and Revised IMO GHG Strategies. The Initial Strategy, adopted at MEPC 72 in 2018, set a carbon intensity target of at least a forty per cent reduction in CO2 emissions per transport work by 2030 while pursuing efforts towards seventy per cent by 2050, and a target of reducing total annual greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping by at least fifty per cent by 2050, both against a 2008 baseline, with a vision of phasing out emissions entirely within this century. The Revised Strategy, adopted at MEPC 80 in July 2023, retained the forty per cent carbon intensity target for 2030 but changed the character of the headline goal from intensity to absolute reduction. It sets net-zero greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping by or around 2050, with indicative checkpoints of at least twenty per cent striving for thirty per cent absolute reduction by 2030, and at least seventy per cent striving for eighty per cent by 2040, both against 2008. It also adds a technology target that zero or near-zero greenhouse gas emission technologies, fuels and energy sources should represent at least five per cent, striving for ten per cent, of the energy used by international shipping by 2030. The important conceptual point is that an intensity target can be met while total emissions rise if trade grows; an absolute target cannot. Q2. What is the current status of the IMO Net-Zero Framework? It is approved but not adopted, and it is not in force. The Framework was approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025 as draft amendments that would insert a new Chapter 5 into MARPOL Annex VI, combining a goal-based greenhouse gas fuel intensity standard on a well-to-wake basis with an economic pricing and reward mechanism, under which ships exceeding the required intensity acquire remedial units and ships outperforming it may earn surplus units. It was submitted for formal adoption at the second extraordinary session of the Marine Environment Protection Committee, held in London from the fourteenth to the seventeenth of October 2025. The session did not adopt it: a motion to adjourn for one year carried by fifty-seven votes to forty-nine with twenty-one abstentions. The Committee returned to it at MEPC 84, held from the twenty-seventh of April to the first of May 2026 and preceded by the twenty-first Intersessional Working Group on GHG emissions, but again reached no final agreement — reporting describes a continuing split between states wanting the original text adopted with minimal change and states wanting a more market-ready approach, although the balance of support was reported to have shifted towards adoption since the October 2025 vote. Work continues through two further intersessional working groups scheduled for September and November 2026, reporting to MEPC 85, which is planned for the thirtieth of November to the third of December 2026, immediately followed by a one-day resumption of the extraordinary session on the fourth of December 2026 — that date is the current decision point, superseding the October 2026 date originally announced in 2025. So the correct statement is that it is a draft instrument that operators should plan for but which has no legal effect, and any figure associated with it, including the 93.3 grams of CO2 equivalent per megajoule reference baseline discussed at MEPC 83, is a draft figure. Q3. Which of the energy efficiency measures do you actually influence as Chief Engineer, and how? EEDI is fixed at design and construction and I cannot change it; my only concern there is that the ship-specific EEDI Technical File is maintained on board and that no machinery or structural modification takes the ship outside its approved design assumptions. EEXI is a one-off calculation for existing ships, most commonly satisfied by engine or shaft power limitation, so my role is to ensure the limitation arrangement is correctly installed, sealed, and that the override arrangement and its recording are understood, since misuse of the override is a compliance failure. The measure I genuinely influence is the CII, the operational carbon intensity rating under MARPOL Annex VI Regulation 28, which is recalculated every year from reported fuel consumption and distance sailed and produces a rating from A to E against a reduction factor that tightens annually. The levers are hull and propeller cleanliness, which is usually the largest single recoverable loss; waste heat recovery output, which degrades with economiser soot fouling and steam leakage; turbocharger and air cooler cleanliness, which govern charge air density and therefore combustion quality; injector condition and timing; use of the shaft generator in place of auxiliary engines where the load profile allows; thermal insulation of exhaust and steam systems; and auxiliary load discipline. The SEEMP Part III is where those measures are formally recorded, and if the ship is rated D for three consecutive years or E once, a plan of corrective actions must be developed and incorporated into it. Q4. Explain the difference between tank-to-wake and well-to-wake accounting and why it matters. Tank-to-wake accounting counts only the emissions produced on board from the fuel as burned, using fixed carbon conversion factors for each fuel type. That is the basis of the CII under MARPOL Annex VI Regulation 28: fuel consumed multiplied by its carbon factor, divided by transport work. It takes no account of how the fuel was produced, extracted, refined or transported. Well-to-wake accounting counts the entire lifecycle, including upstream production and distribution emissions, and is expressed as greenhouse gas intensity per unit of energy in grams of CO2 equivalent per megajoule. That is the basis of FuelEU Maritime under EU Regulation 2023/1805, and of the greenhouse gas fuel intensity metric in the draft IMO Net-Zero Framework. The distinction matters because a fuel can look very different on the two bases. Fossil LNG performs well tank-to-wake because of its favourable carbon-to-hydrogen ratio, but performs considerably less well well-to-wake once upstream methane leakage and any onboard methane slip are counted. Blue and green fuels can show the reverse pattern. The practical rule is that the two are separate regulatory tracks with separate baselines — the draft IMO figure of 93.3 grams of CO2 equivalent per megajoule is a 2008 fleet average, while the FuelEU baseline of 91.16 is a 2020 EU fleet average — and no causal statement should be made across them without checking which boundary applies. ✍ Written Exam Focus 5 Define the Energy Efficiency Design Index, state its units, and explain what a lower attained value signifies. 10 Compare the Initial IMO GHG Strategy of 2018 with the Revised Strategy of 2023, identifying the change in the nature of the targets and stating the 2030 and 2040 indicative checkpoints. 15 Explain the technical and operational measures currently in force under MARPOL Annex VI Chapter 4 — EEDI, EEXI, SEEMP and CII — distinguishing which apply to new and existing ships. Describe the consequences of a poor CII rating, and analyse the engineering measures available to a Chief Engineer to improve the operational carbon intensity of an existing vessel. 🧠 Memory Box 2023 Revised Strategy: net-zero by or around 2050 · 2030 checkpoint −20% striving −30% · 2040 checkpoint −70% striving −80% · ZNZ fuels 5% striving 10% by 2030 · carbon intensity −40% by 2030. All against 2008. EEDI = new ships (design). EEXI = existing ships (one-off). SEEMP = all ≥400 GT. CII = ≥5,000 GT, annual A–E. D for three consecutive years, or E once → corrective action plan in SEEMP Part III. NZF: approved MEPC 83 (Apr 2025) · NOT adopted · adjourned MEPC/ES.2 Oct 2025 (57/49/21) · MEPC 84 (Apr–May 2026) no agreement · MEPC/ES.2 resumes 4 Dec 2026 (after MEPC 85, 30 Nov–3 Dec). CII = tank-to-wake (Reg 28). GFI and FuelEU = well-to-wake. IMO draft baseline 93.3 gCO₂eq/MJ (2008); FuelEU 91.16 gCO₂eq/MJ (2020). Never conflate. EEDI phases: 0 → 1 (10%) → 2 (20%) → 3 (30%) , Phase 3 brought forward to 2022 for container ships, gas carriers, general cargo and LNG carriers. ▶ Deep Dive — Case Study — Degrading Waste Heat Recovery Output on a Laden Passage Symptom A Post-Panamax bulk carrier built to EEDI Phase 3 shows progressively falling turbo-generator output on a steady-state laden passage. Eventually the electrical load can no longer be carried and a second auxiliary diesel generator is brought on line, raising daily fuel consumption and worsening the CII contribution of the voyage. The engine parameters look broadly normal, which is why the problem is allowed to develop. Systematic elimination The output of an exhaust gas economiser depends on exhaust mass flow, exhaust temperature and the heat transfer available. Take them in order. Exhaust temperature and mass flow: check turbocharger speed against load and against the shop test curve, scavenge air pressure and temperature, air cooler differential pressure and cooling water inlet temperature, and air filter condition. A fouled air path reduces charge density, which raises exhaust temperature at the turbine inlet but reduces mass flow, and the net effect on recoverable energy is usually negative. Heat transfer: economiser soot deposits on the tube nest, established from the gas-side differential pressure trend and from the record of soot blowing frequency and effectiveness; water-side scaling from feedwater quality; and any indication of past soot fire, which permanently degrades the nest. Steam side: leakage across the system, drains passing, unlagged or damaged insulation on steam lines, feedwater pump performance, and dump condenser operation. Electrical side: turbo-generator excitation, governor response and load-sharing settings — a generator that is healthy but incorrectly load-shared will drop off unnecessarily. The likely cause and the fix In most cases of progressive rather than sudden loss, the answer is gas-side fouling of the economiser combined with air-path fouling upstream. The remedy is soot blowing restored to correct frequency and pressure, water washing at the next opportunity with the correct chemistry and full drainage, air cooler cleaning, and turbocharger cleaning. The critical precaution is soot fire risk: never water wash without confirming the plant condition, following the manufacturer's procedure, and ensuring drainage is clear, because a wet soot deposit at temperature is exactly the condition that initiates an economiser fire. Closing the loop on compliance Record the intervention against corrected specific fuel consumption and against turbo-generator output at comparable load, so the improvement is demonstrable rather than asserted. Enter the measure and its effect in SEEMP Part III as an implemented energy efficiency action. If the ship is on a charter with a CII clause, the same evidence supports the owner's position on responsibility for the rating. On my vessel (Maersk A/S container tonnage) On container tonnage the equivalent exposure is larger because service speed is dictated by schedule and cannot be traded for efficiency. That concentrates everything on the recoverable losses — hull and propeller condition, air path cleanliness, waste heat recovery availability and reefer-driven auxiliary load. The department that trends these continuously has an argument to make when the CII rating is questioned; the department that does not has only an opinion. 📚 References Resolution MEPC.377(80) — 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships Resolution MEPC.304(72) — Initial IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships Resolution MEPC.328(76) — 2021 revised MARPOL Annex VI (EEXI, CII, SEEMP Part III), in force 1 November 2022 MARPOL Annex VI, Chapter 4, including Regulation 28 (operational carbon intensity rating) IMO — MEPC 83 report (April 2025); 2nd extraordinary session of the MEPC, 14–17 October 2025; MEPC 84 report and ISWG-GHG 21, 20 April – 1 May 2026 Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 (FuelEU Maritime) — for the well-to-wake comparison only Notes-p22 · P22-T3 · v1.0

text: Where a cargo suction well protrudes into the double bottom, it locally reduces the mandated protective depth h. section_title: MARPOL Annex I: Double-Hull Structural Geometry & Tank Segregation
text: Topic 11 MARPOL Annex I: Double-Hull Structural Geometry & Tank Segregation MARPOL Annex I — Structure Uday pp. 51–53 Examiner: Nair ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: The source draft presented the wing-tank width formula W = 0.5 + DWT/20,000 m and the suction-well clearance rule ≥ 0.5h as if they were direct MARPOL Annex I sentences. Neither is printed in that algebraic form in the Annex text itself. Both are re-labelled below as design/unified-interpretation formulas — the double-bottom height rule h = B/15 or 2.0 m, whichever is less (min 1.0 m) is accurately reflected in Reg. 19/13F and is kept as direct regulation wording. 📖 Definition MARPOL Annex I Reg. 19 requires oil tankers of 5,000 DWT and above to be fitted with double-hull and double-bottom tanks or spaces arranged to protect the cargo tank length against collision or grounding — passive containment by structural design, as distinct from the active discharge-control measures covered separately in Topic 12. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) Double-hull geometry defines the physical margin a CE is relying on if the vessel grounds — understanding h and W tells the CE how much sacrificial structure exists before the cargo tank itself is breached. Piping segregation rules (ballast vs cargo) are a direct structural safeguard against a single failure turning into a pollution incident — the CE must be able to explain why this separation exists, not just that it exists. On a Maersk A/S container vessel (non-tanker), Reg. 19 geometry does not apply to the CE's own ship, but it is tested orally on every candidate regardless of vessel type — examiners expect the theory to be solid even without personal operational exposure. 📅 Historical Background 1989 → Exxon Valdez grounding, Prince William Sound 1990 → US Oil Pollution Act (OPA 90) mandates double hulls for US trade 1992 → MARPOL Annex I Reg. 13F (later renumbered Reg. 19) mandates double hull/bottom for new tankers ≥5,000 DWT 1996 → Reg. 19 applies in full to tankers delivered on/after 6 July 1996 ⚖ Regulatory References MARPOL Annex I, Reg. 19 Double-hull/double-bottom requirements for oil tankers ≥5,000 DWT delivered on/after 6 July 1996; reduced dimensions for tankers <5,000 DWT Unified Interpretations to Reg. 19 Flag/class circulars specifying wing tank width and suction well clearance measurement practice 🔧 Double-Hull Geometry (≥5,000 DWT) TYPICAL DOUBLE HULL CROSS-SECTION (≥5,000 DWT) +-----------------------------------------------+ | DECK LINE | +-------+-------------------------------+-------+ | Wing | | Wing | | Tank | CARGO TANK | Tank | | (W) | +-----------------+ | (W) | | | | Suction Well | | | +-------+------+--------+--------+------+-------+ | Double Bottom (h) | ≥0.5h clearance | +-----------------------------------------------+ |============== BOTTOM SHELL PLATING ============| +-----------------------------------------------+ Reg. 19 (verbatim-quotable): h = B/15 (m) or 2.0 m, whichever is the lesser; minimum h = 1.0 m Design/interpretation (not verbatim): W ≈ 0.5 + DWT/20,000 m, bounded 1.0–2.0 m Below 5,000 DWT (unified interpretation): W ≈ 0.76 m, h ≈ 0.76 m Suction well clearance (unified interpretation): ≥ 0.5h from bottom shell Piping segregation: ballast, sounding and vent pipes serving ballast tanks must not pass through cargo tanks; cargo lines must never pass through ballast spaces — this keeps a single structural failure from creating a direct cargo-to-sea or cargo-to-ballast pathway. CE Oral Tip — Nair: When asked "what protects the ship if the wing tank width formula and the 0.5h rule aren't in Annex I word-for-word?" — explain that Reg. 19 sets the legal minimum protective distances and areas, while the algebraic forms are unified interpretations/design practice used industry-wide to satisfy that regulation. Examiners reward candidates who can draw this legal-vs-engineering distinction rather than reciting the formula as if it were quoted convention text. 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1: State the double-bottom height requirement for an oil tanker ≥5,000 DWT under Reg. 19. The distance h between the cargo tank bottom and the bottom shell plating must not be less than B/15 (metres) or 2.0 m, whichever is the lesser, with an absolute minimum of 1.0 m. This forms a continuous sacrificial structural zone that absorbs grounding damage before the cargo tank itself is breached. Q2: Explain the structural logic of the suction-well 0.5h clearance. Where a cargo suction well protrudes into the double bottom, it locally reduces the mandated protective depth h. Unified interpretations require the well to be kept shallow enough that at least half of that protective depth (0.5h) remains between the well bottom and the bottom shell plating, so a bottom-shell breach cannot directly puncture the cargo space through the well. Q3: Why does Reg. 19 mandate piping segregation between ballast and cargo systems? Ballast and cargo piping are kept structurally separate — ballast pipes must not pass through cargo tanks and cargo lines must not pass through ballast spaces — so that a single structural or seal failure cannot create a direct pathway for cargo oil to reach the sea via ballast discharge, or for ballast water to contaminate cargo. Q4: What dimensions apply to oil tankers below 5,000 DWT? Unified interpretations permit reduced protective dimensions for smaller oil tankers: a minimum wing tank width of approximately 0.76 m and a minimum double-bottom height of approximately 0.76 m, reflecting the lower absolute outflow risk of a smaller cargo volume. ✍ Written Exam Questions 5M Sketch a cross-section of an oil tanker ≥5,000 DWT showing the double-hull and double-bottom boundaries and state the governing dimensional criteria. 10M Explain the structural and legal distinction between MARPOL Annex I Reg. 19 requirements and the unified-interpretation design formulas commonly used to satisfy them. 🧠 Memory Box h = B/15 or 2.0 m (min 1.0 m) — quotable Reg. 19 wording W ≈ 0.5 + DWT/20,000 m (1.0–2.0 m) — design interpretation, not verbatim Suction well ≥ 0.5h — unified interpretation <5,000 DWT: W ≈ h ≈ 0.76 m ⚡ Quick Revision Item Key Fact Double bottom height h (≥5,000 DWT) B/15 or 2.0 m, lesser; min 1.0 m Wing tank width W (≥5,000 DWT) ≈0.5+DWT/20,000 m; bounded 1.0–2.0 m (design rule) <5,000 DWT tankers W≈0.76 m, h≈0.76 m (unified interpretation) Suction well clearance ≥0.5h from bottom shell ▶ Deep Dive — Full Reference Detail Why the Formula Isn't "in" MARPOL Reg. 19 expresses the wing-tank requirement as a minimum protective width/area sufficient to reduce accidental outflow, evaluated case-by-case in the tanker's approved outflow analysis. The W = 0.5 + DWT/20,000 m relationship is a simplified design heuristic taught industry-wide and consistent with typical CAS (Condition Assessment Scheme) outflow practice, bounded by the 1.0–2.0 m regulatory limits — but it is not the literal regulation sentence, and examiners who probe this distinction are testing whether the candidate over-quotes derived formulas as primary law. Maersk A/S Container Vessel Context As a non-tanker, the vessel does not carry the Reg. 19 cargo-tank double-hull geometry at all; container vessels have their own hull/void-space arrangement unrelated to oil cargo outflow protection. This topic is tested purely as general MEO Class 1 knowledge. 📚 References IMO — MARPOL Annex I overview Marshall Islands Registry — Unified Interpretations, MARPOL Annex I (suction well/wing tank guidance) 🔗 Related QB Questions: QB3 — MARPOL Discharge Criteria Notes-p3 · T11 · v1.0

section_title: Q1: A PSC officer notes heavy black oil residue inside the OWS overboard sight-glass, but the ORB shows all recent discharges under 15 ppm. How do you respond?
text: I isolate and lock out the OWS overboard line immediately to demonstrate compliance, then launch an internal investigation checking: (1) mechanical failure or seal degradation of the coalescer/filter elements allowing oil slug pass-through; (2) OCM optical-cell scaling or leakage causing a false clean reading; (3) any unauthorised piping bypass ("magic pipe"). I invite the PSC officer to witness a full OCM calibration with certified test fluid and an automated 3-way valve test to confirm system integrity.

section_title: Q2: Why is an MEPC 60(33) unit inadequate on a modern vessel?
text: MEPC 60(33) units rely on gravity/density separation only, so they cannot break the stable chemical emulsions created by modern surfactants, detergents and scavenge soot in machinery bilges — these emulsions pass through at high ppm. MEPC 107(49) units add a secondary emulsion-breaking stage, a fast-response tamper-resistant alarm with automatic stopping/recirculation, and 18-month secure data logging, none of which MEPC 60(33) units are required to have.

All operations must be recorded in the Oil Record Book Part I.

section_title: Q4: The OWS passes on clean water but the OCM spikes above 15 ppm on actual bilge water. What is your troubleshooting sequence?
text: Since it passes on clean water, the fault is not sensor calibration but the unit's inability to break a stable emulsion or handle particulate loading. I check for detergent/surfactant contamination or scavenge soot in the bilge well, isolate ongoing chemical cleaning, inspect and clean/replace the primary coalescer and secondary emulsion-breaking elements, and verify the OCM sample line is free of air bubbles or scale before re-testing.

text: Topic 12 MARPOL Annex I: Oil-Water Separator Evolutionary Design & Operational Discharge Regimes MARPOL Annex I — OWS/OCM Uday pp. 53–56 Examiner: Simon ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: The MEPC 107(49) "5 s sensor response / 20 s total loop" figures are re-framed below as type-approval testing criteria (order-of-magnitude test-protocol benchmarks) rather than quoted Resolution sentences, consistent with standard MIW verification practice for this Resolution. 📖 Definition Where Topic 11 covers passive structural containment, this topic covers active separation : processing machinery-space bilge water and cargo slops through high-efficiency, tamper-resistant monitored equipment before any release to sea, and the operational discharge criteria that govern when and how that release is lawful — with a strict 15 ppm ceiling outside Special Areas and zero discharge in ecologically sensitive zones. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) Every OWS/OCM operation the CE authorises is a statutory act under Reg. 14/15 — a wrong call is a criminal environmental offence in most jurisdictions, not just a company non-conformity. PSC treats OWS/OCM data-log vs ORB mismatches as prima facie evidence of a "magic pipe" bypass — this is one of the single largest sources of criminal prosecution and detention in the tanker/bulk trades. On a Maersk A/S container vessel (non-tanker, ≥400 GT), Reg. 14/15 machinery-space bilge discharge is the CE's day-to-day operational reality — this is the most directly applicable part of Annex I to the CE's own vessel type. 📅 Historical Background 1995 → MEPC 60(33) — first harmonised OWS/OCM type-approval guideline 2005 → MEPC 107(49) supersedes MEPC 60(33) for new OWS installations from 1 Jan 2005, addressing surfactant-stabilised emulsions ⚖ Regulatory References MARPOL Annex I, Reg. 14 Mandatory oil filtering (OWS) equipment for ships ≥400 GT MARPOL Annex I, Reg. 15 & 34 Operational discharge control — machinery spaces (Reg. 15) and cargo areas of oil tankers (Reg. 34) MEPC.60(33) Superseded OWS/OCM type-approval guideline — gravity separation only MEPC.107(49) Current OWS/OCM type-approval guideline — multi-stage emulsion breaking, tamper-resistant alarm, closed-loop recirculation, data logging 🔧 OWS Evolution: MEPC 60(33) vs MEPC 107(49) Parameter MEPC 60(33) MEPC 107(49) Separation principle Gravity/coalescer only — cannot handle surfactant-stabilised emulsions Multi-stage: gravity + secondary emulsion-breaking (ultrafiltration/flocculation/carbon adsorption) Alarm & automation Basic 15 ppm alarm; auto-stop/recirculation not standardised Tamper-resistant 15 ppm alarm + mandatory automatic stopping and closed-loop recirculation OCM sensor response Not tightly constrained Type-approval testing requires a fast sensor response (order of 5 s) and a bounded total control-loop time (order of 20 s) during slug tests Data logging Not required in the instrument — relies on manual ORB entry Mandatory internal electronic log of date/time/alarm status/valve position, secure and recoverable for ≥18 months Sampling point Not standardised Fixed sampling point on a vertical section immediately before the overboard valve 🔧 Operational Discharge Criteria Waste Source Outside Special Area Inside Special Area Machinery bilge (all vessels ≥400 GT) En route; approved 15 ppm OWS; effluent <15 ppm; not from cargo pump-room bilges Same, plus OWS must have automatic stopping and recirculation; Antarctic Area — completely prohibited Cargo oil residues/slops (oil tankers) En route; >12 NM from land; rate ≤30 L/NM instantaneous; total ≤1/30,000 of that cargo; via ODME, below waterline Completely prohibited — retain onboard, shore reception only CE Oral Tip — Simon: Simon frequently frames this as a live-fault scenario ("OWS passes clean water but fails on bilge water — troubleshoot") rather than a definitions question. Lead with the mechanical diagnosis (emulsion-breaking failure, not sensor calibration) before citing the regulatory figures. 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1: A PSC officer notes heavy black oil residue inside the OWS overboard sight-glass, but the ORB shows all recent discharges under 15 ppm. How do you respond? I isolate and lock out the OWS overboard line immediately to demonstrate compliance, then launch an internal investigation checking: (1) mechanical failure or seal degradation of the coalescer/filter elements allowing oil slug pass-through; (2) OCM optical-cell scaling or leakage causing a false clean reading; (3) any unauthorised piping bypass ("magic pipe"). I invite the PSC officer to witness a full OCM calibration with certified test fluid and an automated 3-way valve test to confirm system integrity. Q2: Why is an MEPC 60(33) unit inadequate on a modern vessel? MEPC 60(33) units rely on gravity/density separation only, so they cannot break the stable chemical emulsions created by modern surfactants, detergents and scavenge soot in machinery bilges — these emulsions pass through at high ppm. MEPC 107(49) units add a secondary emulsion-breaking stage, a fast-response tamper-resistant alarm with automatic stopping/recirculation, and 18-month secure data logging, none of which MEPC 60(33) units are required to have. Q3: State the discharge criteria for machinery-space bilge water outside a Special Area. The ship must be en route; the effluent must be processed through an approved 15 ppm OWS as per Reg. 14; oil content after treatment must be under 15 ppm, continuously monitored; and the mixture must not originate from cargo pump-room bilges or be mixed with cargo residues. All operations must be recorded in the Oil Record Book Part I. Q4: The OWS passes on clean water but the OCM spikes above 15 ppm on actual bilge water. What is your troubleshooting sequence? Since it passes on clean water, the fault is not sensor calibration but the unit's inability to break a stable emulsion or handle particulate loading. I check for detergent/surfactant contamination or scavenge soot in the bilge well, isolate ongoing chemical cleaning, inspect and clean/replace the primary coalescer and secondary emulsion-breaking elements, and verify the OCM sample line is free of air bubbles or scale before re-testing. ✍ Written Exam Questions 10M Detail the complete technical and operational differences between OWS equipment type-approved under MEPC 60(33) and MEPC 107(49), focusing on emulsion-breaking capability, response times and data retention. 15M A 150,000 DWT crude tanker needs to discharge cargo slops on an international voyage. State the complete regulatory discharge criteria under MARPOL Annex I inside and outside Special Areas, describe the ODME's function, and outline the immediate action if the automated discharge valve fails to shut during a high-rate discharge event. 🧠 Memory Box 60(33) → 107(49) — gravity-only → multi-stage + data logging + fast alarm Machinery bilge limit: <15 ppm; 0 in Antarctic Area E-12-30-ODME — En route · >12 NM · <30 L/NM · ODME below waterline OCM data retention: ≥18 months ⚡ Quick Revision Item Key Fact Machinery bilge limit <15 ppm; 0 in Antarctic Area Cargo slop discharge rate ≤30 L/NM instantaneous; ≤1/30,000 of cargo total OCM data retention ≥18 months (MEPC 107(49)) OCM sensor response (test benchmark) ~5 s sensor / ~20 s total loop ▶ Deep Dive — Full Reference Detail Special Area vs Antarctic Area Discharge Outside Special Areas, machinery bilge water may be discharged en route, through an approved 15 ppm OWS, provided it does not originate from cargo pump-room bilges. Inside Special Areas the same conditions apply but the OWS must additionally have automatic stopping and recirculation. In the Antarctic Area, any discharge of oil or oily mixtures from machinery spaces is completely prohibited — all bilge and sludge must be retained for shore disposal. Maersk A/S Container Vessel Context Reg. 14/15 OWS/OCM obligations for machinery-space bilges apply in full to the vessel. text: First I confirm the Certificate is within its 5-year validity with current annual/intermediate endorsement stamps. Then I cross-reference every item in the relevant Supplement (Form A or B) against the physical machinery — manufacturer, serial number and type-approval date of the OWS/OCM, and the physical dimensions/soundings of every sludge and bilge tank. section_title: Q2: How and why do you perform a sludge mass-balance check?
text: I estimate expected sludge as roughly 1–2% of total HFO consumed — e.g. 30 t/day HFO gives an expected 300–600 L/day of sludge — then compare that against actual sludge tank accumulation, incinerator running hours, and shore disposal volumes logged in the ORB. A significant shortfall against the estimate, without a matching incineration or shore-disposal record, flags a possible unlogged discharge or data error well before an official survey.

text: Topic 13 MARPOL Annex I Survey Framework, IOPP Certification & Port State Preparedness HSSC / Survey Uday pp. 57–62 Examiner: Paul / Nair ⭐ High Frequency 🔎 Verification note: The source draft's sludge-generation estimate (1–2% of HFO consumption) is presented correctly as an engineering rule-of-thumb, not a regulatory figure, and is kept labelled as such below. HSSC survey window (±3 months) and the 5-year renewal cycle are consistent with IMO Res. A.1207(34) (2025 — supersedes A.1186(33)/2023 and A.1140(31)/2019) and Annex I Reg. 6/7 and are retained as stated. 📖 Definition The Harmonized System of Survey and Certification (HSSC) under MARPOL Annex I sets a structured, time-bound regime to verify that a vessel's hull, equipment, systems and materials conform to Annex I. Mass-balance checking (expected vs actual sludge) is an internal audit tool the CE can run weekly to catch data-logging errors or equipment faults months before a survey or PSC inspection exposes them. On sign-on, a systematic Form A/B cross-check against physical equipment is the single most effective way for a new CE to inherit a clean compliance position rather than an inherited defect. 📅 Historical Background Pre-HSSC → SOLAS/MARPOL/Load Line surveys ran on independent, mismatched schedules HSSC introduced → IMO harmonises survey intervals to a common 5-year cycle across conventions Form A/B split → IOPP Supplement divided into Form A (non-tankers) and Form B (oil tankers) for distinct verification pathways Current → IMO Res. A.1207(34) — current HSSC Survey Guidelines in force (2025, supersedes A.1186(33)/2023 and A.1140(31)/2019) ⚖ Regulatory References MARPOL Annex I, Reg. 6 Mandatory survey types/intervals — oil tankers ≥150 GT, other ships ≥400 GT MARPOL Annex I, Reg. 7/8 Issuance/endorsement of the IOPP Certificate by the Flag Administration or on its behalf MARPOL Annex I, Reg. 12 Mandatory capacity/arrangements for retention and disposal of oil residues (sludge) IMO Res. Mass-balance check: expected sludge ≈ 1–2% of total HFO consumption (engineering rule-of-thumb, not a regulatory figure) — compare against actual tank levels, incinerator hours and shore disposal volumes; large unexplained gaps suggest a bypass or unlogged operation. Hardware: incinerator functional test (dampers, dosing pumps, high-temp cut-outs); OWS/OCM recirculation-loop test with simulated high-ppm signal, confirming 3-way valve response; BHT/OBT/sludge tank high-level alarm float tests; spares inventory per manufacturer's list; overboard pipe inspection piece checked for residual oil film. CE Oral Tip — Paul: Paul frequently probes whether a candidate treats the sludge mass-balance check as a legal requirement or an internal audit tool — it is the latter. State clearly that the 1–2% figure is an engineering estimate used to sanity-check ORB/incinerator/shore-receipt data, not a MARPOL-mandated percentage. 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1: You've just signed on as CE. Any mismatch is treated as a major non-conformity and reported to the company and class immediately. Q2: How and why do you perform a sludge mass-balance check? I estimate expected sludge as roughly 1–2% of total HFO consumed — e.g. 30 t/day HFO gives an expected 300–600 L/day of sludge — then compare that against actual sludge tank accumulation, incinerator running hours, and shore disposal volumes logged in the ORB. A significant shortfall against the estimate, without a matching incineration or shore-disposal record, flags a possible unlogged discharge or data error well before an official survey. Q3: The OWS passes on clean water but the OCM spikes above 15 ppm on actual bilge water. What is your troubleshooting sequence? I check for detergent/surfactant contamination or scavenge soot in the bilge well, isolate ongoing chemical cleaning, inspect and clean/replace the primary coalescer and secondary emulsion-breaking elements, and verify the OCM sample line is free of air bubbles or scale before re-testing. Q4: Differentiate Form A and Form B of the IOPP Supplement. Form A (non-tankers ≥400 GT) covers ship particulars, OWS control, sludge retention, standard discharge connection and SOPEP. Form B (oil tankers ≥150 GT) includes all of Form A plus cargo-specific sections: SBT/COW/double-hull geometry, accidental outflow protection, intact/damage stability, slop tank and ODME arrangements, and STS transfer documentation — reflecting the additional cargo-related pollution risk on a tanker. ✍ Written Exam Questions 5M Differentiate an Annual, Intermediate and Renewal survey under the MARPOL Annex I HSSC framework, with their timing windows. 10M Compile a CE's operational checklist for an upcoming IOPP Renewal Survey, covering documentation, calculation and mechanical verification. 15M Compare IOPP Supplement Form A and Form B in structural detail. Explain why cargo/stability/ballast entries are mandatory only for tankers, and discuss how a PSC officer uses these documents in an expanded inspection. 🧠 Memory Box IOPP validity: max 5 years Survey window: ±3 months of anniversary date A-I-R mnemonic: Annual (yearly, ±3m) → Intermediate (replaces Annual in Yr2/3) → Renewal (exhaustive, Yr5) Form A = non-tankers ≥400 GT; Form B = oil tankers ≥150 GT Sludge estimate: ~1–2% of HFO consumption (engineering rule-of-thumb only) ⚡ Quick Revision Item Key Fact IOPP max validity 5 years Annual/Intermediate window ±3 months of anniversary date Form A scope Non-tankers ≥400 GT Form B scope Oil tankers ≥150 GT Sludge generation estimate 1–2% of total HFO consumed (rule-of-thumb) ▶ Deep Dive — Full Reference Detail PSC Detention Triggers Specific to Survey Documentation Common PSC focus points include: sludge tanks listed on Form A showing signs of fresh paint or clean water (suggesting illegal bypass); incinerator hour-meter readings inconsistent with logged "burned" volumes; hidden fresh-water dilution lines feeding the OCM sample block; and failure of the automated 3-way valve to shift within the tested response window during a live high-ppm simulation. Maersk A/S Application As Danish-flagged vessels, Maersk container ships are surveyed under DMA authority, typically via DNV or LR acting as Recognized Organization. The CE's Form A cross-check on sign-on should specifically verify the OWS/OCM model and sludge tank capacities against the physical engine-room layout before the first PSC call. 📚 References IMO — Harmonized System of Survey and Certification (HSSC) DGMA, India See also — MIW Engineering Management Notes Part 20, Topic 3 : the general HSSC survey-window and Continuous Machinery Survey / Safety Equipment Survey treatment, applying the same mechanics beyond the IOPP Certificate. 🔗 Related QB Questions: QB3 — MARPOL & PSC Notes-p3 · T13 · v1.0

text: Type 1 carries the most hazardous chemicals and has the tightest structural protection — wing tank width ≈B/5 or 11.5 m, double bottom ≈B/15 or 6 m, single tank capped at ≈1250 m³. The "7 knots/4 knots" speed thresholds in the Reg. 13 discharge criteria are widely-taught operational figures consistently used in training material; they are labelled as such rather than quoted as a single Annex II sentence. 📖 Definition MARPOL Annex II controls pollution by Noxious Liquid Substances (NLS) carried in bulk, through cargo categorisation, structural containment standards for chemical tankers, and mandatory physical parameters for any operational residue discharge. Chemical tanker structural design is governed separately by the IBC Code (ships built on/after 1 July 1986) or the older BCH Code (ships built before that date). ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) Chemical cargoes combine toxicity, reactivity and bioaccumulation risk — a stripping or prewash error is both an environmental and a personnel-safety failure, not just a paperwork issue. Cargo Record Book (CRB) gaps around a Category X prewash are one of the highest-yield PSC detention triggers on chemical tankers. Understanding IMO Type 1/2/3 tank geometry lets the CE reason about why a given cargo can or cannot be loaded into a specific tank, independent of what the Certificate of Fitness states. 📅 Historical Background 2 Oct 1983 → MARPOL Annex II enters into force Pre-2007 → Older multi-category NLS evaluation system in use 1 Jan 2007 → Major reclassification: four categories (X, Y, Z, OS); emphasis shifts to efficient stripping systems to minimise onboard residue ⚖ Regulatory References MARPOL Annex II, Reg. 6 Pollution categorisation system for Noxious Liquid Substances (X, Y, Z, OS) MARPOL Annex II, Reg. 13 Operational control and physical discharge criteria for NLS residues IBC Code Chemical tankers constructed on/after 1 July 1986 — Type 1/2/3 structural and tank-capacity criteria BCH Code Chemical tankers constructed before 1 July 1986 🔧 NLS Categorisation (Reg. 6) Category X: major hazard to marine resources/health — discharge strictly prohibited. Category Y: hazard to marine resources/health/amenities — strict quality/quantity discharge limits. Category Z: minor hazard — less stringent restrictions. Other Substances (OS): no hazard — governed by ordinary machinery-space bilge criteria. 🔧 IBC Code Structural Types (design criteria, not MARPOL text) Feature Type 1 Type 2 Type 3 Cargo hazard level Most severe (IBC Ch. 17) Significant Moderate Wing tank spacing ≈B/5 or 11.5 m, lesser ≈760 mm from side shell No minimum specified Double bottom height ≈B/15 or 6 m, lesser ≈B/15 or 6 m, lesser No minimum specified Max single tank volume ≈1250 m³ ≈3000 m³ No cap 🔧 NLS Residue Discharge — Reg. 13 Operational Parameters S-D-S-U — Lawful NLS Overboard Discharge (outside Special Areas) Verify cargo Category (X/Y/Z) from CRB → Cat X: mandatory prewash to shore until ≤0.1% by weight → Cat Y/Z: prewash only if stripping limit not achieved, to shore → S: Speed ≥7 kn (self-propelled) / ≥4 kn (towed) — en route → D: Distance ≥12 NM from nearest land → S: Sea depth ≥25 m minimum → U: Underwater outlet, discharge below the waterline CE Oral Tip — Nair: If asked to quote the Type 1/2/3 figures "as per MARPOL," correct the premise: these are IBC Code design/tabulated criteria that implement the general Annex II hazard categorisation, not Annex II text itself. Q2: Why is surface discharge prohibited and underwater discharge required under Annex II? The underwater outlet releases residues below the waterline into the ship's turbulent boundary layer, using hull motion and propeller wash for rapid dilution. Surface discharge is prohibited because many NLS residues are volatile or toxic to surface marine life and can form persistent, dangerously concentrated slicks or vapour hazards if released at the surface. Q3: Differentiate IMO Type 1, 2 and 3 chemical tanker design. Type 1 carries the most hazardous chemicals and has the tightest structural protection — wing tank width ≈B/5 or 11.5 m, double bottom ≈B/15 or 6 m, single tank capped at ≈1250 m³. Type 2 carries significant-hazard cargoes with reduced spacing (≈760 mm wing clearance, same double-bottom rule) and a ≈3000 m³ cap. Type 3 carries lower-hazard cargoes with no mandatory spacing or volume limit. These are IBC Code criteria, not direct MARPOL Annex II wording. ✍ Written Exam Questions 5M Sketch and label the tank boundary distances for an IMO Type 1 and Type 2 chemical tanker under the IBC Code. 10M Describe the properties and reclassification criteria for Categories X, Y, Z and OS under MARPOL Annex II. 15M A chemical tanker is discharging Category Y residues from tank cleaning. section_title: Q3: A high-viscosity persistent floater cargo is discharged in a Special Area and an H₂S alarm triggers during prewash. What immediate action do you take?
text: I sound the chemical emergency alarm; crew immediately don positive-pressure SCBA. I isolate the tank venting valves, shift to controlled venting, and increase nitrogen blanketing pressure to suppress further vapour generation. I check the integrity of closed gauging seals and vapour-return piping, and do not permit enclosed-space entry until gas-freeing is verified complete with calibrated multi-gas detectors.

text: Topic 15 Advanced Chemical Regulatory Management: P&A Manuals, Tripartite Agreements, HNS & Modern Amendments MARPOL Annex II / IBC Uday pp. 69–75 Examiner: Senthil / Nair Medium Frequency 🔎 Verification note: The persistent-floater viscosity/melting-point criteria and the mandatory prewash/shore-reception requirement are correctly tied to Resolution MEPC.315(74) (2021 Annex II amendments) in the source draft and are retained as stated. The 3-year Tripartite Agreement validity and its MEPC.2 Circular tracking mechanism are consistent with Annex II Reg. 6.3 practice and are kept as direct references. 📖 Definition This topic covers the administrative and procedural layer of chemical cargo management: the Procedures and Arrangements (P&A) Manual mandated for every chemical tanker, the Tripartite Agreement mechanism for provisional carriage of unclassified chemicals, and the 2021 MARPOL Annex II amendments addressing high-viscosity "persistent floater" cargoes such as palm oil. ⚓ Why It Matters (CE Perspective) A Tripartite Agreement addendum that has quietly expired mid-voyage is a common, high-consequence PSC detention trigger — the CE must actively track validity, not just check it at load port. Persistent floater prewash procedures (post-2021) are a frequently outdated item in older P&A Manuals — failure to update the manual is a recurring detention cause. H₂S monitoring and closed gauging requirements for reactive/toxic cargoes are direct crew-safety measures, not just regulatory box-ticking. 📅 Historical Background MEPC.2 Circular → Published annually every December; tracks provisional chemical classifications 2021 → Resolution MEPC.315(74) — Annex II amendments introduce persistent floater controls (palm oil, olive oil, paraffin wax, etc.) ⚖ Regulatory References IBC Code, Ch. 17/18 Lists of chemicals with assigned carriage requirements; a cargo outside these chapters needs a Tripartite Agreement before carriage MEPC.2 Circular Annual (December) IMO publication tracking provisional/Tripartite chemical classifications MEPC.315(74) 2021 Annex II amendments — persistent floating product criteria and mandatory prewash 🔧 Tripartite Agreement Mechanism A Tripartite Agreement is a provisional assessment mechanism used when a manufacturer wants to ship a bulk liquid chemical not yet formally classified in IBC Code Chapters 17/18. It requires consensus of three administrations: the producing/shipping country, the vessel's Flag State, and the receiving country. Maximum validity is 3 years ; it is issued as a formal addendum to the vessel's Certificate of Fitness, and the provisional classification is tracked via the MEPC.2 Circular published every December. 🔧 Persistent Floater Criteria (MEPC.315(74), 2021) Criteria: viscosity ≥50 mPa·s at 20°C, and/or melting point ≥0°C. Operational requirement: mandatory tank prewash at the unloading port within designated areas (e.g. North West European waters); residue-water mixture discharged entirely to shore reception before departure. Mnemonic (V-M-P-S): Viscosity ≥50 mPa·s · Melting point ≥0°C · Port prewash required · Shore reception mandatory. CE Oral Tip — Senthil: Senthil often frames this as an incident-response question ("cargo confirmed as a persistent floater after discharge — what now?") rather than a definitions question. Lead with the operational prewash-to-shore sequence, then cite MEPC.315(74) — examiners reward procedure-first answers on this topic. 🎯 Oral Q&A Q1: What is a Tripartite Agreement, when is it required, and what are its validity boundaries? It is a provisional international assessment mechanism used when a chemical has not yet been formally classified in IBC Code Chapters 17/18, requiring consensus of the producing, flag, and receiving administrations. Maximum validity is 3 years; it must be attached as a formal addendum to the Certificate of Fitness, and the classification is tracked annually via the December MEPC.2 Circular. Q2: Explain the 2021 Annex II persistent floater amendments and the mandatory operational steps. Under MEPC.315(74), persistent floating products such as palm oil, olive oil and paraffin wax are defined by viscosity ≥50 mPa·s at 20°C and/or melting point ≥0°C. When such cargoes are discharged within specified areas, a mandatory tank prewash must be executed at the unloading port and the residue-water mixture discharged completely to shore reception before the vessel departs. Q3: A high-viscosity persistent floater cargo is discharged in a Special Area and an H₂S alarm triggers during prewash. What immediate action do you take? I sound the chemical emergency alarm; crew immediately don positive-pressure SCBA. I isolate the tank venting valves, shift to controlled venting, and increase nitrogen blanketing pressure to suppress further vapour generation. I check the integrity of closed gauging seals and vapour-return piping, and do not permit enclosed-space entry until gas-freeing is verified complete with calibrated multi-gas detectors. ✍ Written Exam Questions 5M Outline the structural sections of a vessel-specific P&A Manual as mandated by MARPOL Annex II. 10M Describe the structural/operational modifications mandated by recent IBC Code revisions for specialised chemical cargoes — controlled venting, tank inerting, closed gauging, H₂S monitoring. 15M A chemical tanker finishes discharging high-viscosity sunflower seed oil inside a designated Special Area. Detail the regulatory criteria and shipboard prewash procedure under the persistent floater amendments, the CE's P&A Manual/CRB responsibilities, and the primary PSC audit items. 🧠 Memory Box Tripartite max validity: 3 years; addendum to Certificate of Fitness MEPC.2 Circular: published every December V-M-P-S: Viscosity ≥50 mPa·s · Melting point ≥0°C · Port prewash · Shore reception ⚡ Quick Revision Item Key Fact Tripartite max validity 3 years Persistent floater viscosity limit ≥50 mPa·s at 20°C Persistent floater melting point ≥0°C Governing resolution MEPC.315(74), 2021 amendments ▶ Deep Dive — Full Reference Detail NLS Certificate vs Certificate of Fitness An NLS Certificate (MARPOL Annex II) applies to standard tankers carrying lower-risk Category Z/OS substances and does not require IBC Code damage-stability compliance. A Certificate of Fitness (IBC Code) applies to specialised chemical tankers carrying Category X/Y/Z cargoes and requires compliance with IMO Type 1/2/3 structural and damage-stability standards, and is the document that carries Tripartite Agreement addendums. PSC Focus Points Expired Tripartite addendums still listed as active cargo; P&A Manuals not updated for persistent floater prewash procedures; bypassed or open venting where controlled arrangements are mandated — all are common detention triggers on advanced chemical inspections. 📚 References IMO — MARPOL Annex II overview IMO — Persistent floater amendments background 🔗 Related QB Questions: QB2_G — Chemical Cargo Hazards Notes-p3 · T15 · v1.0

section_title: Q1: What is HNS and how does it differ from oil pollution liability?
text: HNS is any substance other than oil which, if released into the sea, could harm human health, marine life, amenities, or legitimate sea uses. Unlike the oil pollution regime (CLC/Fund Convention), HNS liability is split into a two-tier system: shipowner strict liability (Tier 1) backed by compulsory insurance, and a post-incident industry-funded HNS Fund (Tier 2) for damages exceeding the shipowner's cap.

section_title: Q2: Why was the original 1996 HNS Convention revised in 2010?
text: Many states found the 1996 Convention's reporting requirements for fragmented, small-volume packaged cargo receivers operationally unworkable — tracking every small packaged HNS shipment was an excessive administrative burden. The 2010 Protocol simplified this by shifting the primary reporting obligation onto major bulk receivers, while keeping the underlying liability structure intact, making ratification practical.

section_title: Q3: Who pays into the HNS Fund, and when is it triggered?
text: The Fund is financed by post-incident contributions from individual receivers of HNS cargo who import quantities above specified threshold volumes — contracting governments make no direct budget contribution. It is triggered once the shipowner's Tier 1 liability cap is exhausted or if the shipowner is financially insolvent.

section_title: Q5: What are the four IMDG segregation categories?
text: "Away From" (minimum practical separation, can share a compartment), "Separated From" (different compartments/holds, wider separation on deck), "Separated by a Complete Compartment or Hold From" (a full steel bulkhead between), and "Separated Longitudinally by an Intervening Complete Compartment or Hold From" (a full intermediate hold as buffer).
