section_title: International Legislation Hierarchy & EIF Process
text: Legislative Hierarchy Convention: Broad multilateral treaty between nations — legally binding. Protocol: Ancillary agreement introducing major changes to a convention. Amendment: Minor modification — fast-tracked via tacit acceptance. Resolution: Resolves protocol disputes; ongoing IMO review loops. Code: Mandatory or recommendatory technical details for execution. Act (domestic): National law passed by Parliament, approved by President. How an IMO Convention Enters into Force — 5 Steps 1. Drafting — IMO technical committees draft text based on safety needs ▼ 2. Adoption — Assembly conference: ≥1/3 of contracting governments present (quorum); ≥2/3 of those present vote in favour ▼ 3. Signature — States declare intention to join; pledge not to act against the convention's spirit ▼ 4. Ratification — States incorporate into domestic law; submit instrument of ratification to IMO ▼ 5. Entry into Force (EIF) — Activates after fixed period once minimum tonnage and state number criteria met ✓ Correction Applied — 27 Jul 2026 Prior revision incorrectly stated 2/3 quorum present for the Adoption step. The correct requirement is a quorum of at least 1/3 of contracting governments present for the vote, with at least 2/3 of those present voting in favour for adoption — consistent with the 1/3–2/3 figures already verified elsewhere in this series (SOLAS Article VIII / MARPOL Article 16 tacit acceptance mnemonic). Reported by a candidate (submitted 27 Jul 2026). Verified against primary source — see Regulatory References below. ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "How does an IMO convention enter into force?" — All 5 steps. Then he may ask: "What is the difference between signature and ratification?" — Signature = declaration of intent; ratification = domestic law incorporation with binding effect. He may also ask: "What is accession?" — A state joining a convention already in force (not an original signatory). ⚖ Regulatory References Vienna Convention 1969 "Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969" — defines signing, ratification, accession, and entry-into-force procedures SOLAS Preamble / Art. IX "Article IX — Entry into force" (SOLAS 1974) — required 25 States representing 50% of world merchant gross tonnage for original entry into force IMO Convention 1948 "Convention on the International Maritime Organization, 1948" — establishes IMO's committee structure (MSC, MEPC, etc.) responsible for drafting conventions

keywords: CBDR-RC equity climate justice Kyoto Rio developed developing nations
section_subtitle: 1992 Earth Summit — developed vs developing nations framework
section_title: CBDR — Common But Differentiated Responsibilities
text: Definition & Origin A fundamental legal and environmental principle first formalised in the UNFCCC framework, adopted at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro . Recognises that while all nations share responsibility for solving climate change, their historical contributions and current capacities differ significantly. Core Framework Developed nations: Emitting GHGs since the Industrial Era; account for over 50% of cumulative global emissions. Must take greater financial and technical responsibility for reduction. Developing nations: Historically low emissions, limited wealth and technology for clean transition — receive support rather than bearing equal burden. Maritime Relevance IMO's approach has historically been flag-neutral (same rules for all ships regardless of flag state), which conflicts with CBDR. This tension is ongoing — developing nations argue CBDR should apply to maritime GHG measures. IMO's 2023 GHG Strategy acknowledges this by including provisions for technology transfer and capacity building. ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What is CBDR and how does it relate to IMO?" — Origin at Rio 1992, embedded in UNFCCC/Paris Agreement. The tension: IMO applies same standards to all ships regardless of flag, while CBDR says developed nations should do more. Simon Sir may ask: "Does CBDR apply to MARPOL?" — Not explicitly, but it influences IMO mid-term measure negotiations. ⚖ Regulatory References UNFCCC 1992 / Art. 3.1 "Article 3.1 — Principles" (UNFCCC, 1992) — Common But Differentiated Responsibilities principle first codified Rio Declaration 1992 "Principle 7" (Rio Declaration on Environment and Development, 1992) — states cooperate to conserve Earth's ecosystem; developed states acknowledge their responsibility IMO 2023 GHG Strategy "2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships" — acknowledges CBDR; includes capacity-building and technology transfer provisions

text: 4 Types of P&I Capital Calls ETC (Estimated Total Call): Baseline premium calculated and billed at the start of the policy year — based on estimated annual claims. Unbudgeted Supplementary Call: Additional premium levied on all members if annual claims outpace the club's financial reserves. Release Call: Premium charged when a shipowner withdraws a vessel from the club — covers outstanding liability before the policy year closes. Overspill Call: Catastrophic assessment levied if a massive claim exceeds the club's standard reinsurance limits — pooled across the International Group of P&I Clubs. ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What is a P&I Club?" — A mutual insurance association covering third-party liabilities (pollution, cargo damage, crew injury, collision). section_title: FMEA — Failure Mode and Effect Analysis
text: Definition A proactive, structured risk assessment methodology originally developed by the U.S. Military to systematically identify, analyse, and mitigate potential failure modes before they occur. 4 Standard Execution Steps Identify the system, sub-system, or component to be analysed. Identify all potential failure modes for each component. Determine the underlying causes of each potential failure. Evaluate the operational effects and consequences of each failure mode. Risk Priority Number (RPN) — FMEA Metric RPN = Occurrence (O) × Severity (S) × Detectability (D) Each scored 1–10 | Maximum RPN: 1,000 Action threshold: RPN > 100 → immediate corrective action required ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What is FMEA and how is RPN calculated?" — Define FMEA, list 4 steps, quote RPN = O × S × D, max 1000, action threshold 100. He may link this to ISM Code Cl. 7 (shipboard operations — risk assessment) and ask how FMEA differs from HAZID/HAZOP. FMEA is component-level; HAZOP is process/flow-level. ⚖ Regulatory References ISM Code / Cl. 7 "7. Development of Plans for Shipboard Operations" (ISM Code Part A) — FMEA is a recognised risk-assessment tool within this framework IEC 60812 "IEC 60812 — Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA and FMECA)" — defines RPN methodology and procedure IACS UR S11 "IACS Unified Requirement S11 — Longitudinal Strength Standard" — structural failure-mode principles applied in hull design approval; verify exact UR number before quoting

section_subtitle: Definition per MS Notice 09/2014 · document control & amendment authority explained
section_title: ISM "Apex" Safety Management Manual
text: Definition — per the primary source D.G. Shipping's own MS Notice 09 of 2014 (para 6.2.1.1) is the actual origin of the term "Apex Manual." It defines it as: the company's Safety Management Manual , which must contain policies, objectives, organisational structure, and responsibilities/authorities of relevant personnel, and which addresses all elements of the ISM Code. The apex manual cross-references subordinate operational manuals, instructions, checklists, and forms — but the Notice itself does not split the manual into named "Tier 1/2/3" categories, and does not assign different approval authorities to different parts of it. Common Teaching Simplification Many oral-coaching sources (including earlier versions of this note) describe the SMS documentation as a 3-tier ISO 9001-style hierarchy for teaching purposes: Tier 1 — Policy: Company safety/environmental policy, objectives, organisational structure. Tier 2 — Procedures: Specific shipboard plans and operational safety procedures. Tier 3 — Forms: Working forms, checklists, and record sheets. This structure is a useful way to organise the manual's contents — but it is not found in MS Notice 09/2014, the ISM Code, or any DGMA circular, and neither is a rule assigning specific tiers to Flag/RO vs. DPA approval. Amendment Authority — what is actually verified Neither MS Notice 09/2014 nor the ISM Code (Cl. 11) assigns approval of "Tier 1," "Tier 2," or "Tier 3" specifically to Flag/RO vs. DPA. Cl. 11 requires only that document changes be "reviewed and approved by authorized personnel" under the Company's own document-control procedure. What Flag/RO (D.G. Shipping / DGMA) does control, per MS Notice 09/2014: (a) preliminary scrutiny of the apex SMS manual as part of the initial DOC application (§8.1.1.5, §8.1.2); (b) issuing/endorsing the DOC and SMC; (c) verifying, at annual/intermediate/renewal audit, that the Company's document-control system functions correctly; (d) DPA/ADPA qualification and any *change of DPA* must be reported to DGS (§7.3.1) — this is the one genuine "must-report-to-Flag" trigger in the Notice, and it concerns the *person*, not a manual tier. Day-to-day content amendments across the manual (whichever "tier" they sit in) are approved internally per the Company's own document-control procedure — subject to audit, not pre-approval, by Flag/RO. ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What is the ISM apex manual?" — the top-level Safety Management Manual per MS Notice 09/2014 §6.2.1.1, addressing all ISM Code elements and cross-referencing subordinate manuals/forms. If he frames it as "3 tiers," describe Policy → Procedures → Forms as the standard way of organising it. If he probes "who approves changes to each tier," the defensible answer is: neither the Code nor MS Notice 09/2014 mandates a fixed Tier-vs-Flag/RO split — document changes are approved by "authorized personnel" under the Company's own document-control procedure (Cl. 11); Flag/RO's role is scrutiny at initial DOC application and periodic audit, not routine amendment sign-off. Be ready to describe your own company's document-control hierarchy in practice. ⚖ Regulatory References MS Notice 09/2014 "International Safety Management (ISM) Code on Indian ships" (No. ENG/ISM/59(4)/97, dated 15.05.2014) — §6.2 "SMS Manuals" is the primary source defining the "Apex Manual." Supersedes MS Notices 09/2003 & 28/2003 and 33 Engineering Circulars. Documentation" (ISM Code Part A) — requires procedures ensuring valid documents are available at relevant locations, that changes are reviewed and approved by authorized personnel, and obsolete documents are removed. Company Verification, Review and Evaluation" (ISM Code Part A) SOLAS IX / Reg 3 "Regulation 3 — Requirements for a Safety Management System" (SOLAS IX) — mandates ISM Code compliance for both company and ship

section_title: STP Code & Duties of a Principal Officer (PO)
text: STP Code — Special Trade Passenger Ships Agreement Developed in cooperation with the World Health Organization (WHO) . Governs safe transport of large numbers of unberthed passengers in specific sea trade areas. Applies to any mechanically propelled passenger ship carrying more than 30 special trade passengers . Special trade = passengers accommodated on weather decks, upper decks, or between-deck spaces. Principal Officer (PO) — 7 Statutory Duties Regional head of the Mercantile Marine Department (MMD) under DGMA: Managing formal ship registration and ownership tracking. Overseeing statutory certification and endorsement of marine officers. Supreme regional authority over statutory vessel certification. Supervising and scheduling Flag State Inspections. Directing PSC enforcement inspections. Ordering and overseeing marine casualty investigations. Apex Nodal Officer for regional ISPS Code compliance. ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What is the role of the Principal Officer?" — Know all 7 duties. He is the regional head of the MMD — the PO is the person who authorises your COC endorsements, schedules FSIs, and directs casualty investigations. Simon Sir at Kochi MMD reports up through this structure. Shows awareness of the DGS administrative hierarchy. ⚖ Regulatory References Merchant Shipping Act, 2025, Part II Appointment and powers of Principal Officers, MMD — in force 15 March 2026 (formerly Section 7 of the repealed 1958 Act; verify exact section number against current India Code text before quoting) ISPS Code / Part A "Part A" (ISPS Code) — Principal Officer's role as regional ISPS enforcement/reporting nodal authority under Indian implementation STP Agreement 1971 "Special Trade Passenger Ships Agreement, 1971 (STP)" — WHO/IMO cooperation framework for unberthed passenger carriage

text: SEO — Seamen's Employment Office Locations: Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata. Functions: Recruitment regulation, seafarer registration, RPS licence issuance and renewal, monitoring suspended agencies, repatriation of stranded crews using RPS bank guarantees or welfare funds. Statutory Obligations of an RPS Provider Maintain complete records of all recruited seafarers and crew manifests. All fees/charges borne entirely by employer — never by the seafarer. Verify all personnel hold valid STCW documentation. Emergency Reporting: Report any seafarer death or major disability to SEO and next of kin within 48 hours . Pay statutory fee of ₹6,000 per seafarer per year to the shipowner (welfare fund contribution). ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What is the SEO?" — Government body in Mumbai/Chennai/Kolkata regulating seafarer recruitment and placement. He may ask: "Can a recruitment agency charge the seafarer fees?" — No — MLC Regulation 1.4 and Indian RPS rules prohibit fees being charged to seafarers. Know the 48-hour death reporting obligation — critical for CE awareness when a crew member is lost or seriously injured. ⚖ Regulatory References MLC 2006 / Reg 1.4 "Regulation 1.4 — Recruitment and placement" (MLC 2006) — no recruitment fees to seafarers; record-keeping, complaints mechanism, repatriation obligations Merchant Shipping Act, 2025, Sec 62 (Part V) Statutory basis for the Seamen's Employment Office and RPS licensing — in force 15 March 2026 (formerly Section 96 of the repealed 1958 Act) MS Labour Rules 2016 "Merchant Shipping (Recruitment and Placement of Seafarers) Rules" — 48-hour reporting, bank guarantee, welfare contribution requirements; verify current rule year/number and exact contribution figure before quoting, as these are periodically revised

section_title: NSB & Merchant Shipping Act 2025
text: NSB — National Shipping Board Permanent statutory advisory body established 1 March 1959 under Section 4 of the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 (provision carried forward under the new MSA 2025 as the "Shipping Board"). Under the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (MoPSW). Statutory composition — Section 4, MSA 2025 (verified against Gazette text, Act No. 24 of 2025): Total up to 22 members — (a) 6 members of Parliament (4 elected by/from the Lok Sabha + 2 elected by/from the Rajya Sabha); (b) up to 16 additional members nominated by the Central Government to represent Central Government, shipowners, seafarers and other interests, of which at least 4 shall be women , with an equal number of shipowner and seafarer representatives mandated among the 16. The Chairperson is nominated by the Central Government from among the Board's own members (not necessarily an MP). Current seated board (2025 reconstitution, pre-MSA 2025 rules): 16 members total (Chairman + 15) — DG Shipping/Chief Surveyor, Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas rep, Indian Navy rep, Indian Coast Guard rep, INSA (shipowners), ICCSA/coastal shipping assoc., NUSI/MUI (seafarer unions), IRS, an academic (IIT), and port/industry representatives — no sitting MPs on this particular board. Know both the exact statutory formula (22 max, 4 women minimum) and that the practical seated board can look different pending fresh reconstitution under the new Act's rules. Advisory scope: national shipping policies, coastal/international shipping, seafarer training, welfare, marine safety, environmental protection, maritime law amendments. Merchant Shipping Act 2025 — Key Changes (from the former MS Bill 2024) Introduced in Lok Sabha December 2024; passed by Lok Sabha 6 Aug 2025 and Rajya Sabha 11 Aug 2025; received Presidential assent 18 Aug 2025 as the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (No. 24 of 2025) ; brought into force by government notification from 15 March 2026 , repealing the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 (except Part XIV) and the Coasting Vessels Act 1838. Structure: Condenses 561 sections (1958 Act) into 325 sections across 16 Parts. DG Shipping renamed: Director-General now styled Director-General of Maritime Administration (DGMA) . NRI/OCI/foreign corporate ownership: Enables NRIs, OCIs, and other Central-Government-notified entities to register vessels under Indian flag; wholly-owned-by-Indian requirement relaxed. Bareboat Charter Registry: Registration of foreign vessels under bareboat charter-cum-demise (BBCD) agreements, ownership intended to transfer to the Indian charterer. Vessel definition expanded: Submersibles, hydrofoils, MODUs, non-displacement craft included. Registration mandatory regardless of propulsion or size — removes the old 15-ton non-mechanically-propelled coastal exemption. Seafarer welfare: Extends statutory protection and social security to Indian seafarers, aligns with MLC 2006; retains National Welfare Board for Seafarers. MTI regulation: DGMA empowered to approve/regulate Maritime Training Institutes and courses. MARPOL/SOLAS/Wreck Removal: Incorporates SOLAS, MARPOL, Ballast Water Management Convention and Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention obligations, including shipowner-funded wreck removal costs. Compliance transparency: Mandatory disclosure of all shipping charges to exporters/importers; penalties up to ₹5 lakh for non-disclosure. ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What is the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 and when did it come into force?" — Key answer: repeals the 1958 Act, in force from 15 March 2026, allows NRI/OCI/foreign flag registration, expands vessel definitions, renames DG Shipping to DGMA, aligns with MLC. This is a very current topic and status changes fast — re-verify the in-force date and any pending Rules (draft MS Rules were still under stakeholder consultation as of early 2026) close to your oral date. On composition: if asked "how many members and what's the women representation?" — up to 22 total (6 MPs + up to 16 nominated), at least 4 of the 16 must be women, equal shipowner/seafarer representation among the 16 (Section 4, MSA 2025 — verified against the Gazette text). ⚖ Regulatory References MSA 2025 (No. 24 of 2025) "Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (No. 24 of 2025)" — verify exact commencement date and repeal scope directly against the Gazette notification before quoting, as this is very recent legislation MLC 2006 "Maritime Labour Convention, 2006" — the MSA 2025 is understood to align Indian domestic law with MLC standards; verify specific alignment provisions against the enacted text MSA 2025, Section 4 "Section 4" (Merchant Shipping Act, 2025) — National Shipping Board composition; verify exact composition figures against the enacted text before quoting, as this is very recent legislation

section_title: ISO 8217:2024 & FAME Biofuel
text: ISO 8217:2024 — Seventh Edition Key Changes Expanded from 2 to 4 reference tables to accommodate modern alternative fuel blends. Table 1: Distillate and bio-distillate grades — allows 100% FAME . Table 2: Residual fuels with sulphur caps below 0.50% — includes new RMA 20 grade. Tables 3 & 4: Bio-residuals and residual fuels with sulphur ≥0.50%. Removed winter/summer quality distinction — replaced with cold filter plugging and pour point limits. Added minimum Cetane number, oxidation stability limit, and Net Heat of Combustion reporting. FAME — Fatty Acid Methyl Ester Transesterification Reaction Vegetable oils / Animal fats + Methanol → (KOH/NaOH catalyst, heat) → FAME (Esters) + Glycerol Advantages: Reduces GHG emissions; high biodegradability; improved lubricity for injectors. Disadvantages: Prone to oxidation and degradation in storage; microbial growth risk; minor incompatibility with natural rubbers. ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What is ISO 8217:2024 and what changed?" — 7th edition, 4 tables, 100% FAME in distillates. He may ask: "What is FAME?" — Biofuel produced by transesterification (vegetable oils + methanol + KOH/NaOH catalyst → FAME + glycerol). Key concern: FAME degrades in storage — important for bunker quality management on your Maersk vessel. ⚖ Regulatory References ISO 8217:2024 "Products from petroleum, synthetic and renewable sources — Fuels (Class F) — Specifications of marine fuels" (ISO 8217:2024) — 7th edition; expanded to 4 tables; allows up to 100% FAME in DF distillate grades MARPOL VI / Reg 14 "Regulation 14 — Sulphur oxides (SOₓ) and particulate matter" (MARPOL VI) — ISO 8217 is the referenced quality standard for compliant fuels MARPOL VI / Reg 18 "Regulation 18 — Fuel oil availability and quality" (MARPOL VI) — BDN must reference ISO 8217 grade

section_title: UNFCCC & COP Historical Milestones
text: UNFCCC United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change — international treaty established 1992 to coordinate global climate action. The Conference of the Parties (COP) is its supreme decision-making body, meeting annually. Key COP Milestones COP 3 (1997 — Kyoto): Adopted the Kyoto Protocol — first binding emission targets and carbon credit system. COP 21 (2015 — Paris): Paris Agreement — limit warming to well below 2.0°C , pursue 1.5°C. Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). COP 26 (2021 — Glasgow): Pledges to phase down coal; methane pledge; Article 6 carbon markets rules (not finalised). COP 28 (2023 — Dubai): First global stocktake; fossil fuel transition language; triple renewables; Loss & Damage Fund operational. COP 29 (2024 — Baku): Climate finance — new NCQG goal; Article 6 carbon market rules finalised. ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What is UNFCCC and what is COP?" — UNFCCC = the treaty; COP = the annual decision-making body. Know the 4 key COP milestones: Kyoto (1997), Paris (2015), Glasgow (2021), Dubai (2023). Simon Sir may ask how the Paris Agreement relates to the IMO strategy — both target net-zero 2050 but IMO acts through MARPOL regulations, not NDCs. ⚖ Regulatory References UNFCCC 1992 "United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, 1992 (UNFCCC)" — establishes the Conference of the Parties (COP) as supreme governing body Kyoto Protocol 1997 "Kyoto Protocol" (adopted COP3, 1997) — binding emission targets for developed (Annex I) nations Paris Agreement 2015 "Paris Agreement" (adopted COP21, 2015) — Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) based commitments; 5-year review/ratchet cycles

text: Definition Commercial practice of registering a merchant ship in a foreign nation rather than the shipowner's country of citizenship — typically to take advantage of relaxed regulations, minimal taxation, and flexible labour laws. Common FOC Registries Panama, Liberia, Marshall Islands, Bahamas, Malta, Vanuatu, Cambodia. He may ask: "What are the advantages and risks of FOC?" — Advantages: lower tax, lower costs, flexible manning. Risks: weaker flag state oversight, lower safety standards historically, ITF labour disputes, potential PSC targeting based on flag performance. PSC MOUs maintain flag state blacklists/grey lists. ⚖ Regulatory References UNCLOS Art. 91 "Article 91 — Nationality of ships" (UNCLOS 1982) — genuine link requirement between ship and flag State, frequently challenged in Flag of Convenience arrangements MLC 2006 "Maritime Labour Convention, 2006" — minimum labour standards apply regardless of flag, limiting the labour-cost advantage of Flags of Convenience IOMOU / Paris MOU "Indian Ocean MOU / Paris MOU" — publish flag performance black/grey/white lists; Flags of Convenience are disproportionately represented on grey/black lists

keywords: broaching pooping following sea stability loss surf riding course keeping
section_subtitle: Rudder out of water — wave orbital motion — extreme heel
section_title: Broaching — Course Control Failure in Following Seas
text: Definition A dangerous hydrodynamic phenomenon where a vessel running with a following sea loses directional control and turns abruptly beam-on to the waves , creating extreme heel risk. Mechanism Ship travels down a wave face at a speed close to the wave propagation speed. Stern lifts out of the water — rudder emerges from the water , destroying steering control. Wave orbital water motion causes the vessel to swing sideways. Combined wind and wave forces induce an extreme angle of heel — capsizing risk. ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What is broaching?" — Explain the mechanism: stern lifts → rudder out of water → loss of steering → beam-on. He may ask: "How do you prevent broaching?" — Reduce speed (increase period ratio ship/wave), alter course to take seas on quarter, increase engine power momentarily to maintain steerage. Broaching is covered under heavy weather manoeuvring — SOLAS V/34 Master's responsibility. ⚖ Regulatory References SOLAS V / Reg 34 "Regulation 34 — Safe navigation and avoidance of dangerous situations" (SOLAS V) IS Code 2008 / Part B "Part B — Recommendations" (IS Code 2008) — non-mandatory guidance on vulnerability to parametric rolling and broaching-to IMO MSC-MEPC.2/Circ.13 "Interim Guidelines on the Second Generation Intact Stability Criteria" (MSC.1/Circ.1627, or successor circular) — covers broaching-to/surf-riding vulnerability criteria; verify exact current circular number, this area has been revised multiple times

keywords: rescue boat position propeller walk single screw ship stern

section_title: Rescue Boat — Starboard Side Placement
text: Design Rationale Most merchant vessels use a right-handed propeller (clockwise viewed from aft). When astern power is applied (e.g., MOB emergency stop), transverse thrust (propeller walk) pushes the stern to port , swinging the bow to starboard. Placing the rescue boat on the starboard side positions it away from the port-swinging stern and propeller hazard. This enables faster, safer launching and recovery of the person in the water. ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "Why is the rescue boat placed on the starboard side?" — Propeller walk: right-handed screw → stern swings port under astern thrust → starboard side is clear of stern and propeller. He may test this with: "What if your vessel has a CPP (Controllable Pitch Propeller)?" — CPP vessels can go astern without stern walk, but starboard placement remains standard by convention. ⚖ Regulatory References SOLAS III / Reg 26 "5.1.2" (LSA Code Ch. section_title: Life Cycle Assessment — Well-to-Wake Framework
text: Well-to-Wake (WTW) = WTT + TTW WTT (Well-to-Tank): GHG from feedstock → refining → transport → bunker tank TTW (Tank-to-Wake): GHG from onboard combustion → exhaust LCA Implications for Alternative Fuels LNG: Low TTW CO₂ but methane slip (CH₄, GWP 27–30) can negate the advantage. Ammonia: Zero TTW CO₂ but N₂O combustion byproduct (GWP 273); grey ammonia production is energy-intensive. Green H₂: Zero WTW if from renewable electrolysis — but expensive. FAME: Low WTW from waste oils; higher if from food crops (land use change). ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What is Well-to-Wake?" — WTW = WTT + TTW. "Why isn't LNG zero-carbon?" — Methane slip — unburned CH₄ escapes, GWP 27–30. Smart Contracts: Self-executing contracts triggered by real-world events (e.g., port arrival triggers freight payment automatically). ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What is blockchain and how is it used in shipping?" — 3 pillars: decentralised, cryptographic, immutable. Maritime: Smart BOL, Smart BDN, Smart Contracts. "What is a Smart Contract?" — Self-executing programme that automatically performs contract terms when conditions are met — no intermediary needed. ⚖ Regulatory References IMO FAL 44 (2019) "FAL Committee, 44th session (2019) — output on electronic data exchange / e-B/L" — recognises electronic bills of lading; blockchain cited as an enabling technology — verify exact FAL 44 output/circular reference before quoting a specific resolution number MARPOL VI / Reg 18 "Regulation 18 — Fuel oil availability and quality" — Bunker Delivery Note requirement; blockchain-based "Smart BDN" is an industry application, not itself an IMO-mandated format

section_title: Great Circle Navigation
text: Definition: Shortest possible distance between two points on a sphere. On Mercator chart: Appears as a curved arc — not a straight line. Rhumb Line: Constant heading, straight on Mercator, longer distance. Great circle: Shorter but requires continuous course adjustment. Composite sailing: Limits poleward extent — used to avoid ice/harsh weather at high latitudes. ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What is great circle navigation?" — Shortest route on a sphere, curved on Mercator, continuous course changes. When NOT to use: polar/ice regions, short voyages (negligible saving), shallow water. Composite great circle limits the latitude reached. ⚖ Regulatory References SOLAS V / Reg 34 "Regulation 34 — Safe navigation and avoidance of dangerous situations" — voyage planning must consider route type, including great circle options SOLAS V / Reg 27 "Regulation 27 — Nautical charts and publications" — adequate and up-to-date charts required to cover the intended voyage

text: 5 Vs of Big Data Volume: Sheer scale and amount of data collected. Velocity: Rapid speed at which data is generated in real time. Variety: Different data types — text, logs, images, sensor feeds. Veracity: Accuracy, reliability, and trustworthiness of data. Value: Actionable insights and business intelligence derived. Maritime Applications Dynamic voyage optimisation: Real-time sea/weather/traffic analysis → optimise routes, fuel, emissions. Predictive asset analytics: Machinery parameter monitoring → predict failures before breakdown. Supply chain management: Port data + vessel locations → accurate ETA computation. ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What is big data and what are the 5 Vs?" — Quote all five. He links to IoT (generates the data) and AI/ML (analyses it). As CE, predictive maintenance using big data is highly relevant — vibration, temperature, and pressure sensor data feeds predictive maintenance systems replacing time-based PMS. ⚖ Regulatory References MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3 "Guidelines on Maritime Cyber Risk Management" (MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3) read with "Maritime Cyber Risk Management in Safety Management Systems" (Resolution MSC.428(98)) — big data/IT systems treated as cyber assets requiring protection under the SMS MARPOL VI / Reg 26 "Regulation 26 — Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP)" — big-data-driven voyage optimisation is a recognised measure supporting CII improvement

keywords: IWIS In-Water Survey Preparation Drydock 10-step checklist cathodic protection 5-yr paint bead welds propeller
section_subtitle: 10-step checklist · cathodic protection · 5-yr paint · bead welds · propeller numbering
section_title: IWIS — In-Water Survey Preparation in Drydock
text: 10 IWIS Preparation Steps (in drydock) Fit approved cathodic protection system . Paint hull with coating designed to last 5 years . Paint colour provides optimal contrast with underwater environment (assists diver visibility). Shell openings with gratings: secure hinged openings . All suction, discharge, and shell openings marked by bead welding for easy diver identification. All transverse and longitudinal butt welds clearly marked . Propeller blades numbered (normally pre-marked). Hull areas inaccessible at LWL during IWIS given particular attention. Documentation to diver: shell expansion plan, drain plug plan, rudder/stern frame drawings. Agreed method for blanking shell openings established for diver safety. Note: propeller blade count and engine unit count should NOT be integral multiples — avoids resonance. ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What is IWIS and how do you prepare for it?" — In-Water International Survey — underwater hull inspection in lieu of drydocking (requires BIS class notation). He expects the 10-step drydock preparation checklist. "What is the advantage of IWIS?" — Avoids drydocking costs and off-hire time. ⚖ Regulatory References IACS UR Z17 "IACS UR Z17 — Procedural Requirement for In-Water Survey" — conditions under which an in-water survey may substitute for drydocking; requires BIS (Bottom Inspection in lieu of Survey) class notation — verify exact UR designation/number SOLAS I / Reg 10 "Regulation 10 — Surveys" (SOLAS I) — periodical surveys including bottom/underwater inspection; Administration may permit in-water survey in lieu of drydocking

keywords: Multiple Load Lines One valid time non-active concealed logbook entry assignment booklet

section_title: Multiple Load Lines
text: Used when a vessel needs to operate with greater freeboard allowance (e.g., draft restrictions at specific ports, low-density cargo). At any time only one load line is valid . Non-active load lines painted the same colour as the ship's hull to conceal them. Master must make an entry in the official logbook whenever a load line is changed. Procedure for changing load lines must be in the vessel's Environmental Management System (EMS). Procedure to Obtain Multiple Load Lines Owner sends request to Administration. RO carries out calculations, performs surveys, and issues full-term certificate. Freeboard assignment and approved copies sent to Administration. Administration issues an assignment booklet . Each load line change entered in assignment booklet — endorsed at annual and renewal surveys. ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What are multiple load lines?" — Only ONE active at a time; non-active lines concealed (painted hull colour); Master logs every change. He may ask about the alternate tonnage certificate — issued by Administration showing both original and reduced tonnage. ⚖ Regulatory References ILLC 1966 / Annex I "Annex I — Regulations for Determining Load Lines" (International Convention on Load Lines, 1966) — permits assignment of multiple load lines with specified marking/concealment conditions LL Protocol 1988 "Protocol of 1988 relating to the International Convention on Load Lines, 1966" — aligns load line survey/certification cycle with the Harmonised System of Survey and Certification (HSSC)

keywords: Sustainable Development Incineration Port Restrictions SDG 2030 incinerator 850°C continuous port incineration ban PVC
section_subtitle: UN SDG 2030 · incinerator 850°C continuous · port incineration ban · PVC prohibited
section_title: Sustainable Development, Incineration & Port Restrictions
text: Sustainable Development Meeting present needs without compromising future generations. Guided by UN SDG 2030 Agenda (17 goals). IMO aligns GHG strategy with UN SDGs — net-zero shipping by or around 2050. Incinerator Regulations (MARPOL VI / Reg 16) Incinerator Temperature Requirements Continuous feed: flue gas temperature ≥ 850°C Batch-loaded: must reach 600°C within 5 minutes Onboard incineration outside approved incinerator: prohibited Exception: sewage sludge and oil sludge may be burned in auxiliary boilers/power plants when NOT in port Port Incineration Restrictions Incineration prohibited while in port or at offshore terminals. Prohibited items: PVC (unless type-approved incinerator), EGCS residues, cargo residues with heavy metals/PCBs, refined petroleum products containing halogens, MARPOL Annex V HME cargo residues. ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What are the incinerator temperature requirements?" — 850°C continuous, 600°C within 5 minutes for batch. "Can you incinerate PVC?" — Only in a type-approved incinerator. "Can sewage sludge be incinerated in port?" — No, only at sea in boilers/auxiliary engines. ⚖ Regulatory References MARPOL VI / Reg 16 "Regulation 16 — Shipboard incineration" (MARPOL Annex VI) — 850°C continuous/600°C within 5 min batch temperature requirements; prohibited substances; port incineration restrictions MEPC.244(66) "2014 Standard Specification for Shipboard Incinerators" (Resolution MEPC.244(66)) — updates MEPC.76(40); operational/type-approval standards for shipboard incinerators UN SDG 2030 "Transforming Our World: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development" (UN General Assembly Resolution A/RES/70/1) — 17 SDGs framework IMO references when aligning its GHG strategy with broader sustainability goals

keywords: Maintenance Strategies Preventive Predictive Time-based scheduled condition-based IoT sensor triggered
section_subtitle: Time-based scheduled vs condition-based IoT/sensor triggered
section_title: Maintenance Strategies — Preventive vs Predictive
text: Parameter Preventive Maintenance Predictive Maintenance Basis Schedule-based — fixed time intervals Condition-based — real-time sensor data Trigger Calendar/running hours — regardless of condition Triggered when condition data indicates need Tools PMS, checklists, class survey schedules IoT sensors, vibration analysis, thermal imaging, oil analysis Advantage Simple, reliable, class-compliant Reduces unnecessary overhauls; lower cost; higher availability Disadvantage May overhaul items that don't need it — wasted resources Requires investment in sensor infrastructure and data analytics ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What is the difference between preventive and predictive maintenance?" — Preventive = time-based (do it regardless of condition). Predictive = condition-based (IoT/sensors tell you when to act). "Which does your company use?" — Maersk uses a hybrid PMS: calendar-based for safety-critical items; condition monitoring for machinery systems under ISM Code Cl. 10. ⚖ Regulatory References ISM Code / Cl. 10 "10. Maintenance of the Ship and Equipment" (ISM Code Part A) — PMS must cover critical systems; condition-based monitoring is an acceptable maintenance strategy IACS UR M28 "IACS UR M28 — Condition-based maintenance for machinery" — IACS guidance framework for sensor-based predictive maintenance eligibility — verify exact UR designation/number before quoting

keywords: PSC Action Codes Form Code 10–99 detention

Form B: Deficiencies by code — description + action code. ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What is PSC Code 30?" — Detainable deficiency — ship cannot sail. Know Code 16 (14 days), Code 17 (before departure), Code 45 (fix detention-worthy deficiency at next port). Form B is what the CE must action. ⚖ Regulatory References IMO Res. A.1206(34) "Procedures for Port State Control, 2025" (adopted 3 Dec 2025, effective 1 Jan 2026, supersedes A.1185(33) of 2023) — action codes, inspection procedures, Form 13/Form A&B IOMOU Procedures "Indian Ocean Memorandum of Understanding on Port State Control — Procedures" — regional action code definitions and deficiency classification

keywords: PSC Inspection Types Clear Grounds Initial More Detailed Expanded CIC clear grounds triggers
section_subtitle: Initial → More Detailed → Expanded → CIC · 6 clear grounds triggers
section_title: PSC Inspection Types & Clear Grounds
text: 4 PSC Inspection Types Initial: Baseline walk-through — certificates, general condition, cleanliness. More Detailed: Triggered by clear grounds — deep equipment verification. Expanded: High-risk vessel categories by age, type, or flag performance. CIC (Concentrated Inspection Campaign): Regional campaign on specific system — 3-month window, announced annually by MOUs. 6 Clear Grounds Triggers Structural issues, severe hull corrosion, compromised watertight integrity. Critical safety or pollution equipment missing or non-operational. Invalid, missing, or expired seafarer certificates. Bridge or E/R crew unable to communicate effectively. Master or crew unfamiliar with essential shipboard procedures. Third-party report or crew complaint alleging substandard conditions. ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What triggers a more detailed PSC inspection?" — Any of the 6 clear grounds. CIC — MOU announces annual focus area. Maersk vessels receive CIC briefings before port calls. Prepare by ensuring equipment in the focus area is operational and records are complete. ⚖ Regulatory References IMO Res. A.1206(34) "Procedures for Port State Control, 2025" (supersedes A.1185(33), effective 1 Jan 2026) — Chapter 2 defines inspection types (Initial/More Detailed/Expanded/CIC) and clear grounds criteria IOMOU / Paris MOU "Indian Ocean MOU / Paris MOU — Concentrated Inspection Campaign announcements" — annual campaign topics published on each MOU's website

keywords: PSC Suspension Post-Detention Steps Flag notified Superintendent SMC audit separate surveyor clear before sailing
section_subtitle: Flag/RO notified · Superintendent SMC audit · separate RO surveyor · clear before sailing
section_title: PSC Suspension & Post-Detention — 4 Steps
text: Suspension Protocol PSCO logs all detainable deficiencies found up to point of suspension ▼ Formally notify Flag Administration and acting RO ▼ Vessel frozen in port — Flag/RO commits to full independent survey before reinspection 4 Mandatory Steps to Clear Detention Company deploys Superintendent — full structural inspection + internal SMC audit . Full survey by Classification surveyor from RO different from the last annual survey . Rectify every logged deficiency — prepare for final PSC reinspection. Once PSC order cleared — mandatory additional external SMC audit before vessel sails. ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "Your ship has been detained in Singapore — walk me through the steps." — All 4 steps. Critical: clearance surveyor must be a DIFFERENT RO from last annual survey — ensures independence. Two SMC audits total (internal Superintendent + external post-clearance). ⚖ Regulatory References IMO Res. A.1206(34) "Procedures for Port State Control, 2025" (supersedes A.1185(33), effective 1 Jan 2026) — Chapter 3, suspension of inspection and conditions for detention/release ISM Code / Cl. 12 "12. Company Verification, Review and Evaluation" (ISM Code Part A) — post-detention SMC audit falls under Company verification obligations; DPA oversight mandatory

keywords: PSC Detention Appeal National MOU Panel days national 3-member independent panel CIS clearance

text: Pathway National Procedure MOU Panel Procedure Deadline Within 30 days Within 80 days Route Domestic legal channels Via Flag State/RO to MOU Secretariat Panel Domestic legal process Independent 3-member — excludes Port State and Flag State If upheld Detention reversed Port State requested to reconsider; CIS entry cleared PSCO obligation: must inform the Master of right to appeal and provide documentation at time of detention. ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "How can a PSC detention be appealed?" — Two pathways: national (30 days) or MOU panel (80 days via Flag/RO). 3-member panel excludes both Port State and Flag State. IOMOU: www.iomou.org. PSCO has a duty to inform the Master of appeal rights at time of detention. ⚖ Regulatory References IMO Res. A.1206(34) "Procedures for Port State Control, 2025" (supersedes A.1185(33), effective 1 Jan 2026) — right of appeal provisions; national procedure and MOU independent panel review pathway IOMOU Procedures "Indian Ocean Memorandum of Understanding — Appeal Procedures" — 80-day independent panel review; 3-member panel excluding Port and Flag State

keywords: SOLAS Liferaft Packs Pack extended ocean short coastal has extra provisions
section_subtitle: Pack A = extended ocean · Pack B = short/coastal · Pack A has extra provisions
section_title: SOLAS Liferaft Packs — A vs B
text: Pack A: Extended survival on international ocean voyages. Contains everything in Pack B plus: extra drinking water, survival food, additional hull repair kits, extra flares, expanded first aid kits. Pack B: Scaled-down inventory for short international voyages or domestic coastal routes. Your Maersk container vessel on international voyages carries Pack A liferafts. ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What is the difference between SOLAS Pack A and Pack B?" — Pack A = ocean (more equipment). Pack B = short/coastal (reduced). He may ask specific Pack A extras: extra drinking water, survival food, additional flares, expanded first aid. ⚖ Regulatory References LSA Code / 4.1.5 "4.1 Inflatable Liferafts" (LSA Code Ch. IV) — Pack A (ocean) and Pack B (coastal) equipment content specification SOLAS III / Reg 13 "Regulation 13 — Stowage of survival craft" — SOLAS III sets stowage/carriage numbers; Pack A content requirement itself derives from LSA Code 4.1.5, not Reg 13 directly — cross-reference both when citing

keywords: Lifejacket Classifications Specs Testing 150N adult upright sec 120mm freeboard 24hr ≤5% loss 2-sec
section_subtitle: 150N adult · upright 5 sec · 120mm freeboard · 24hr/≤5% loss · 2-sec fire test
section_title: Lifejacket Classifications, Specs & Testing
text: 3 Categories Adult: Age 12+ or ≥43 kg → min buoyancy 150 N Child: Age 2–12 or 15–43 kg → min buoyancy 88–150 N Infant: Under 2 years or <15 kg → min buoyancy 88 N Lifejacket Performance Standards (LSA Code) Automatic uprighting: unconscious person face-up within 5 seconds Mouth clearance: mouth ≥ 120 mm above water Buoyancy test: submerge 24 hrs → loss ≤ 5% Fire resistance: withstand 2-second oil fire without burning/melting Inflatable lifejackets: annual inspection by certified service station. Must have separate independent buoyancy compartments. ⚡ Simon Sir typically asks "What are the specifications of a lifejacket?" — 150 N adult, upright in 5 seconds, 120 mm freeboard, 24-hour buoyancy test ≤5% loss, 2-second fire test. "How often are inflatable lifejackets serviced?" — Annually by certified station. ⚖ Regulatory References LSA Code / 2.2 "2.2 Lifejackets" (LSA Code Ch. II) — buoyancy (150N adult), automatic uprighting (5 sec), freeboard (120mm), and testing requirements MSC.81(70) "Revised Recommendation on Testing of Life-Saving Appliances" (Resolution MSC.81(70)) — detailed lifejacket test protocols (buoyancy loss, fire, uprighting) SOLAS III / Reg 7 "Regulation 7 — Personal life-saving appliances" — one lifejacket per person plus additional lifejackets for watchkeepers/remote stations

keywords: Bonjean Curves Definition Uses Applications Stability Naval Arch
section_title: Bonjean Curves — Definition, Uses & Applications
text: Definition A Bonjean curve is a graph that plots the relationship between the area of a ship's transverse cross-section and its draft. A separate curve is drawn for each transverse station along the ship's length. Primary Uses Displacement volume: Calculate the ship's total displacement volume at any waterline. LCB: Determine the longitudinal centre of buoyancy. Block coefficient: Compute the displacement block coefficient. Centre of flotation: Find the longitudinal centre of the waterplane area. Structural & Launching Calculations Calculate the distribution of the buoyancy force during ship launching — critical as the stern lifts before the bow clears the slipway. Determine longitudinal bending moments and shear forces for structural strength calculations in non-uniform loading conditions. ⚖ Regulatory References IS Code 2008 IMO Intact Stability Code — stability criteria that Bonjean-derived hydrostatics must satisfy SOLAS II-1 / Pt B Subdivision and stability — hydrostatic data requirements for passenger and cargo ships IACS UR S1 Longitudinal strength standard — uses buoyancy distribution data derived from Bonjean curves Simon Sir typically asks: "What is a Bonjean curve and where do you use it?" Key answer: graph of section area vs. draft at each station; used for displacement, LCB, and launching calculations. Simon Sir may then ask how launching calculations differ — emphasise the dynamic buoyancy shift as the stern lifts.

keywords: LSA Code Chapters 2024 Amendments Lowering Speeds Pages 113–114 SOLAS
section_title: LSA Code — Chapters, 2024 Amendments & Lowering Speeds (Pages 113–114)
text: LSA Code — 7 Chapters Chapter Subject 1 General 2 Personal Life-Saving Appliances 3 Visual Signals 4 Survival Craft 5 Rescue Boats 6 Launching and Embarkation Appliances 7 Other Life-Saving Appliances LSA Code Amendments — Effective 1 January 2024 Rescue Boat Launching: Stored mechanical power may be waived if one person can recover the rescue boat using manual crank handles, provided crank force ≤ 160 N . Lifeboats with two independent propulsion systems or free-fall lifeboats: Adequate buoyancy arrangements must be provided. LSA Code Amendments — Effective 1 January 2026 Single Fall Hook System: Shall be designed so it cannot support any load unless completely reset; prevents accidental release during recovery. Lifeboat Lowering Speeds Maximum lowering speed: 1.3 m/s (upper safety limit) Minimum lowering speed: V = 0.4 + 0.02H Where V = speed (m/s); H = height from davit head to waterline (m) ⚖ Regulatory References LSA Code (MSC.48(66)) International Life-Saving Appliance Code — mandatory under SOLAS III SOLAS III / Reg 6 Maintenance, thorough examination, operational testing, overhaul and repair of LSA MSC.471(101) 2019 LSA Code amendments — single fall hook systems and lifeboat engine requirements MSC.520(106) Amendments to SOLAS Chapter II-2 (fire protection) — in force 1 January 2026 Simon Sir typically asks: "How many chapters in the LSA Code?" — Answer: 7 chapters . He may ask the lowering speed formula — give both maximum (1.3 m/s) and the minimum formula. The 2024 and 2026 amendments are current exam hot topics — know the 160 N crank force limit and the single-fall hook requirement.

keywords: FSS Code FTP Structure Test Procedures Page 115–116 Fire SOLAS
section_title: FSS Code & FTP Code — Structure & Test Procedures (Page 115–116)
text: FSS Code — International Code for Fire Safety Systems (2000) Mandatory under SOLAS Chapter II-2 . Provides international standards for fire safety systems and fire-fighting equipment. Contains 15 Chapters : Ch. Subject 1 General 2 International Shore Connection 3 Personal Protection 4 Fire Extinguishers 5 Fixed Gas Fire Extinguishing Systems (CO₂) 6 Fixed Foam Systems 7 Fixed Pressure Water-Spray & Water Mist Systems 8 Automatic Sprinkler, Detection & Alarm Systems 9 Fixed Fire Detection & Alarm Systems 10 Sample Extraction Smoke Detection 11 Low Location Lighting 12 Fixed Emergency Fire Pumps 13 Means of Escape 14 Fixed Deck Foam Systems 15 Inert Gas Systems FTP Code — International Code for Fire Test Procedures (2010) Applicable under SOLAS Chapter II-2 . Provides laboratory testing, type approval, and fire test procedures for materials and products installed onboard ships. Non-Combustibility Test: Material behaviour under high temperatures. Smoke and Toxicity Test: Smoke density and toxic gas generation. Class Divisions Test: Fire testing for "A", "B", and "F" class structural divisions. Control Systems Test: Fire testing for fire door control systems. Surface Flammability Test: Surface flammability properties. Primary Deck Coverings: Testing deck covering materials. Textiles and Films: Upholstered furniture, bedding, vertically suspended textiles. ⚖ Regulatory References FSS Code (MSC.98(73)) International Fire Safety Systems Code — mandatory under SOLAS II-2 FTP Code (MSC.307(88)) International Code for Application of Fire Test Procedures — mandatory under SOLAS II-2 SOLAS II-2 / Reg 17 Alternative design and arrangements for fire protection — must meet FSS/FTP Code equivalency Simon Sir typically asks: "How many chapters in the FSS Code?" — Answer: 15 chapters . He may then ask which chapter covers CO₂ fixed systems — Chapter 5 . For FTP Code, key question: "What is the FTP Code used for?" — Type approval testing of materials installed onboard. Know the "A", "B", "F" class division fire test.

keywords: Curve Statical Dynamic Stability Page 102 Code
section_title: GZ Curve — Statical & Dynamic Stability (Page 102)
text: The GZ Curve (Curve of Statical Stability) Plots the righting lever (GZ) against angle of heel (θ) for a specific displacement (Δ) and KG. Three key features: Range of Stability: Angular range over which GZ is positive. Angle of Vanishing Stability: Angle at which GZ returns to zero — beyond this, vessel capsizes. Point of Inflection (Contraflexure): Where the curve changes from concave to convex — occurs at deck edge immersion because the waterplane area begins to decrease. Key Stability Formulas Small angles (θ ≤ 10–12°): GZ = GM × sin θ Wall-Sided Formula (large angles): GZ = (GM + ½ BM tan²θ) × sin θ Approximate GM from curve slope: GM = GZ_θ / θ (at θ = 1 radian = 57.3°) Dynamic Stability Definition: Total work done in inclining the vessel to a specific angle of heel. Calculation: Area under the GZ curve up to that angle — expressed in tonne-metre-radians . Maximum energy absorption occurs at the angle of vanishing stability; beyond this, the vessel cannot right itself. IS Code 2008 Minimum Criteria (reference) Area under GZ curve: ≥ 0.055 m·rad (to 30°); ≥ 0.090 m·rad (to 40° or flooding angle); ≥ 0.030 m·rad between 30° and 40°. GZ at 30°: ≥ 0.20 m ; Initial GM: ≥ 0.15 m . ⚖ Regulatory References IS Code 2008 IMO Resolution MSC.267(85) — mandatory intact stability criteria for all ship types SOLAS II-1 / Reg 5 Requires stability information booklet and inclining experiment approval SOLAS II-1 / Reg 22 Damage stability — residual GZ requirements after flooding Simon Sir typically asks: "Draw the GZ curve and explain the features." Draw axes clearly, mark the range of stability, point of inflection, max GZ, and angle of vanishing stability. He may ask: "What is the difference between statical and dynamic stability?" — Statical = GZ at a fixed angle; Dynamic = area under the curve (energy absorbed).

keywords: Smart Sensors IOPP Certificate Supplements Page 103 Machinery MARPOL
section_title: Smart Sensors & IOPP Certificate Supplements (Page 103)
text: Smart Sensors in the Engine Room Definition: Advanced instruments with integrated microprocessors that process and communicate data rather than merely transmit raw signals. They act as "sensors with a brain." IoT integration: Used in predictive maintenance frameworks — sensors detect early bearing wear, temperature deviations, and vibration anomalies. Applications: Fuel efficiency optimisation, emission control (NOx/SOx monitoring), automated alarm management, UMS (Unattended Machinery Space) operation. IOPP Certificate Supplements (MARPOL Annex I) Form A: Supplement for ships other than oil tankers — records bilge water systems, OWS, 15 ppm alarm, ORB Part I. Form B: Supplement for oil tankers — records additional crude oil washing, inert gas system, SBT/CBT arrangements, COW. Must be permanently attached to the IOPP Certificate — guides PSC surveyors during inspections. Key Contents of IOPP Supplement Ship particulars: Name, Port of Registry, IMO number, GT. OWS configuration and 15 ppm alarm details. Sludge tank, bilge tank, and waste oil tank volumes and locations. Standard Discharge Connection (SDC) specifications. SOPEP (Shipboard Oil Pollution Emergency Plan) status. ⚖ Regulatory References MARPOL Annex I / Reg 14 Surveys — requirements for IOPP certificate survey and endorsement MARPOL Annex I / Reg 38 Form of IOPP Certificate and Supplement (Appendix II) — Form A and Form B MARPOL Annex I / Reg 15 Control of discharge of oil — 15 ppm bilge water discharge standard Simon Sir typically asks: "What is the difference between Form A and Form B of the IOPP supplement?" Form A = non-tankers; Form B = oil tankers. He may also ask about smart sensors — emphasise IoT + predictive maintenance + UMS context for container vessels.

keywords: VDR Safety Equipment Certificate Number Pages 103–105 SOLAS LSA Survey
section_title: VDR, Safety Equipment Certificate & Equipment Number (Pages 103–105)
text: Safety Equipment Certificate — Supplement Form E Official addendum to the Cargo Ship Safety Equipment Certificate. Key contents: LSA details: lifeboat/liferaft types and capacities, rescue boat specs, lifebuoy/lifejacket/immersion suit inventory, SARTs and EPIRBs. Navigation equipment: magnetic compass, gyrocompass, ECDIS (with backup), radar units, LRIT, VDR/S-VDR, echo sounder. Equipment Number (EN) A dimensionless technical parameter used to determine the mandatory size, weight, and quantity of anchors, chain cables, mooring lines, and towing lines for new ship installations. Found on the classification society's portal or in the Equipment Number Calculation document within the approved Towing and Mooring Arrangement Plan. Voyage Data Recorder (VDR) — SOLAS Chapter V Reg 20 Maritime equivalent of an aircraft "black box." Mandatory on cargo ships ≥ 3,000 GT built on or after 1 July 2002. Data recorded: Date/time, GPS position, speed, heading, bridge audio, radar/AIS captures, echo sounder, engine orders, rudder commands, wind, watertight door status. Primary recording: Continuous loop covering at least 48 hours — older data overwritten. Protected capsule: Retains at least 12 hours of data; withstands fire, impact, and deep-sea pressure. Long-Term Recording Medium: Accessible bridge location; retains at least 30 days (720 hours) . VDR Capsule Types Fixed Capsule: Hardened steel; 48-hour loop; 2-year data retention; fitted with ULB (Underwater Locating Beacon). Float-Free Capsule: HRU + EPIRB integrated; 48-hour loop; 6-month retention. Long-Term Recording Medium: Bridge accessible; 30-day data history. ⚖ Regulatory References SOLAS V / Reg 20 VDR requirements — mandatory for cargo ships ≥ 3,000 GT; S-VDR for existing ships MSC.333(90) Performance standards for VDR — data parameters, capsule specifications, ULB SOLAS III / Reg 4 Surveys of life-saving appliances — Safety Equipment Certificate survey requirements IACS UR A1 Equipment number — anchor and mooring equipment determination criteria Simon Sir typically asks: "How long does a VDR retain data?" — Give all three: 48 hours (primary loop), 12 hours (protected capsule), 30 days (long-term medium). He may also ask about the ULB — it transmits a 37.5 kHz signal to aid capsule location after sinking.

keywords: ARPA Suez Canal Tonnage Flag Duties Pages 106–107 SOLAS Navigation UNCLOS
section_title: ARPA, Suez Canal Tonnage & Flag State Duties (Pages 106–107)
text: ARPA (Automatic Radar Plotting Aid) An automated tracking system integrated into the vessel's radar that automatically processes targets and calculates their true course, speed, CPA (Closest Point of Approach), and TCPA (Time to CPA). Replaces manual plotting to mitigate collision risks. Suez Canal Net Tonnage (SCNT) Derived from the historical Moorsom System's Net Registered Tonnage (NRT) with modifications specific to Suez Canal transit authorities. All canal tariffs, pilotage fees, and dues are based on the Suez Canal Special Tonnage Certificate , issued by recognized classification societies. Flag State Duties (UNCLOS Article 94) Effectively exercise jurisdiction and administrative, technical, and social control over ships flying its flag. Maintain a national ship register . Ensure safety at sea regarding structural construction, equipment standards, and seaworthiness. Safe manning, labour conditions, and crew training in accordance with STCW. Regular structural surveys by qualified surveyors; ensure navigational charts and equipment meet safety criteria. Verify Master, officers, and crew hold appropriate qualifications and are present in required numbers. Ensure crew is conversant with SOLAS, COLREGs, and MARPOL requirements. Conduct official marine casualty investigations involving their flag vessels on the high seas when loss of life, serious injury, or major environmental damage occurs. ⚖ Regulatory References UNCLOS Art. 94 Duties of the Flag State — exclusive jurisdiction and control over ships on the high seas SOLAS V / Reg 19 Carriage requirements for navigational systems including ARPA MSC.116(73) Revised performance standards for gyrocompasses (including radar bearing repeater integration) Simon Sir typically asks: "What are the Flag State's duties under UNCLOS?" — State UNCLOS Article 94 clearly. Key points: maintain register, survey ships, verify STCW compliance, investigate casualties. He may link this to Port State Control — PSC inspects what Flag State is responsible to ensure.

keywords: Coastal Rights DOC Club Correspondent Pages 108–109 UNCLOS SOLAS Commercial
section_title: Coastal State Rights, DG DOC & P&I Club Correspondent (Pages 108–109)
text: Rights and Duties of a Coastal State Regulate marine traffic and enforce navigational safety zones. Maintain visual/electronic navigational aids and offshore installations. Enforce protection over subsea cables and pipelines. Conserve living marine resources within EEZ. Preserve coastal environment — prevent, reduce, and control marine pollution. Issue hydrographic surveys and meteorological warnings. Enforce customs, fiscal, immigration, and sanitary laws without blocking innocent passage of foreign vessels. Dangerous Goods Document of Compliance (DG DOC) Governed under SOLAS Chapter II-2 Reg 19 and Chapter VII. Confirms vessel's construction and machinery comply with requirements for carrying dangerous goods. Schedule 1: Matrix of DG classes approved for carriage and permitted stowage locations. Schedule 2: Physical/structural requirements the vessel must maintain. Validity: Maximum 5 years ; must not extend beyond the Safety Construction Certificate. Role of a P&I Correspondent Local on-scene representative for P&I Clubs — the "eyes and ears" at each port. 24/7 assistance during maritime incidents, collisions, structural failures, emergencies. Handle local claims: crew injuries, repatriation, cargo damage, oil pollution. Coordinate investigations and gather legal evidence. Provide local maritime law and customs expertise. Primary communication link between P&I Club HQ and shipowner/Master. Appoint local legal representation for court proceedings. ⚖ Regulatory References SOLAS II-2 / Reg 19 Special requirements for ships carrying dangerous goods — DG DOC requirements SOLAS VII / Ch A Carriage of dangerous goods in packaged form — IMDG Code compliance UNCLOS Art. 17–26 Right of innocent passage and coastal state enforcement rights in territorial sea Simon Sir typically asks: "What is a DG Doc?" — Emphasise it's issued for 5 years and covers two schedules: what you can carry and where you can carry it. P&I Correspondent is less likely from Simon, but Rajappan or Nair may ask it in a cargo/commercial context.

keywords: Engine Comparison Components Omitted Pages 109–110 Machinery 2-Stroke
section_title: ME vs MC Engine — Comparison & Components Omitted (Pages 109–110)
text: Technical Design Comparison System Component MC Engine (Mechanical) ME Engine (Electronic) Timing Control Mechanical chain drive & camshaft Hydraulic Power Supply (HPS) + ECU Fuel Injection Mechanical fuel pumps & roller guides Electronically regulated fuel pressure boosters Exhaust Valves Mechanical cam actuating profiles Electronic actuation — FIVA / ELFI valves Starting Air Mechanical starting air distributor Electronically controlled solenoid starting valves Speed Governor Mechanical / hydraulic governor Integrated digital governor in ECU software Control Stand Local mechanical maneuvering stand Electronic Local Operating Panel (ELOP) Operational Advantages of ME over MC Efficiency: Precise fuel injection timing and variable exhaust valve operation → lower SFOC across all load profiles. Flexibility: Injection parameters adjustable dynamically for varying fuel qualities (VLSFO, biofuels, methanol) — not possible with fixed mechanical cams. Emissions: Precise combustion control reduces smoke and NOx compared to MC engines. Components Eliminated in ME Engine (vs MC) Chain drive, chain wheel frame, camshaft. Fuel pump cam and roller guide. Exhaust valve cam, fuel pump actuator. Starting air distributor, mechanical governor, mechanical control stand. ⚖ Regulatory References NOx Technical Code 2008 Tier II/III NOx compliance — ME electronic control enables optimised combustion to meet limits MARPOL Annex VI / Reg 13 NOx emission limits — Tier I/II/III thresholds by rpm and build date IRS / MAN B&W Rules Maker's classification rules for ME engine type approval and maintenance intervals Simon Sir's favourite question: "Explain the difference between an ME and MC engine — what is eliminated?" List the 9 components eliminated. Then explain the FIVA (Fuel Injection & Valve Actuation) valve — this is the key component that replaces the camshaft in ME engines. He may ask: "What happens if the hydraulic oil pressure to the HPS fails?" — Safety system activates; engine goes to slow/stop; backup manual ELOP available.

keywords: Port Place Refuge Protocol Request Procedure Pages 110–111 SOLAS ISM Emergency
section_title: Port / Place of Refuge — Protocol & Request Procedure (Pages 110–111)
text: Definition A Port/Place of Refuge (PoR) is a port or sheltered coastal anchorage chosen by a vessel in distress to stabilise her structural condition, ensure crew safety, or prevent environmental pollution hazards. Triggers for Seeking PoR Critical machinery breakdown, fire/explosion, severe structural damage. Cargo shifting, extreme weather, hull damage, progressive flooding. Formal Request Procedure — Form A submitted to: Coastal State Competent Authority. Flag State administration. Vessel's insurance company (P&I Club). Classification Society. The request includes: ship particulars, nature of distress (fire/machinery breakdown/pollution), crew and passenger count, safety measures taken, and pollution/environmental risks. Competent Authority Assessment — Factors Considered Threat to life onboard and risk to public safety. Possibility of oil spill or hazardous cargo pollution. Fire or explosion risk; impact on nearby communities. Validity of the vessel's insurance (P&I Club cover). Master requests PoR │ ▼ Form A submitted to Coastal State / Flag / P&I / Class │ ▼ Competent Authority Assessment │ ┌──┴──┐ ▼ ▼ Approved Rejected │ ▼ Coastal State permits entry ⚖ Regulatory References IMO Res. A.1184(33) Guidelines on places of refuge for ships in need of assistance (2023; revoked A.949(23)) IMO MSC-MEPC.3/Circ.3 Revised guidance on the role of the Competent Authority in evaluating places of refuge UNCLOS Art. 18 Innocent passage — requires coastal states to allow passage of ships in distress ISM Code Sec. 8 Emergency preparedness — DPA and company must be notified in emergency situations Simon Sir typically asks: "What is a port of refuge and what is the procedure?" Give the 4-party notification list: Coastal Authority, Flag State, P&I Club, Classification Society. He may ask: "Who decides if refuge is granted?" — the Coastal State Competent Authority, not the Master or the company.

keywords: Polar Code Requirements Certificate Preparations Pages 111–113 SOLAS Survey
section_title: Polar Code — Requirements, Certificate & CE Preparations (Pages 111–113)
text: Definition & Scope The International Code for Ships Operating in Polar Waters (Polar Code) — mandatory under SOLAS XIV and MARPOL Annexes I, II, IV, V, VI. Covers Arctic and Antarctic waters. Covers: ship design, construction, equipment, operational procedures, training, SAR, and protection of the polar ecosystem. Hazards in Polar Waters Severe weather; poor/unreliable charts; difficult rescue and clean-up operations. Machinery affected by extreme low temperatures; increased hull and propeller loading from ice. Ship Categories (Polar Ship Certificate) Category A: Designed for heavy multi-year ice; can operate year-round in polar conditions. Category B: Less robust — not capable in severe ice; summer operation only. Category C: Designed to operate in open water or low ice concentration. Requirements for Issue of Polar Ship Certificate Risk Assessment: Assessment of anticipated operating conditions and polar hazards. PWOM (Polar Water Operational Manual): Covers ship capabilities, limitations, decision-making, and emergency procedures for owner/operator/Master/crew. Survey: Class survey to verify structural and equipment compliance. CE Preparations Before Entering Polar Waters (key items) Drain fire line and freshwater deck lines to prevent freezing. Check anchor wash valves; start hydraulic pumps well before operation; run winches slowly to warm hydraulic oil. Check accommodation heating coils; verify lifeboat coolant contains antifreeze. Ensure fuel tanks contain winter-grade fuel ; check pour point of lubricating oils. Verify stern tube oil specification for low-temperature operation. Plan alternate sea suction arrangements (change to low suction when ice risk increases). Spread rock salt at gangways, ER entrances, emergency exits, skylight areas, mooring stations. Check bridge window heaters; verify freshwater cooling systems contain antifreeze. Provide adequate winter PPE: gloves, parka, insulated boots, ski goggles. ⚖ Regulatory References SOLAS XIV Safety measures for ships operating in polar waters — Polar Code mandatory under this chapter MARPOL Annexes I/II/IV/V/VI Environmental protection requirements for polar waters (HFO ban, garbage, discharge standards) STCW Reg V/4 Training and certification for officers on ships operating in polar waters MARPOL Annex I / Reg 43A Heavy Fuel Oil ban in Arctic waters — general prohibition from 1 July 2024 Simon Sir typically asks: "What are the CE's preparations before entering polar waters?" — List at minimum 10 from the list above. Critical ones: drain lines, antifreeze in lifeboat/cooling systems, winter-grade fuel, alternate sea suction, stern tube oil check. He may also ask: "What are the three categories of polar ships?"

keywords: Formal Safety Assessment FSA Steps Risk Matrix Page 117 ISM IMO Methodology
section_title: Formal Safety Assessment (FSA) — 5 Steps & Risk Matrix (Page 117)
text: Definition FSA is a structured risk assessment and cost-benefit methodology used by IMO member states, committees, and organisations with consultative status when proposing new or revised maritime regulations. It is a tool — not a regulation itself. Five Steps of FSA 1. Hazard Identification (HAZID) │ Identify and prioritise hazards ▼ 2. Risk Analysis │ Likelihood × Consequence assessment ▼ 3. Risk Control Options │ Formulate risk control measures ▼ 4. Cost–Benefit Assessment │ Does risk reduction outweigh cost? ▼ 5. Recommendations for Decision Making │ Final implementation proposal to IMO Risk Score Formula Risk Score = Likelihood × Consequence Likelihood scale: 1 (Low) → 2 (Medium) → 3 (High). Consequence scale: 1 (Minor) → 2 (Major) → 3 (Catastrophic). Higher scores receive priority for risk control measures. ⚖ Regulatory References IMO MSC-MEPC.2/Circ.12 Revised guidelines for FSA for use in the IMO rule-making process ISM Code Sec. 1.2.3 Safety management objectives — risk assessment as a foundation of ISM culture SOLAS XI-1 / Reg 3 Requirements for enhanced surveys and structural assessment linked to FSA findings Simon Sir typically asks: "What are the 5 steps of FSA?" — State them in order with the acronym: Hazard Identification → Risk Analysis → Risk Control Options → Cost-Benefit → Recommendations. He may ask: "What tool is used in Step 1?" — HAZID (Hazard Identification study).

keywords: Inclining Experiment Conditions Method Formulas Pages 137–138 Stability Survey
section_title: Inclining Experiment — Conditions, Method & Formulas (Pages 137–138)
text: Objective Determines the precise vertical centre of gravity (KG) and baseline metacentric height (GM) of a newly built vessel or one that has undergone major structural modification. Mandatory Conditions Vessel must be structurally complete, upright, and floating in sheltered water — free from wind, waves, tides, or current. All tanks completely empty or completely full — minimise free surface effect. Mooring ropes kept slack; gangway lifted; ship floating freely. Record drafts at 6 points (FP, AP, midships both sides) and measure dock water density. All loose gear secured, bilges pumped dry, cranes/derricks in sea-going position. Non-essential personnel must leave the vessel. Procedure Equal test weights (w) placed away from centreline on both sides of midships deck. Weights must induce a list of 1° to 4° — enough to be measurable, not too large to invalidate. Minimum two pendulums (stabilograph) suspended at maximum vertical distance — bobs submerged in oil or water to dampen oscillation. Weights shifted transversely over distance (d) across 8 separate movements — recording deflections each time. Key Formulas tan θ = Deflection / Pendulum Length GM = (w × d) / (Δ × tan θ) Where: w = weight shifted; d = distance moved; Δ = displacement KG = KM − GM KM taken from hydrostatic tables at measured draft ⚖ Regulatory References SOLAS II-1 / Reg 5 Stability information — inclining experiment required for new ships; results form basis of stability booklet IS Code 2008 / Sec. 7 Procedures for conducting inclining experiments and lightweight checks IMO MSC.1/Circ.1591 Revised guidelines on inclining experiment and lightweight check for ships Simon Sir typically asks: "What are the conditions required for an inclining experiment?" — Give 6 conditions. Then give the formula: GM = (w × d)/(Δ × tanθ). He may ask: "Why must the list be between 1° and 4°?" — Less than 1° is too small to measure accurately; more than 4° invalidates the wall-sided formula assumption.

keywords: Free Surface Effect Angle Loll Tender Stiff Ships Pages 139–141 Stability
section_title: Free Surface Effect, Angle of Loll & Tender vs Stiff Ships (Pages 139–141)
text: Free Surface Effect (FSE) Mechanism: Liquid in a partially filled tank shifts to the low side when the vessel heels → centre of gravity shifts (G → G₁) → reduces righting lever (GZ) → increases effective KG. FSE represents a virtual rise in KG (reduction in effective GM). Mitigation: Subdivide tanks with liquid-tight longitudinal bulkheads, swash plates, or baffles. Formula: Free Surface Moment = ρ × i / Δ , where i = second moment of area of the free surface about its own longitudinal axis. Angle of Loll (AOL) The angle to which an unstable vessel (negative initial GM) will heel under environmental forces. At this angle, GZ = 0 and B₁ is directly below G — temporary neutral equilibrium. Behaviour: Vessel lists to AOL — if heeled further in same direction, a transient positive GM pushes back to AOL. If heeled to the other side, vessel lolls aggressively. Causes: Improper ballasting, top-heavy cargo, emptying low DB tanks, structural errors, excessive FSE. CORRECT remedy: Ballast low DB tanks first (to lower G) — do NOT use transverse weight shifting (extremely dangerous). Tender vs Stiff Ships Feature Tender Ship (small GM) Stiff Ship (large GM) Cause Heavy topside weights → G raised Heavy low weights → G lowered Rolling period ≈ 30–35 seconds (slow, comfortable) ≈ 15–18 seconds (fast, violent) Risk Easy to incline, slow to recover Violent snapping motion — structural stress Remedy Lower heavy weights to DB tanks Raise weights to increase rolling period ⚖ Regulatory References IS Code 2008 / Part A Reg 2.3 Stability criteria — FSE correction mandatory in all GM calculations IS Code 2008 / Sec. 2.2.3 Angle of loll — vessel with negative GM, stability at angles of inclination SOLAS II-1 / Reg 22 Damage stability — residual stability requirements with FSE included Simon Sir typically asks: "What is free surface effect?" — Virtual rise in G due to liquid shift in partially filled tanks. "What is angle of loll and how do you correct it?" — Loll = neutral equilibrium when GM is zero due to initial negative GM; correct by ballasting DB tanks (never use cranes). Tender (30–35 s) vs stiff (15–18 s) rolling periods are oral exam standards.

keywords: Competency Proficiency Audit Survey Pages 117–118 STCW ISM
section_title: Competency vs Proficiency & Audit vs Survey (Pages 117–118)
text: Competency vs Proficiency Feature Competency Proficiency Scope Holistic ability to perform all duties of a specific rank Mastery of a specific skill or task Certificate Certificate of Competency (CoC) Certificate of Proficiency (CoP) Elements Sea time + education + examination Targeted training + assessment Examples Chief Engineer, Master Mariner Firefighting, Medical First Aid, STS, SDSD, tanker familiarisation Audit vs Survey Criteria Audit Survey Timeline Focus Past activities — detect systemic faults Future — ensure vessel stays seaworthy until next survey Target Documentation, procedures, SMS, forms Physical product — machinery, equipment, structure Method Sampling basis — cannot audit entire system at once Entire system evaluated (full scope) Outcome Non-conformities (NCs) and recommendations Issue, endorse, or renew statutory/class certificates ⚖ Regulatory References STCW Reg I/2 Certificates of Competency — minimum standards, format, and endorsement STCW Reg VI/1–VI/3 Basic safety training — Certificates of Proficiency for firefighting, medical, survival ISM Code Sec. 12 Company verification, review and evaluation — audit requirements under ISM SOLAS I / Reg 6 Inspection and survey of ships — initial, annual, intermediate, renewal surveys Simon Sir typically asks: "What is the difference between a competency and a proficiency?" — Key: Competency = CoC = rank eligibility; Proficiency = CoP = specific task (firefighting, SDSD). He may also ask: "What is the difference between an audit and a survey?" — Audit = past/documentation/sampling; Survey = future/physical/full scope.

keywords: Certificate Class Statutory Certificates Shipping Pages 118–119 ISM Survey IACS
section_title: Certificate of Class vs Statutory Certificates & AR/VR in Shipping (Pages 118–119)
text: Certificate of Class Mandatory but NOT statutory — required commercially, not by a convention directly. Issued by a Classification Society confirming compliance with Class Rules for design, construction, and maintenance. Required for: P&I Club coverage, Hull & Machinery insurance, charter party commitments. Statutory Certificates Issued by the Flag Administration or Recognised Organisation (RO) acting on its behalf. Confirms compliance with international conventions (SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, MLC). Legal requirement for global trade — cannot operate commercially without them. AR vs VR in Shipping AR (Augmented Reality): Overlays digital information onto the real world — uses smartphones, tablets, or smart glasses. Example: Wärtsilä AR system where seafarers receive live shore-based repair instructions on a see-through display during stern tube maintenance. VR (Virtual Reality): Creates a completely artificial simulated environment — requires VR headsets. Used for engine room emergency drills, stability training, enclosed space rescue simulation. ⚖ Regulatory References SOLAS I / Reg 6 Survey and certification — flag state or RO statutory certification obligations IMO RO Code (Res. A.739(18)) Recognition of organisations acting on behalf of the Administration — RO authorisation IACS PR 1 IACS procedure for condition of class — classification survey standards Simon Sir typically asks: "What is the difference between a Class certificate and a statutory certificate?" — Class = society-issued, mandatory for insurance/charter; Statutory = administration/RO-issued, legally required by convention. AR question likely from Srivastava; Simon may ask as a technology update question.

keywords: COP-29 Key Outcomes Latest MARPOL Amendments Pages 119–120 GHG
section_title: COP-29 Key Outcomes & Latest MARPOL Amendments (Pages 119–120)
