text: COP-29 — Key Takeaways (Baku, Azerbaijan, Nov 2024) NCQG (New Collective Quantified Goal): Replaced the historic $100 billion annual climate finance target. Designed to reflect actual financial needs of developing nations. Global Carbon Market: Agreement reached on UN-backed global carbon trading rules under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Finance Target: Discussions around tripling climate finance to $300 billion — notable disagreements between developing nations on implementation remained. MARPOL Annex VI — Latest Amendments Mediterranean Sea ECA (SOx): Designated as an Emission Control Area for SOx and PM — effective 1 May 2025 . Max sulphur content 0.10% in ECA. BDN Flash Point: Bunker Delivery Note must now include the measured flash point or a declaration confirming flash point ≥ 70°C (SOLAS requirement). EEXI and CII: Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index and Carbon Intensity Indicator regulations now in force under Annex VI. MARPOL Annex I — Latest Amendments HFO Arctic Ban: Carriage and use of Heavy Fuel Oil in Arctic waters prohibited from 1 July 2024 (with certain flag state exemptions for coastal state vessels). IOPP Certificate simplification: Administrative changes for ships flying non-party flags. Form B Simplification: Simplified completion for Supplement Form B — entries relating to SBT, protective location, double hull, and dedicated clean ballast tanks. ⚖ Regulatory References MARPOL Annex VI / Reg 14 Sulphur oxide (SOx) control — 0.5% global cap; 0.1% in ECAs; Mediterranean ECA from May 2025 MARPOL Annex VI / Reg 28 Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) — operational rating system A–E, annual reporting MARPOL Annex I / Reg 43A Prohibition on carriage and use of HFO as fuel in Arctic waters from 1 July 2024 MEPC.338(76) Guidelines on operational carbon intensity rating of ships — CII rating guidelines Simon Sir typically asks: "What is the latest ECA added under MARPOL Annex VI?" — Mediterranean Sea, effective 1 May 2025. He may ask about the HFO ban in Arctic waters — effective 1 July 2024. BDN flash point amendment is an examiner favourite for Chief Engineer orals on Maersk container vessels bunkering VLSFO.

keywords: Casualty Investigator GESAMP AMS Ballast Water Page 121 ISM MARPOL Survey
section_title: Casualty Investigator, GESAMP & AMS — Ballast Water (Page 121)
text: Marine Casualty Investigator Qualifications (MS Act S.359) Academic: M.Sc. in Maritime Affairs from World Maritime University (WMU), Malmö, Sweden. Field training: Casualty investigation training at WMU. Practical experience: Under Part XI (Investigation of Marine Incidents), Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 — in force 15 March 2026, formerly Section 359 of the repealed 1958 Act — complete at least one Preliminary Inquiry under an approved experienced investigator. CPD: Periodic refresher training in advanced casualty investigation techniques. GESAMP — Joint Group of Experts Stands for: Joint Group of Experts on the Scientific Aspects of Marine Environmental Protection . Established: 1969 . Jointly sponsored by 10 UN organisations including IMO. Function: Conducts studies and reviews on marine environmental protection — advises the UN system. EHS Working Group: Evaluates environmental hazards of harmful substances carried by ships — provides technical advice directly to IMO. Alternate Management Systems (AMS) — USCG Definition: A Ballast Water Treatment System (BWTS) type-approved by a foreign Administration but not yet USCG-approved . USCG allows temporary use in US waters while the system undergoes formal USCG type-approval testing. Validity window: Maximum 5 years . ⚖ Regulatory References Merchant Shipping Act, 2025, Part XI Preliminary inquiry — qualification and appointment of marine casualty investigators in India; in force 15 March 2026 (formerly Sec 359 of the repealed 1958 Act) Casualty Investigation Code (Res. A.849(20)) Code for the investigation of marine casualties and incidents — international framework BWM Convention Reg D-3 Type approval of BWTS using active substances — GESAMP BWWG evaluation required USCG 33 CFR Part 151 AMS provisions — allows IMO-approved systems in US waters during USCG evaluation period Simon Sir typically asks: "What is GESAMP?" — Give the full form, 1969 establishment, 10 UN bodies, and EHS Working Group. AMS and USCG 5-year window is more likely from Nair or Srivastava given its regulatory complexity. Casualty investigator qualifications are a Kochi MMD examiner favourite — S.359 is the key section number.

keywords: Maritime Zones Act 1976 BDN Bunker Calculations Pages 126–127 MARPOL Commercial
section_title: Maritime Zones Act 1976, BDN & Bunker Calculations (Pages 126–127)
text: Maritime Zones Act 1976 (India) Official title: The Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone, and Other Maritime Zones Act 1976. Defines India's maritime boundaries and sovereign rights — aligned with UNCLOS. Protects marine resources and regulates fishing, oil exploration, and shipping in Indian maritime zones. Bunker Delivery Note (BDN) — MARPOL Annex VI Reg 18 Official legal record of a fuel transfer between bunker supplier and receiving vessel. Mandatory contents: Vessel name, IMO number, port, delivery date, supplier details, quantity/volume, fuel type (VLSFO/ULSFO/MGO), density, kinematic viscosity, sulphur content %, and seal numbers of collected fuel samples. Signatures: Must be signed and stamped by both Chief Engineer and bunker barge representative . Retention: BDN retained onboard for minimum 3 years ; fuel sample retained for minimum 12 months . NEW: BDN must now include measured flash point or declaration that flash point ≥ 70°C. CE Decision-Making Hierarchy Safety of Life & Ship (First priority) │ ▼ Regulatory Compliance (SOLAS · MARPOL · Flag State) │ ▼ Company SMS │ ▼ Risk Assessment → Best Course of Action Volumetric-to-Mass Bunker Calculations Fuel ordered in MT but delivered in m³ — must correct for temperature and density. V₁₅ = Vt × [1 − α(T − 15)] Where: Vt = observed volume; α = expansion coefficient; T = fuel temp (°C) HFO: α = 0.00065/°C | MGO: α = 0.00085/°C Mass (MT) = V₁₅ × ρ₁₅ (density at 15°C in t/m³) Always apply: temperature correction, trim correction, and list correction before accepting BDN quantity. ⚖ Regulatory References MARPOL Annex VI / Reg 18 Fuel oil availability and quality — BDN mandatory; sample retention 12 months; BDN retention 3 years MARPOL Annex VI / Reg 14 SOx control — BDN sulphur content must demonstrate compliance with applicable limits ISO 8217:2024 Marine fuel oil specification — density, viscosity, flash point, and sulphur content standards Simon Sir typically asks: "What is a BDN and what does it contain?" — Give the 3-year retention for BDN and 12-month for sample — these are the most tested figures. The volumetric correction formula is a CE-level exam staple. Know HFO coefficient (0.00065) vs MGO (0.00085).

keywords: Documents Classification Flag State–RO Delegation Pages 127–128 Survey IACS ISM
section_title: Ship Documents, Classification & Flag State–RO Delegation (Pages 127–128)
text: Instrument of Sale vs Builder's Certificate Feature Instrument of Sale (Bill of Sale) Builder's Certificate Applicability New-build AND second-hand vessel transfers Issued exclusively for new-build vessels only Issued by Current legal shipowner Shipyard (construction yard) Primary use Ship registration under new owner after sale First-time vessel registration and initial hull insurance Contents Transaction details, title transfer, ownership covenants Builder ID, construction date, technical specifications Why Classification is Important A vessel requires Class throughout its service life to demonstrate structural and machinery compliance with Class Rules. Required for: Design approval and construction supervision. P&I Club and H&M insurance coverage. Charter party terms. Technical support and statutory compliance. Periodic surveys to confirm continued seaworthiness. Flag State Delegation to RO — Process Step 1 — Application: Organisation applies to become an RO under the IMO RO Code. Step 2 — Credential Verification: Flag State audits technical credentials and capabilities. Step 3 — MoU: Memorandum of Understanding signed defining scope, limitations, and oversight programme. Step 4 — Validity: Instructions on duration and periodic renewal of delegated authority. ⚖ Regulatory References IMO Res. A.739(18) Guidelines for authorisation of organisations acting on behalf of the Administration (RO Code) IMO RO Code (Res. MSC.349(92)) Mandatory RO Code — requirements for recognised organisations' technical competence SOLAS I / Reg 6 Surveys — Administration may entrust surveys to inspectors or ROs Simon Sir typically asks: "What is a Builder's Certificate?" — New-build only, from the shipyard, used for first registration. The RO delegation process (MoU, IMO RO Code) is a Nair/Srivastava question. Know the 4-step process clearly — it appears in commercial law orals.

keywords: Load Line Survey SAFCON Act 1958 Structure Pages 128–130 SOLAS
section_title: Load Line Survey, SAFCON Survey & MS Act 2025 Structure (Pages 128–130)
text: Load Line Survey Protocol Certificate validity: International Load Line Certificate valid for maximum 5 years . Mandatory documents: Trim and Stability Booklet, Loading Manual, Record of Conditions of Assignment, Cargo Loading Indicator Type-Approval Certificate, Bow Height Certificate. Inspection checklist: Freeboard marks, draft marks, vent heads/flame screens, scuppers and freeing ports, weathertight doors, guard rails, gangway condition, machinery space openings, overboard valves, bilge pumps, emergency bilge suction, sounding pipes. SAFCON Survey — Practical Examination Steps Anchoring equipment → Collision bulkhead → Watertight doors (local & remote) → Bilge system → Main engine remote stops → Steam piping insulation → Standby machinery auto-start → Engineers' alarm → Electrical insulation (megger) → Emergency power (generator/batteries) → Review previous survey memoranda Merchant Shipping (MS) Act 1958 — Structure (historical — replaced by the MS Act 2025, in force 15 March 2026, except Part XIV) 18 Parts, 460 Sections. Key sections for CEOs (1958 numbering, for legacy reference; the current Act is the MS Act 2025 — 16 Parts, 325 sections) : Section 334: Unseaworthy ships — detention provisions. Section 336: Owner's obligation — duty to ensure vessel safety. Section 359: Preliminary inquiry — appointment of marine casualty investigators. Section 360: Formal investigation — judicial courts. Part VII (Sec. 95): Relief and Repatriation of Seamen (RPS). Part IX: Safety — covers LSA Code and FSS Code. ⚖ Regulatory References LL Convention 1966 / Art. 14 Surveys — initial, annual, and renewal survey requirements for Load Line Certificate SOLAS I / Reg 10 Maintenance of conditions after survey — SAFCON continuous obligations Merchant Shipping Act, 2025, Part XI Preliminary inquiry and formal investigation of marine casualties under Indian law; in force 15 March 2026 (formerly Sec 359–360 of the repealed 1958 Act) Simon Sir typically asks: "What do you check during a SAFCON survey?" — Give the 10-step sequence. Key MS Act sections: 334 (unseaworthy), 336 (owner's duty), 359 (preliminary inquiry), 360 (formal investigation). Load Line Certificate: 5-year validity with annual endorsements.

keywords: Parametric Rolling Synchronous Container Risk Pages 136–137 Stability
section_title: Parametric Rolling & Synchronous Rolling — Container Ship Risk (Pages 136–137)
text: Parametric Rolling Occurs on modern vessels with fine bow lines and wide transom sterns when wave length matches ship length and waves encounter the vessel from ahead or astern. Core condition: Pitching period = rolling period, OR pitching period = ½ rolling period . Mechanism: As vessel pitches, submerged hull area forward and aft changes dynamically → shifting centre of buoyancy → oscillating rolling moment. Vessel behaviour: Alternates between: — Wave crest under midship → waterplane narrows → lower GM → tender condition. — Wave trough under midship → wider waterplane → higher GM → stiff condition. Hazards: Severe structural stress, stack failures, loss of containers overboard, risk of capsizing. Corrective action: Immediate alteration of course and speed . Synchronous Rolling Definition: Resonance phenomenon when the vessel's natural rolling period matches the wave encounter period . Hazards: Heavy water on deck, cargo shifting, loss of stability, capsizing. Corrective action: Change course, change speed, or ballast to alter the rolling period. ⚖ Regulatory References IS Code 2008 / Part B Guidance for dynamic stability — parametric rolling and pure loss of stability scenarios IMO MSC.1/Circ.1228 Revised guidance on avoiding dangerous situations in adverse weather and sea conditions SOLAS VI / Reg 5-2 Container securing — lashing requirements to resist parametric roll-induced forces Simon Sir typically asks: "What is parametric rolling and how do you correct it?" — Explain the pitching = ½ rolling period condition; the tender-stiff alternation; and that course and speed change is the immediate corrective action. As a Maersk container ship 2/E, this is directly relevant — know it thoroughly.

keywords: CO₂ System Properties Pressure Testing Measurement Methods Pages 151–152 Fire SOLAS
section_title: CO₂ System — Properties, Pressure Testing & Measurement Methods (Pages 151–152)
text: Physical Properties of CO₂ Critical Temperature: 31.1°C — above this, CO₂ cannot be liquefied regardless of pressure. Critical Pressure: 75 bar — pressure needed to liquefy at critical temperature. Bottle pressure: 56 bar at 20°C; 64 bar at 25°C; 71 bar at 30°C — room temperature must be kept below 55°C. Specific free gas volume: 0.56 m³/kg at 21.1°C and 1 bar. Pressure Testing of CO₂ Flooding System Lines Line Section Test Medium Test Pressure Cylinder to Master Valve Liquid (hydraulic) 190 bar Master Valve to ER/Cargo Hold Valve Liquid (hydraulic) 80 bar ER/Cargo Hold Valve to Nozzles Air blowing test 6–7 bar Pilot Control Line (copper tube) Burst test 56 bar CO₂ Bottle Stamping Requirements Manufacturer name, official stamp, serial number, tare weight (empty bottle weight), test pressure, and hydrostatic test date. CO₂ Quantity Measurement Methods Beam scale (physical weighing). Thermal strip indicators. Infrared (IR) camera. Ultrasonic liquid level indicator. Radioactive isotope liquid level gauge. Hydrostatic pressure testing history. Capacity Requirements Machinery space (excl. casing): CO₂ = 40% of gross volume. Machinery space (incl. casing): CO₂ = 35% of gross volume. Cargo hold: CO₂ = 30% of gross volume of largest cargo hold. Discharge requirement: 50% within 1 minute; 85% within 2 minutes . ⚖ Regulatory References FSS Code Ch. 5 Fixed CO₂ fire extinguishing systems — capacity, discharge rate, room regulations SOLAS II-2 / Reg 10 Fire-fighting systems — fixed CO₂ installation requirements for machinery spaces IRS / DNV Rules Class rules for CO₂ system installation, bottle pressure testing intervals Simon Sir typically asks: "What pressure is the CO₂ line tested to?" — Give all three sections: 190 bar (cylinder to master valve), 80 bar (master valve to ER valve), 6–7 bar air blow (nozzle section). He will ask about capacity — know 40%/35%/30% by heart. Pilot line is copper — he may ask why (corrosion resistance, flexibility, ease of installation).

keywords: Container Marking ISO 6346 Identification Large Problems Pages 169–170 SOLAS
section_title: Container Marking (ISO 6346), Identification & Large Ship Problems (Pages 169–170)
text: Container Marking Structure (ISO 6346) Owner's Prefix: 3 capital letters (owner/operator). Equipment Category Identifier: 1 capital letter: U = All freight containers. J = Detachable freight container-related equipment. Z = Trailers and chassis carrying storage containers. Serial Number: 6-digit unique number within owner's fleet. Check Digit: Single digit validating accuracy of prefix and serial number. Problems Associated with Large Container Ships Stacking of light containers & Windage: Large above-deck container stacks catch wind — reduces manoeuvrability (e.g., Ever Given grounding, Suez Canal 2021). Torsional forces & Parametric Rolling: G-forces during pitch and roll cause container stack failures and loss overboard. Infrastructure demands: Massive capital investment required (e.g., Panama Canal expansion 2016 = $5 billion). Prototype Tests on Containers (carried out regardless of single or series build) Dimension check; Lifting test (top corner, bottom corner, forklift). Stacking test; Concentrated load on roof and floor. Transverse racking test; Longitudinal restraint test. Endwall and sidewall test; Door operation test. Cargo securing device test; Weather tightness test. ⚖ Regulatory References ISO 6346 Container coding, identification, and marking — owner prefix, equipment identifier, serial, check digit CSC Convention 1972 Prototype testing requirements for new container designs and series production SOLAS VI / Reg 5-1 Container weight verification — VGM mandatory before loading since 2016 Simon Sir typically asks: "What are the prototype tests for containers?" — List all 9+ tests; emphasise they apply irrespective of whether a single container or a series is built . He may ask about windage on large container ships — direct link to the Ever Given. Know container ID structure: 3+1+6+1 (XXXU-123456-7).

keywords: Container Logistics VGM Reefer PTI New Regulations Pages 171–174 SOLAS
section_title: Container Logistics, VGM, Reefer PTI & New Regulations (Pages 171–174)
text: Key Logistics Definitions Liner Trade: Fixed routes, strict schedules, published timetables — predictable for exporters/importers. SOC: Shipper Owned Container; COC: Carrier Owned Container (negotiated under NVOCC). ICD (Inland Container Depot): Inland site where shipping and customs clearance for containerised cargo can be processed. CFS (Container Freight Station): Physical extension of the port for temporary storage. VGM — Verified Gross Mass (SOLAS Ch. VI, from 2016) Shippers must declare the actual weight before loading. Without VGM, container is denied loading . Method 1: Direct weighing on a certified weighbridge — VGM = total weight of packed, sealed container. Method 2: Calculated — VGM = Σ(individual package weights + dunnage/securing materials) + container tare weight. Weighing equipment must meet National Certification and Calibration requirements (India: Legal Metrology Dept). Reefer Container PTI (Pre-Trip Inspection) Functional check on empty refrigerated container before release to shipper. Valid PTI certificate: 30 to 180 days (varies by carrier). Checklist: cooling unit, temperature recording device, structural integrity, cleaning, connection to main control module. New Container Ship Regulations (2026) Electronic Inclinometers: Mandatory from January 2026 for container ships and bulk carriers > 7,000 GT. Mandatory Reporting of Lost Containers: Strictly mandatory from January 2026 . Fire Fighting for Containers (Post-2016 ships) At least one water mist lance for container fires in open spaces. Two water monitors if ship beam ≤ 30 m; four monitors if beam > 30 m. Thermal imaging camera mandatory. ⚖ Regulatory References SOLAS VI / Reg 2 VGM — Verified Gross Mass; shippers must verify and provide weight before loading; mandatory from 2016 SOLAS II-2 / Reg 10.10 Portable monitors and water mist lances for fighting fires in cargo areas MSC.380(94) Amendments to SOLAS VI Regulation 2 — VGM provision, responsibilities of shippers and masters Simon Sir / Rajappan typically ask: "What is VGM and what are the two methods?" — Method 1 = certified weighbridge; Method 2 = calculated sum + tare weight. Both methods require certified/calibrated equipment. 2026 regulations (inclinometers + lost container reporting) are current affairs hot topics for container vessel orals at Kochi MMD.

keywords: CO₂ Room Regulations Maintenance Schedule Certificates Pages 146–150 Fire SOLAS
section_title: CO₂ Room Regulations, Maintenance Schedule & Certificates (Pages 146–150)
text: CO₂ Room Regulations (FSS Code Ch. 5) Must not be used for any other purpose; located aft of the collision bulkhead . Access doors must open outward ; room must be gas-tight. Access directly possible from the open deck . Room temperature must be maintained below 55°C . Exhaust duct of mechanical ventilation routed to the bottom of the space (CO₂ is 1.5× heavier than air). Minimum 6 air changes per hour ; minimum clear height: 2,000 mm. Must not be located lower than one deck below the open deck if below deck. CO₂ System Maintenance Schedule Interval Key Tasks Monthly Open control cabinet — test audible/visual alarms, ventilation cut-off. Check room ventilation fan. Verify cylinders properly clamped. Check operating levers and flexible hoses. Yearly All monthly checks + blow through distribution pipes with service air + check general physical condition of installation. 2-Yearly (Biennial) All yearly checks + weigh CO₂ bottles (max 10% content reduction per cylinder allowed) + blow pipes at 6–7 bar service air. 5-Yearly All previous + uncouple all main bottles. Open one pilot bottle and test time delay unit, master valve auto-open, and high-pressure leak alarm. Check manifold relief valve lifts at 180 bar. Pressure test isolated piping sections at 25 bar air . 10-Yearly Renew all flexible hoses. Internal inspection of bottles (check dip tubes). Hydrostatic test at 250 bar — test 10% of bottles; if any fail → test 50%; if more fail → test 100%. After 20 years of age: hydrostatic test every 5 years . Required Certificates Installation Certificate. Shore maintenance/weighing certificate ( every 2 years ). Bottle pressure test certificate ( every 10 years ; every 5 years after 20 years of age). ⚖ Regulatory References FSS Code Ch. 5 / Sec. 2.2.5 CO₂ room location, construction, and ventilation requirements MSC.1/Circ.1318 Revised guidelines for maintenance and inspection of fixed CO₂ fire-extinguishing systems SOLAS II-2 / Reg 14 Operational readiness, maintenance and inspections of fire protection systems Simon Sir's most-tested CO₂ question: "What is the 10-yearly maintenance of the CO₂ system?" — Renew flexible hoses, internal bottle inspection, hydrostatic test at 250 bar, test 10%/50%/100% batch rule. He will also ask: "Why is the ventilation exhaust at the bottom of the CO₂ room?" — CO₂ is 1.5× heavier than air → sinks → must be extracted from the bottom to prevent accumulation.

keywords: TQM Total Quality Management Shipping Pages 152–153 ISM
section_title: TQM — Total Quality Management in Shipping (Pages 152–153)
text: Definition TQM is a comprehensive management philosophy seeking to continually improve products, services, and processes through quality focus and the active involvement of all employees. Quality is not a single department's responsibility — it is a collective effort. 8 Principles of TQM 1. Customer Focus: Align strategy to meet and exceed customer expectations. 2. Continuous Improvement (Kaizen): Ongoing structured efforts to improve processes. 3. Employee Involvement: Every employee participates in quality improvement. 4. Process-Centred Approach: Identify hidden inefficiencies through systematic workflows. 5. Integrated System: All departments work seamlessly toward quality objectives. 6. Fact-Based Decision Making: Decisions based on empirical data, not intuition. 7. Strategic & Systematic Approach: TQM aligned with organisation's long-term goals. 8. Communication: Open channels ensuring everyone understands their role in quality. TQM Aims in Shipping Operations Zero Cargo Claims; Zero Lost Time Incidents (LTI). Zero Detentions or PSC deficiencies. Minimum operating costs; no MARPOL fines. No major Non-Conformities (NC) under the ISM Code. Safe, high-efficiency cargo turnaround. ⚖ Regulatory References ISO 9001:2015 Quality Management Systems — High Level Structure (HLS) enabling integration with ISM, OHSAS, ISO 14001 ISM Code Sec. 11 Documentation requirements — SMS documentation as part of integrated quality management ISO 14001:2015 Environmental Management Systems — integrated with TQM for shipping environmental compliance Simon Sir typically asks: "What is TQM and what are its principles?" — Give all 8 principles with "Kaizen" for principle 2. He may link it to ISO 9001:2015 — know that the HLS (High Level Structure) of 2015 allows integration of Quality + Safety + Environmental + Energy management systems into one IMS.

keywords: GISIS FAL Convention Standardised Forms Pages 154–155 Survey Commercial
section_title: GISIS, FAL Convention & Standardised FAL Forms (Pages 154–155)
text: GISIS — Global Integrated Shipping Information System IMO's centralised online platform collecting, processing, storing, and sharing regulatory and operational data on global shipping and maritime safety. Used for ship surveys, port state inspections, flag state data. FAL Convention (1965 / EIF March 1967) Facilitates international maritime traffic by streamlining administrative formalities, port procedures, and documentary requirements for ships arriving at, staying in, and departing from international ports. Prevent unnecessary delays: Reduce bureaucratic paperwork and time in international maritime traffic. Standardised documentation: Promote global standardisation of clearance documents. Maritime Single Window (MSW): Mandatory from 1 January 2024 — electronic exchange between ships and ports mandatory. Standardised FAL Forms Form Document Name FAL Form 1 General Declaration (vessel particulars, voyage info, dimensions) FAL Form 2 Cargo Declaration FAL Form 3 Ship's Stores Declaration FAL Form 4 Crew's Effects Declaration FAL Form 5 Crew List FAL Form 6 Passenger List (if applicable) FAL Form 7 Dangerous Goods Manifest ⚖ Regulatory References FAL Convention 1965 Convention on Facilitation of International Maritime Traffic — standardised port entry/exit documentation FAL.6(18) / FAL.8(34) Amendments to FAL Convention — revised standardised forms; MSW mandatory from Jan 2024 SOLAS XI-2 / Reg 9.2.2 ISPS pre-arrival security information — required in addition to FAL forms Simon Sir typically asks: "What is the FAL Convention?" — 1965, facilitates international maritime traffic, standardises documents. Know the 7 FAL forms by name and number. MSW mandatory from 1 January 2024 is a current hot topic. He may ask: "What is GISIS?" — IMO's centralised maritime information platform.

keywords: Maritime Single Window IRS Electronic Certificates Pages 156–157 Survey IACS
section_title: Maritime Single Window & IRS Electronic Certificates (Pages 156–157)
text: Maritime Single Window (MSW) A unified digital platform for rapid exchange of electronic information between ships, port authorities, customs, immigration, and shipping companies — mandatory from 1 January 2024 under FAL Convention amendments. Single point of entry: All regulatory data submitted through one portal — eliminates repetitive paperwork to multiple government authorities. India — SWIFT: Single Window Interface for Facilitating Trade + NLP-Marine (National Logistics Portal Marine). Singapore — NSW: National Single Window. IRS Electronic Certificates IRS implemented e-certificates from July 2018 for all vessels classed under IRS. All statutory and class certificates issued as E-Certificates — digitally signed with a Unique Tracking Number (UTN) for online verification. Initially not extended to passenger ships; requires MoU between Flag State and RO. Advantages of Electronic Certificates Rapid delivery onboard — no physical mailing. Easy document management — no bulky paper folders. No risk of physical document loss, theft, or deterioration. Cyber security must be integrated into ship's SMS (audited during DOC/SMC renewal). ⚖ Regulatory References FAL.6(18) Amendments to FAL Convention — electronic exchange of information mandatory from April 2019 MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3 Guidelines on Maritime Cyber Risk Management MSC-FAL.1/Circ.8 Guidelines for setting up and operating a Maritime Single Window Simon Sir typically asks: "What is the Maritime Single Window?" — Unified digital port clearance platform; mandatory from 1 January 2024. IRS e-certificate from July 2018 with UTN is a current affairs question. He may ask: "What is a UTN?" — Unique Tracking Number on e-certificates for instant online authenticity verification.

keywords: Five Categories Maritime Liens True Lien Pages 158–159 Commercial Admiralty
section_title: Five Categories of Maritime Liens & True Maritime Lien (Pages 158–159)
text: Five Categories of Maritime Liens 1. Maritime Lien (True): Attaches to crew wages, salvage, or physical damage caused by ship's action. 2. Statutory Lien: Government/statutory bodies for port charges, customs dues. Valid for 6 months (60 days after sale of vessel, whichever is earlier). 3. Possessory Lien: Arises while holding physical possession — ship repair yard, ship chandler claims. Lost if possession is surrendered. 4. Contractual Lien: Established via express contract terms — shipowner's lien on cargo for unpaid freight. 5. Judicial Lien: Generated by court order — attachment lien, execution lien. Maritime lien can attach only to: The Ship, The Cargo, or The Freight. True Maritime Lien — Key Characteristics Privileged claim: Priority over ship mortgages, possessory liens, and statutory rights in rem. Secret and indelible: Travels with the property even if the vessel is sold — invisible, not registered in any public registry. Accrues automatically at the moment of the event giving rise to the cause of action. Enforcement: By Action in Rem — the ship (res) is physically arrested by the Admiralty Court and may be sold to satisfy creditors. Legal Glossary Res: Latin for "thing" — the maritime property (ship, cargo, freight). Action in Rem: Legal action directed against the property itself. Action in Personam: Legal action against a person, company, or entity. Pari Passu: Claims of the same class rank equally — proceeds shared proportionately. ⚖ Regulatory References Admiralty Act 2017 (India) Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act — replaces archaic British admiralty statutes Admiralty Act 2017 / Sec. 9 Maritime liens — priority, nature, enforcement, and expiry provisions UNCLOS Art. 113–114 Damage by submarine cables/pipelines — liability provisions relevant to maritime claims Simon Sir (or Rajappan/Nair) typically asks: "What are the types of maritime liens?" — Give all 5 types. Key distinction: True maritime lien = secret + indelible + travels with ship even after sale. Statutory lien expires in 6 months. Possessory lien is lost if possession is surrendered. "Pari Passu" = equal ranking within the same class — must know the Latin term.

keywords: Priority Maritime Liens Admiralty Act 2017 Pages 160–162 Commercial
section_title: Priority of Maritime Liens & Admiralty Act 2017 (Pages 160–162)
text: Common True Maritime Lien Claims (in rank order) Salvage claims. Crew wages and Master's disbursements. Damage done by a ship (collision claims). Bottomry and Respondentia bonds. Bottomry Bond: Ship pledged as collateral by the Master to secure emergency funds. Respondentia Bond: Cargo pledged as collateral. Priority Rule — "Last in Time, First in Right" Last in Time, First in Right (Most recent lien preserving the vessel takes precedence) Salvage claims: ranked in inverse chronological order — latest salvage operation has highest priority. Liens of the same class: rank Pari Passu (equal, proportional payment). Admiralty Act 2017 (India) — Key Provisions Maritime lien continues even if vessel changes ownership, registration, or flag. General maritime lien expiry: 1 year unless the vessel is seized and sold by the High Court. Wage-related claims: 2 years from date claim becomes due (wages, repatriation, contractual sums). Statutory lien: 6 months ; 60 days after sale, whichever expires first. Admiralty Assessor Rules 2018 — Qualifications MEO Class 1 Engineer. Sea experience including 5+ years in survey and inspection of merchant ships; at least 1 year as CE or 2E . Appeal: Plaintiff may approach the Supreme Court of India. ⚖ Regulatory References Admiralty Act 2017 / Sec. 9–10 Maritime liens — rank, priority, and duration of various categories of maritime claims Admiralty Act 2017 / Sec. 22 Inter se priority — ranking of maritime liens of the same and different classes Admiralty Assessors Rules 2018 Qualifications and appointment of Admiralty Assessors in Indian High Courts Key exam points: "Last in Time, First in Right" principle for maritime liens of different classes. "Pari Passu" for same class. Duration: 1 year (general), 2 years (wages), 6 months (statutory). Admiralty Assessor: MEO Class 1 + 5 years survey experience — this is directly relevant to your career path.

keywords: UNCLOS Maritime Zones EEZ International Seabed Authority Pages 163–166 Commercial
section_title: UNCLOS Maritime Zones, EEZ & International Seabed Authority (Pages 163–166)
text: UNCLOS III (1982) — Maritime Zones Baseline ├─ Territorial Sea (TS): up to 12 NM ├─ Contiguous Zone: up to 24 NM ├─ Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ): up to 200 NM (excl. TS) └─ Continental Shelf: to outer continental margin Max: 350 NM from baseline OR 100 NM seaward of the 2,500m isobath (whichever is further) Area Beyond National Jurisdiction (ABNJ): beyond all the above Key UNCLOS Articles Art. 33: Contiguous Zone — coastal state may enforce customs, fiscal, immigration, sanitary laws. Art. 56: EEZ rights — sovereign rights to exploit natural resources; jurisdiction over artificial islands, marine research, environment protection. Art. 77: Continental shelf — sovereign rights for exploring and exploiting natural resources. Art. 192: General obligation to protect and preserve the marine environment. Art. 195: No transfer of hazards — states must not transfer pollution from one area to another. Art. 218/220: Port State and Coastal State enforcement of environmental regulations. International Seabed Authority (ISA) Established under UNCLOS — headquartered in Kingston, Jamaica . Regulates all mineral-related activities in the international seabed area (The Area — ABNJ). All UNCLOS state parties are ISA members. ⚖ Regulatory References UNCLOS 1982 / Art. 55–75 EEZ — rights, jurisdiction, duties of coastal states; due regard for other states UNCLOS 1982 / Art. 192–196 Environmental protection obligations — prevent, reduce, control marine pollution Maritime Zones Act 1976 (India) Indian legislation defining maritime boundaries aligned with UNCLOS provisions Simon Sir / Nair typically asks: "What are the maritime zones under UNCLOS?" — Give all zones with distances from baseline. Key articles: 94 (Flag State duties), 192 (protect marine environment), 218/220 (PSC/coastal state enforcement). ISA headquarters: Kingston, Jamaica.

keywords: CSC Convention Safety Approval Plate Inspection Schemes Pages 167–168 SOLAS Container
section_title: CSC Convention, Safety Approval Plate & Inspection Schemes (Pages 167–168)
text: CSC Convention Adopted: December 1972; EIF: September 1977. Convened jointly by UN and IMO. BIC (Bureau International des Containers): Non-profit organisation assigning owner prefixes and managing the BIC Code Register. Follows ISO 6346 for container coding, identification, and marking. CSC Safety Approval Plate Attached to the outside left door of the container. Contains: "CSC SAFETY APPROVAL" stamping (bold characters ≥ 8mm height). Classification company approval code, manufacturing date, manufacturer's container ID number. Maximum Gross Weight: Container + cargo weight safely transportable. Stacking Load Value: Weight stackable on top at 1.8G force. Racking Test Load Value: Transverse force before frame twists. First maintenance examination date. Container Weight Formulas Gross Weight = Tare Weight + Cargo Weight Payload = Maximum cargo weight the container can hold Container Inspection Schemes PES (Periodic Examination Scheme): First exam ≤ 5 years after manufacture; thereafter at intervals ≤ 30 months. Next inspection date marked on CSC plate. ACEP (Approved Continuous Examination Programme): Container examined every time repair is carried out; must align with PES intervals minimum; ACEP number displayed on plate. CSC plate validity note: A CSC plate is valid only if the container is in good order. Any authorised agent can take a container out of service immediately if damaged to a dangerous level — regardless of inspection scheme. ⚖ Regulatory References CSC Convention 1972 International Convention for Safe Containers — safety approval, inspection, and marking requirements ISO 6346 Freight containers — coding, identification, and marking including owner prefix and equipment identifier SOLAS VI / Reg 2 Safe loading and securing — container CSC compliance required before loading on ships Simon Sir / Rajappan typically asks: "What information is on the CSC Safety Approval Plate?" — List all items; emphasise it is on the outside left door . He may ask the difference between PES and ACEP — PES = periodic time-based; ACEP = repair-triggered + continuous. CSC plate validity depends on condition, not just inspection date.

keywords: SUA Convention History Scope Jurisdiction Pages 175–176 ISPS SOLAS
section_title: SUA Convention — History, Scope & Jurisdiction (Pages 175–176)
text: Full Name & Background Convention for the Suppression of Unlawful Acts Against the Safety of Maritime Navigation (SUA). Triggered by the hijacking of the Italian cruise ship Achille Lauro on 7 October 1985 near Alexandria, Egypt — resulting in the murder of a passenger. IMO was mandated by member states to develop a framework protecting ships from terrorist acts. Resolutions and MSC circulars were deemed insufficient → full convention adopted in Rome, March 1988 . Operational Timeline Instrument Adopted EIF Original SUA Convention March 1988 March 1992 Fixed Platforms Protocol March 1988 March 1992 2005 SUA Protocol 2005 July 2, 2010 Scope — Unlawful Acts Under SUA Forcible seizure or hijacking of a vessel. Acts of violence against any person onboard. Planting devices likely to damage or destroy the vessel, cargo, or equipment. Destroying or tampering with maritime navigational facilities. Communicating intentionally false information endangering the vessel. Extradite or Prosecute: Contracting governments must either extradite offenders or prosecute them domestically. Jurisdictional Limits Territorial waters (≤ 12 NM): National domestic laws apply — coastal state has full sovereign authority. International waters (> 12 NM): SUA jurisdiction governs. No state may board a foreign vessel without flag state permission. Vessel exemptions: Warships, state-owned vessels (naval/customs/police), vessels fully withdrawn from commercial navigation. ⚖ Regulatory References SUA Convention 1988 Convention for Suppression of Unlawful Acts — base maritime security framework SUA Protocol 2005 Expanded SUA — WMD transport, use of ships as weapons, knowingly transporting terrorists SOLAS XI-2 Special measures to enhance maritime security — ISPS Code, continuous synopsis record Simon Sir typically asks: "What is the SUA Convention and what triggered it?" — Achille Lauro 1985 → Rome 1988 adoption. Key point: applies in international waters only; flag state permission required for boarding. The 2005 Protocol added WMD transport and using ships as weapons — new criminal offences under Article 3 bis.

keywords: SUA Boarding Protocol Offender Handling 2005 Pages 177–180 ISPS SOLAS
section_title: SUA — Boarding Protocol, Offender Handling & 2005 Protocol (Pages 177–180)
text: Protocols for Onboard Offenders Master may deliver the suspect to competent authorities of any contracting state at the vessel's next port (the Receiving State). Master must notify the receiving state before entering territorial sea . Master must preserve all physical evidence and hand it to the receiving state. In India: Indian Coast Guard is authorised to take custody on behalf of the government. High-Seas Boarding Protocol Requesting State has reasonable suspicion │ ▼ Request sent to Flag State to confirm nationality │ ▼ Nationality confirmed → Request authorisation to board │ ┌──┴──┐ ▼ ▼ Authorised Denied │ │ ▼ ▼ Board, search, Abort / Diplomatic question, inspect dispute channels Flag State's Four Response Options Option I: Authorise boarding and search. Option II: Formally decline. Option III: Permit boarding conditional on own law enforcement officers being present. Option IV: Conduct a joint boarding operation. 2005 SUA Protocol — New Offences (Article 3 bis) Using ships as weapons/platforms to cause death, injury, or intimidate governments. Transporting Weapons of Mass Destruction (WMD) — nuclear, biological, chemical, explosive. Knowingly transporting a person who has committed a SUA offence. 4-Hour Urgent Boarding Rule (2005 Protocol) A state party may notify the IMO Secretary-General that if an urgent boarding request receives no response within 4 hours , the requesting state may proceed with stopping, boarding, and searching the vessel. Extradition Principles Dual criminality: Act must be criminal under both states' law for extradition to apply. Extradition may be denied if politically motivated or based on persecution of race/religion/nationality. ⚖ Regulatory References SUA Convention 1988 / Art. 7–10 Master's duties, custody transfer, extradition, and prosecution obligations SUA Protocol 2005 / Art. 3bis New offences — WMD transport, ships as weapons, transporting terrorists UNCLOS Art. 110 Right of visit — warships may board foreign ships on the high seas under specified circumstances Simon Sir typically asks: "What are the Flag State's options when a boarding request is received under SUA?" — Give all four options clearly. The 4-hour rule under the 2005 Protocol is a hot exam question. Know Article 3 bis for WMD transport — this expanded SUA beyond basic hijacking to counter modern terrorism.

keywords: London Dumping Convention LC-72 1996 Protocol Comparison Pages 181–186 MARPOL Environmental
section_title: London Dumping Convention (LC-72) & 1996 Protocol — Comparison (Pages 181–186)
text: Overview Convention Name: Convention on Prevention of Marine Pollution by Dumping of Wastes and Other Matter. LC-72: Adopted 1972; EIF August 1975. 1996 Protocol: Adopted 1996; EIF March 2006 — replaces the original convention. Definition of Dumping IS Dumping: Deliberate disposal at sea of waste from vessels, aircraft, platforms, or deliberate disposal of vessels/platforms themselves. NOT Dumping: Operational discharges from vessels; pipeline discharges; waste to rivers; placement of matter for a purpose other than disposal. Activities incidental to normal operation of vessels are not considered dumping. Exemptions: Safety of life or property; force majeure; emergency situations. Convention vs 1996 Protocol — Key Comparison Element LC-72 (Original) 1996 Protocol Approach Black-list & Grey-list — permitted everything except listed items Reverse List — prohibits ALL dumping except explicitly listed waste Annex 1 Black-list: complete prohibition of hazardous materials Reverse List: permitted materials subject to stringent permits Annex 2 Grey-list: special permit required Waste Assessment Framework Annex 3 Technical criteria for permits Evaluation criteria Annex 4 Not present Marine geo-engineering regulation 1996 Protocol — Permitted Reverse List (Annex 1) Dredged material; sewage sludge; fish waste; inert inorganic geological material; mining waste; organic material; CO₂ streams from carbon capture processes. 1996 Protocol Amendments 2006 Carbon Sequestration: Allows long-term storage of CO₂ beneath the seabed; 2019 update allows transboundary export of CO₂ for sequestration. 2013 Marine Geo-engineering (Annex 4): Regulates and prohibits most ocean fertilisation activities unless for legitimate scientific research. ⚖ Regulatory References London Convention 1972 Convention on Prevention of Marine Pollution by Dumping — original black-list/grey-list framework London Protocol 1996 Replaces LC-72 — reverse list approach; precautionary principle; waste assessment mandatory LP.4(8) 2006 Amendment to London Protocol — CO₂ sequestration under seabed permissible Simon Sir / Nair typically asks: "What is the difference between the London Dumping Convention and the 1996 Protocol?" — Original: everything permitted except black-listed items. Protocol: everything prohibited except Reverse List items. Key principle of 1996 Protocol: Precautionary Approach — take action even without conclusive scientific proof of harm.

keywords: Basel Convention Hazardous Waste Trade Control PIC Procedure Pages 187–189 MARPOL Environmental
section_title: Basel Convention — Hazardous Waste Trade Control & PIC Procedure (Pages 187–189)
text: Overview Full name: Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and Their Disposal. Adopted: 1989; EIF: 1992. Context: Created to combat "toxic trade" — developed countries disposing hazardous waste in developing nations (e.g., Africa). Objective: Protect human health and the environment from adverse effects of hazardous and other wastes. Core Aims Reduce hazardous waste generation; promote Environmentally Sound Management (ESM). Restrict transboundary movements except under ESM frameworks. Treat and dispose of waste as close as possible to the place of generation . Prior Informed Consent (PIC) Procedure Step 1: Exporter notifies home Competent Authority │ ▼ Step 2: Authority forwards dossier to importing & transit states │ ▼ Step 3 & 4: Importing state reviews (≈ 60-day window) Options: Consent / Refuse / Request more details │ ▼ Step 5: If consented → export authorised Shipment must carry Movement Document │ ▼ Step 6: Disposal facility issues Certificate of Disposal/Recovery Note for India: Designated national authority for PIC = MOEFCC (Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change). Key Basel Amendments Ban Amendment (adopted 1994, EIF Dec 2019): Prohibits export of hazardous wastes from OECD (developed) to developing countries. Plastic Waste Amendment (EIF Jan 2021): Most plastic waste exports require PIC procedure. E-Waste Amendment (effective Jan 2025): All electronic/electrical waste trade subject to PIC procedures. ⚖ Regulatory References Basel Convention 1989 Transboundary hazardous waste control — PIC procedure, ESM principles, national competent authorities Basel Ban Amendment (COP.2) Prohibition on export of hazardous wastes from Annex VII (OECD) to non-Annex VII countries Hong Kong Convention 2009 Ship Recycling Convention — end-of-life vessels subject to hazardous material control similar to Basel principles Simon Sir typically asks: "What is the Basel Convention?" — 1989, hazardous waste transboundary control, PIC procedure. India's competent authority: MOEFCC. Current affairs: E-Waste Amendment effective January 2025 — examiners are asking this in 2025–2026 orals. Governing body: Conference of the Parties (COP).

keywords: HNS Convention Liability Fund Compensation Tiers Pages 190–195 MARPOL Commercial
section_title: HNS Convention — Liability, Fund & Compensation Tiers (Pages 190–195)
text: Overview Full name: International Convention on Liability and Compensation for Damage in Connection with the Carriage of Hazardous and Noxious Substances by Sea. 1996 version: Never entered into force. 2010 Protocol: Awaiting ratification — not yet in force. Purpose: Final major IMO liability convention filling gaps left by CLC and Bunker Convention — specifically covers personal injury, death, property damage from chemical fires/explosions. HNS Categories Oils carried in bulk (MARPOL Annex I). Noxious liquid substances in bulk (MARPOL Annex II). Dangerous liquids in bulk (IBC Code). Liquefied gases; liquid substances with flash point ≤ 60°C; hazardous solid bulk materials. Packaged dangerous goods (IMDG Code). Two-Tier Compensation System Tier I: Paid by the shipowner's insurance. Bulk HNS: Max 100 million SDR ; Packaged HNS: Max 115 million SDR . Tier II: Paid by the HNS Fund (funded by receivers of contributing cargo — bulk HNS only). Total compensation cap: 250 million SDR (inclusive of Tier I). HNS Fund Accounts (4 accounts when operational) Oil Account; LNG Account; LPG Account; General Account (Bulk Solids + Other HNS). No cross-subsidisation — compensation from same account as the substance causing damage. Shipowner Liability Limits (Bulk HNS) Ships ≤ 2,000 GT: 10 million SDR . 2,001–50,000 GT: 10 million SDR + 1,500 SDR/ton. > 50,000 GT: 10M + 1,500/ton (to 50k) + 360 SDR/ton thereafter. EIF Requirements for 2010 HNS Protocol At least 12 states ratified; total registered tonnage ≥ 2 million GT ; contributing bulk HNS cargo ≥ 40 million tonnes per year. ⚖ Regulatory References HNS Convention 1996 Original convention — never entered into force; replaced by 2010 Protocol structure HNS Protocol 2010 Revised convention — two-tier system, fund accounts, strict liability, awaiting ratification CLC 1992 / IOPC Fund 1992 Related oil pollution conventions — HNS explicitly excludes CLC-covered pollution to avoid overlap Simon Sir / Nair typically asks: "What is the HNS Convention?" — Full name, 2-tier system, why it fills gaps (covers fire/explosion/injury that CLC doesn't). Total cap: 250 million SDR. Fund contributor: the RECEIVER of contributing cargo (bulk HNS). Not yet in force — 2010 Protocol still awaiting ratification as of 2026.

keywords: BWM Convention Overview D-1 D-2 Standards BWMS Code Pages 196–197 MARPOL Survey
section_title: BWM Convention — Overview, D-1/D-2 Standards & BWMS Code (Pages 196–197)
text: Overview Full name: International Convention for the Control and Management of Ships' Ballast Water and Sediments, 2004. EIF: September 2017. Purpose: Prevent transfer of harmful aquatic organisms and pathogens via ballast water discharge — protect biodiversity and prevent invasive species. Compliance Standards D-1 (Ballast Water Exchange): Exchange ballast water at ≥ 200 NM from nearest land and in ≥ 200 m water depth. Efficiency ≥ 95% volumetric exchange (flow-through: pump ≥ 3 × volume). D-2 (Ballast Water Performance Standard): Treated ballast water must contain: E. coli Applicability Applies to all ships designed to carry ballast water. Ships ≥ 400 GT: Must hold approved BWMP, maintain BWRB, meet D-1/D-2 standards with approved BWTS. Exceptions: Vessels operating exclusively within a state's jurisdiction; warships; permanent sealed ballast tanks. BWMS Code — Transition from G8 Guideline G8 Guideline (2016): Recommendatory — allowed non-uniform type approval across states. BWMS Code (MEPC 72, mandatory): Systems installed on or after 28 October 2020 must comply with this Code for type approval — ensures uniformity across flag states and ROs. ⚖ Regulatory References BWM Convention 2004 Base convention — D-1 exchange standard, D-2 performance standard, Regulation D-3 type approval MEPC.300(72) BWMS Code — mandatory code for type approval of ballast water management systems from Oct 2020 BWM Convention Reg D-3 Type approval — systems using active substances require GESAMP BWWG evaluation and MEPC approval Simon Sir typically asks: "What is the D-2 standard?" —

keywords: BWTS Type Approval Land Shipboard Testing Pages 198–199 MARPOL Survey
section_title: BWTS Type Approval — G8/G9, Land & Shipboard Testing (Pages 198–199)
text: Type Approval Phases for Non-Active Substance Systems (G8/BWMS Code) Phase 1: Pre-Test Evaluation Technical specs, piping diagrams, manuals, SDL submitted │ ▼ Phase 2: Type Approval Testing ├── Land-Based Performance Testing (independent labs) ├── Environmental Testing (vibration, temp, moisture) └── Shipboard Operational Testing (≥ 6 months aboard) │ ▼ Phase 3: Issuance of Type Approval Certificate │ ▼ Phase 4: Final On-Board Installation & Inspection Salinity Testing (Land-Based) — 3 Salinities Required Marine Water: 28 to 35 PSU. Brackish Water: 10 to 20 PSU. Freshwater: Previously, single-salinity testing gave restricted approval. Now all 3 required for unrestricted Type Approval Certificate. SDL (System Design Limitations) stamped on certificate. Shipboard Testing Full-scale test onboard an active vessel in normal sea conditions. System must operate in continuous compliant condition for at least 6 months . Failed Test Cycle: Non-compliant D-2 discharge results, or engineering failure interrupting the run. Invalid Test Cycle: Environmental conditions (salinity/temperature) outside SDL limits — does not count as failure; can be re-run. G9 — Active Substance Systems Applies to: electrolytic disinfection, chemical dosing, electrochemical reactions, ozone treatment. GESAMP BWWG: Must evaluate toxicological impact, persistence, bioaccumulation, corrosion effects. System requires formal MEPC/IMO approval. Basic Approval → Land/Ship Testing → Final Approval (resubmitted to IMO). UV + TiO₂ (Advanced Oxidation) systems require G9 approval because hydroxyl radicals function as an active chemical biocide. ⚖ Regulatory References BWM Convention Reg D-3 Active substance approval — GESAMP BWWG evaluation required; MEPC final approval MEPC.300(72) — BWMS Code Land-based and shipboard testing protocols; 3-salinity requirement; SDL stamping on certificate MEPC.126(53) Revised G8 guidelines (superseded by BWMS Code for systems installed from Oct 2020) Simon Sir typically asks: "How is a BWTS type-approved?" — Give the 4 phases. Key: land-based testing in 3 salinities; shipboard testing for minimum 6 months. He may ask: "What is an Invalid Test Cycle?" — Environmental conditions outside SDL limits; can be re-run without penalty. G9 = active substance systems → GESAMP evaluation required.

keywords: IMO USCG BWTS Requirements Key Differences Page 200 MARPOL Survey
section_title: IMO vs USCG BWTS Requirements — Key Differences (Page 200)
text: IMO vs USCG Type Approval — Comparison Parameter IMO (BWMS Code / G8) USCG (46 CFR Part 162) Organism metric Viable organisms (capable of reproduction) Living organisms (direct mortality counts) Testing method Most Probable Number (MPN) Vital Stain (FDA/CMFDA) Discharge limit Test cycle quantity 3 onboard + 5 land-based cycles 5 ashore land-based cycles Minimum holding time 5 days in tanks 24 hours only Oxidant monitoring IMO TRO standards US-TRO (Total Residual Oxidant) Validation framework G8/G9 guidelines + BWMS Code US-ETV (Environmental Technology Verification) Practical Implication for Maersk Container Vessels Vessels calling US ports must have a USCG type-approved BWTS (or use an AMS — Alternate Management System for up to 5 years during evaluation). IMO-approved systems alone are insufficient for US port entry compliance. Dual-approved systems or AMS status must be verified before calling US ports. ⚖ Regulatory References USCG 33 CFR Part 151 USCG ballast water management regulations — D-2 equivalent standards for US ports USCG 46 CFR Part 162 USCG BWTS type approval — living organism metric, vital stain method, 24-hour holding BWM Convention Reg D-2 IMO performance standard — viable organism metric, MPN method, 5-day holding USCG AMS Policy Alternate Management System — 5-year temporary authorization for IMO-approved systems in US waters Simon Sir typically asks: "What is the difference between IMO and USCG BWTS requirements?" — Key differences: IMO measures VIABLE organisms (MPN method); USCG measures LIVING organisms (vital stain). IMO: 5-day minimum holding; USCG: 24 hours. As a Maersk 2/E on container vessels calling US ports, you must understand AMS status and dual approval requirements.

section_subtitle: The Hong Kong Convention (HKC) — Significance for India & Ship Recycling Regulation
section_title: What is the significance of the Hong Kong Convention for India and how does India's ship-breaking industry stand to benefit or be impacted by its implementation?
The Hong Kong Convention (HKC) — Significance for India & Ship Recycling Regulation
text: ⚓ MIW Marine Intelligence Weekly WRITTEN QUESTION NOTES · WA1 · HKC & SHIP RECYCLING · WA1-HKC1 The Hong Kong Convention (HKC) — Significance for India & Ship Recycling Regulation Expanded model-answer notes for MEO Class 1 written & oral exam preparation — Engineering Management & Regulatory Compliance 📚 Chapter X 🏷 Tags: HKC · IHM · Ship Recycling · MARPOL-adjacent ✅ Verified against IMO primary sources 🕐 ~14 min read 🔎 Verification note (read before studying) This note has been fact-checked against IMO primary sources and classification-society publications (see reference list at the end). Where a source could not be independently confirmed, it has been flagged rather than presented as fact — a discipline this series follows strictly, since answer-drafting tools are known to occasionally invent plausible-sounding regulation numbers. Model Answer · Written Question What is the significance of the Hong Kong Convention for India and how does India's ship-breaking industry stand to benefit or be impacted by its implementation?

section_title: 1 · Definition & Purpose
text: 1 · Definition & Purpose The Hong Kong International Convention for the Safe and Environmentally Sound Recycling of Ships (HKC) is a legally binding IMO treaty ensuring that ships, at the end of their operational lives, do not pose unnecessary risks to human health, safety, or the marine environment during recycling. Its purpose is to regulate the entire lifecycle of a vessel from an environmental-engineering perspective: controlling hazardous materials embedded in a ship's structure and machinery, setting technical criteria for Ship Recycling Facilities (SRFs), and enforcing compliance through continuous documentation, certification, and verification.

10 · Expanded Model Answer
text: 10 · Expanded Model Answer 1. Introduction & Structural Alignment The ratification and enforcement of the HKC is a major turning point for India's maritime economy. India accounts for a substantial share of global ship recycling volumes, concentrated primarily at the Alang-Sosiya hub in Gujarat. By enacting the Recycling of Ships Act, 2019, India aligned its national legal framework with the HKC well ahead of global entry into force, enabling recycling yards to upgrade to international green standards before 26 June 2025 . 2. Structural & Strategic Benefits Market consolidation & higher tonnage inflow: Shipowners who previously avoided South Asian beaching yards on ESG grounds can now route vessels to compliant Indian facilities. Circular economic linkage (recycled steel): Indian yards recover large volumes of high-grade marine steel annually; processing recycled steel requires markedly less energy than virgin ore smelting, feeding domestic construction and manufacturing. Shipbreaking Credit Note Scheme: Under Maritime India Vision 2030, the government offers a scrap-value credit note to shipowners recycling at compliant domestic yards, fundable toward new construction at Indian shipyards. 3. Technical Impacts & Operational Challenges CapEx for secondary infrastructure: Shift from mud-beach dismantling to hybrid systems using impermeable concrete heavy-lift intertidal landing pads. Downstream waste-management infrastructure: The core challenge is building authorised, high-capacity Treatment, Storage and Disposal Facilities (TSDFs) for PCB, asbestos, and bilge-sludge volumes. "Double compliance" pressure: European shipowners remain bound by the stricter EU-SRR, which does not permit intertidal beaching — pushing Indian yards to keep upgrading to compete with dry-docked facilities elsewhere. 8 marks Detail the specific survey and certification requirements that an active vessel must undergo under the HKC framework prior to entering an authorized ship recycling facility. Regulatory reference: HKC Annex Regulations 8, 9 and 10; harmonisation guidance in MEPC.222(64). 4-stage survey cycle: Initial → Renewal (5-year loop) → Additional → Final. Documentation output: ICIHM (operational-life certificate) → IRRC (pre-recycling certificate, valid ≤ 3 months). Cross-check requirement: Surveyor confirms the vessel-specific SRP is formally authorised by the recycling state's competent authority before the final IRRC is issued. 10 marks As Chief Engineer, explain how you would establish a robust on-board maintenance programme to ensure continuous validity of the IHM Part I throughout a ship's operational lifespan. System integration: Embed IHM-updating into the PMS and ISM Safety Management Manual. MD/SDoC procurement control: No spares, paint drums, or seals aboard without MD and SDoC. Crew training & sampling restrictions: Prohibit unrecorded installation of gaskets, linings, or insulation potentially containing Appendix 1 materials. Auditing: Quarterly audit by the Designated Person (IHM DP), cross-checking repair logs against the electronic IHM Part I register. 15 marks Analyze the technical conflicts and regulatory intersections between the HKC, the EU-SRR, and the Basel Convention, and their impact on commercial engineering choices of global ship operators. Jurisdictional core: HKC — flag-and-recycling-state treaty; EU-SRR — regional mechanism with global port-state application; Basel — transboundary hazardous-waste dumping. Beaching debate: HKC permits controlled intertidal beaching; EU-SRR requires impermeable concrete structures, narrowing EU-flagged vessel options. The "waste challenge": An end-of-life ship can be simultaneously a transport asset under IMO rules and "hazardous waste" under Basel — driving enforcement actions for unapproved exports. Commercial mitigation: Operators use independent Recognized Organizations to maintain one hyper-compliant IHM profile satisfying all three regimes.

section_title: 2 · Importance to International Shipping
text: 2 · Importance to International Shipping Before global enforcement, the industry relied largely on unregulated beaching operations, associated with toxic spills, occupational illness, and fatal accidents. The HKC introduces global harmonisation, removing incentives for "flag-hopping" or "yard-shopping" to weaker jurisdictions. The Convention converts ship recycling from an unmonitored scrap transaction into a structured, audited, and traceable industrial process — enforcing a "cradle-to-grave" asset-management concept across shipowners, shipbuilders, equipment manufacturers, classification societies, and recycling yards.

section_title: 3 · Historical Background & Timeline
text: 3 · Historical Background & Timeline Date Milestone May 2009 HKC formally adopted at a Diplomatic Conference in Hong Kong, China, developed jointly with IMO, ILO, and Parties to the Basel Convention. 2019 India enacts the Recycling of Ships Act, 2019 , transposing HKC technical provisions into domestic law, establishing the Directorate General of Shipping (DGS) as National Authority. June 2023 Bangladesh and Liberia ratify, satisfying Article 17 entry-into-force criteria: ratification by ≥15 States representing ≥40% of world merchant shipping GT, with combined annual recycling volume ≥3% of that GT. 26 June 2025 HKC enters into force globally — 24 months after the 2023 threshold was met — shifting the industry from voluntary to binding compliance. CE Oral Tip: Examiners at Kochi MMD frequently probe the Article 17 mechanics — be ready to state the dual criteria (15 States / 40% GT / 3% recycling volume) and that entry into force followed 24 months after the June 2023 threshold, landing on 26 June 2025 .

section_title: 4 · IMO / International Regulatory References
text: 4 · IMO / International Regulatory References ⚖ Regulatory References HKC Annex — Reg. 4 Controls on Ships' Hazardous Materials — prohibits/restricts installation of Appendix 1 materials. HKC Annex — Reg. 5 Inventory of Hazardous Materials (IHM) — every ship must maintain an active, verified IHM. HKC Annex — Reg. 8 & 9 Statutory survey regime — Initial, Renewal, Additional, and Final surveys. MEPC.222(64) 2012 Guidelines for the survey and certification of ships under the HKC — governs harmonisation of the Initial Survey with other statutory certificates. MEPC.379(80) 2023 Guidelines for the Development of the IHM — adopted 7 July 2023, applicable no later than 26 June 2025. MEPC.211(63) 2012 Guidelines for the Authorization of Ship Recycling Facilities. MEPC.353(78) 2022 Guidelines for the Development of the Ship Recycling Plan (SRP).

section_title: 5 · Engineering Explanation & Core Technical Mechanisms
text: 5 · Engineering Explanation & Core Technical Mechanisms The IHM Framework — Three-Part Engineering Logbook +-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | INVENTORY OF HAZARDOUS MATERIALS (IHM) | +-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | PART I: Materials in Ship's Structure and Equipment | | - Maintained continuously throughout the ship's operational life. | | - Covers paint systems, insulation, machinery seals, and piping. | +-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | PART II: Operationally Generated Wastes | | - Compiled prior to recycling by the Shipboard Management team. | | - Quantifies sludges, bilge waters, and tank residues. | +-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | PART III: Stores (Consumables, Spare Parts, Provisioning Liquids) | | - Logged immediately before decommissioning/sale to the SRF. | | - Identifies refrigerant gases, chemical treats, and batteries. | +-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ Appendix 1 vs. Appendix 2 Materials Appendix 1 — Strictly Prohibited / Restricted Installation: Asbestos, Ozone Depleting Substances (ODS), Polychlorinated Biphenyls (PCBs), Organotin Compounds (anti-fouling TBT). Appendix 2 — Compulsory Monitoring & Quantification: Cadmium, Hexavalent Chromium, Lead, Mercury, Polybrominated Biphenyls (PBBs), Polybrominated Diphenyl Ethers (PBDEs), Radioactive Substances, Short-Chain Chlorinated Paraffins (SCCPs). Technical Calculation — Safe Yard Capacity An authorised Ship Recycling Facility (SRF) calculates its Maximum Annual Ship Recycling Capacity (C SRF ) in Gross Tonnage using an empirically-framed throughput relation: C SRF = Σ [ (GT i × D operational ) ⁄ T dismantle, i ] × η yard GT i — Gross Tonnage of representative vessel type i . D operational — Active operational days of the facility per year (typically normalised to 300 days). T dismantle, i — Structural cutting/processing time (days) to fully reduce vessel i to zero blocks. η yard — Yard Efficiency & Safety Factor (≤ 1.0), set by crane capacity, cutting-zone area, and waste-storage constraints. CE Oral Tip: This capacity relation is a teaching construct to illustrate the engineering variables a yard must control (throughput days, dismantling time per vessel type, efficiency factor) — it is not a formula printed in the HKC Annex itself. Present it as "an illustrative capacity-planning relation," not as a quoted regulatory formula, if an examiner asks for its source.

section_title: 6 · Chief Engineer & Flag State Responsibilities
text: 6 · Chief Engineer & Flag State Responsibilities Chief Engineer Responsibilities IHM Maintenance — MD/SDoC Protocol: Statutory custodian of IHM Part I. Every repair, pump overhaul, or repaint requires extracting a Material Declaration (MD) and Supplier's Declaration of Conformity (SDoC) , logged in the SMS to update the IHM. Pre-Recycling Preparation: On decommissioning instructions, draft Part II (wastes) and Part III (stores) of the IHM. System Optimisation: Transfer remaining HFO to settling tanks; keep gas-freeing certificates current for cargo blocks, bunker tanks, and pump rooms. Flag State Responsibilities Survey Verification: Flag State / authorised RO verifies onboard systems match the IHM log via periodic surveys. Certification: Issues the ICIHM on satisfactory survey; issues the IRRC prior to scrapping, following the verified Final Survey — the IRRC is normally valid for a period not exceeding three months , timed to cover the ship's final voyage.

section_title: 7 · Practical Shipboard Application
text: 7 · Practical Shipboard Application Case Study — End-of-Life Capesize Bulk Carrier, Alang A 180,000 DWT Capesize bulk carrier reaches end of commercial life, scheduled for dismantling at an authorised yard in Alang, India. STEP 1: IHM PART I, II & III CONSOLIDATION - Chief Engineer collects MD/SDoCs from past drydocks. - Quantifies remaining fuel oil, lubes, sludge, ODS inventory. | v STEP 2: SHORE-SIDE FACILITY AUDIT & SRP MATCHING - Yard provides a vessel-specific Ship Recycling Plan (SRP). - Plan maps cutting sequence to protect structural integrity. | v STEP 3: STATUTORY FINAL SURVEY BY FLAG STATE RO - Surveyor verifies onboard items against submitted IHM. - Confirms tanks are ready for safe access and hot work. | v STEP 4: IRRC ISSUANCE & SAFE TRANSIT TO ALANG - International Ready for Recycling Certificate issued. - Vessel departs for beaching at the authorized facility. Incident: Unmapped Asbestos Found During Pre-Recycling Inspection Immediate Isolation & Containment: Isolate the auxiliary boiler room space; secure ventilation fans, seal dampers to prevent fibre migration into engine room casing or accommodation. Statutory Logging & IHM Amendment: Log location, estimated volume, physical state in IHM Part I; notify the DGS/RO surveyor. SRP Revision Request: Transmit the amended IHM to the SRF; the SRF revises its SRP to include wet-containment and hazardous disposal protocols before torch-cutting proceeds in that block.

section_title: 8 · Survey Requirements (HSSC) & Port State Control Focus
text: 8 · Survey Requirements (HSSC) & Port State Control Focus Survey Scope Initial At new construction, or when HKC becomes retroactively applicable. Verifies IHM Part I. Renewal Not exceeding 5 years , validates the ICIHM; focuses on changes altering the hazardous-material matrix. Additional Triggered by major structural modification or significant equipment change. Final Before the ship is taken out of service and recycling begins; verifies IHM Parts I–III, enables IRRC issuance, confirms the SRF's vessel-specific SRP is ready. ⚠ PSC Alert — Deficiency Codes & Detention Risk Code 14101 — IHM Missing/Invalid: immediate grounds for detention if no valid ICIHM is onboard. Code 14104 — IHM Not Maintained / Lack of MD or SDoC: logged overhauls lacking matching declarations draw a Code 17 (rectify before departure) or Code 30 detention if illegal Appendix 1 materials are found.

Engineering Design for Recycling (EDfR) — Green Shipbuilding

It has been removed rather than corrected to a guessed number, since no verifiable IACS PR/UR reference for MD/SDoC construction-survey audit methodology could be confirmed from public sources. Model Answer · Written Question Explain the core principles of Engineering Design for Recycling (EDfR) as applied to modern green shipbuilding. Discuss how lifecycle engineering solutions mitigate future environmental liabilities during a vessel's decommissioning phase.

section_title: 1 · Definition & Purpose
text: 1 · Definition & Purpose Engineering Design for Recycling (EDfR), colloquially termed "Green Shipbuilding," is a proactive structural and systems-engineering discipline applied at the conceptual, detailed, and production design stages of a marine asset. Its objective is to optimise a vessel's life-cycle efficiency by systematically minimising the integration of hazardous, restricted, or unrecyclable materials, while shaping structural configuration and machinery arrangements to enable safe, rapid, and environmentally sound decommissioning. Rather than treating a ship solely as an operational commercial instrument, EDfR treats the hull, machinery spaces, and accommodation blocks as a modular repository of recyclable components and controlled hazardous-waste streams — aligning newbuild design with the Hong Kong Convention (HKC) and the EU Ship Recycling Regulation (EU-SRR) from the first day of fabrication.

10 · Expanded Model Answer
text: 10 · Expanded Model Answer 1. Introduction & Core Philosophy EDfR is a proactive engineering methodology that integrates end-of-life disposal criteria into the initial asset design phase. Under the global mandate of the HKC, shipbuilding can no longer ignore a vessel's ultimate dismantling phase. By evaluating material lifecycles, chemical compositions, and structural disassembly mechanics, EDfR minimises uncontained hazardous-waste streams and reduces downstream decommissioning costs. 2. Key Technical Principles Proactive substitution: Eliminating toxic chemicals at the design stage — exfoliated graphite or aramid fibres instead of asbestos gaskets, non-biocidal silicone coatings instead of organotin anti-fouling. Deconstruction engineering (design for disassembly): Integrated extraction corridors, bolted rather than fully-welded non-structural casings, clear access paths to high-value recyclable components. Material stream homogeneity: Specifying steel alloys and non-ferrous metals with unmixed chemical compositions to avoid complex composites that hinder separation and reduce scrap purity/value. 3. Mitigation of Environmental & Financial Liabilities When a vessel engineered under EDfR reaches end-of-life, its asset profile is transparent: the SRF receives a fully-updated IHM Part I database mapping every steel component. This clear data environment lets the yard execute its SRP safely and efficiently, reducing dismantling time, lowering insurance premiums, and preventing toxic-exposure claims or environmental remediation penalties for the shipowner. 8 marks Explain the difference between a Material Declaration (MD) and a Supplier's Declaration of Conformity (SDoC). Discuss their roles in maintaining the validity of the IHM Part I register. Defining the MD: A technical document from an equipment vendor identifying the presence and mass of any Appendix 1 or 2 materials in the delivered product, above reporting thresholds set in MEPC.379(80). Defining the SDoC: A formal corporate statement confirming the supplied component complies with relevant maritime regulations, providing a legal link back to the manufacturer. The verification chain: Chief Engineer uses both documents to update the digital IHM Part I register whenever an onboard system is repaired or replaced, creating an unbroken compliance trail for class and PSC audits. 10 marks Design an engineering procedure for tracking and logging Appendix 2 tracked substances during a major mid-life vessel conversion (e.g. installation of an alternative fuel delivery system). Pre-conversion risk assessment: Identify which new components contain regulated Appendix 2 substances (e.g. cadmium in electronics, lead in heavy valving sleeves). Procurement documentation control: Strict quality-control loop requiring verified MD and SDoC before components are accepted on site. Physical verification & frame mapping: Installation engineers log the exact location of components by frame number, deck level, and system sub-category in the electronic IHM Part I register. Statutory survey triggering: Notify the Flag State RO to conduct an Additional Survey, validating updated IHM Part I data and re-issuing the ICIHM. 15 marks Formulate a technical and economic evaluation comparing a standard legacy container vessel design with an advanced EDfR container vessel design over a 25-year operational lifecycle, focusing on end-of-life residual values and regulatory non-compliance risks. Operational baseline phase: EDfR designs typically carry a modest CapEx premium (certified material sourcing, modular layout additions) versus a standard design. Mid-life maintenance/upgrade phase: EDfR designs reduce OpEx during major overhauls through integrated extraction corridors and accessible soft patches, cutting dry-dock down-time. Regulatory compliance risk: Legacy designs face financial risk under post-2025 HKC enforcement — potential fines, port restrictions, or structural retrofitting costs if undocumented hazardous materials surface during PSC inspections. End-of-life scrap valuation: An EDfR vessel's pure material streams and documented absence of toxic contaminants command a premium residual scrap value per lightship displacement tonne at recycling, since the yard can process the steel and machinery streams faster and with less specialised hazardous-waste handling. Legacy vessels, by contrast, face cost deductions for hazardous-waste remediation and extended dismantling schedules where the IHM is incomplete or unverifiable.

section_title: 11 · Summary & Memory Boxes
text: 11 · Summary & Memory Boxes 📌 EXAM FOCUS EDfR requires newbuild specifications to completely omit Appendix 1 substances and clearly log Appendix 2 substances above the thresholds set in MEPC.379(80). Structural Extraction Corridors are a core design requirement to allow heavy machinery removal without destroying the hull girder. CE Oral Tip: During shipyard construction inspections, verify that soft patches in the engine room casing are unencumbered by secondary piping, cable trays, or ventilation trunks. A sub-contractor routing generic lines across a designated soft patch invalidates the design's disassembly capability. ⚠ PSC Alert — Key Design Audit Targets Retrofitted components lacking matching MD or SDoC records in the master folder. Discrepancies between actual structural modifications (e.g. bulkhead changes) and the schematics appended to the ICIHM. 🧠 MEMORY BOX Remember the chain: clean material selection at design → structural extraction corridors → complete MD/SDoC paper trail → transparent IHM at end-of-life → higher scrap value, lower liability. That single chain is the spine of almost every EDfR written answer. 📖 Reference Sources IMO — Recycling of Ships & Hong Kong Convention: imo.org/en/mediacentre/hottopics/pages/recycling-of-ships-and-hong-kong-convention.aspx · IMO — HKC Convention text & FAQ (wwwcdn.imo.org, Ship Recycling documents) · ISO 30005:2012 — iso.org/standard/55907.html · ClassNK — Ship Recycling Convention outline (T1311e, Jan 2025) · DNV — HKC / IHM certification guidance (2025) · IACS — Procedural Requirements register, iacs.org.uk (used to confirm/reject PR numbering before citation).
