section_title: 2 · Importance to International Shipping
text: 2 · Importance to International Shipping Historically, maritime assets were designed exclusively for operational survivability, hydrodynamic efficiency, and payload volume. This legacy approach embedded toxic materials in critical structural zones — chrysotile asbestos in high-temperature steam gaskets, or PCBs in electrical cable insulation — creating severe occupational hazards and contamination risk at decommissioning. EDfR shifts the maritime economic model from linear ("take-make-dispose") to circular. Structural layout adaptations, standardised components, and end-of-life accessibility reduce future decommissioning costs, mitigate ESG liabilities, and maximise the scrap residual value of the asset.

section_title: 3 · Historical Background & Origins
text: 3 · Historical Background & Origins The baseline problem (legacy tonnage): Late-20th-century shipyards relied on composite, synthetic, and chemically-stabilised materials. The discovery of widespread occupational health degradation — notably mesothelioma among shipyard and recycling workers — prompted reassessment of marine engineering material specifications. The paradigm shift (early 2000s): IMO began moving from reactive pollution response to life-cycle monitoring, introducing "cradle-to-grave" asset-monitoring thinking that would later underpin the HKC. Post-2025 enforcement: With the HKC taking full global effect on 26 June 2025 , the shipbuilding market moved from voluntary eco-notations (e.g. DNV's Green Passport or Lloyd's Register's ECO notation) toward mandatory, statutorily-audited design practices verifying compliance with prohibited-material constraints before steel cutting begins.

section_title: 4 · IMO / International Regulatory References
text: 4 · IMO / International Regulatory References ⚖ Regulatory References HKC Annex — Ch. 2 Requirements for Ships — controls the design and construction phase of newbuild tonnage. HKC Annex — Reg. 4 Controls on Ships' Hazardous Materials — prohibits/restricts installation of Appendix 1 materials on all newbuildings. HKC Annex — Reg. 5 Requires the new-ship IHM Part I to be developed at the construction stage and verified before delivery. MEPC.379(80) 2023 Guidelines for the Development of the IHM — defines MD/SDoC formats and material-detection thresholds. MEPC.222(64) 2012 Guidelines for survey and certification of ships under the HKC — governs the Initial Survey at delivery. ISO 30005:2012 Ship recycling management systems — information control for hazardous materials in the shipbuilding manufacturing chain (guidance document supporting HKC compliance). CE Oral Tip: If an examiner asks which IACS document governs MD/SDoC audit procedure at construction survey, the safe, defensible answer is that this sits under each class society's own survey procedures implementing HKC Regulation 5 and MEPC.379(80) — not a single universal IACS PR/UR number. Don't quote a specific IACS PR number unless you've verified it against the current IACS register yourself.

section_title: 5 · Engineering Explanation & Core Technical Mechanisms
text: 5 · Engineering Explanation & Core Technical Mechanisms Material Selection Optimisation & Prohibited Substitutions The fundamental engineering pillar of green shipbuilding is the absolute omission of Appendix 1 hazardous materials and the disciplined reduction of Appendix 2 monitored substances, using non-toxic alternatives capable of withstanding the marine environment. +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | MATERIAL SELECTION OPTIMIZATION MATRIX | +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | LEGACY PROHIBITED MATERIAL (APPENDIX 1) ===> GREEN ENGINEERING ALTERNATIVE SOLUTION | +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | Chrysotile Asbestos (High-Temp Gaskets) ===> Exfoliated Graphite bonded to 316SS Tanged Inserts | | Polyurethane / Phenolic Foam Insulation ===> Mineral Wool / Rigid Glass-Fiber Eco-Mats | | Tributyltin (TBT) Anti-Fouling Coatings ===> Fluoropolymer / Silicone Fouling Release Coatings | | Lead-Acid Storage Banks (Aux Power) ===> Lithium Iron Phosphate (LiFePO4) Modular Racks | | Cadmium-Plated Sea-Water Fasteners ===> Duplex Stainless Steel (UNS S31803) / Titanium Alloys | +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+ Structural Modular Design & Decommissioning Access Paths A primary technical bottleneck during recycling is extracting high-value machinery (auxiliary diesel engines, purifiers, condenser heat exchangers) buried deep in the lower engine room. Traditional designs require destructive torch-cutting of decks and watertight bulkheads, disrupting hull structural stability. EDfR mitigates this with Structural Extraction Corridors — bolted access plates, removable deck beams, and unencumbered vertical soft patches engineered into the general arrangement, allowing a recycling-yard crane to lift heavy machinery out without compromising the hull girder's global structural integrity.

section_title: 6 · Chief Engineer & Flag State Responsibilities
text: 6 · Chief Engineer & Flag State Responsibilities Chief Engineer Responsibilities (Newbuild Construction & Delivery Oversight) Technical gatekeeper policy: Review shipyard production drawings to ensure scheduled deviations (e.g. valve gland packing changes during fit-out) are supported by a corresponding MD. Baseline Part I entry verification: Audit the shipyard's initial IHM Part I draft; cross-verify that Appendix 2 item locations (lead ballast keel blocks, mercury instruments) are precisely mapped to frame-spacing coordinates on the general arrangement plan. Flag State & Recognized Organization (RO) Responsibilities Plan approval audit: Design plan approval before keel laying, verifying material specifications match Appendix 1 prohibition criteria. Initial verification survey: Physical Initial Survey during sea trials to issue the ICIHM, confirming the physical ship matches the audited IHM structure.

section_title: 7 · Practical Shipboard Application
text: 7 · Practical Shipboard Application Case Study — IHM Verification Audit on a Newly Delivered Green VLCC A 300,000 DWT VLCC, engineered under EDfR criteria, is delivered from a South Korean shipyard with a digitally-mapped IHM Part I database integrated into its asset-management software. STEP 1: COMPILING THE SHIPYARD MASTER IHM FILE - Shipyard collects MDs and SDoCs from vendors, indexed to component serial codes. | v STEP 2: VERIFYING MODULAR MECHANICAL REMOVAL COMPLIANCE - Chief Engineer inspects designated "Soft Patches" in the casing. - Confirms heavy lube oil purifiers can clear structural frames easily. | v STEP 3: STATUTORY INITIAL SURVEY BY RO CLASS SURVEYOR - Random non-destructive testing (NDT) audits on pipe lagging. - Confirms zero trace of prohibited chrysotile fibers via lab assays. | v STEP 4: ICIHM GENERATION & ASSET REGISTRATION - Class issues the statutory International Certificate on IHM. - Digital IHM locked into the vessel's SMS for lifetime updates. Incident: Unauthorized Spares Supply in an Outport Isolate and log the component: Second Engineer notes the newly installed mechanical seal lacks an MD/SDoC. Chief Engineer logs serial number, frame location, and installation date in the engine room logbook as an unverified modification. Issue formal vendor demand: Demand a verified MD detailing the exact composition of seal faces and elastomers within a defined window (typically 48 hours). Physical testing or replacement: If unresolved, classify the component as an unmapped potential hazard. At the next major hub port, replace with a certified OEM spare carrying full HKC documentation, and correct the IHM Part I entry.

section_title: 8 · Survey Requirements (HSSC) & Port State Control Focus
text: 8 · Survey Requirements (HSSC) & Port State Control Focus Initial Survey (HSSC Framework) Material Declaration folder: Verification of completeness of MDs and SDoCs for all Appendix 1 and 2 listed components. Visual and sampling verification: Surveyor checks materials against submitted plans — e.g. dry-film sampling of anti-fouling coatings for AFS Convention / HKC Regulation 4 compliance. PSC Inspection Focus Audit trail inspection: PSCO selects a randomly retrofitted component (e.g. emergency air compressor, auxiliary heat exchanger) and requests the corresponding MD/SDoC. Physical label cross-check: Verifies components with monitored Appendix 2 substances (e.g. electronic control cards with heavy-metal solder) carry correct tracking labels cross-referenced to the electronic IHM registry. ⚠ PSC Alert — Deficiency Risk Areas IHM Part I not updated after structural modification: An upgrade (e.g. scrubber retrofit) not reflected in the IHM Part I is a major deficiency. Illegal Appendix 1 installation: Discovery of newly-installed prohibited asbestos or unapproved ODS gases triggers detention, requiring physical remediation before sailing.

section_title: 9 · Structural Comparison — Traditional vs. EDfR Design
text: 9 · Structural Comparison — Traditional vs. EDfR Design Parameter Traditional Design Green EDfR Design Material documentation Disjointed vendor spec sheets; no centralised chemical tracking. Unified digital database mapped to MD and SDoC structures. Machinery extraction "Buried asset" layout; requires structural deck destruction to remove. Structural Extraction Corridors with engineered soft patches and bolted frames. Insulation/lagging Cheap composite synthetic fibres; asbestos cross-contamination risk. Certified pure mineral wool or high-purity glass-fibre mats. Anti-fouling Heavy-metal or reactive biocides needing specialised stripping. Advanced fluoropolymer fouling-release coatings, minimal toxic residue. Component standardisation Proprietary alloy mixes hinder scrap processing. High-homogeneity alloys for efficient recycling-facility separation.

section_subtitle: Industrial Safety & Waste Stream Management at Authorized Ship Recycling Facilities
section_title: Detail the technical infrastructure required for an authorized Ship Recycling Facility to achieve compliance under the Hong Kong Convention framework. Explain how a facility manages and tracks downstream hazardous waste streams to prevent environmental degradation.
Industrial Safety & Waste Stream Management at Authorized Ship Recycling Facilities
text: ⚓ MIW Marine Intelligence Weekly WRITTEN QUESTION NOTES · WA1 · HKC & SHIP RECYCLING · WA1-HKC3 Industrial Safety & Waste Stream Management at Authorized Ship Recycling Facilities Expanded model-answer notes for MEO Class 1 written & oral exam preparation — Industrial Safety & Waste Stream Management 📚 Chapter Z 🏷 Tags: HKC · SRFP · TSDF · Facility Safety ✅ Verified against IMO/class sources 🕐 ~13 min read 🔎 Verification note (read before studying) The original draft of this chapter included a "mass-balance tracking equation" with a specific ≤2% regulatory tolerance figure for reconciling incoming IHM hazardous-material mass against downstream TSDF receipts. No IMO, HKC Annex, or class-society source could confirm a published numeric tolerance of this kind, so the formula and the 2% figure have been removed rather than presented as regulation. The underlying concept — that a yard must reconcile what it logged in against what it sent to disposal — is real and is explained in plain terms in Section 5 below. Everything else in this chapter has been checked against IMO and classification-society sources. Model Answer · Written Question Detail the technical infrastructure required for an authorized Ship Recycling Facility to achieve compliance under the Hong Kong Convention framework. Explain how a facility manages and tracks downstream hazardous waste streams to prevent environmental degradation.

section_title: 1 · Definition & Purpose
text: 1 · Definition & Purpose Industrial Safety and Waste Stream Management at an authorized Ship Recycling Facility (SRF) is the systematic application of environmental engineering, occupational hygiene, and chemical-containment protocols to vessel deconstruction. The objective is to control, isolate, and safely process all hazardous-material streams generated during dismantling. This discipline turns traditional scrap-yard operations into a regulated industrial process — preventing transboundary pollutant migration, eliminating occupational exposure to toxic compounds (friable asbestos, heavy-metal dusts, volatile organic compounds), and ensuring all outputs pass through verified downstream treatment infrastructure.

10 · Expanded Model Answer
text: 10 · Expanded Model Answer 1. Introduction & Structural Requirements To achieve formal authorisation under the HKC and pass classification-society audits, an SRF must move away from unregulated dismantling methods and install engineered infrastructure that contains pollutants at the primary point of cutting — structural barrier pads, multi-stage filtration systems, and a strict, transparent chain-of-custody framework for downstream waste. 2. Core Environmental Engineering Infrastructure Impermeable catchment pad: Heavy-lift reinforced concrete pad above the intertidal zone, able to withstand dropped steel blocks and support crawler cranes, sealed with oil-resistant coating and sloped toward collection points. Advanced drainage & separation: Multi-stage oil-water separator extracts hydrocarbons; chelating filter units precipitate and capture suspended heavy metals (lead, cadmium, hexavalent chromium) before discharge or reuse. Atmospheric isolation equipment: Negative-pressure containment tents, HEPA-filtered industrial vacuums, and wet-stripping systems for friable asbestos. 3. Downstream Hazardous Waste Tracking Once hazardous materials are extracted, they enter a structured tracking pipeline. The facility cannot store toxic waste indefinitely on site; it must partner with state-authorised TSDFs. Every consignment — asbestos sheets, PCB-laden cables, chemical sludges — is logged with a unique tracking code; the TSDF weighs the waste on arrival and issues an official destruction receipt, which is cross-referenced against the vessel's original IHM to confirm nothing was diverted or dumped. 8 marks Explain the purpose of a Document of Authorization to Ship Recycling (DASR) and list the key technical audits a facility must pass to secure this certification. Defining the DASR: The statutory certificate issued by the competent national authority under HKC Regulation 16, confirming the facility complies with international environmental and safety requirements. Infrastructure audit focus: Structural integrity of impermeable concrete cutting pads, capacity of oil-water separators, effectiveness of stormwater containment sumps. Procedural/management review: Audit of the master SRFP, verifying documented worker safety training, medical surveillance records, and formal contracts with authorised downstream TSDF networks. 10 marks Formulate an operational engineering procedure for gas-freeing and certifying a heavy fuel oil (HFO) double-bottom tank on an end-of-life vessel prior to commencing primary torch-cutting at an authorized facility. Initial mechanical stripping: Deep-pump the tank using specialised positive-displacement shore pumps to remove pumpable residual sludge and HFO. Thermal/chemical washing: Inject high-pressure steam or chemical emulsifiers to loosen and wash away hydrocarbon residues clinging to bulkheads and floor plates. Mechanical ventilation & gas-freeing: Deploy explosion-proof air blowers to ventilate the space and displace volatile hydrocarbon vapours. Atmospheric testing & certification: An independent Marine Chemist uses calibrated gas detectors to measure oxygen (≥20.9%), lower explosive limit (LEL <1%), and toxic gas concentrations (e.g. H 2 S), formally issuing the "Safe-for-Hot-Work" certificate before cutting begins. 15 marks Evaluate the occupational health and safety risks associated with handling Appendix 1 materials during ship dismantling. Design a comprehensive facility management program to achieve a "Zero-Harm" operational target for yard workers. Identifying Appendix 1 hazards: Mesothelioma from asbestos exposure, central-nervous-system damage from lead dust, toxicity from PCBs. Engineering control architecture: Negative-pressure isolation tents for asbestos stripping, specialised cutters to reduce toxic fumes versus open-flame torches, dedicated enclosed hazardous-waste storage lockers. Administrative & PPE controls: Mandatory respiratory-protection programmes with particulate respirators, colour-coded work zones to prevent cross-contamination, continuous automated air-monitoring along the yard perimeter. Medical surveillance: Long-term worker health monitoring — regular lung-function testing, blood lead-level assays, detailed occupational-health tracking logs to sustain a verified Zero-Harm environment.

section_title: 11 · Summary & Memory Boxes
text: 11 · Summary & Memory Boxes 📌 EXAM FOCUS Authorised facilities operate under an approved Ship Recycling Facility Plan (SRFP) and generate a custom Vessel-Specific SRP for every ship handled. Every hazardous-material volume extracted from a vessel must be reconciled against certified TSDF destruction receipts — an unexplained gap is the primary audit red flag. CE Oral Tip: When preparing a vessel for hand-off to an authorised yard, ensure all internal pipe valves connecting clean-water systems to fuel lines are closed and locked. This prevents unexpected hydrocarbon migration during structural cutting, which can cause localised flash fires or contaminate clean scrap-metal streams. ⚠ Facility Audit — High-Risk Target Areas Discrepancies between the volume of electronic waste (e.g. PCB-coated wiring) logged in the vessel's IHM and physical TSDF receipts. Deterioration of oil-resistant epoxy coating on the primary catchment pad, allowing toxic chemical runoff to leach into the underlying ground. 🧠 MEMORY BOX Remember the chain: SRFP (yard's master plan) → SRP (this ship's specific plan) → catchment pad + separator + chelating filter (containment) → HEPA tent + wet-stripping (asbestos) → weighed, coded waste → TSDF receipt → reconciled against the IHM. Walking an examiner through this chain in order answers most facility-management questions. 📖 Reference Sources IMO — HKC FAQ & Convention text (wwwcdn.imo.org, Ship Recycling documents) · IMO — Recycling of Ships & Hong Kong Convention: imo.org/en/mediacentre/hottopics · Gleiss Lutz — HKC entry into force legal briefing (Regulation 16 & 18 references) · Britannia P&I — Ship Recycling: Hong Kong Convention in force (DASR validity) · IMO FAQ — Implementing the Hong Kong Convention (SRFP/authorisation process). section_title: 2 · Importance to International Shipping
text: 2 · Importance to International Shipping The final phase of a vessel's life cycle carries significant regulatory, legal, and reputational risk for operators. Under the HKC, shipowners face liability if an end-of-life vessel is dismantled at a facility permitting uncontained chemical spills or experiencing high occupational casualty rates. Rigorous facility management gives shipping audited, high-transparency disposal routes. Yards enforcing explicit controls — impermeable concrete pads, advanced drainage catchments, specialised hazardous-waste tracking — help operators protect ESG standing, meet flag/port state compliance, and reduce litigation exposure.

section_title: 3 · Historical Background & Origins
text: 3 · Historical Background & Origins The legacy era (unregulated beaching): For decades, vessels were run aground on tidal beaches; residual fuel oils, heavy metals, and toxic anti-fouling paints frequently washed directly into the marine environment. The regulatory transition: IMO established explicit facility authorisation criteria under the HKC. India concurrently enacted the Recycling of Ships Act, 2019 , giving a statutory framework to upgrade domestic yards. Modern global enforcement (post-2025): Following the HKC's global entry into force on 26 June 2025 , yards using intertidal beaching had to adapt — Alang, India installed impermeable heavy-lift concrete structures and advanced drainage recovery systems to remain internationally authorised.

section_title: 4 · IMO / International Regulatory References
text: 4 · IMO / International Regulatory References ⚖ Regulatory References HKC Annex — Ch. 3 Requirements for Ship Recycling Facilities — core criteria for authorisation and operation of SRFs. HKC Annex — Reg. 16 Authorization of Ship Recycling Facilities — competent national authority audits and formally authorises yards via a DASR. HKC Annex — Reg. 18 Ship Recycling Facility Plan (SRFP) — mandates a comprehensive manual of technical capability, safety equipment, and waste-management infrastructure. HKC Annex — Reg. 9 Vessel-specific Ship Recycling Plan (SRP) — approved by the recycling company and the responsible flag state. MEPC.211(63) 2012 Guidelines for the Authorization of Ship Recycling Facilities — technical benchmarks for environmental monitoring and infrastructure design. CE Oral Tip: Nair-style examiners like exact regulation numbers here. Know that the DASR is issued under Regulation 16 and is valid for a maximum of 5 years , and that the SRFP obligation sits under Regulation 18 — these two numbers come up repeatedly in facility-authorisation questions.

section_title: 5 · Engineering Explanation & Core Technical Mechanisms
text: 5 · Engineering Explanation & Core Technical Mechanisms SRFP vs. Vessel-Specific SRP An authorised facility operates under two distinct documentation layers: Ship Recycling Facility Plan (SRFP): The yard's master operational manual — physical footprint, crane capacities, maximum GT limits, emergency response plans, worker training programmes, downstream hazardous-waste contracts. Vessel-Specific Ship Recycling Plan (SRP): A customised deconstruction manual for each ship, cross-referencing its IHM with the yard's cutting capabilities — cutting sequence, stability calculations during mass reduction, and containment procedures for materials found on board. Intertidal Impermeable Catchment Pad & Drainage Mechanics To prevent hydrocarbon and heavy-metal leaching into the coastal ecosystem, modern yards use an engineered Intertidal Catchment Pad — a thick, reinforced concrete pad positioned above the high-tide zone, extending down to interface safely with the vessel's primary cutting block. INTERTIDAL CATCHMENT PAD & FILTER STRUCTURE [ Vessel Hull Block ] ---> ( Primary Cutting Area / Heavy-Duty Reinforced Concrete Pad ) | v (Gravity-Driven Surface Runoff) +-------------------------------+ | Impermeable Coated Sump Drain | +-------------------------------+ | v +-------------------------------+ | Multi-Stage Coalescing Plate | | Oil-Water Separator | +-------------------------------+ | | v (Recovered Oil) v (Pre-Treated Effluent) [ Sludge Holding ] [ Heavy Metal Chelating Filters ] | v [ Evaporation Ponds / Municipal Treatment ] The concrete surface is treated with an oil-resistant epoxy coating and sloped toward dedicated collection sumps. Rain run-off and industrial wash-water are directed into a multi-stage gravity-driven coalescing-plate oil-water separator, which isolates oils for recovery while channelling the water through chelating filters to capture suspended heavy metals before disposal. Downstream Waste Reconciliation — the Mass-Balance Principle To prevent illegal toxic dumping, an authorised facility must be able to demonstrate that the hazardous-material quantities logged in the incoming vessel's IHM roughly match what was actually sent for treatment. In practice this means: every waste stream extracted from the ship (asbestos lagging, PCB-laden cables, oily sludge, heavy-metal residues) is weighed, logged with a unique tracking code, and matched against a certified destruction or treatment receipt issued by the receiving TSDF. A significant, unexplained gap between the IHM-declared quantity and the TSDF-received quantity is the red flag a Competent Authority audit is designed to catch — it points either to under-declaration in the original IHM or to undocumented dumping. Exam answers should describe this reconciliation principle in these terms rather than quoting a specific numeric tolerance, since no such figure is published in the HKC Annex or IMO guidelines.

section_title: 6 · Chief Engineer & Flag State Responsibilities
text: 6 · Chief Engineer & Flag State Responsibilities Chief Engineer Responsibilities (Handover & Decommissioning Phase) Safe-for-Hot-Work verification: Supervise deep-pumping and mechanical cleaning of residual bunker tanks; ensure independent certified marine chemists inspect enclosed machinery spaces, pump rooms, and double-bottom tanks to issue valid "Safe-for-Entry" and "Safe-for-Hot-Work" certificates before torch cutting. Data integrity handover: Provide the yard's safety officer with the finalised, verified IHM Parts I, II and III; point out exact locations of fixed hazardous materials (heavy lead ballast, mercury switches) to match the yard's cutting plan. Flag State & Competent National Authority Responsibilities Final verification audit: Flag State surveyor reviews the complete documentation package to confirm operational-lifetime IHM updates match the vessel's final physical condition. IRRC issuance: Upon confirming the yard's SRP is officially approved by the recycling state's National Authority, the Flag State issues the IRRC, authorising the vessel's final voyage to the facility.

section_title: 7 · Practical Shipboard Application
text: 7 · Practical Shipboard Application Case Study — Removal of Friable Asbestos Insulation, Alang An international cargo vessel arrives at an authorised recycling facility in Alang. Its SRP identifies friable asbestos lagging around an obsolete auxiliary exhaust gas economiser line in the upper engine room casing. STEP 1: CONSTRUCTING THE NEGATIVE-PRESSURE CONTAINMENT TENT - Enclose the work zone using heavy-gauge polyethylene sheets. - Install HEPA filtration units to maintain internal negative pressure. | v STEP 2: WET-STRIPPING EXTRACTION PROTOCOLS - Technicians wear positive-pressure respirators and protective suits. - Wet the lagging with surfactant-treated water to suppress toxic fibers. | v STEP 3: DOUBLE-BAG SEALING & MASS VERIFICATION - Place stripped insulation into labeled, heavy-gauge plastic bags. - Seal, weigh, and log each bag with a unique hazardous tracking code. | v STEP 4: TSDF TRANSFER & FINAL DESTRUCTION LANDFILL - Secure waste in sealed containers for transport to an approved TSDF. - TSDF issues a waste receipt certificate to close the tracking loop. Incident: Hydrocarbon Spill on the Catchment Pad During Block Lifting During the crane lift of a 45-metric-tonne lower engine room block, an unmapped auxiliary lube oil line ruptures, spilling residual medium-viscosity lubricant onto the concrete pad. Immediate drainage isolation: Activate the emergency manual shut-off valve at the catchment pad's primary drain outlet, isolating the pad and protecting the oil-water separator from overload. Absorbent boom deployment: Deploy hydrophobic absorbent booms around the slick; apply granular oil-binding silicate polymers onto the pad to absorb the liquid phase. Mechanical scraping & log verification: Use non-sparking scrapers to collect saturated absorbent into hazardous-waste drums; log recovered oil volume and contaminated-absorbent mass for TSDF transfer, then reopen the drainage path.

section_title: 8 · Survey Requirements & Port State Control Focus
text: 8 · Survey Requirements & Port State Control Focus Facility Authorisation & Continuous Audit Requirements Initial authorisation audit: Technical review of infrastructure, verification of the master SRFP, physical testing of containment pads and drainage systems — leads to DASR issuance, valid up to 5 years . Annual surveillance audits: Unannounced inspections verifying worker health records, PPE compliance logs, air-monitoring samples, and TSDF receipts against active operational volumes. Vessel-specific inspections: Physical spot-checks before, during, and after cutting each vessel to confirm the yard follows its approved SRP. National Authority Inspection Focus Air and soil monitoring verification: Independent laboratory records for airborne asbestos-fibre counts and heavy-metal soil contamination around the facility perimeter. Enclosed-space entry control audits: "Safe-for-Entry" logs and calibrated, bump-tested four-gas atmospheric monitors before enclosed-space entry. ⚠ PSC / National Authority Alert — Common Non-Compliance Findings Improper downstream chain-of-custody logging: Missing certified TSDF receipts within the required timeframe can lead to temporary suspension of the operating license. Catchment pad cracking/degradation: Structural cracks allowing oily water to leach into the soil trigger an immediate halt to cutting in that zone until repairs and re-coating are complete.

section_title: 9 · Structural Comparison — Legacy Beaching vs. Compliant Authorized SRF
text: 9 · Structural Comparison — Legacy Beaching vs. Compliant Authorized SRF Parameter Legacy Beaching Scrap Yard Compliant Authorized SRF (HKC) Primary structural deck Unprotected intertidal mud/sand surfaces. Impermeable reinforced concrete pads with oil-resistant epoxy coating. Drainage catchment Zero containment; runoff drains directly to sea. Gravity-sloped pad channels to multi-stage oil-water separators. Asbestos remediation Open-air manual ripping; high airborne-fibre risk. Negative-pressure containment tents with certified HEPA filtration. Downstream waste accountability Unregulated third-party scrap dealers, no tracking. Direct integration with authorised TSDF networks via electronic tracking logs. Gas-freeing & entry protocols Ad-hoc checks, reliant on natural ventilation. Mandatory Marine Chemist certification, continuous gas-monitoring logs.

section_title: 1 · Definition & Purpose
text: 1 · Definition & Purpose The 2023 IMO Strategy on the Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships (the "2023 IMO GHG Strategy"), adopted by Resolution MEPC.377(80) at MEPC 80 on 7 July 2023, is the binding international policy framework governing the phased decarbonisation of the global merchant fleet. It supersedes the more modest 2018 Initial Strategy and commits international shipping to a pathway that peaks GHG emissions as soon as possible and reaches net-zero GHG emissions by or around (i.e. close to) 2050 . The Strategy itself is a policy instrument, not a self-executing regulation — it is implemented through binding amendments to MARPOL Annex VI . The short-term measures (EEXI, CII, enhanced SEEMP) already give the Strategy legal teeth today; the mid-term technical and economic measures (a goal-based fuel standard and GHG pricing mechanism, intended as a new Chapter 5 of Annex VI) are still working through the IMO's adoption process — see the status note in Section 4.

section_subtitle: 10 · Examination Question Bank

10 · Examination Question Bank
text: 10 · Examination Question Bank Part 1 — Strategic Architecture of the 2023 Revised Strategy The 2023 IMO Revised GHG Strategy accelerates the regulatory path to full decarbonisation, replacing the 2018 Initial Strategy's 50% absolute-reduction goal with net-zero GHG emissions by or around 2050. Intermediate indicative checkpoints — at least 20% (striving for 30%) reduction by 2030 and at least 70% (striving for 80%) by 2040, both against 2008 — track progress, alongside a target that ZNZ energy sources reach at least 5% (striving for 10%) of total fleet energy use by 2030. Part 2 — Mechanics of Short-Term Carbon Intensity Indicators EEXI is a one-off design constraint (attained EEXI ≤ required EEXI), verified for the International Energy Efficiency Certificate. CII is a retrospective annual operational index producing an A–E rating from real logged performance. Part 3 — Enforcement and Corrective Action Enforcement runs through the Statement of Compliance: a vessel cannot trade internationally without a valid SoC. A single-year 'E' rating, or 'D' for three consecutive years, triggers a mandatory SEEMP Part III corrective action plan, which must identify the operational root causes and be audited/approved by the Flag Administration or an authorised RO before a new SoC issues. Part 4 — Technical and Operational Remediation Pathways Engine Power Limitation (EPL): mechanical or electronic fuel-rack lock capping maximum shaft output, forcing a lower, more efficient operating speed. Hydrodynamic upgrades: Mewis ducts, propeller boss cap fins, low-friction anti-fouling coatings. Energy-saving technologies: wind-assisted propulsion (e.g. Flettner rotors), air lubrication systems. Fuel transition: biofuel blending, or conversion/dual-fuel retrofit to LNG, methanol, or ammonia. 8 marks Explain the technical differences between EEXI and CII, and outline the administrative consequences of an 'E' rating. EEXI: design constraint, attained ≤ required, single verification event tied to the IEE Certificate. CII: retrospective operational metric, recalculated every calendar year from DCS-logged performance. 'E' rating consequence: mandatory SEEMP Part III revision with a documented corrective action plan, audited and approved by the Flag Administration/RO before a Statement of Compliance can be reissued. 10 marks Describe the structural updates of the 2023 IMO Revised GHG Strategy over the 2018 Initial Strategy, focusing on interim checkpoints and alternative energy targets. 2018 vs 2023 headline target: 50% absolute reduction by 2050 (2018) superseded by net-zero by or around 2050 (2023). Interim checkpoints: at least 20% (striving 30%) reduction by 2030; at least 70% (striving 80%) by 2040, both vs 2008. Fleet carbon-intensity target: at least 40% reduction per transport work by 2030. New 2030 alternative-energy target: ZNZ technologies/fuels at least 5% (striving 10%) of total shipping energy use.

section_title: 2 · Importance to International Shipping
text: 2 · Importance to International Shipping The Strategy fundamentally reshapes vessel valuation, chartering, and shipboard engineering management. Its headline levels of ambition, benchmarked against a 2008 baseline, are: Carbon intensity of the ship: continued reduction through EEDI/EEXI phases for new and existing ships. Fleet carbon intensity: reduce CO 2 emissions per transport work, across international shipping, by at least 40% by 2030 . Uptake of zero or near-zero (ZNZ) GHG technologies, fuels and energy sources: at least 5%, striving for 10% , of the energy used by international shipping by 2030. Net-zero target: peak emissions as soon as possible and reach net-zero by or around 2050 . Indicative checkpoints support these levels of ambition: at least 20%, striving for 30%, total annual GHG reduction by 2030 versus 2008; and at least 70%, striving for 80%, by 2040. For a Chief Engineer, these targets translate directly into carbon budgets that bind a ship's commercial trading life to its measured operational efficiency.

text: 4 · IMO / International Regulatory References Statutory Architecture — Short-Term Measures (in force) MARPOL Annex VI Ch.4 Regulations on Energy Efficiency of Ships. Reg. 20 & 21 EEDI requirement and calculation for new ships. Reg. 22 & 23 SEEMP and EEXI requirements for existing ships. Reg. 26 Verification of attained EEXI on existing ships. Reg. 27 & 28 Data collection (IMO DCS) and operational CII rating. Res. MEPC.328(76) 2021 amendments introducing EEXI/CII/enhanced SEEMP (in force 1 Nov 2022). Res. MEPC.354(78) 2022 Guidelines on the Operational Carbon Intensity Rating of Ships (CII Rating Guidelines, G4) — the A–E boundary scale; see the full G1–G5 guideline table in Section 5C. Res. MEPC.377(80) 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships. ⚠ Regulatory status note — mid-term measures (Chapter 5) are NOT yet in force MEPC 83 (April 2025) approved draft amendments introducing a new Chapter 5 — IMO Net-Zero Framework (goal-based fuel standard + carbon pricing/reward mechanism) by a vote of 63 in favour, 16 against, 24 abstentions . The extraordinary session convened to formally adopt the text, MEPC/ES.2 (14–17 October 2025), did not vote on adoption at all — instead, a procedural motion to adjourn consideration for one year (moved by Singapore, put to a vote by Saudi Arabia) passed 57 in favour, 49 against, 21 abstentions, 8 absent . Adoption is now deferred to a reconvened session tentatively scheduled for 30 November–3 December 2026 — MEPC 85 (30 Nov–3 Dec) followed by a resumed one-day MEPC/ES.2 session on 4 December, per MEPC 84's April 2026 outcome — though this remains provisional and subject to further confirmation; do not state this date as settled fact in an exam answer. As a direct consequence of the 2025 delay, the earliest possible entry into force has shifted from March 2027 to on/around March 2028 . Do not state in an exam answer that Chapter 5 is "in force" or give a fixed entry-into-force date as settled fact — describe it as approved at MEPC 83, adoption deferred at MEPC/ES.2, and pending the tentative late-2026 reconvened session. This chapter covers only the short-term measures (EEXI/CII/SEEMP), which are already in force; the mid-term GFI framework is covered separately once adopted.

section_title: 5 · Engineering Explanation & Core Technical Mechanisms
text: 5 · Engineering Explanation & Core Technical Mechanisms A. Energy Efficiency Design and Existing Ship Indices (EEDI / EEXI) EEDI (newbuilds) and EEXI (existing ships) are structural, design-verification indices — calculated once per vessel (barring major conversion) — expressing theoretical CO 2 grams emitted per tonne-mile of transport work at a reference design condition: $$EEDI\ /\ EEXI = \frac{\left(\prod_{j} f_j\right)\left(\sum_i P_{ME(i)} \cdot C_{F\,ME(i)} \cdot SFC_{ME(i)}\right) + \left(P_{AE} \cdot C_{FAE} \cdot SFC_{AE}\right) - \left(\sum_l f_{eff(l)} \cdot P_{eff(l)} \cdot C_{FME} \cdot SFC_{ME}\right)}{f_i \cdot f_c \cdot Capacity \cdot V_{ref}}$$ EEDI / EEXI Formula in Words EEDI / EEXI = Net CO₂ Emitted ÷ Transport Work Capacity Numerator (Net CO₂ Emitted, per Voyage-Equivalent) Take the main engine's rated power, multiply by that engine's carbon factor and its specific fuel consumption — this gives main-engine CO₂ output. Do the same for the auxiliary engines and add the two together. Then subtract any CO₂ credit earned from innovative energy-saving devices (e.g. shaft generators, waste-heat recovery) that reduce the effective power draw. Finally, multiply the whole result by a correction-factor product that accounts for ship-type features such as ice-class or general cargo capacity adjustments. Denominator (Transport Work Capacity) Multiply the ship's cargo-carrying capacity (deadweight or gross tonnage, depending on ship type) by its reference speed at that capacity, then apply the capacity- and speed-correction factors. Spoken Version "Sir, EEDI and EEXI express grams of CO₂ emitted per tonne-mile of transport work at a reference design condition. The numerator is the net CO₂ output — main engine power times its carbon factor times specific fuel consumption, plus the same for the auxiliary engines, minus any credit for energy-saving devices, all scaled by ship-type correction factors. The denominator is the ship's capacity multiplied by its reference speed. A ship complies when its attained value is at or below the required value for its size and ship-type phase." Same Formula Shape — So What Actually Differs? EEDI and EEXI use the identical structure above, but they are not the same calculation in practice, because the value plugged into $P_{ME}$ differs: Point of Difference EEDI (newbuild) EEXI (existing ship) When calculated Once, at the design stage, before the ship is built — a forward-looking design commitment. Once, retrospectively, at the ship's first survey on or after 1 Jan 2023 — a one-time check on a ship already in service. Power value used ($P_{ME}$) 75% of the engine's as-built Maximum Continuous Rating (MCR) — the power the engine was actually designed to deliver. Also 75% of MCR normally, but if the owner has fitted an overridable Engine Power Limitation (EPL) or Shaft Power Limitation (ShaPoLi) system, the calculation instead uses 83% of the limited power ($MCR_{lim}$) — i.e. a deliberately derated figure, per the 2021 Guidelines (Res. MEPC.335(76)). Why this matters A newbuild is designed from scratch to meet its EEDI target — no retrofit needed. An existing ship with an oversized engine can mechanically or electronically cap its power via EPL/ShaPoLi, which lowers $MCR$, lowers $C_F \cdot SFC \cdot P_{ME}$, and brings attained EEXI below the required value without any hardware change to the engine itself — this is why EPL is the single most common EEXI compliance route across the fleet today. Reference speed source Taken from the ship's own EEDI sea-trial data (mandatory for ships in the EEDI scope). For ships that were never subject to EEDI (built before the phase-in), $V_{ref}$ may instead come from an estimated speed-power curve per the 2022 EEXI survey guidelines (Res. MEPC.351(78)), since no EEDI sea-trial record exists. Applicability Ships ≥400 GT across the 11 MARPOL Annex VI ship-type categories, keel-laid/delivered per the EEDI phase-in schedule since 1 Jan 2013. Ships ≥400 GT built before 1 Jan 2023, same 11 categories. Caution: the MARPOL reg. 2.13/2.18 definition of "existing ship" (built before 1 Jan 2013) applies only to EEDI major-conversion rules — it does not define EEXI applicability. A common oral-exam trap. Required-value reduction-factor phase (the primary regulatory difference) Progressive Phase 1 → 2 → 3 reduction factors, tied to build/delivery year — later phases are stricter. Required EEXI is generally set at the same level as EEDI Phase 2 for most ship types, but four categories — container ships, cruise ships, LNG carriers, and gas carriers — must meet the tougher, accelerated Phase 3 level (applicable from 1 April 2022). This reduction-factor linkage, not just the power/speed inputs, is what most classification-society guidance treats as the main EEDI/EEXI difference. Governing calculation guideline Res. MEPC.364(79) (2022) — current in-force EEDI Calculation Guidelines, consolidating the earlier MEPC.245(66)/MEPC.308(73) lineage. Res. MEPC.350(78) (2022) — EEXI Calculation Guidelines, which explicitly cross-refer to the EEDI guidelines, instructing the reader to substitute "EEXI" wherever "EEDI" appears. Carry-forward option N/A If a ship already has an attained EEDI on file (i.e. it was EEDI-scope at build) and that attained EEDI ≤ the required EEXI, the existing EEDI value may be declared directly as the attained EEXI — no fresh EEXI calculation is required (Res. MEPC.350(78)). Scope of power considered Both indices account only for propulsion (main engine) power, plus a fixed 2.5% allowance for auxiliary engine power — neither is a whole-ship energy audit. A common misconception worth pre-empting in an oral answer: EEDI/EEXI say nothing about hotel load, cargo-handling power, or reefer container consumption — that is what CII (Section 5B) captures instead. Where $P_{ME}$/$P_{AE}$ are design power outputs (kW); $C_F$ is the fuel's carbon factor (e.g. ≈3.114 g-CO₂/g-fuel for standard fuel oil, per MARPOL Annex VI Appendix VI); $SFC$ is specific fuel consumption (g/kWh) from NO x Technical Code test-bed trials; $Capacity$ is deadweight or gross tonnage at summer load draft; $V_{ref}$ is service speed at that capacity/power setting. A ship complies when its attained EEDI/EEXI is at or below the required value set by the applicable reduction-factor phase. Required EEDI / Required EEXI — MARPOL Annex VI, Regulations 24 & 25 The formulas above give the ship's attained value. Compliance is judged against a separate required value, defined directly in the Convention text (MARPOL Annex VI consolidated edition, as amended by Res. MEPC.328(76), MEPC.361(79), MEPC.362(79)): $$Required\ EEDI = \left(1 - \frac{X}{100}\right) \cdot \text{Reference line value} \qquad \text{[Reg. 24]}$$ $$Required\ EEXI = \left(1 - \frac{Y}{100}\right) \cdot \text{Reference line value} \qquad \text{[Reg. 25]}$$ $$\text{Reference line value} = a \cdot b^{-c} \qquad \text{[common to both]}$$ Required EEDI / EEXI Formula in Words Required Value = (1 − Reduction Factor) × Reference Line Value Reference Line Value (the common baseline) A curve fitted to historical fleet performance for each ship type, expressed as a constant $a$ multiplied by the ship's own size parameter (DWT or GT, called $b$ here) raised to a negative exponent $c$ — larger ships sit lower on the curve. Both EEDI and EEXI are measured against the same reference line for a given ship type; only the reduction factor applied to it differs. Reduction Factor — X (EEDI) vs Y (EEXI) Subtract the reduction factor (as a percentage) from 100%, then multiply that surviving fraction by the reference line value. X (Table 1) increases through EEDI Phase 1 → 2 → 3 as build year gets later — a newbuild delivered today faces a stricter X than one delivered in 2015. Y (Table 3) is fixed at whatever percentage corresponds to the EEDI Phase 2 level for most ship types — except container ships, cruise ships, LNG carriers and gas carriers, which are held to the accelerated Phase 3 level instead (see the table above). Spoken Version "Sir, both Required EEDI and Required EEXI are calculated the same way — one minus the reduction factor, over 100, multiplied by the EEDI reference line value for that ship type. The reference line itself is a curve, a times the ship's capacity to the power of minus c, common to both indices. What differs is only which reduction-factor table applies: X from Table 1 for EEDI, which gets stricter with each build-year phase, or Y from Table 3 for EEXI, which is generally frozen at the Phase 2 level, except for four ship types held to Phase 3." B. Operational Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) Unlike the design indices, CII is a dynamic, retrospective operational metric calculated at the close of each calendar year from actual logged performance: $$Attained\ CII_{annual} = \frac{\sum_j M_j \cdot C_{Fj}}{Capacity \cdot D_{att}}$$ Attained CII Formula in Words Attained CII = Total CO₂ Emitted (year) ÷ (Capacity × Distance Sailed) Numerator (Total CO₂ Emitted Over the Calendar Year) For each fuel type consumed over the year, take the total mass burned and multiply it by that fuel's carbon conversion factor. Add these fuel-wise totals together to get the ship's total logged CO₂ output for the year. Denominator (Transport Work Actually Performed) Multiply the ship's capacity (deadweight or gross tonnage) by the total distance actually sailed over the year, taken from the oil record book or GPS log. Spoken Version "Sir, the Attained CII numerator is the total CO₂ emitted over the calendar year — the sum, across all fuels burned, of each fuel's mass multiplied by its carbon conversion factor. The denominator is the ship's capacity multiplied by the actual distance sailed that year. Dividing the two gives grams of CO₂ per capacity-mile, which is then compared against the Required CII reference line to assign the annual A-to-E rating." Numerator Worked as a Formula — Multi-Fuel Ship (e.g. VLSFO + MDO) A container ship rarely burns one fuel all year — main engine on VLSFO (Heavy Fuel Oil family), auxiliary/boiler on MDO (Marine Diesel Oil) during ECA transits and manoeuvring. The numerator is simply each fuel's annual mass multiplied by its own $C_F$, added together: $$\text{Numerator} = \left(M_{VLSFO} \times C_{F,\,HFO}\right) + \left(M_{MDO} \times C_{F,\,MDO}\right) + \dots$$ Using the IMO's standard $C_F$ values (Res. MEPC.281(70), Appendix IX table — same factors used for IMO DCS reporting): HFO/VLSFO family = 3.114 , MDO/MGO = 3.206 , LFO = 3.151, LNG = 2.750, Methanol = 1.375, Ethanol = 1.913 (all in tonnes CO₂ per tonne fuel). Worked example: a ship burning 8,000 t VLSFO and 500 t MDO in a calendar year — $$\text{Numerator} = (8{,}000 \times 3.114) + (500 \times 3.206) = 24{,}912 + 1{,}603 = 26{,}515\ \text{t CO}_2$$ This 26,515 t CO₂ figure is then divided by (Capacity × Distance Sailed) to give the Attained CII in grams CO₂ per capacity-mile. Every additional fuel type on board — LNG, methanol, biofuel blends — simply adds one more $(M_j \times C_{Fj})$ term to the same sum; the formula structure never changes, only the number of terms. Where $M_j$ is total mass (g) of fuel type $j$ consumed over the calendar year; $C_{Fj}$ is the carbon conversion factor for fuel $j$; $D_{att}$ is total distance travelled over ground (nautical miles), from the oil record book / GPS log. The Attained CII is compared against a ship-type- and size-specific Required CII reference line to assign an annual rating of A (major superior) through E (inferior). C. The CII Guideline Family (G1–G5) — Know All Five for the Oral CII is not governed by a single resolution — it is a suite of five linked guideline documents, each covering one part of the calculation-to-rating chain. Examiners frequently ask "what does G-series mean for CII?" as a rapid-fire check. Note the resolution numbers below are the current, in-force 2022 versions — several sources online (including AI-generated ones) still cite the original 2021 resolutions, which were revoked and replaced at MEPC 78 in June 2022. Guide Current Resolution Purpose G1 Res. MEPC.352(78) (2022) (revoked 2021 original, Res. MEPC.336(76)) Calculation methods and applicability of Attained CII for individual ships — the formula and worked example above. G2 Res. MEPC.353(78) (2022) (revoked 2021 original, Res. MEPC.337(76)) Reference lines for use with operational carbon intensity indicators — the baseline curve each ship type is measured against. G3 Res. MEPC.338(76) (2021), as amended by Res. MEPC.400(83) (2025) Annual reduction factors ("Z" factors) relative to the reference line — see the confirmed 2023–2030 table below. G4 Res. MEPC.354(78) (2022) (revoked 2021 original, Res. MEPC.339(76)) Operational carbon intensity rating boundaries — the A–E scale itself. G5 Res. MEPC.355(78) (2022) Interim correction factors and voyage adjustments — see below; this is the guideline candidates most often forget entirely. Confirmed CII Reduction ("Z") Factors, 2023–2030 The 2027–2030 figures were previously undecided in earlier editions of the G3 guidelines; MEPC 83 (April 2025) closed that gap by adopting Res. MEPC.400(83), fixing the annual increment at 2.625% per year from 2027 onward, reaching 21.5% by 2030: Year 2023 2024 2025 2026 2027 2028 2029 2030 Z factor (vs 2019 baseline) 5% 7% 9% 11% 13.625% 16.25% 18.875% 21.5% Correction Factors & Voyage Adjustments (G5) — Often Omitted, Heavily Tested Attained CII is not simply raw annual fuel mass over distance — Res. MEPC.355(78) allows specific, legitimate deductions from the numerator before the final A–E rating is struck, recognising that some fuel consumption is not representative of the ship's normal carbon efficiency: Voyage adjustments ($FC_{voyage}$): fuel consumption may be excluded for voyages undertaken solely for securing the safety of the ship or saving life at sea (applies to all ships), and for voyages in ice conditions (ice-classed ships only). $AF_{TankerSTS}$: a correction factor for oil tankers engaged in ship-to-ship (STS) transfer voyages, recognising the additional fuel burned manoeuvring alongside another tanker rather than on passage. $AF_{TankerShuttle}$: a correction for shuttle tankers operating with dynamic positioning during offshore loading. $FC_{electrical}$: deducts fuel used to generate additional electrical load for reefer containers, gas-carrier cargo handling, or LNG/tanker cargo-system equipment — cargo-driven consumption, not propulsion inefficiency. $FC_{boiler}$ and $FC_{others}$: deduct fuel used for tanker cargo heating or inert gas system operation. Each correction is applied to the relevant fuel-mass term before it enters the $\sum_j M_j \cdot C_{Fj}$ numerator — this is the practical answer to "how is Attained CII actually calculated," and a candidate who only states the raw formula without mentioning corrections is giving an incomplete answer. "Is CII Being Combined with EEXI?" — What's Actually Happening There is no literal merger of the two indices into a single formula — this is a common misconception worth pre-empting directly in an oral answer. What is true: MEPC 83 (April 2025) completed Phase 1 of the IMO's review of the short-term GHG measures, which examined CII, SEEMP, and EEXI together as one package , since all three share the same enforcement chain under MARPOL Annex VI regulation 28 (technical file → SEEMP Part III → Statement of Compliance). Out of that joint review: the CII G3 reduction factors were extended to 2030 (above), while EEXI itself was not substantively reopened. Phase 2 of the review is now underway — per IMO's own published timeline it runs Spring 2026 to Spring 2028 , and will look at further developing CII metrics, enhancing the SEEMP framework, and — most relevant to your question — ensuring synergies between the CII/EEXI energy-efficiency framework and the IMO Net-Zero Framework (Chapter 5) once that is adopted. So: EEXI and CII remain two separate, independently certified regimes (EEXI under the one-time IEE Certificate, CII under the annual Statement of Compliance) linked only structurally — a ship's EEXI technical-file parameters (capacity, reference speed) feed conceptually into CII's denominator logic, but there is no regulatory plan to fuse them into one index. Treat any claim of a fixed "MEPC 85, October 2026" decision date on this with caution — IMO's own Phase 2 work plan gives a two-year window (Spring 2026–Spring 2028), not a single decisive session.

section_title: 6 · Chief Engineer & Flag State Responsibilities
text: 6 · Chief Engineer & Flag State Responsibilities Chief Engineer Directives DCS data integrity: daily logging of fuel consumption by distinct consumer (main engine, auxiliary engines, boilers), split "underway"/"not underway", from calibrated flow meters or verified soundings. SEEMP Part III execution: implement the ship-specific 3-year rolling improvement plan to maintain or recover at least a 'C' rating. Voyage optimisation: weather routing, main engine RPM/shaft-power limits (EPL/ShaPoLi), and trim management to minimise fuel burn without breaching safe operating limits. Flag State / Recognized Organization (RO) Responsibilities Verification: audit annual fuel-consumption data submitted under IMO DCS, due by 31 March of the following year. Certification: issue the annual Statement of Compliance (SoC) for fuel consumption and carbon intensity. Enforcement: require a SEEMP Part III corrective action plan for a 'D' rating three years running, or a single-year 'E' rating.

section_title: 7 · Practical Shipboard Application & Case Study
text: 7 · Practical Shipboard Application & Case Study Case Study — Capesize Bulk Carrier Trending to a 'D' Rating A large bulk carrier on standard VLSFO projects a 'D' rating by Q3 year-end. Main engine: 2-stroke, electronically controlled, MCR 16,500 kW; average consumption ≈46.5 MT/day at 13.5 knots; boiler ≈1.8 MT/day in port, ≈0.5 MT/day at sea. [Analyse Q3 DCS data] -> [Apply overridable EPL] -> [Trim & routing optimisation] -> [Re-project year-end CII] Engine Power Limitation (EPL): electronically de-rate maximum shaft output (e.g. to ~65% MCR), enforcing an eco-speed. Fuel consumption falls with the cube of speed for a given hull/propeller combination: $$P_{new} = P_{old} \cdot \left(\frac{V_{new}}{V_{old}}\right)^{3}$$ Speed–Power Cube Law in Words New Power = Old Power × (New Speed ÷ Old Speed)³ Take the ratio of the new speed to the old speed, cube that ratio (multiply it by itself three times), then multiply by the old power requirement to get the new power requirement. In plain terms: a small cut in speed produces a much larger cut in power — and therefore fuel burn — because resistance grows disproportionately with speed for a fixed hull and propeller. For example, a 10% speed reduction (ratio 0.9) cuts power demand by roughly 27% (0.9³ ≈ 0.73), not 10%. Spoken Version "Sir, the cube law states that required power is proportional to the cube of speed for a given hull and propeller. So the new power equals the old power multiplied by the ratio of new speed to old speed, raised to the power of three. This is why modest speed reduction under EPL delivers a disproportionately large fuel and CII benefit." Auxiliary load optimisation: clean boiler smoke tubes to improve heat-transfer efficiency; concentrate non-essential high electrical loads (ballast treatment, deck-crane testing) into port stays; run a single auxiliary engine at sea where safe. Trim optimisation: adjust ballast distribution to keep the bulbous bow effectively submerged and minimise wave-making resistance. Result: reducing speed and cleaning up auxiliary consumption lowers grams of CO 2 per tonne-mile enough to move the projected rating from 'D' back toward 'C' by the December 31 close — illustrating how CII is managed operationally rather than through hardware retrofit alone.

section_title: 8 · Survey Requirements (HSSC) & Port State Control Focus
text: 8 · Survey Requirements (HSSC) & Port State Control Focus Survey Requirements Initial survey: on delivery, or before issue of the International Energy Efficiency (IEE) Certificate — verifies the EEDI/EEXI technical file and certified SEEMP Part I. Sea-trial verification (tightened from 1 May 2026): Res. MEPC.403(83) (adopted 11 April 2025, MEPC 83) amends the EEDI Survey & Certification Guidelines (Res. MEPC.365(79)) so that, for sea trials conducted on or after 1 May 2026 , power curves must be built from measured ship speed and measured main engine output, corrected per the updated ISO 15016:2025 standard or ITTC Recommended Procedure 7.5-04-01-01.1 (2024) — the older ISO 15016:2015 basis is no longer valid after that date. Practical tightening: ship-length-dependent maximum wind-speed limits, mandatory wave-buoy calibration data submitted to the verifier, and a stricter, standardised wave-correction priority sequence. This is a genuine increase in verification rigor at the final (sea-trial) stage — not a shift to ongoing operational EEDI monitoring; EEDI remains a one-time design-stage index. Periodical/annual audits: confirm any retrofit affecting installed power (ducting, propeller boss fins, EPL seals) matches the technical file. SEEMP Part III verification: confirms an approved, ship-specific, multi-year improvement plan exists and is followed. Port State Control Focus Document check: validity of the Statement of Compliance for the preceding calendar year. SEEMP Part III onboard verification: documented evidence the crew is executing the plan's stated optimisation measures. EPL/ShaPoLi integrity: physical check of tamper-evident seals on fuel-rack limiters, or electronic shaft-power-limiting logs. ⚠ High-Risk Detention Vectors Missing or expired Statement of Compliance after 31 May of the reporting year. Broken or unlogged EPL override without a documented safety justification in the engine room logbook. No corrective action plan filed in SEEMP Part III after consecutive non-compliant ratings.

Model Answer · Written Question (15 marks) Discuss the key elements of the revised IMO strategy on the reduction of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from ships, including the new Chapter 5 of MARPOL Annex VI, and explain the mid-term and long-term measures proposed to achieve the targets and their potential impact on the shipping industry.

section_title: 1 · Definition & Purpose
text: 1 · Definition & Purpose The IMO Net-Zero Framework is the set of mid-term technical and economic measures that will implement the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy's decarbonisation targets. It is drafted as a new Chapter 5 of MARPOL Annex VI ("Regulations on the IMO Net-Zero Framework") and combines two elements: A technical element — a goal-based marine fuel standard mandating a phased reduction in the Well-to-Wake (WtW) GHG Fuel Intensity (GFI) of the energy used on board. An economic element — a global maritime GHG emissions pricing mechanism , linking a ship's compliance balance to a levy/reward system. Unlike the short-term measures covered in Chapter 1 (EEXI, CII), which regulate a ship's own operational efficiency, Chapter 5 regulates the carbon content of the fuel itself , evaluated across its full lifecycle rather than only at the exhaust stack.

10 · Examination Question Bank
text: 10 · Examination Question Bank Part 1 — Strategic Architecture and the Role of Chapter 5 The 2023 IMO GHG Strategy commits the fleet to net-zero by or around 2050. Chapter 5 of MARPOL Annex VI, approved at MEPC 83 and pending formal adoption, is the primary regulatory vehicle for the mid-term measures: a technical goal-based marine fuel standard (GFS) and an economic GHG pricing mechanism, working together to force annual reductions in fuel lifecycle intensity. Part 2 — Technical Mechanics of the GFS The GFS caps the annual Well-to-Wake GHG intensity (GFI) of shipboard energy, in gCO 2 eq/MJ. By including the Well-to-Tank component, it prevents shifting emissions upstream during fuel production, and by weighting CH 4 and N 2 O by their global warming potentials it captures the true lifecycle footprint, not just tailpipe CO 2 . Part 3 — Compliance Mechanics Ships beating their Direct Compliance Target earn Surplus Units, bankable or tradeable. Ships in deficit must buy Remedial Units, priced by tier (Tier 1 between the Direct Compliance and Base lines at $100/tCO 2 eq; a materially higher rate above the Base line). Long-term compliance eventually phases out conventional fuel oil entirely as targets tighten toward 2050. Part 4 — Evaluation of Shipping Industry Impact A strong "evaluate" answer weighs both the enabling and the burdensome effects, then reaches a judgement — not just a list. Enabling / Positive Impacts First-mover commercial advantage: ships beating the Direct Compliance Target generate Surplus Units, bankable and tradeable across a corporate fleet — compliance becomes a potential revenue stream rather than a pure cost centre for early adopters. Asset value protection: fuel-flexible tonnage (dual-fuel, methanol-ready) retains charter appeal and resale value as the compliance curve tightens toward 2035 and beyond; single-fuel VLSFO-only ships face accelerating commercial obsolescence. Single global benchmark: once adopted, one worldwide GFI curve replaces a patchwork of regional schemes, giving owners a stable target to design newbuilds against rather than reconciling multiple overlapping frameworks. Burdensome / Negative Impacts Fuel infrastructure hurdles: cryogenic/low-flashpoint handling systems, dedicated fuel-preparation spaces, double-walled high-pressure piping for methanol/ammonia. Energy density penalty: alternative fuels need materially larger storage volume for equivalent range, reducing cargo capacity — approximate volumetric comparison for equivalent energy: VLSFO/MGO ≈1×, LNG ≈1.8×, green methanol ≈2.4×, liquid ammonia ≈3×. Capex barrier for older/smaller tonnage: retrofit costs are often uneconomic on ships with limited remaining trading life, creating a two-tier fleet split between compliant tonnage and ships that simply absorb Remedial Unit costs until scrapping. Fuel availability and bunkering-route risk: ZNZ fuel supply infrastructure is not yet globally distributed; a technically compliant ship may still face routing constraints based on where green methanol or ammonia is actually bunkerable. Overlap with regional schemes: until international and regional carbon frameworks (e.g. EU ETS, FuelEU Maritime) are reconciled with Chapter 5, some owners face compounding cost exposure on the same voyage. Evaluative Judgement The framework's structure — a lenient Base Target as a floor, a materially stricter Direct Compliance Target as the real bar, and Tier 1 pricing at $100/tCO 2 eq — is designed to reward early movers financially while pricing laggards out gradually, rather than banning non-compliant ships outright. Net effect: the framework accelerates fleet renewal and fuel diversification, but the transition cost falls disproportionately on operators of older, less flexible tonnage, and the pace of real-world benefit depends heavily on how quickly ZNZ fuel supply chains scale — a factor outside any individual shipowner's control. 🎯 ACTIVE RECALL — before you re-read this section Close your eyes and answer, out loud, in your own words: "Who wins and who loses under Chapter 5, and why is the two-tier target structured that way?" If you can name at least one enabling impact, one burden, and the reason for the Base/Direct split without looking — you've retained it. If not, that's the gap to drill, not the whole section again. Spaced check: revisit this specific question again tomorrow, then in 3 days, then in a week — recall speed on "who wins/who loses" is a good proxy for whether this is exam-ready. 8 marks Explain how Well-to-Wake (WtW) lifecycle accounting differs from traditional Tank-to-Wake (TtW) observations under MARPOL Annex VI. TtW: emissions from the vessel's exhaust stack only — the basis for EEDI/EEXI/CII. WtW (Chapter 5): combines upstream production emissions (WtT) with operational combustion emissions (TtW). Why it matters: prevents alternative fuels like ammonia or hydrogen being credited as "zero-emission" if produced from unabated fossil energy upstream. 10 marks Describe the two-tier compliance target system under the IMO Net-Zero Framework, focusing on the Base Target and Direct Compliance Target and the consequences of a compliance deficit. Base Target: minimum survival curve — 4% (2028) to 30% (2035) reduction vs reference. Direct Compliance Target: the target ships must actually meet — 17% (2028) to 43% (2035) reduction vs reference. Deficit consequence: Tier 1 (between the two lines) priced at $100/tCO 2 eq; falling below the Base Target line attracts a materially higher penalty rate, creating a strong economic incentive toward ZNZ fuel adoption.

section_title: 2 · Importance to International Shipping
text: 2 · Importance to International Shipping International shipping accounts for roughly 3% of global anthropogenic GHG emissions, but because it operates across international jurisdictions, territorial frameworks such as the Paris Agreement cannot directly regulate it. MARPOL Annex VI Chapter 5 fills that gap with a single global standard, preventing operators from routing tonnage through less-regulated flags to avoid climate obligations. For marine engineers, it shifts the centre of gravity of fuel-related compliance from tank-to-wake operational efficiency (CII) to full life-cycle well-to-wake fuel accounting — making zero/near-zero (ZNZ) fuel adoption a matter of commercial necessity rather than voluntary ESG positioning.

section_title: 3 · Historical Background & Origins
text: 3 · Historical Background & Origins [2023 / MEPC 80] 2023 Revised GHG Strategy adopted (Res. MEPC.377(80)) — mid-term "basket of measures" work plan launched | v [2024 / MEPC 81-82] Draft outline of the IMO Net-Zero Framework developed; candidate technical (fuel standard) and economic (pricing) measures narrowed via ISWG-GHG sessions | v [April 2025 / MEPC 83] New Chapter 5 (Regs 30-39) APPROVED by majority vote (63 in favour, 16 against, 24 abstentions) — not yet a formal Article 16 decision | v [October 2025 / MEPC ES.2] Extraordinary session called to formally ADOPT the text — no adoption vote was taken; a motion to ADJOURN for 1 year passed 57-49-21(abst)-8(absent) | v [Nov/Dec 2026] MEPC 85 (30 Nov-3 Dec, tentative) + resumed ES.2 (4 Dec) to consider adoption — date provisional as of MEPC 84 (Apr 2026); EIF shifts to ~Mar 2028 if adopted This is the single most important timeline fact for an oral or written answer on this topic: Chapter 5 has been approved in draft, but not yet formally adopted. Examiners tracking current affairs (particularly Nair) will test whether a candidate overstates the chapter's legal status.

Reg. 31 Goal — phased reduction of marine fuel GHG intensity, aligned with the 2023 Strategy. Reg. 32 Functional requirements — continuous improvement of attained GFI plus economic contribution. Reg. 33 Attained Annual GFI calculation — the formal Well-to-Wake formula. Regs 35 & 36 GFI targets and compliance approaches — Base Target, Direct Compliance Target, Remedial Unit mechanism. Res. MEPC.376(80) Guidelines on Life Cycle GHG Intensity of Marine Fuels (LCA Guidelines) — WtT/TtW emission factors. ⚠ Regulatory status note — do not state Chapter 5 is "in force" MEPC 83 (April 2025) approved the draft text by a vote of 63 in favour, 16 against, 24 abstentions . MEPC/ES.2 (14–17 October 2025), the session convened to formally adopt it, never actually voted on adoption — instead a procedural motion to adjourn consideration for one year (moved by Singapore, put to a vote by Saudi Arabia) passed 57 in favour, 49 against, 21 abstentions, 8 absent . Adoption is deferred to a reconvened session tentatively scheduled for 30 November–3 December 2026 — MEPC 85 (30 Nov–3 Dec) followed by a resumed one-day MEPC/ES.2 session on 4 December, per MEPC 84's April 2026 outcome — though this remains provisional and subject to further confirmation; do not state this date as settled fact in an exam answer. As a direct consequence, the earliest possible entry into force has shifted from the original 1 March 2027 target to on/around 1 March 2028 , with the first reporting period likely 1 January 2029 — treat both as the proposed timeline, not settled fact, until formal adoption occurs. In an exam answer, always frame this chapter as "approved at MEPC 83, adoption deferred, reconvened session tentatively late Nov/early Dec 2026."

section_title: 5 · Engineering Explanation & Core Technical Mechanisms
text: 5 · Engineering Explanation & Core Technical Mechanisms A. Well-to-Wake (WtW) Accounting Principles Traditional MARPOL Annex VI regulation (EEDI/EEXI/CII) measures emissions only from the ship's exhaust stack — a Tank-to-Wake (TtW) boundary. Chapter 5 instead measures the complete fuel lifecycle, from production through combustion — Well-to-Wake (WtW) : $$\text{Total WtW Intensity} = \text{Well-to-Tank (WtT)} + \text{Tank-to-Wake (TtW)}$$ | | | | | | | | +------------------------+ Bunkered onto +---------------------+ Combusted +--------------+ | Extraction, Refining, |------------------->| Shipboard Storage |----------->| Propulsion & | | Transport, Logistics | the Vessel | Tanks & Fuel Lines | in Engine | Stack Gas | +------------------------+ +---------------------+ +--------------+ This boundary shift ensures alternative fuels are only credited as low-emission if produced sustainably — e.g. "grey" hydrogen or ammonia made from unabated fossil energy shows a poor WtT score even though it burns cleanly on board. Three greenhouse gases are tracked, normalised by 100-year Global Warming Potential ($GWP_{100}$): CO 2 = 1, CH 4 = 28, N 2 O = 265. B. The Attained Annual GFI Equation The Attained Annual GHG Fuel Intensity ($GFI_{attained}$), in grams of CO 2 -equivalent per megajoule of energy delivered on board: $$GFI_{attained} = \frac{\sum_{i} \left(M_{i} \times LCF_{WtW,\,i}\right) + E_{remedial}}{\sum_{i} \left(M_{i} \times LHV_{i}\right) \times f_{s}}\ \ \left[gCO_2eq/MJ\right]$$ GFI Formula in Words GFI(attained) = Numerator ÷ Denominator Numerator (Total GHG Emissions, Well-to-Wake, Plus Remedial Adjustment) Sum, across all fuel types used on board, of the mass of that fuel burned multiplied by its Well-to-Wake life-cycle GHG emission factor — which already bundles together the upstream (production/transport) footprint, the downstream (combustion) footprint, and any methane or nitrous oxide slip penalty weighted by Global Warming Potential. Add these fuel-wise totals together, then add any emissions adjustment carried from purchased Remedial Units. Denominator (Total Energy Delivered, Structurally Corrected) Sum, across all fuel types, of the mass of fuel burned multiplied by its Lower Heating Value, to get total energy delivered in megajoules. Then apply a structural correction factor that credits specialised energy systems such as wind-assist propulsion or onboard carbon capture. Spoken Version "Sir, the GFI numerator is the total Well-to-Wake greenhouse gas emissions — the sum over all fuels used of each fuel's mass multiplied by its combined upstream, downstream, and methane/nitrous-oxide-slip emission factor, plus any Remedial Unit adjustment. The denominator is the total energy delivered — the sum over all fuels of each fuel's mass multiplied by its Lower Heating Value, corrected for any wind-assist or carbon-capture credit. Dividing the two gives the attained GFI in grams of CO2-equivalent per megajoule, which is then compared against the Target GFI to determine the compliance balance." Where: $M_i$ = mass of fuel type $i$ consumed in the 12-month reporting period (tonnes); $LCF_{WtW,i}$ = Well-to-Wake life-cycle GHG emission factor for fuel $i$ (combining CO 2 , CH 4 , N 2 O via $GWP_{100}$), sourced from the IMO LCA Guidelines (Res. MEPC.376(80)); $LHV_i$ = lower heating value of fuel $i$ (MJ/g); $E_{remedial}$ = emission adjustment from purchased Remedial Units; $f_s$ = structural correction factor for specialised energy systems (wind-assist, onboard carbon capture). C. The Two-Tier Target Mechanism Chapter 5 sets two parallel reduction trajectories against a 2008 WtW reference value (≈93.3 gCO 2 eq/MJ): Element Base Target Direct Compliance Target Objective Minimum baseline decarbonisation curve for fleet-wide survival. Accelerated curve driving faster ZNZ fuel adoption — the target every ship must actually meet. 2028 reduction 4% vs reference. 17% vs reference. 2035 reduction 30% vs reference. 43% vs reference. 2036–2040 targets To be decided by 2032 (5-yearly review mechanism). Emissions between the Direct Compliance line and the (less strict) Base Target line fall in Tier 1 , priced at US$100 per tonne CO 2 eq (well-to-wake basis). Emissions above the Base Target — i.e. failing even the minimum curve — attract a materially higher penalty rate under Tier 2. A ship is required to meet the Direct Compliance Target; the Base Target functions as the higher-penalty backstop. D. The GFI Compliance Balance At the close of each reporting period, the compliance balance (CB), in tonnes of CO 2 -equivalent, is: $$CB = \left(GFI_{Target} - GFI_{attained}\right) \times Energy_{total} \times 10^{-6}$$ Compliance Balance Formula in Words CB = (Target GFI − Attained GFI) × Total Energy × 10⁻⁶ Subtract the ship's attained GFI from its Target GFI for the applicable tier — a positive result means the ship performed better than the target, a negative result means it fell short. Multiply that difference by the total energy delivered on board over the reporting period (in megajoules), then apply the unit conversion (10⁻⁶) to express the result in tonnes of CO₂-equivalent rather than grams. Spoken Version "Sir, the compliance balance is the Target GFI minus the Attained GFI, multiplied by the total energy the ship consumed that year, converted from grams to tonnes of CO2-equivalent. A positive balance means the ship beat its target and earns Surplus Units; a negative balance means it must buy Remedial Units to cover the shortfall at the applicable tier price." where $Energy_{total} = \sum_i (M_i \times LHV_i)$ in MJ. If $CB \geq 0$, the ship is in direct compliance and generates Surplus Units — bankable, poolable within a corporate fleet, or tradeable via the IMO GFS/Net-Zero Fund register. If $CB Remedial Units at the applicable tier price.

section_title: 6 · Chief Engineer & Flag State Responsibilities
text: 6 · Chief Engineer & Flag State Responsibilities Fuel Lifecycle Label (FLL) verification: confirm every bunker delivery carries a certified FLL with WtT and TtW emission factors; a BDN without a certified FLL defaults the fuel to a worst-case fossil baseline in the GFI calculation. GFI Register data integrity: maintain accurate consumption records by fuel type to support the annual attained GFI submission through IMO DCS. Flag State role: verify annual GFI submissions, issue the Statement of Compliance, and administer Surplus/Remedial Unit transactions through the (proposed) IMO GFS Register once the framework is adopted and in force.

section_title: 7 · Practical Shipboard Application
text: 7 · Practical Shipboard Application Engineering Viability of Candidate Alternative Fuels LNG: clean stack combustion (TtW CO 2 roughly 20–25% below conventional fuel oil), but WtW performance is undermined by upstream extraction venting and unburnt methane slip in the engine — since CH 4 carries a $GWP_{100}$ of 28, even modest slip can push $GFI_{attained}$ into deficit. Bio-methanol: clean, sulphur-free combustion; sustainably sourced biomass feedstock can give a very low or even negative WtT value, making it one of the stronger near-term paths to the Direct Compliance Target. Green ammonia (NH 3 ): carbon-free combustion (no CO 2 from the fuel molecule itself), but only credited as low-emission if produced via renewable electrolysis — "grey" (fossil-derived) ammonia carries a poor WtT score. Unburnt ammonia slip and N 2 O formation ($GWP_{100}$ = 265) must be minimised. On My Vessel (Maersk Container, 2-Stroke Main Engine) For a large ABS-classed container vessel on a conventional 2-stroke main engine burning VLSFO, Chapter 5 compliance today means preparing the ground rather than reacting to a live obligation: verifying that current bunker deliveries already carry FLL-equivalent emission-factor data where the supplier provides it, and flagging any future dual-fuel retrofit decision (methanol-ready newbuild orders, in particular) as directly tied to the Direct Compliance Target trajectory rather than the more lenient Base Target.

section_title: 8 · Survey & PSC Focus
text: 8 · Survey & PSC Focus Statement of Compliance (SoC): once in force, ships must hold an SoC certifying the prior year's attained GFI and compliance balance, verified by the Flag Administration or an authorised RO. Enhanced SEEMP Part II data collection: fuel consumption reporting by consumer type and by "underway"/"not underway" status underpins the GFI calculation, mirroring the existing IMO DCS enhancements already in force for CII. FLL/BDN cross-check: PSC and RO auditors will expect Fuel Lifecycle Labels to accompany the Bunker Delivery Note for any fuel claiming a non-default emission factor.
